q.q: One of the most frequent uses of mechanical ventilation is for the management of ____ patients recovering from anesthesia and medications.
q.e: Managing postoperative patients recovering from anesthesia and medications is one of the most frequent clinical uses of mechanical ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 2)

q.q: Normal airway resistance in healthy adults is between ____.
q.e: Normal airway resistance in healthy adults is 0.5 to 2.5 cm H2O/L/sec; it is higher in intubated patients because of the smaller ET tube diameter. (Chang 4th ed., p. 3)

q.q: Which condition increases airway resistance through a change in the wall of the airway rather than inside or outside the airway?
o: Neoplasm of the bronchial muscle structure
Retained secretions inside the bronchial lumen
Foreign body aspiration in the upper airways
Tumors surrounding and compressing the airway
q.e: Airflow obstruction may result from changes inside the airway (retained secretions), changes in the airway wall (neoplasm of the bronchial muscle structure), or compression from tumors outside the airway. (Chang 4th ed., p. 3)

q.q: According to the simplified form of Poiseuille's Law, by what factor must driving pressure increase to maintain constant airflow when the airway radius is reduced by half?
q.e: Based on Poiseuille's Law, reducing the airway radius by half of its original size increases the driving pressure (work of breathing) required to maintain the same airflow by 16-fold. (Chang 4th ed., p. 3)

q.q: What is the normal range of airway resistance in healthy nonintubated adults?
q.e: Normal airway resistance in healthy adults is 0.5 to 2.5 cm H2O/L/sec, and it is higher in intubated patients because of the smaller internal diameter of the endotracheal tube. (Chang 4th ed., p. 3)

q.q: At a fixed flow, which combination of changes to an endotracheal tube would increase airway resistance?
o: Increasing length and decreasing internal diameter
Decreasing length with internal diameter unchanged
Decreasing length and increasing internal diameter
Increasing internal diameter with length unchanged
q.e: Airway resistance varies directly with length and inversely with diameter, making the internal diameter of the endotracheal tube the major contributor to tube-related airway resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 3)

q.q: Among causes of increased airway resistance, which condition is classified as an infectious cause?
q.e: Laryngotracheobronchitis (croup), epiglottitis, and bronchiolitis are infectious causes of increased airway resistance, whereas postintubation obstruction, foreign body aspiration, the ET tube, and circuit condensation are mechanical obstructions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 4)

q.q: During mechanical ventilation, ____ may be used to compensate for the effects of airflow resistance and to augment spontaneous tidal volume.
q.e: Pressure support ventilation (PSV) is used during mechanical ventilation to compensate for airflow resistance from the endotracheal tube and ventilator circuit and to augment spontaneous tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 4)

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient has a peak inspiratory pressure of 36 cm H2O, a plateau pressure of 24 cm H2O, and an inspiratory flow of 1.5 L/sec. What is the airway resistance?
q.e: Airway resistance equals pressure change (Peak Inspiratory Pressure − Plateau Pressure) divided by flow: (36 − 24) / 1.5 = 8.0 cm H2O/L/sec. (Chang 4th ed., p. 4)

q.q: If the resistive pressure difference stays constant while airway resistance doubles, inspiratory flow will ____.
o: fall to half its original value
fall to one-quarter of its original value
q.e: Inspiratory flow equals the resistive pressure difference divided by airway resistance. With the pressure difference held constant, doubling resistance halves flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 4)

q.q: As a result of chronic air trapping and highly compliant lung parenchyma, patients with chronic airway obstruction use a breathing pattern that is ____.
q.e: Patients with chronic airway obstruction who develop highly compliant lungs may breathe more deeply and slowly. Chang contrasts this with the shallow, rapid breathing pattern of restrictive lung disease. (Chang 4th ed., p. 5)

q.q: Sustained abnormally high airway resistance can cause respiratory muscle fatigue and ventilatory failure, which occurs when minute ventilation cannot keep up with ____.
q.e: Ventilatory failure occurs when a patient's minute ventilation cannot keep up with CO2 production, resulting in an abnormally high PaCO2; oxygenation failure usually follows when oxygen needs for metabolism are unmet. (Chang 4th ed., p. 5)

q.q: While reviewing a ventilator's pressure-volume loop display, a therapist observes outward bowing of the inspiratory limb (from A1 to A2) without expiratory bowing. What is the likely cause?
q.e: Increased bowing of the pressure-volume loop reflects higher airflow resistance; specifically, bowing of the inspiratory limb (from A1 to A2) may be caused by excessive inspiratory flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 5)

q.q: On a pressure-volume loop, outward bowing of the expiratory limb (line B2) occurs when expiratory airflow resistance is increased, such as in ____.
q.e: When expiratory airflow resistance is increased, such as during bronchospasm, bowing of the expiratory limb (line B2) occurs on the pressure-volume loop. (Chang 4th ed., p. 6)

q.q: Refractory hypoxemia is a persistent low blood oxygen level unresponsive to medium to high concentrations of inspired oxygen and is usually caused by ____.
q.e: Low compliance conditions such as ARDS are associated with refractory hypoxemia, which fails to respond to medium to high inspired oxygen concentrations and is usually caused by intrapulmonary shunting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 6)

q.q: How is plateau pressure obtained on a mechanical ventilator to calculate static compliance?
o: Applying an inspiratory hold or occluding the exhalation port at end-inspiration
Measuring baseline circuit pressure maintained at the end of passive exhalation
Recording the peak airway pressure reached while inspiratory gas flow is active
Applying an expiratory hold maneuver immediately before the next mandatory breath
q.e: Plateau pressure—the pressure needed to maintain lung inflation in the absence of airflow—is measured by applying an inspiratory hold or occluding the exhalation port at end-inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 6)

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient has a corrected expired tidal volume of 480 mL, a peak inspiratory pressure of 31 cm H2O, a plateau pressure of 21 cm H2O, and 5 cm H2O of PEEP. What is the static compliance?
q.e: Static compliance (CST) equals Corrected Tidal Volume divided by (Plateau Pressure − PEEP): 480 mL / (21 − 5 cm H2O) = 30 mL/cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 6)

q.q: In conditions of extremely high lung compliance such as emphysema, why is exhalation often incomplete?
o: Lack of elastic recoil by the lungs
Decreased total lung capacity at rest
q.e: In extreme high compliance states like emphysema, destruction of lung tissue causes a lack of elastic recoil by the lungs, leading to incomplete exhalation, air trapping, and elevated functional residual capacity and total lung capacity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 7)

q.q: Which clinical condition decreases static lung compliance?
q.e: Static compliance reflects the elastic resistance of the lung and chest wall when airflow is absent; conditions that decrease it include ARDS, atelectasis, tension pneumothorax, obesity, and retained secretions. Bronchospasm, ET tube kinking, and airway obstruction affect dynamic compliance (airflow resistance). (Chang 4th ed., p. 7)

q.q: During volume-controlled ventilation, a patient develops acute bronchospasm. Corrected expired tidal volume and total PEEP remain unchanged. Peak inspiratory pressure rises from 24 to 38 cm H2O, and plateau pressure remains 18 cm H2O. How do dynamic and static compliance change?
o: Dynamic compliance decreases while static compliance stays the same
Both static compliance and dynamic compliance increase above baseline
Static compliance decreases while dynamic compliance stays the same
Both static compliance and dynamic compliance decrease proportionally
q.e: When airflow resistance increases (such as in bronchospasm), peak inspiratory pressure rises while plateau pressure remains unchanged, causing dynamic compliance to decrease while static compliance stays the same. (Chang 4th ed., p. 8)

q.q: At the same delivered tidal volume, a shift of the pressure-volume slope toward the volume axis indicates ____.
o: a smaller pressure change and higher compliance
a larger pressure change and higher compliance
a smaller pressure change and lower compliance
a larger pressure change and lower compliance
q.e: On a pressure-volume loop, shifting of the slope toward the volume axis indicates an increase in compliance, whereas shifting toward the pressure axis indicates a decrease in compliance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 9)

q.q: Which practice is essential when interpreting lung compliance measurements clinically?
o: Establishing a trend from serial measurements without comparing static to dynamic values
Comparing static compliance directly with dynamic compliance to quantify elastic recoil
Recording dynamic compliance during an end-inspiratory hold with zero airway flow
Using a single static compliance measurement to diagnose acute parenchymal lung disease
q.e: A single compliance measurement has little interpretive value; measurements should be repeated to establish a trend, and static compliance must not be compared with dynamic compliance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 9)

q.q: For critically ill patients, what is the normal clinical range for static compliance?
q.e: For critically ill patients, static compliance is normally between 40 and 60 mL/cm H2O, whereas dynamic compliance is between 30 and 40 mL/cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 10)

q.q: Deadspace ventilation is defined as wasted ventilation, or a condition in which ____.
o: ventilation is in excess of perfusion
ventilation and perfusion increase in proportion
perfusion is in excess of ventilation
ventilation and perfusion decrease in proportion
q.e: Deadspace is wasted ventilation. Physiologic deadspace comprises anatomic deadspace in the conducting airways and alveolar deadspace from ventilation of inadequately perfused alveoli. (Chang 4th ed., p. 10)

q.q: Anatomic deadspace in the conducting airways normally accounts for about 30% of tidal volume and can be estimated as ____ of ideal body weight.
q.e: Anatomic deadspace is estimated at 1 mL/lb of ideal body weight. In Chang’s example, 150 mL of a 500 mL tidal volume occupies the conducting airways, giving an anatomic deadspace fraction of 30%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 11)

q.q: A patient has an anatomic deadspace of 150 mL. If the tidal volume decreases from 500 mL to 300 mL, what does the anatomic deadspace-to-tidal-volume percentage become?
q.e: Decreasing tidal volume increases the relative anatomic deadspace-to-tidal-volume percent; reducing tidal volume from 500 mL to 300 mL with 150 mL deadspace increases the ratio from 30% (150/500) to 50% (150/300). (Chang 4th ed., p. 11)

q.q: ____ is the sum of anatomic and alveolar deadspace volumes and approximates anatomic deadspace under normal conditions.
q.e: Physiologic deadspace equals the sum of anatomic and alveolar deadspace; it approximates anatomic deadspace normally, but rises above it when low cardiac output or vessel obstruction increases alveolar deadspace. (Chang 4th ed., p. 11)

q.q: Simultaneous arterial blood and mixed expired gas samples show a PaCO2 of 50 mm Hg and a mixed expired PCO2 of 30 mm Hg. What is the physiologic VD/VT ratio?
q.e: Physiologic deadspace-to-tidal-volume ratio is calculated as (PaCO2 − PE−CO2) / PaCO2: (50 − 30) / 50 = 0.40, or 40%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 12)

q.q: In patients on mechanical ventilation, a VD/VT ratio below what threshold is considered acceptable and suggests adequate ventilatory function upon weaning?
q.e: In mechanically ventilated patients, a VD/VT ratio of less than 60% is considered acceptable and suggests adequate ventilatory function for weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 12)

q.q: How can drug overdose and neuromuscular disease raise the physiologic deadspace-to-tidal-volume ratio?
o: Decreasing tidal volume and causing a relative increase in VD/VT
Dilating conducting bronchi and enlarging anatomic deadspace volume
Lowering cardiac output and halting pulmonary capillary perfusion
Obstructing pulmonary vessels and creating true alveolar deadspace
q.e: Drug overdose and neuromuscular disease decrease tidal volume to cause a relative increase in VD/VT, whereas heart failure, blood loss, vasoconstriction, and pulmonary embolism increase alveolar deadspace. (Chang 4th ed., p. 12)

q.q: A patient has a tidal volume of 500 mL, a deadspace volume of 150 mL, and a respiratory frequency of 12 breaths/min. What is the minute alveolar ventilation?
q.e: Alveolar volume is tidal volume minus deadspace volume (500 − 150 = 350 mL), and multiplying by the respiratory frequency of 12 breaths/min yields a minute alveolar ventilation of 4,200 mL/min (4.2 L/min). (Chang 4th ed., p. 13)

q.q: Hypoventilation leading to ventilatory failure is characterized by a PaCO2 greater than 45 mm Hg, or greater than ____ for patients with COPD.
q.e: The clinical finding for hypoventilation in ventilatory failure is a PaCO2 greater than 45 mm Hg, or greater than 50 mm Hg for patients with COPD. (Chang 4th ed., p. 13)

q.q: A persistent diffusion defect contributing to ventilatory failure is identified by a gas diffusion rate less than ____ of predicted normal.
q.e: A persistent diffusion defect leading to ventilatory failure features a gas diffusion rate less than 75% of predicted normal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 13)

q.q: Because pulmonary blood flow is gravity-dependent, the V/Q ratio increases from about 0.4 in the lower lung zone to what value in the upper lung zone?
q.e: Gravity-dependent blood flow produces more perfusion at the bases and less perfusion at the apices, so the V/Q ratio ranges from 0.4 in the lower lung zone to 3.0 in the upper lung zone. (Chang 4th ed., p. 14)

q.q: With sufficient pulmonary reserve, a patient usually compensates for hypoxemia caused by uncomplicated V/Q mismatch through ____.
q.e: When pulmonary reserve is sufficient, a patient usually compensates for V/Q mismatch hypoxemia by hyperventilation, and uncomplicated V/Q mismatch is readily reversible with oxygen therapy. (Chang 4th ed., p. 14)

q.q: What upper cutoff does Chang give for normal physiologic shunt in healthy individuals?
q.e: In healthy individuals, the physiologic shunt approximates the anatomic shunt and is less than 5%, whereas for noncritically ill patients a normal physiologic shunt is less than 10%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 14)

q.q: Which requirement makes the classic physiologic shunt equation more invasive than the estimated shunt equations?
o: Obtaining a mixed venous blood sample from the pulmonary artery in addition to arterial blood
Collecting a timed mixed expired carbon dioxide bag simultaneously with arterial blood sampling
Measuring continuous end-tidal carbon dioxide tension alongside arterial co-oximetry levels
Using an assumed arteriovenous oxygen content difference of 5 mL/dL in noncritical patients
q.e: The classic physiologic shunt equation is the most accurate among all shunt equations, requiring both an arterial blood sample and a mixed venous blood sample from the pulmonary artery. (Chang 4th ed., p. 15)

q.q: A physiologic shunt of 25% in a hospitalized patient is interpreted as a ____.
q.e: Physiologic shunt values are interpreted as normal (<10%), mild shunt (10% to 20%), significant shunt (20% to 30%), and critical and severe shunt (>30%). (Chang 4th ed., p. 15)

q.q: Because intrapulmonary shunting results from collapsed or fluid-filled lung units, ____ may be applied during spontaneous breathing to open and ventilate those units.
q.e: Collapsed or fluid-filled lung units causing intrapulmonary shunting may be opened and ventilated using PEEP during mechanical ventilation or continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) during spontaneous breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 15)

q.q: Across the alveolar-capillary membrane, oxygen diffuses from the alveoli (PAO2 = 109 mm Hg) to the pulmonary arterial capillaries (PvO2 = 40 mm Hg) with a pressure gradient of ____.
q.e: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli (PAO2 = 109 mm Hg) to the pulmonary arterial capillaries (PvO2 = 40 mm Hg) across a pressure gradient of 69 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 15)

q.q: Carbon dioxide diffuses across the alveolar-capillary membrane with a net pressure gradient of only 6 mm Hg because its gas diffusion coefficient is ____ greater than that for oxygen.
q.e: Carbon dioxide diffuses from pulmonary arterial capillaries (46 mm Hg) to the alveoli (40 mm Hg) across a 6 mm Hg gradient because its gas diffusion coefficient is 19 times greater than that for oxygen. (Chang 4th ed., p. 16)

q.q: Which mechanism explains how pulmonary fibrosis decreases the gas diffusion rate?
o: Decreased surface area of the alveolar-capillary membrane
Insufficient capillary transit time for gas diffusion
Reduced inspired oxygen tension from fire combustion
q.e: Emphysema and pulmonary fibrosis decrease the surface area of the alveolar-capillary membrane, whereas pulmonary edema and retained secretions thicken the membrane and tachycardia leaves insufficient diffusion time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 16)

q.q: Lack of oxygen in the organs and tissues due to a reduction in inspired oxygen tension, such as at high altitude or in a burning enclosure, is called ____.
q.e: Hypoxic hypoxia is a lack of oxygen in organs and tissues caused by reduced inspired oxygen tension (PIO2), such as at high altitude or during fire combustion; severe hypoxia may lead to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. (Chang 4th ed., p. 16)

q.q: At a barometric pressure of 760 mm Hg, a PaO2 of 40 to 59 mm Hg is interpreted as ____.
q.e: Per Chang, at PB 760 mm Hg: normal 80–100, mild 60–79, moderate 40–59, and severe less than 40 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 17)

q.q: At a barometric pressure of 760 mm Hg, mild hypoxemia corresponds to a PaO2 of ____.
q.e: Per Chang, at PB 760 mm Hg, mild hypoxemia is a PaO2 of 60 to 79 mm Hg; at PB 630 mm Hg, 60 to 79 mm Hg is normal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 17)

q.q: Why can arterial oxygen content reveal reduced oxygen-carrying capacity in an anemic patient whose PaO2 is normal?
o: CaO2 includes hemoglobin-bound oxygen, which can fall with anemia despite a normal PaO2.
Co-oximetry directly measures intracellular aerobic metabolism in body tissues.
PaO2 increases above normal whenever hemoglobin concentration falls significantly.
PaO2 reflects only hemoglobin-bound oxygen and misses dissolved plasma oxygen.
q.e: PaO2 reflects dissolved plasma oxygen. CaO2 also accounts for hemoglobin-bound oxygen, so a reduced hemoglobin concentration can lower CaO2 even when PaO2 is normal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 17)

q.q: In the arterial oxygen content equation, CaO2 equals (Hb × 1.34 × SaO2) plus (PaO2 × ____).
q.e: Arterial oxygen content combines hemoglobin-bound oxygen and dissolved plasma oxygen using the formula CaO2 = (Hb × 1.34 × SaO2) + (PaO2 × 0.003). (Chang 4th ed., p. 17)

q.q: At a barometric pressure of 630 mm Hg, an adult has a PaO2 of 68 mm Hg. Which hypoxemia category applies at this altitude?
q.e: At a barometric pressure of 630 mm Hg, a PaO2 of 60 to 79 mm Hg is considered normal (whereas 80 to 100 mm Hg is normal at 760 mm Hg). (Chang 4th ed., p. 17)

q.q: Oxygenation failure may develop when severe hypoxemia (PaO2 < 40 mm Hg) does not respond to supplemental oxygen concentrations of ____.
q.e: Oxygenation failure may develop when severe hypoxemia (PaO2 < 40 mm Hg) fails to respond to a moderate to high level (50% to 100%) of supplemental oxygen. (Chang 4th ed., p. 17)

q.q: Patients requiring mechanical ventilation due to a ____ may have normal pulmonary function, but their respiratory muscles lack adequate neuromuscular impulses.
q.e: Clinical conditions leading to mechanical ventilation include depressed respiratory drive, excessive ventilatory workload, and failure of the ventilatory pump; patients with depressed respiratory drive may have normal pulmonary function while lacking adequate neuromuscular impulses. (Chang 4th ed., p. 18)

q.q: In a tetraplegic patient, an acute spinal cord injury at the ____ level can interrupt motor signals to the diaphragm and cause respiratory paralysis.
q.e: Chang identifies C1–C3 as the injury level associated with respiratory paralysis in tetraplegia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 19)

q.q: In Chang’s classification of drug-induced increases in ventilatory workload, which drug class is listed under bronchospasm?
q.e: Beta-blockers, hydrocortisone, and neuromuscular blocking agents are causes of drug-induced bronchospasm, whereas narcotics, naloxone, thiazide diuretics, and insulin are causes of drug-induced acute pulmonary edema. (Chang 4th ed., p. 20)

q.q: Chang identifies ____ as an example of an electrolyte imbalance that can cause ventilatory pump failure.
q.e: Causes of ventilatory pump failure include hyperkalemia (electrolyte imbalance), flail chest and tension pneumothorax (chest trauma), idiopathic respiratory distress syndrome (premature birth), and respiratory muscle fatigue (geriatric patients). (Chang 4th ed., p. 21)

sections.title: Ch 2 · Effects of Positive Pressure Ventilation

q.q: During negative pressure ventilation, pressures in the airways, alveoli, and pleura are ____ during inspiration.
q.e: Negative pressure ventilation creates negative pressure on the chest wall, so airway, alveolar, and pleural pressures decrease during inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 28)

q.q: In an illustrative example of airway pressure gradients, the alveolar-to-atmospheric pressure difference has a magnitude of 5 cm H2O during expiratory flow. If atmospheric pressure is assigned zero, what is alveolar pressure?
q.e: In this example, alveolar pressure is 5 cm H2O above atmospheric pressure during expiratory flow, so its gauge pressure is +5 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 28)

q.q: Which combination of factors determines the level of positive airway pressure generated during volume-controlled ventilation?
o: Mechanical tidal volume, compliance, and airflow resistance
Preset inspiratory pressure, PEEP, and expiratory duration
Barometric pressure, pleural pressure, and respiratory drive
Spontaneous tidal volume, heart rate, and arterial oxygen
q.e: In volume-controlled ventilation, the tidal volume is preset and the resulting level of positive pressure depends on mechanical tidal volume, lung compliance, and airflow resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 28)

q.q: Which of the following conditions limits the volume delivered during positive pressure ventilation because the ventilator is unable to reach peak inspiratory pressure?
q.e: An ET tube cuff leak or ventilator circuit leak prevents the ventilator from reaching peak inspiratory pressure, whereas obstruction, kinking, bronchospasm, and low compliance cause PIP to be reached too soon. (Chang 4th ed., p. 29)

q.q: A patient receiving pressure-controlled ventilation develops acute bronchospasm and high airway resistance. Because the preset peak inspiratory pressure is reached prematurely, what happens to the delivered breath?
o: The inspiratory phase ends early and delivers a smaller volume
Expiratory flow stops early to maintain alveolar recruitment
Peak inspiratory pressure rises well above the preset pressure
Inspiratory time automatically lengthens to preserve tidal volume
q.e: During pressure-controlled ventilation, inspiration terminates as soon as the preset PIP is reached, so premature pressure attainment from high resistance or low compliance reduces delivered volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 29)

q.q: At the start of expiration during positive pressure ventilation, airway-opening pressure falls to 0 cm H2O while alveolar pressure is 20 cm H2O. What is the signed pressure gradient, defined as airway-opening pressure minus alveolar pressure?
q.e: During expiration PI returns to 0 cm H2O while PALV is 20 cm H2O, creating a ∆P of −20 cm H2O as gas flows out of the lungs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 29)

q.q: In positive pressure ventilation, peak inspiratory pressure and mean airway pressure are directly related to tidal volume, airway resistance, and peak inspiratory flow rate and inversely related to ____.
q.e: Airway pressures (PIP and mPaw) vary directly with tidal volume, airway resistance, and peak inspiratory flow rate, and vary inversely with compliance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 30)

q.q: In lungs with normal compliance, about ____ of the airway pressure is transmitted to the thoracic cavity.
q.e: Approximately 50% of airway pressure is transmitted to the thoracic cavity when lung compliance is normal, whereas stiff lungs transmit much less. (Chang 4th ed., p. 30)

q.q: Two mechanically ventilated patients receive the same high PEEP setting: Patient A has severe ARDS with stiff, noncompliant lungs, and Patient B has normal lung compliance. Compared with Patient B, the decrease in cardiac output in Patient A will be:
o: less severe due to dampening by nonelastic lung tissues
more severe because stiff lungs transmit more pressure to the thorax
identical because the same PEEP produces the same intrathoracic pressure
more severe due to increased pulmonary venous return
q.e: Nonelastic, stiff lung tissues dampen airway pressure transmission to the thoracic cavity, making the reduction in cardiac output from high PIP or PEEP less severe than in normal-compliance lungs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 30)

q.q: To keep mean airway pressure at the lowest level possible and preserve cardiac output, inspiratory time, respiratory frequency, peak inspiratory pressure, and ____ should be kept to a minimum.
q.e: Mean airway pressure is directly related to inspiratory time, respiratory frequency, PIP, and PEEP, so keeping these four parameters minimal helps prevent reductions in cardiac output. (Chang 4th ed., p. 30)

q.q: Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) raises baseline airway pressure above atmospheric pressure and is used to treat refractory hypoxemia caused by ____.
q.e: PEEP increases end-expiratory airway pressure above atmospheric pressure to treat refractory hypoxemia caused by intrapulmonary shunting, though it lowers cardiac output more than CPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 30)

q.q: Because oxygen delivery is the product of ____, a ventilator-induced reduction in stroke volume and cardiac output decreases oxygen delivery.
q.e: Higher intrathoracic pressure compresses the great vessels and reduces venous return, stroke volume, and cardiac output; since O2 delivery equals O2 content multiplied by cardiac output, O2 delivery falls. (Chang 4th ed., p. 31)

q.q: In cardiac tamponade or acute asthma exacerbation, pulsus paradoxus is defined as an exaggerated inspiratory decrease in systolic blood pressure of:
q.e: During spontaneous inspiration arterial blood pressure transiently falls; in cardiac tamponade or acute asthma exacerbation, a systolic pressure drop exceeding 10 mm Hg is called pulsus paradoxus. (Chang 4th ed., p. 31)

q.q: During positive pressure ventilation, inward displacement of the ventricular walls during systole produces reverse pulsus paradoxus, whose mechanism appears to be a reduction in ____.
q.e: Positive pressure ventilation displaces ventricular walls inward during systole to enhance emptying and slightly raise systolic pressure; this reverse pulsus paradoxus appears to stem from reduced left ventricular afterload. (Chang 4th ed., p. 31)

q.q: During positive pressure ventilation, a patient exhibits a 20 mm Hg inspiratory increase in systolic blood pressure (significant reverse pulsus paradoxus of >15 mm Hg). This finding is a sensitive indicator of:
q.e: A significant reverse pulsus paradoxus (an inspiratory rise in systolic blood pressure >15 mm Hg during positive pressure ventilation) is a sensitive clinical indicator of hypovolemia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 31)

q.q: Unlike hypotensive patients, in hypertensive patients the use of large tidal volumes ____ venous return to the left ventricle.
q.e: In hypotensive conditions large tidal volumes compress pulmonary vessels and decrease blood flow to the left heart, whereas in hypertensive patients minimal vessel compression and the thoracic pump mechanism increase left ventricular venous return. (Chang 4th ed., p. 32)

q.q: According to the thoracic pump mechanism, pulmonary blood vessels are relieved of alveolar compression and blood flow from the right to the left ventricle increases during the ____ of positive pressure ventilation.
q.e: During inspiration, positive pressure compresses pulmonary vessels and limits blood flow from right to left ventricle; during expiration, alveolar compression resolves and right-to-left blood flow increases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 33)

q.q: In children with right ventricular dysfunction, high positive pressure (up to 40 cm H2O) and large tidal volumes of ____ may reduce the workload of the right heart via the thoracic pump mechanism.
q.e: In the pediatric setting Chang describes, positive pressures up to 40 cm H2O and tidal volumes of 20 to 30 mL/kg may reduce right ventricular workload through the thoracic pump mechanism. (Chang 4th ed., p. 34)

q.q: The ____ reflects left ventricular preload and is not affected to a great extent by positive pressure ventilation because the systemic venous circulation compensates.
q.e: CVP (right ventricular preload) and PAP (right ventricular afterload) are major hemodynamic values altered by positive pressure ventilation, whereas PCWP (left ventricular preload) is minimally affected due to systemic venous compensation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 34)

q.q: At a mechanical tidal volume of 1 L during positive pressure ventilation, approximately what percentage of the pulmonary blood volume is shifted to the systemic circulation?
q.e: Compression of pulmonary blood vessels during positive pressure ventilation at a 1 L tidal volume shifts an estimated 15% to 20% of pulmonary blood volume into the systemic circulation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 34)

q.q: A decline in cardiac output caused by positive pressure ventilation and PEEP can be minimized by maintaining adequate intravascular volume and administering a ____.
q.e: Decreased cardiac output during positive pressure ventilation and PEEP is managed with intravascular volume expansion and positive inotropic support. (Chang 4th ed., p. 34)

q.q: The kidneys are highly vascular and at any one time receive about ____ of the circulating blood volume.
q.e: At any given time the kidneys receive about 25% of circulating blood volume, making renal filtration and urine output highly vulnerable to ventilator-induced reductions in cardiac output. (Chang 4th ed., p. 35)

q.q: During the inspiratory phase of positive pressure ventilation without PEEP, why does shifting pulmonary blood volume to the systemic circulation fail to increase central venous pressure (CVP)?
o: The systemic venous circulation readily absorbs the extra volume
The pulmonary capillary bed retains blood during peak lung inflation
The kidneys rapidly excrete the shifted intravascular fluid volume
The right ventricle immediately pumps the extra blood into the lungs
q.e: Although inspiration shifts a fraction of pulmonary blood to the systemic circulation, CVP does not rise because the systemic venous circulation readily absorbs the extra volume while higher intrathoracic pressure impedes venous return. (Chang 4th ed., p. 35)

q.q: For adequate removal of body wastes, urine output must remain above ____ in a 24-hour period, below which oliguria is present.
q.e: Adequate waste removal requires urine output above 400 mL in 24 hours; oliguria is defined as urine output less than 400 mL in 24 hours (or less than 160 mL in 8 hours). (Chang 4th ed., p. 36)

q.q: Why does central venous pressure rise when PEEP is added to positive pressure ventilation?
o: elevated PAP raises right ventricular pressure and hinders venous return
decreased intrathoracic pressure pulls systemic venous blood into the thorax
increased left ventricular stroke volume backs blood into the vena cava
systemic arterial vasodilation increases blood flow into the right atrium
q.e: PEEP compresses pulmonary vessels and increases PAP, which raises right ventricular pressure, impedes systemic venous return to the right heart, and backs up blood pressure in the systemic veins. (Chang 4th ed., p. 36)

q.q: A ventilated patient with acute renal failure remains paralyzed after short-term drug administration. Which pair of drugs does Chang associate with this complication and delayed weaning?
q.e: Because pancuronium and vecuronium rely on renal clearance, renal failure can prolong neuromuscular blockade for up to 7 days after more than 2 days of vecuronium use and hinder weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 36)

q.q: Glomerular ultrafiltration depends on elevated capillary pressure maintained because the afferent arteriole is somewhat dilated relative to the ____, which is always somewhat constricted.
q.e: A relatively dilated afferent arteriole paired with a partially constricted efferent arteriole maintains the high glomerular hydrostatic pressure needed to filter drugs such as digoxin, vancomycin, beta-lactams, and aminoglycosides. (Chang 4th ed., p. 37)

q.q: Which group of drugs is eliminated via renal tubular secretion from the peritubular capillaries into the renal tubule, leading to higher circulating levels when renal blood flow falls?
o: Digoxin, furosemide, procainamide, and some penicillins
Pancuronium, vecuronium, propranolol, and morphine sulfate
q.e: Drugs cleared by active renal tubular secretion include digoxin, furosemide, procainamide, and some penicillins; decreased renal blood flow reduces their secretion and raises plasma levels. (Chang 4th ed., p. 37)

q.q: Which glomerular filtration rate range does Chang give as an indicator of renal failure?
q.e: Normal GFR is 90 to 120 mL/min/1.73 m2 (with normal male creatinine clearance of 97 to 137 mL/min), and renal failure is defined as a GFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 37)

q.q: Which serum electrolyte pattern is typically observed in a patient with renal failure?
o: Increased serum potassium and decreased serum sodium
Increased serum potassium and increased serum sodium
Decreased serum potassium and increased serum sodium
Decreased serum potassium and decreased serum sodium
q.e: In renal failure, serum BUN (normal 10 to 20 mg/dL), creatinine (normal 0.7 to 1.5 mg/dL), and potassium (normal 3 to 5 mEq/L) usually increase, whereas serum sodium (normal 138 to 142 mEq/L) usually decreases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 37)

q.q: Chang defines the prothrombin-time criterion for likely liver impairment as a prolongation greater than a specified cutoff. What is that cutoff, in seconds above control?
q.e: Liver dysfunction is monitored by prothrombin time, bilirubin, and albumin; impairment is likely when prothrombin time is >4 sec over control. (Chang 4th ed., p. 38)

q.q: When mechanical ventilation reduces cardiac output and concentrates the urine, an enhanced tubular reabsorption gradient increases reabsorption back into the circulation of aminoglycosides and ____.
q.e: Reduced renal blood flow and concentrated urine increase the passive tubular reabsorption gradient for drugs in the glomerular filtrate, including aminoglycosides, theophylline, and phenobarbital. (Chang 4th ed., p. 38)

q.q: Hepatic perfusion normally accounts for about 15% of cardiac output and varies inversely with PEEP; in one study, increasing PEEP to 20 cm H2O decreased hepatic blood flow by:
q.e: Positive pressure ventilation alone leaves the 15% hepatic share of cardiac output unchanged, whereas PEEP of 10, 15, and 20 cm H2O reduced hepatic blood flow by 3%, 12%, and 32%, respectively. (Chang 4th ed., p. 38)

q.q: Which prothrombin-time result meets Chang’s criterion for likely impairment of liver function?
q.e: Chang’s prothrombin-time criterion is more than 4 seconds above control. A prolongation of 5 seconds meets it. A prolongation of exactly 4 seconds does not. (Chang 4th ed., p. 38)

q.q: Which intensive care medications rely on hepatic perfusion for clearance and may reach elevated serum concentrations when PEEP reduces liver blood flow?
q.e: ICU medications whose clearance depends on hepatic blood flow include lidocaine, meperidine, propranolol, and verapamil; liver hypoperfusion raises their circulating concentrations. (Chang 4th ed., p. 38)

q.q: In Chang’s description of bedside measurement of intra-abdominal pressure, the pressure transducer is connected to a ____.
q.e: Intra-abdominal pressure is measured with a pressure transducer connected to a transurethral bladder catheter and may rise with ascites, bowel edema or obstruction, antishock garments, or hernia repair. (Chang 4th ed., p. 39)

q.q: A ventilated patient with massive ascites has an intra-abdominal pressure of 24 mm Hg, and an increase in PEEP to 18 cm H2O is proposed. Why does combining PEEP above 15 cm H2O with IAP above 20 mm Hg require caution?
o: It potentiates the pressures exerted on the heart and great vessels
It increases functional residual capacity and causes hyperinflation
It shifts blood into the lungs and elevates left ventricular preload
It dilates renal arterioles and causes excessive diuresis and fluid loss
q.e: Elevated IAP transmits pressure across the diaphragm; applying high PEEP (>15 cm H2O) when IAP exceeds 20 mm Hg requires caution because it potentiates the pressures exerted on the heart and great vessels. (Chang 4th ed., p. 39)

q.q: Combining PEEP with increased intra-abdominal pressure produces which set of cardiovascular changes alongside decreased cardiac output?
o: Increased peripheral vascular resistance and decreased ventricular compliance
Decreased peripheral vascular resistance and increased compliance of ventricles
Decreased peripheral vascular resistance and increased stroke volume output
Increased compliance of ventricles and decreased venous admixture fraction
q.e: PEEP with elevated IAP causes increased peripheral vascular resistance, decreased ventricular compliance, and decreased cardiac output, along with reduced GFR and reduced FRC. (Chang 4th ed., p. 39)

q.q: Morphine sulfate is commonly used for pain control during mechanical ventilation and may cause gastrointestinal side effects including ____.
o: increased bowel sounds and accelerated gastric emptying
q.e: GI complications during mechanical ventilation result from GI hypoperfusion and common ICU drugs; morphine sulfate used for pain control can cause constipation and vomiting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 40)

q.q: Mechanical ventilation with high levels of PEEP reduces gastrointestinal perfusion by increasing intrathoracic and right atrial pressures and:
o: reducing the gradient between mean systemic venous and right atrial pressures
increasing the gradient between aortic systolic and left atrial pressures
dilating the splanchnic vascular bed and accelerating intestinal motility
increasing the gradient between mean systemic venous and right atrial pressures
q.e: High-PEEP mechanical ventilation raises intrathoracic and right atrial pressures, narrowing the pressure gradient between mean systemic venous and right atrial pressures and reducing cardiac output and GI perfusion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 40)

q.q: What daily energy expenditure does Chang report for the work of breathing in patients with COPD?
q.e: Because of high airway resistance and V/Q abnormalities, COPD patients expend 430 to 720 kcal/day on the work of breathing—roughly 10 times the normal 38 to 72 kcal/day. (Chang 4th ed., p. 41)

q.q: Which of the following causes of respiratory muscle fatigue is classified as a mechanical factor rather than a nonmechanical factor?
q.e: High airway resistance, low lung compliance, and low chest wall compliance are mechanical factors in respiratory muscle fatigue, whereas malnutrition, endocrine diseases, electrolyte disorders, drugs, and persistent hypoxemia are nonmechanical factors. (Chang 4th ed., p. 41)

q.q: During prolonged mechanical ventilation, diaphragm muscle atrophy can occur as a result of ____.
o: muscle proteolysis and a decrease in myofiber content
neuromuscular junction sprouting and collagen deposition
excessive phrenic nerve firing and calcium accumulation
glycogen overaccumulation and skeletal myofiber hypertrophy
q.e: Muscle proteolysis and reduced myofiber content can cause diaphragm atrophy. Chang also describes a time-dependent loss of diaphragm force. (Chang 4th ed., p. 41)

q.q: Most mechanically ventilated patients who are fed enterally do not receive their energy requirement mainly because of ____.
o: routine use of dilute enteral formulas
systematic underestimation of prescribed calorie targets
excessive losses of nutrients in stool
q.e: Frequent interruptions in enteral feedings prevent most enterally fed ventilated patients from meeting energy needs, leading to protein catabolism and depletion of diaphragmatic glycogen and protein stores. (Chang 4th ed., p. 42)

q.q: What full range of stress multipliers does Chang give for estimating energy needs from REE in a mechanically ventilated burn patient?
q.e: For burns, Chang estimates total calorie needs by multiplying REE by a factor from 1.5 to 2.1. (Chang 4th ed., p. 42)

q.q: When total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is administered, dextrose is kept minimal to avoid lipogenesis and excess CO2 production, with glucose contributing ____ of total caloric needs.
q.e: Excess dextrose during TPN causes lipogenesis and increases O2 consumption and CO2 production, so glucose should contribute 40% to 60% of total caloric needs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 42)

q.q: Compared with hydrous dextrose (3.4 kcal/g), how many kilocalories per gram does fat emulsion provide in a fat-based TPN regimen for fluid-restricted or CO2-retaining patients?
q.e: Hydrous dextrose generates 3.4 kcal/g whereas fat emulsion provides 9.1 kcal/g, delivering maximum caloric intake with minimum fluid volume and CO2 production. (Chang 4th ed., p. 42)

q.q: Prolonged hyperventilation (>24 hours) shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve to the left, which leads to ____.
o: increased O2 affinity for hemoglobin and reduced O2 release to tissues
decreased O2 affinity for hemoglobin and reduced O2 release to tissues
decreased O2 affinity for hemoglobin and increased O2 release to tissues
increased O2 affinity for hemoglobin and increased O2 release to tissues
q.e: Per Chang, a leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve increases O2 affinity for hemoglobin and reduces O2 release to tissues, causing cerebral tissue hypoxia and neurologic dysfunction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 43)

q.q: Sustained hyperventilation of less than 24 hours causes respiratory alkalosis, which ____.
o: reduces cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure
increases cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure
increases cerebral blood flow but reduces intracranial pressure
reduces cerebral blood flow but increases intracranial pressure
q.e: CO2 is a cerebral vasodilator; hyperventilation for less than 24 hours causes respiratory alkalosis, reducing cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 43)

q.q: A head-trauma patient receives controlled hyperventilation to lower intracranial pressure, which succeeds during the first day. Why does controlled hyperventilation lose its cerebral vasoconstrictor effect after 24 hours?
o: Buffering returns pH toward normal, reducing cerebral vasoconstriction.
Phosphate moves out of cells and dilates cerebral blood vessels.
Prolonged alkalosis shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve to the right.
Cerebral chemoreceptors lose sensitivity to CO₂.
q.e: Sustained hyperventilation of less than 24 hours causes respiratory alkalosis that constricts cerebral vessels and lowers ICP, but after 24 hours body buffer systems return pH toward normal and negate vasoconstriction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 43)

q.q: Sustained hyperventilation (>24 hours) shifts phosphate into cells, producing significant ____ that reduces ATP stores and 2,3-BPG (2,3-DPG) levels and shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve further leftward.
q.e: Prolonged hyperventilation causes leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve and intracellular phosphate shift (hypophosphatemia), depleting ATP and 2,3-BPG and worsening cerebral tissue hypoxia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 43)

q.q: In patients with hypercapnia, cerebral vasodilation and elevated intracranial pressure can produce ____, defined as swelling where the optic nerve exits the back of the eye.
q.e: Hypercapnia causes morning headaches from sleep-related cerebral vasodilation, muscle tremor from sympathetic catecholamine release, and papilledema from cerebral vasodilation and elevated intracranial pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 44)

q.q: Whereas hypercapnia with a normal pH increases cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure, hypercapnia accompanied by a low pH causes:
o: a leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve
q.e: Hypercapnia with normal pH increases cerebral blood flow and ICP, hypercapnia with low pH impairs cerebral metabolism, and hypoxemia decreases mental and motor functions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 44)

q.q: Ventilator technology has evolved since the 1951 introduction of the ____, the first volume-controlled mechanical ventilator.
q.e: The Engström 100, introduced in 1951, was the first volume-controlled mechanical ventilator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 52)

q.q: Robert Chatburn proposed a flexible system to classify mechanical ventilators based on ____ rather than manufacturer terminology.
o: patient age groups, care settings, and cost
proprietary mode names and brand generations
circuit tubing diameters and valve materials
q.e: Chatburn's classification system groups mechanical ventilators by related features, physics, and engineering rather than narrow manufacturer terms. (Chang 4th ed., p. 52)

q.q: During inspiration, how does the elastic load of the respiratory system relate to tidal volume and lung compliance?
o: Proportional to volume and inversely proportional to compliance
Inversely proportional to volume and proportional to compliance
Proportional to airway resistance and inspiratory gas flow rate
Inversely proportional to both tidal volume and lung compliance
q.e: During inspiration, the elastic load is proportional to volume and inversely proportional to compliance, whereas the resistance load depends on airway resistance and flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 52)

q.q: If the patient's ventilatory muscles contribute no work (e.g., sedation or paralysis), the mechanical ventilator provides ____.
q.e: When the patient's muscles contribute no work the ventilator provides full support; when the muscles sustain all requirements support is zero; in between, partial support is provided. (Chang 4th ed., p. 53)

q.q: According to the equation of motion for the respiratory system, muscle pressure plus ventilator pressure equals which expression?
q.e: The equation of motion relates elastic and resistive loads as Muscle Pressure + Ventilator Pressure = (Volume / Compliance) + (Resistance × Flow). (Chang 4th ed., p. 53)

q.q: A spontaneously breathing patient connected to a ventilator sustains all of the ventilatory requirements with the respiratory muscles. What level of ventilatory support is the machine providing?
q.e: When a patient's ventilatory muscles sustain all ventilatory requirements without assistance from the machine, ventilatory support is zero. (Chang 4th ed., p. 53)

q.q: Pneumatically powered ventilators such as the Bird Mark 7 operate using anhydrous, oil-free compressed medical gases supplied at what standard pressure?
q.e: Pneumatically powered ventilators rely on compressed medical gases that are anhydrous, oil-free, and supplied at 50 psi. (Chang 4th ed., p. 53)

q.q: Electrically powered ventilators such as the CareFusion LTV 1150 and Puritan Bennett 540 operate using 120 V 60 Hz alternating current (AC) or ____.
q.e: Electrically powered ventilators use either 120 V 60 Hz alternating current (AC) or 12 V direct current (DC) to run motors, pistons, or compressors. (Chang 4th ed., p. 53)

q.q: The ____ is the system used by the ventilator to transmit or convert input power into useful ventilatory work.
q.e: The drive mechanism converts or transmits the ventilator's input power into useful ventilatory work and shapes its characteristic flow and pressure patterns. (Chang 4th ed., p. 53)

q.q: Which of the following lists the three primary drive mechanisms of a mechanical ventilator?
o: Levers, fluidic logic gates, and rotors
q.e: The three primary ventilator drive mechanisms are pistons, bellows, and microprocessor-controlled pneumatic circuits. (Chang 4th ed., p. 54)

q.q: A ____ is a valve controlled by an electronic switching device that is used to regulate the specific functions of a ventilator.
q.e: Solenoid valves are electronically switched valves used with microprocessors to regulate gas flow and specific ventilator functions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 54)

q.q: Which three methods of bellows compression does the chapter identify for delivering gas to the patient?
o: A spring, a weight, or gas pressure in a sealed chamber
A heated wire grid, a strain gauge, or a vortex sensor
A rotary cam, a linear shaft, or an electric servomotor
A Coanda jet, a separation bubble, or a fluidic splitter
q.e: In a bellows drive mechanism, gas admitted through a one-way valve is delivered when the bellows is compressed by a spring, a weight, or gas pressure in a sealed chamber. (Chang 4th ed., p. 55)

q.q: A ventilator generates selectable flow and pressure waveforms by varying the opening of proportional solenoid valves. This ventilator uses a ____.
o: rotary-driven dual check-valve piston drive system
q.e: Ventilators that pair programmed microprocessor algorithms with proportional solenoid valves to generate diverse flow or pressure patterns use a microprocessor-controlled pneumatic drive mechanism. (Chang 4th ed., p. 55)

q.q: A ventilator continuously measures its output and adjusts its input to maintain a selected value. This closed-loop feedback system is called a ____.
q.e: A closed-loop (servo-controlled) circuit uses a sensing element, an amplifier, and a servomotor to measure output continuously and adjust input automatically. (Chang 4th ed., p. 56)

q.q: Early mechanical control circuits using levers, pulleys, or cams were very durable yet lacked flexibility because they functioned as which type of control circuit?
q.e: Mechanical control circuits using simple machines like levers, pulleys, and cams were durable, yet lacked flexibility because they were open-loop systems without feedback adjustment. (Chang 4th ed., p. 56)

q.q: Which components make up the pneumatic control circuits used in IPPB ventilators and Percussionaire IPV and VDR ventilators?
o: Valves, nozzles, ducted ejectors, and diaphragms
Resistors, diodes, transistors, and logic gates
Levers, pulleys, rotating cams, and drive shafts
Vortex sensors, heated wire grids, and venturis
q.e: Pneumatic control circuits, such as those in IPPB and Percussionaire IPV/VDR ventilators, use valves, nozzles, ducted ejectors, and diaphragms. (Chang 4th ed., p. 56)

q.q: Fluidic control elements, such as those in the Sechrist IV 100B, operate using ____, in which a high-velocity jet of gas attaches to an adjacent wall.
q.e: Fluidic logic elements rely on the Coanda effect, where a high-velocity gas jet forms a low-pressure separation bubble that attaches the flow to an adjacent wall. (Chang 4th ed., p. 56)

q.q: Electronic control circuits provide greater flexibility, but using more sophisticated control circuitry often increases system ____.
q.e: Contemporary electronic control circuits deliver sophisticated drive control and greater flexibility, though at the cost of increased complexity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 57)

q.q: A ____ is defined as the mechanism that provides a mode of ventilation within a specific parameter (pressure, time, volume, or flow).
q.e: During inspiration, a ventilator controls one of four primary variables—pressure, volume, flow, or time—and the mechanism governing that parameter is a controller. (Chang 4th ed., p. 57)

q.q: Using Chatburn's control-variable criteria, a clinician notes that when patient resistance and compliance change, the pressure waveform changes, the volume waveform stays unchanged, and volume is derived via a flow transducer rather than volumetric displacement. How is this ventilator classified?
q.e: Under Chatburn's criteria, when pressure varies, volume remains constant, and volume is derived from a flow transducer rather than measured directly by volumetric displacement, the ventilator is a flow controller. (Chang 4th ed., p. 58)

q.q: Regardless of whether a ventilator is classified as a positive or negative pressure device, the lungs expand as a result of the ____ generated.
q.e: Both positive pressure ventilators (raising airway pressure) and negative pressure ventilators (lowering body surface pressure) inflate the lungs by generating positive transrespiratory system pressures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 58)

q.q: How does a true volume controller directly measure and control the tidal volume delivered to a patient?
o: By the displacement of the piston or bellows
By sensing pressure drop in a venturi tube
By integrating flow across a heated wire grid
By counting vortices with an ultrasonic probe
q.e: A true volume controller measures and controls volume directly through the volumetric displacement of the piston or bellows drive mechanism. (Chang 4th ed., p. 59)

q.q: A ventilator that normally measures flow with a heated wire grid or venturi pneumotachometer is switched into pressure support mode. How is the ventilator classified while operating in this mode?
q.e: When a ventilator is operated in pressure support or pressure-controlled mode, it becomes a pressure controller because pressure is the variable measured and controlled. (Chang 4th ed., p. 59)

q.q: ____ measure and control inspiratory and expiratory time while allowing both pressure and volume to vary with changes in pulmonary compliance and resistance.
q.e: Time controllers regulate inspiratory and expiratory time without using pressure or volume feedback, so both pressure and volume vary when compliance or resistance changes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 59)

q.q: Which ventilator control functions as a time-triggering mechanism?
q.e: A time-triggered breath is delivered when a preset time interval has elapsed; the frequency control on the ventilator is a time-triggering mechanism. (Chang 4th ed., p. 60)

q.q: When a ventilator's frequency control is preset at 12 breaths per minute in a time-triggered mode, what is the time-triggering interval for each complete breath?
q.e: At a preset mandatory rate of 12 breaths per minute (60 sec / 12 breaths), the time-triggering interval is 5 sec per complete breath cycle. (Chang 4th ed., p. 60)

q.q: Expressed as trigger pressure minus baseline airway pressure, what signed pressure range does Chang give for acceptable pressure-trigger settings?
q.e: The trigger threshold is 1 to 5 cm H2O below baseline, corresponding to a signed pressure change of −1 to −5 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 60)

q.q: A clinician changes the pressure-trigger sensitivity setting on a ventilator from −3 cm H2O to −5 cm H2O. How does this adjustment affect ventilator sensitivity and patient effort?
o: Decreases sensitivity and requires more patient effort
Decreases sensitivity and requires less patient effort
Increases sensitivity and requires less patient effort
Increases sensitivity and requires more patient effort
q.e: Changing pressure-trigger sensitivity from −3 to −5 cm H2O decreases the ventilator's sensitivity and requires greater patient inspiratory effort to trigger a breath. (Chang 4th ed., p. 60)

q.q: When auto-PEEP is present during pressure triggering, the patient must overcome both the ____ for the ventilator to sense a successful triggering effort.
o: auto-PEEP level and the sensitivity setting
plateau airway pressure and the cycle time
peak inspiratory pressure and the flow limit
transairway resistance and the tidal volume
q.e: Presence of auto-PEEP increases the required triggering effort because the patient must overcome both the auto-PEEP level and the set trigger sensitivity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 60)

q.q: To reduce the inspiratory effort imposed on the patient, a flow-triggered breath combines ____ mechanisms.
q.e: Flow triggering combines continuous flow and demand flow mechanisms, making it more responsive than pressure triggering and reducing imposed inspiratory work. (Chang 4th ed., p. 61)

q.q: During flow triggering, what flow relationship signals the ventilator to deliver a breath when the patient initiates inspiration?
o: Return flow drops below delivered flow
Delivered flow and return flow stay equal
Return flow rises above delivered flow
Delivered flow drops to zero before inspiration
q.e: Before inspiration, delivered flow equals return flow; as the patient inhales part of the bias flow, return flow decreases below delivered flow and triggers the breath. (Chang 4th ed., p. 61)

q.q: What occurs during inspiration when a ventilator variable reaches its preset limit variable?
o: Breath delivery continues while the variable is held at its preset value
The ventilator allows the variable to rise above the limit until inspiration ends
The ventilator aborts inspiration just like a high-pressure alarm limit
Inspiratory gas flow stops immediately and the exhalation valve opens up
q.e: Unlike a cycle variable or high-pressure alarm limit, reaching a limit variable does not end inspiration; breath delivery continues with the variable held at its preset ceiling. (Chang 4th ed., p. 62)

q.q: Because most newer ventilators are flow controllers that derive volume from flow and inspiratory time without measuring volume directly, their mandatory volume breaths are actually ____.
q.e: In flow-controlling ventilators, volume is a function of flow times inspiratory time rather than a direct volume measurement, so inspiration ends when a preset time elapses (time-cycled). (Chang 4th ed., p. 62)

q.q: The variable controlled during the expiratory phase is termed the ____, which is most commonly pressure when PEEP or CPAP is applied.
q.e: The parameter controlled during the expiratory time between breaths is the baseline variable, most commonly airway pressure via PEEP or CPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 63)

q.q: When titrating PEEP or CPAP to increase FRC and prevent alveolar collapse, which parameters must be monitored to achieve maximum benefit with minimal side effects?
o: Hemodynamic functions, blood gases or oximetry, and compliance
Bellows chamber pressure, bias flow rate, and battery voltage
Anatomical dead space, inspiratory rise time, and gas humidity
Expiratory valve resistance, tube cuff pressure, and circuit length
q.e: PEEP and CPAP must be titrated while monitoring hemodynamic functions, blood gases or oximetry, and pulmonary compliance to balance oxygenation benefits against adverse effects. (Chang 4th ed., p. 63)

q.q: Under Chatburn's phase-variable criteria, if neither peak pressure, peak volume, nor peak flow reaches a preset value before inspiration ends, how is the breath described?
o: No variables are limited during inspiration
Pressure, volume, and flow are limited by default
q.e: When peak pressure, peak volume, and peak flow do not reach a preset threshold prior to the end of inspiration, no variables are limited during inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 63)

q.q: In Chatburn's mode classification, what conditional variable governs switching from machine-triggered to patient-triggered breaths in A/C and SIMV?
q.e: Elapsed time initiates a machine-triggered breath. A qualifying inspiratory effort can initiate a patient-triggered breath. (Chang 4th ed., p. 64)

q.q: In Chatburn's classification of ventilator modes, which conditional variables cause mandatory minute ventilation (MMV) to switch from spontaneous to mandatory breaths?
o: Minute ventilation and peak inspiratory pressure
Tidal volume and peak inspiratory pressure
q.e: In Chatburn's mode classification, mandatory minute ventilation (MMV) uses minute ventilation and time as conditional variables to switch from spontaneous to mandatory breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 65)

q.q: In Chatburn's classification of ventilator modes, volume-assisted pressure support (VAPS) uses ____ as the conditional variable to switch from pressure control to volume control.
q.e: VAPS monitors tidal volume as its conditional variable to transition from pressure control to volume control. (Chang 4th ed., p. 65)

q.q: Chatburn defines a mechanical ventilation mode as a specific combination of breathing pattern, control type, and ____.
q.e: A mechanical ventilation mode is defined as a specific combination of breathing pattern, control type, and operational algorithms. (Chang 4th ed., p. 66)

q.q: During volume-controlled ventilation, airway pressure varies with compliance and resistance so that the ventilator can deliver the prescribed ____.
q.e: In volume-controlled ventilation, delivered volume remains constant despite changes in compliance or airway resistance, allowing regulation of tidal volume and minute ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 66)

q.q: The primary advantage of the pressure-controlled mode is protecting the lungs from excessive pressures, preventing ____.
q.e: Pressure-controlled ventilation caps peak inspiratory pressure to protect the lungs from excessive pressures and prevent ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI). (Chang 4th ed., p. 66)

q.q: During intermittent mandatory ventilation (IMV), why may spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths be augmented with pressure support?
o: To increase spontaneous tidal volume and reduce work from endotracheal tube resistance
To deliver a higher FIO2 concentration during spontaneous breaths than mandatory breaths
To hold exhaled tidal volume constant whenever lung compliance worsens during PCV breaths
To convert spontaneous patient efforts into time-triggered mandatory breaths
q.e: In IMV, adding pressure support augments spontaneous tidal volumes and reduces the inspiratory work imposed by endotracheal tube resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 67)

q.q: In pressure support ventilation, inspiration ends and expiration begins when the inspiratory flow rate decays to what percentage of peak inspiratory flow?
q.e: During pressure support, a constant preset pressure is maintained until inspiratory flow falls to between 10% and 40% of peak inspiratory flow, cycling the breath into expiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 67)

q.q: During dual control within-a-breath modes such as pressure augmentation and volume-assured pressure support, the ventilator switches from ____ within the same breath.
o: mandatory control to baseline CPAP control
q.e: Dual control within-a-breath modes start inspiration as a pressure controller for high initial flow and switch to volume control within the same breath to guarantee tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 68)

q.q: In dual control breath-to-breath pressure-limited, time-cycled modes such as VC+ and PRVC, in what increments is inspiratory pressure adjusted between breaths to reach the target tidal volume?
q.e: After a test breath determines resistance and compliance in VC+ or PRVC, pressure is adjusted automatically in increments of 1 to 3 cm H2O between breaths without exceeding the upper pressure limit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 68)

q.q: A patient breathing in Volume Support Ventilation (VSV) on a Maquet Servo-i becomes apneic. How does the ventilator respond?
o: Switches to a volume-controlled backup ventilation mode
Maintains spontaneous flow cycling without backup breaths
Switches within the same breath to continuous CPAP mode
Increases baseline PEEP in 3 cm H2O steps until triggered
q.e: Volume Support Ventilation (VSV) is a pressure-limited, flow-cycled spontaneous mode that automatically switches to a volume-controlled backup mode if the patient becomes apneic. (Chang 4th ed., p. 69)

q.q: In Automode, after two consecutive spontaneous breaths switch the ventilator from PRVC to volume support, what apnea duration switches it back to PRVC mode?
o: 12 seconds for adults and 8 seconds for pediatrics
20 seconds for adults and 10 seconds for pediatrics
8 seconds for adults and 12 seconds for pediatrics
15 seconds for adults and 5 seconds for pediatrics
q.e: Automode switches from PRVC to VSV after two consecutive spontaneous breaths and reverts to PRVC if apnea lasts 12 seconds in adults or 8 seconds in pediatric patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 69)

q.q: ____ is a spontaneous mode on the Puritan-Bennett 840 that increases pressure assistance within the same breath in proportion to the patient’s measured inspiratory flow and volume.
q.e: Proportional assist ventilation (PAV) tailors pressure support relative to patient effort by amplifying delivered pressure in proportion to measured inspiratory flow and volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 69)

q.q: Which characteristic of automatic tube compensation (ATC) helps reduce air trapping and intrinsic PEEP?
o: It is active during both inspiration and expiration to offset artificial airway resistance
It holds airway pressure at an elevated CPAP level throughout the entire breathing cycle
It terminates inspiratory gas flow whenever exhaled tidal volume reaches the target level
It delivers a mandatory compliance test breath before patient-triggered inspiration
q.e: ATC adjusts pressure to compensate for artificial airway resistance during both inspiration and expiration. This compensation may reduce air trapping and intrinsic PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 69)

q.q: In airway pressure release ventilation (APRV), the higher pressure is typically set initially above the ____ of the lung's pressure-volume curve to enhance recruitment, while brief release to Plow facilitates CO2 removal.
o: end point of the inspiratory limb
q.e: In APRV, the higher CPAP level (with Thigh longer than Tlow) is set initially above the lower inflection point of the pressure-volume curve to keep alveoli inflated, and brief release removes CO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 70)

q.q: By convention on ventilator waveforms, flow values plotted above the horizontal axis are ____, whereas flow values below the horizontal axis are expiratory.
q.e: Waveform convention places inspiratory flow values above the horizontal axis and expiratory flow values below the horizontal axis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 70)

q.q: Some ventilators display flow-versus-volume waveforms to aid in assessing ____ during mechanical ventilation.
o: airway obstruction and the effectiveness of bronchodilator therapy
alveolar dead space ratios and systemic oxygen consumption rates
inspired gas temperature stability and servo-humidifier function
lower inflection points and minimal patient work of breathing
q.e: Pressure-versus-volume loops help minimize work of breathing, whereas flow-versus-volume waveforms aid in assessing airway obstruction and bronchodilator effectiveness. (Chang 4th ed., p. 71)

q.q: In Chatburn's theoretical output waveforms, which relationship holds true for a pressure-controlled inspiration with a rectangular pressure waveform?
o: Mean inspiratory pressure equals peak inspiratory pressure
Mean inspiratory pressure is half of peak inspiratory pressure
Mean airway pressure exceeds peak inspiratory airway pressure
Mean inspiratory pressure equals end-expiratory baseline pressure
q.e: For a rectangular pressure waveform during pressure-controlled inspiration, pressure rises instantaneously and stays constant, so mean inspiratory pressure equals peak inspiratory pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 71)

q.q: Which four shapes classify ventilator pressure waveforms when pressure is the control variable?
o: Triangular, trapezoidal, biphasic, and decelerating ramp
Constant, parabolic, logarithmic, and intermittent pulse
Ascending ramp, descending ramp, constant, and parabolic
q.e: When pressure is the control variable, the four types of pressure waveforms are rectangular, exponential, sinusoidal, and oscillating. (Chang 4th ed., p. 72)

q.q: A graphic presentation of flow and time that has a horizontal 'S' appearance is defined as a ____.
q.e: A sine wave is defined as a graphic presentation of flow and time with a horizontal 'S' appearance; sinusoidal ventilator waveforms resemble its positive half. (Chang 4th ed., p. 72)

q.q: Sinusoidal pressure, volume, and flow waveforms are characteristically produced by ventilators such as the Emerson 3-MV and Bear 33 that use a ____.
q.e: Ventilators with a rotary-driven piston drive mechanism (such as the Emerson 3-MV, Respironics PLV-100, Bear 33, and Puritan-Bennett LP-10/LP-20) produce sinusoidal waveforms. (Chang 4th ed., p. 73)

q.q: During volume-controlled ventilation, which volume waveform produces a rectangular inspiratory flow waveform?
q.e: Because flow is the derivative of volume with respect to time, an ascending-ramp volume waveform produces a constant (rectangular) inspiratory flow waveform. (Chang 4th ed., p. 74)

q.q: When alternating current (AC) electrical power is lost, most ventilator battery backup alarms are powered by ____.
q.e: Loss of AC electrical power triggers audible and visual backup alarms typically powered by rechargeable nickel cadmium batteries that recharge while AC power is connected. (Chang 4th ed., p. 75)

q.q: During ventilator setup, a clinician enters an incompatible parameter outside acceptable specifications, and on another unit a self-diagnostic test failure renders the ventilator inoperative. Which alarm system alerts the clinician in both cases?
q.e: Control circuit alarms warn the clinician of incompatible settings outside acceptable specifications or failure of an internal self-diagnostic test. (Chang 4th ed., p. 75)

q.q: Among ventilator output alarms, flow alarms are limited to monitoring ____.
q.e: The chapter identifies exhaled minute volume as the quantity monitored by flow alarms. Some ventilators allow high and low alarm thresholds for that quantity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 76)

q.q: Monitoring exhaled oxygen tension and end-tidal carbon dioxide tension with output gas alarms assists the clinician in determining which parameters?
o: VD/VT, gas exchange, and the respiratory exchange ratio (R)
Circuit compliance, endotracheal cuff pressure, and PEEP
Inspired gas temperature, FIO2, and humidifier servo output
Auto-PEEP sensitivity, inspiratory rise time, and I:E ratio
q.e: Exhaled oxygen and end-tidal carbon dioxide monitoring systems trigger high/low alarms and help determine dead-space-to-tidal-volume ratio (VD/VT), gas exchange, and the respiratory exchange ratio (R). (Chang 4th ed., p. 76)

sections.title: Ch 4 · Operating Modes of Mechanical Ventilation

q.q: The pressure gradient that must be generated between the airway opening and the alveoli to produce inspiratory flow is known as the ____.
q.e: A mechanical ventilator must generate a pressure difference between the airway opening and the alveoli, called the transairway pressure, to produce inspiratory flow and volume delivery. (Chang 4th ed., p. 82)

q.q: Which equation correctly expresses transairway pressure (PTA)?
q.e: Transairway pressure (PTA) equals the pressure at the airway opening (PAO) minus the alveolar pressure (PALV). (Chang 4th ed., p. 82)

q.q: In a patient breathing room air without applied PEEP or air trapping, pressures at the airway opening and alveoli equilibrate with ____ at the end of a normal exhalation, resulting in no flow.
q.e: Once exhalation is complete under these conditions, airway opening pressure and alveolar pressure both equal atmospheric pressure. The transairway pressure gradient is zero. (Chang 4th ed., p. 82)

q.q: Negative pressure ventilation does not require an artificial airway unless ____ is present.
q.e: Negative pressure ventilation lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure and does not require an artificial airway unless airway obstruction is present. (Chang 4th ed., p. 83)

q.q: During negative pressure ventilation in an iron lung, the tidal volume delivered to the patient is directly related to the ____.
q.e: Evacuating air from an iron lung creates negative pressure around the thorax, and the delivered tidal volume is directly related to the magnitude of the negative pressure gradient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 83)

q.q: A patient with chronic ventilatory failure placed in an iron lung develops decreased cardiac output known as tank shock. What mechanism produces this complication?
o: Negative pressure on peripheral veins reduces venous return
Hyperinflation of upper lung zones increases right heart load
Excessive vagal tone slows conduction at the sinoatrial node
Positive pleural pressure compresses the pulmonary capillaries
q.e: Exposing the peripheral vasculature inside an iron lung to negative pressure matching pleural pressure eliminates the normal venous pressure gradient, decreasing venous blood return to the right atrium and cardiac output. (Chang 4th ed., p. 83)

q.q: Although the chest cuirass improves patient access and reduces tank shock compared with an iron lung, what problem commonly limits its clinical effectiveness?
o: Difficulty maintaining an airtight seal on the chest wall
Requirement for high-pressure compressed oxygen gas sources
Enclosure of the arms and lower body inside a rigid chamber
Inability to ventilate patients without tracheal intubation
q.e: A chest cuirass covers only the chest and leaves the arms and lower body exposed, but ventilation may be limited by difficulty maintaining an airtight seal against the chest wall. (Chang 4th ed., p. 83)

q.q: Individually designed cuirass respirators minimize air leaks and have been used successfully to ventilate patients with chest wall diseases such as ____.
q.e: Custom-fitted cuirass respirators reduce air leakage around the shell and have been used successfully in patients with chest wall diseases such as scoliosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 83)

q.q: Why are chest cuirass ventilators useful in selected home care settings even though they are seldom used in acute care facilities?
o: Ease of maintenance for noninvasive home ventilation
High end-expiratory pressure for alveolar recruitment
Precise volume delivery despite severe bronchial spasm
Automated closed-loop servo control of inspired oxygen
q.e: Chest cuirass ventilators are useful in selected home care settings because they are easy to maintain and can ventilate patients without an artificial airway. (Chang 4th ed., p. 84)

q.q: Positive pressure ventilation generates inspiratory flow and tidal volume by applying a pressure greater than atmospheric pressure at the ____.
q.e: Positive pressure ventilation applies supra-atmospheric pressure at the airway opening, creating a positive transairway pressure gradient directly related to the delivered tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 84)

q.q: Which set lists the four main clinical goals that any selected ventilator operating mode should achieve?
o: Gas exchange, avoiding lung injury, synchrony, and weaning
Gas exchange, lung protection, synchrony, and a fixed rate
Adequate gas exchange, lung protection, constant tidal volume, and weaning
Adequate gas exchange, constant inspiratory flow, synchrony, and weaning
q.e: Regardless of the operating mode chosen, it should provide adequate ventilation and oxygenation, avoid ventilator-induced lung injury, provide patient-ventilator synchrony, and allow successful weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 84)

q.q: Two or more ventilator modes are often combined, such as pairing SIMV with ____ to provide mechanical ventilation and reduce the work of spontaneous breathing.
q.e: Modes are frequently combined for complementary effects; for example, spontaneous plus PEEP equals CPAP, and SIMV may be combined with PSV to lower the work of spontaneous breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 84)

q.q: In mechanical breath terminology, the ____ variable is the mechanism used to start inspiration, such as a patient-generated pressure or flow change or a preset ventilator time interval.
q.e: The trigger variable is the mechanism that starts inspiration, whereas the control variable delivers the breath and the cycle variable ends inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 85)

q.q: In ventilator mode terminology, the ____ variable is the mechanism that ends inspiration, such as volume, pressure, flow, or time.
q.e: The cycle variable is the mechanism that terminates inspiration, including volume-cycled, pressure-cycled, flow-cycled, and time-cycled breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 85)

q.q: In the classification of breath sequences, the ____ breath sequence describes modes such as PSV and CPAP in which all breaths are initiated by the patient with or without assistance.
q.e: In a continuous spontaneous breath sequence, every breath is spontaneous either with assistance (such as PSV) or without assistance (such as CPAP). (Chang 4th ed., p. 85)

q.q: Under a ____ target scheme, the ventilator adjusts its output to suit a patient variable, as when PAV adjusts pressure to meet flow demand.
q.e: A servo control scheme adjusts ventilator output proportionally to a patient variable, such as proportional assist ventilation adjusting pressure to match inspiratory flow demand. (Chang 4th ed., p. 85)

q.q: The ____ targeting scheme adjusts one set point to achieve a different target, as in pressure-regulated volume control.
q.e: An adaptive control scheme automatically adjusts one set point (such as inspiratory pressure via flow and I-time in PRVC) to achieve a different target set point (tidal volume). (Chang 4th ed., p. 85)

q.q: Which targeting scheme uses a mathematical model to adjust frequency, tidal volume, and pressure to achieve a target minute ventilation?
q.e: An optimal target scheme applies a mathematical model to adjust multiple set points—as adaptive support ventilation alters rate, tidal volume, and pressure—to meet a target minute ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 85)

q.q: In mechanical ventilation, a simple operating mode such as ____ provides one constant output based on one constant input rather than using a closed-loop system.
q.e: In simple volume-controlled ventilation, the clinician sets a constant tidal volume (input) and the ventilator delivers it using a constant inspiratory flow (output). (Chang 4th ed., p. 86)

q.q: Why is pressure support ventilation classified as a closed-loop system?
o: Set pressure input is constant while flow output varies
Set volume input is constant while flow output stays fixed
Set flow input varies while airway pressure rises linearly
Set rate input is fixed while exhalation is time-triggered
q.e: During pressure support ventilation, the clinician sets a constant peak pressure plateau (input) and the ventilator varies inspiratory flow (output) according to changing airway and lung characteristics. (Chang 4th ed., p. 86)

q.q: The spontaneous setting on a mechanical ventilator is not an actual mode because the ____ are determined by the patient.
q.e: Spontaneous is not a true ventilator mode because the patient determines both respiratory frequency and tidal volume while the ventilator supplies gas flow and supplemental oxygen. (Chang 4th ed., p. 86)

q.q: What is the role of the mechanical ventilator while operating in the spontaneous breathing setting?
o: Provide timely adequate flow and adjunctive modes like PEEP
Provide supplemental oxygen and end each inspiration at a preset time
Maintain baseline pressure and initiate each breath at a preset interval
Deliver a preset tidal volume on demand
