q.e: During spontaneous breathing, the ventilator provides timely inspiratory flow sufficient to meet the patient's demand along with adjunctive features such as PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 87)

q.q: ____ is a safety feature incorporated with the spontaneous breathing mode that delivers predetermined backup settings if apnea or an extremely low frequency occurs.
q.e: Apnea ventilation is a backup safety feature paired with spontaneous breathing that delivers a preset tidal volume, frequency, and FIO2 if apnea or a dangerously low rate occurs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 87)

q.q: Which set lists the three major clinical indications for applying PEEP?
o: Shunt with refractory hypoxemia, reduced FRC and compliance, and auto-PEEP persisting despite ventilator adjustments
Shunt with refractory hypoxemia, increased FRC and compliance, and auto-PEEP persisting despite ventilator adjustments
Hypoxemia corrected by supplemental oxygen, increased FRC and compliance, and hypotension following a PEEP increase
Shunt with refractory hypoxemia, reduced FRC and compliance, and respiratory alkalosis from excessive mandatory ventilation
q.e: The three major indications for PEEP are intrapulmonary shunt with refractory hypoxemia, decreased functional residual capacity and lung compliance, and auto-PEEP unresponsive to ventilator adjustments. (Chang 4th ed., p. 87)

q.q: As a clinical guideline, refractory hypoxemia is present when the patient's PaO2 is ____ or lower at an FIO2 of 50% or higher.
q.e: Refractory hypoxemia responds poorly to moderate-to-high oxygen levels and is clinically identified when PaO2 is 60 mm Hg or lower on an FIO2 of 50% or higher. (Chang 4th ed., p. 88)

q.q: A PaO2 of 60 mm Hg on an FIO2 of 0.50 gives a P/F ratio of 120 mm Hg. Below what P/F cutoff does this chapter place the oxygenation criterion for ARDS?
q.e: A PaO2 ≤ 60 mm Hg at an FIO2 ≥ 50% gives a calculated P/F ratio ≤ 120 mm Hg, which is well below the < 200 mm Hg threshold for ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 88)

q.q: Which ventilator adjustments help correct air trapping caused by insufficient expiratory time?
o: Increase peak flow, or decrease frequency or tidal volume
Decrease flow cycling threshold, or raise tidal volumes
Decrease peak inspiratory flow, or raise the set frequency
Increase inspiratory pause time, or invert the I:E ratio
q.e: Insufficient expiratory time leading to air trapping and auto-PEEP can be corrected by increasing peak inspiratory flow or by decreasing respiratory frequency or tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 88)

q.q: A ventilated patient has an auto-PEEP of 6 cm H2O and a pressure sensitivity set at 2 cm H2O below baseline. What total negative airway pressure must the patient generate to trigger a breath?
q.e: Because the patient must overcome both auto-PEEP (6 cm H2O) and the sensitivity setting (2 cm H2O), a total negative airway pressure of 8 cm H2O is required to trigger inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 88)

q.q: To raise baseline airway pressure and reduce the work of breath triggering caused by air trapping, extrinsic PEEP may be set ____ the auto-PEEP level.
q.e: Setting extrinsic PEEP slightly below the patient's auto-PEEP level elevates the end-expiratory baseline pressure and decreases the negative pressure effort needed to trigger the ventilator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 88)

q.q: During assist/control ventilation with pressure triggering and 10 cm H2O of PEEP, which airway pressure change indicates that the patient triggered a breath?
o: A negative pressure deflection at the start of inspiration
A prolonged expiratory hold plateau below atmospheric level
An absence of peak airway pressure above the PEEP baseline
A drop of baseline pressure to 0 cm H2O during exhalation
q.e: The patient’s inspiratory effort briefly lowers airway pressure below the 10 cm H2O baseline before the ventilator delivers the breath. A time-triggered breath requires no preceding patient effort. (Chang 4th ed., p. 88)

q.q: Normally at end-exhalation, atmospheric alveolar pressure (0 cm H2O) and an average pleural pressure of –5 cm H2O create what alveolar distending pressure?
q.e: With end-expiratory alveolar pressure at 0 cm H2O and average pleural pressure at –5 cm H2O, the normal alveolar distending (alveolar-pleural) pressure is 5 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 89)

q.q: PEEP increases alveolar end-expiratory pressure, which decreases the ____ for alveolar inflation, increases FRC, and reverses intrapulmonary shunting.
q.e: By maintaining alveolar inflation during exhalation, PEEP lowers the pressure threshold required for alveolar opening, increases FRC, improves V/Q matching and oxygenation, and reduces work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 89)

q.q: Through what hemodynamic mechanism can PEEP reduce cardiac output and cause systemic hypotension?
o: Pleural pressure becomes less negative, reducing venous return
Alveolar recruitment lowers central venous pressure directly
Pleural pressure becomes more negative, trapping thoracic blood
Mean airway pressure drops, collapsing pulmonary capillaries
q.e: PEEP increases peak and mean airway pressures and makes pleural pressure less negative, narrowing the pressure gradient for central venous blood return to the right atrium and lowering cardiac output. (Chang 4th ed., p. 89)

q.q: Shortly after PEEP is applied or increased to a high level, a patient's blood pressure decreases. What should the clinician ensure first before lowering the PEEP level?
o: That the patient is not hypovolemic
That the arterial carbon dioxide is high
That the ventilator circuit is unheated
That the endotracheal cuff is deflated
q.e: If PEEP lowers blood pressure, the clinician should first verify that the patient is not hypovolemic; if intravascular blood volume is adequate, PEEP should then be reduced until blood pressure recovers. (Chang 4th ed., p. 90)

q.q: In which patient will a given PEEP-induced rise in alveolar pressure be transmitted more readily to the pleural space, increasing the likelihood of reduced venous return?
o: A patient with normal or elevated lung compliance
A patient with markedly reduced compliance from pulmonary fibrosis
A patient with extremely low compliance from ARDS
A patient with severely reduced compliance from pulmonary edema
q.e: Extremely low lung compliance (as in ARDS) shields the pleural space from alveolar pressure, whereas normal or elevated lung compliance readily transmits PEEP into the pleural space and impedes venous return. (Chang 4th ed., p. 90)

q.q: What PEEP cutoff does Chang report alongside mean airway pressure of 30 cm H2O and peak inspiratory pressure of 50 cm H2O as a threshold above which barotrauma becomes more frequent?
q.e: A PEEP greater than 10 cm H2O (or mean airway pressure > 30 cm H2O, or peak inspiratory pressure > 50 cm H2O) is associated with an increased incidence of alveolar rupture and barotrauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 90)

q.q: ____ of unknown cause in a ventilated patient should always be interpreted as a clinical sign that barotrauma has occurred.
o: New fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases
New coarse rhonchi over the central airways
q.e: Alveolar rupture can cause pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, pneumopericardium, or pneumoperitoneum, and unexplained subcutaneous emphysema or crepitus indicates barotrauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 90)

q.q: In patients with normal lung compliance, PEEP may impede cerebral venous return and elevate intracranial pressure above its normal range of what values?
q.e: Normal intracranial pressure is 8 to 12 cm H2O; in patients with normal lung compliance, PEEP can raise ICP by impeding cerebral venous drainage. (Chang 4th ed., p. 90)

q.q: Because the kidneys receive approximately what percentage of circulating blood volume at any one time, positive pressure ventilation can reduce glomerular perfusion and urine output?
q.e: The kidneys receive about 25% of the body's circulating blood volume, making them highly vulnerable to decreased blood flow, reduced glomerular filtration, and fluid retention during positive pressure ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 90)

q.q: To use CPAP safely, a spontaneously breathing patient must be able to sustain ____, defined as the amount of ventilation needed to bring PaCO2 to normal.
q.e: CPAP has the same indications as PEEP with the added requirement that the patient's spontaneous lung function can maintain eucapnic ventilation (a normal PaCO2). (Chang 4th ed., p. 91)

q.q: Although adult CPAP can be delivered through a face mask, nasal mask, or endotracheal tube, ____ is the method of choice in neonates.
q.e: In neonates, nasal CPAP is the preferred interface for continuous positive airway pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 91)

q.q: During bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) therapy, ____ provides positive pressure breaths to improve ventilation and hypoxemia caused by hypoventilation.
q.e: In BiPAP, IPAP delivers inspiratory positive pressure breaths to improve ventilation, whereas EPAP acts like CPAP to raise FRC and reduce intrapulmonary shunting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 91)

q.q: BiPAP appears to be of particular value in preventing intubation of the ____ patient and in supporting chronic ventilatory failure.
q.e: BiPAP is valuable in preventing intubation in end-stage COPD and supporting patients with chronic ventilatory failure, restrictive chest wall disease, neuromuscular disease, and nocturnal hypoventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 91)

q.q: When initiating BiPAP on a spontaneously breathing patient, what are the typical starting IPAP and EPAP settings before titrating toward 5 to 7 mL/kg?
o: IPAP 8 cm H2O and EPAP 4 cm H2O
IPAP 15 cm H2O and EPAP 10 cm H2O
IPAP 20 cm H2O and EPAP 12 cm H2O
IPAP 4 cm H2O and EPAP 8 cm H2O
q.e: For a spontaneously breathing patient, IPAP and EPAP are initially set at 8 cm H2O and 4 cm H2O, respectively, and titrated toward a target tidal volume of 5 to 7 mL/kg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 92)

q.q: In the BiPAP spontaneous/timed backup mode, where should the backup respiratory frequency (f/min) be set relative to the patient's spontaneous rate?
o: 2 to 5 breaths/min below the spontaneous frequency
2 to 5 breaths/min above the spontaneous frequency
Exactly equal to the patient's spontaneous frequency
10 to 12 breaths/min above the spontaneous frequency
q.e: In the BiPAP spontaneous/timed mode, the backup rate is set two to five breaths per minute below the patient's spontaneous respiratory frequency, whereas in timed mode it is set slightly higher. (Chang 4th ed., p. 92)

q.q: In the BiPAP timed mode, setting the % IPAP control at 33% or 50% yields which respective I:E ratios?
q.e: Setting % IPAP at 33% produces an I:E ratio of 1:2, while setting % IPAP at 50% produces an I:E ratio of 1:1. (Chang 4th ed., p. 92)

q.q: When adjusting BiPAP settings to improve alveolar ventilation with IPAP or oxygenation with EPAP, in what increments should IPAP or EPAP be raised?
q.e: Both IPAP (for ventilation and PaCO2 normalization) and EPAP (for FRC and oxygenation in intrapulmonary shunting) are increased in increments of 2 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 92)

q.q: Because BiPAP is pressure-targeted rather than volume-controlled, which adjustment or patient change yields a larger delivered tidal volume?
o: Increasing the IPAP level or decreasing the EPAP level
Decreasing the IPAP level or increasing the EPAP level
Setting the EPAP level equal to the preset IPAP pressure
Decreasing lung compliance or increasing airway resistance
q.e: Delivered volume during BiPAP increases with a wider IPAP-to-EPAP gradient (higher IPAP or lower EPAP), higher lung-thorax compliance, and lower airflow resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 92)

q.q: When the EPAP setting is made equal to the IPAP setting on a BiPAP unit, ____ results, and EPAP cannot be set higher than IPAP.
q.e: A BiPAP device functions as a CPAP device when IPAP and EPAP are set to the same pressure level, and EPAP cannot exceed IPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 92)

q.q: Why must control mode ventilation be instituted with sedatives and neuromuscular blockers rather than by making trigger sensitivity unresponsive to patient effort?
o: Spontaneous efforts feel like inspiring against an obstructed airway
Insensitive triggering forces the high-pressure relief valve wide open
Low trigger sensitivity causes rapid hyperventilation and alkalosis
Turning sensitivity down converts time-triggered breaths to flow cycling
q.e: Locking out patient triggering via sensitivity leaves no gas flow during spontaneous efforts, mimicking a completely obstructed airway and causing severe psychological distress. (Chang 4th ed., p. 93)

q.q: During a volume-targeted mandatory breath, a patient actively exhales and airway pressure rises sharply. On a ventilator configured for high-pressure limit cycling, what happens if the pressure reaches that limit?
o: High-pressure limit cycling ends inspiration early, so less than the preset volume is delivered
Inspiration pauses at the pressure limit and then resumes until the preset volume is delivered
Inspiration ends at the pressure limit, but the full preset volume has already been delivered
Inspiration continues at the limiting pressure until the full preset volume is delivered
q.e: Active exhalation during mechanical inflation spikes airway pressure to the high pressure limit, prematurely terminating inspiration and reducing the delivered tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 93)

q.q: Chang lists crushed chest injury as a possible indication for control mode when spontaneous inspiration produces significant ____.
q.e: In a patient with a crushed chest injury, significant paradoxical chest wall movement during spontaneous inspiration is one indication Chang gives for control mode. Other examples include tetanus or seizure activity that interrupts ventilation and a need for a period of complete rest. (Chang 4th ed., p. 93)

q.q: In a sedated and paralyzed patient on control mode ventilation, the primary hazard if accidental circuit disconnection or ventilator failure occurs is ____.
q.e: Because spontaneous respiratory drive is blunted in the control mode, accidental disconnection or mechanical/electrical failure creates an immediate hazard of apnea and hypoxia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 94)

q.q: In the human study Chang cites, what range of complete diaphragmatic inactivity was documented in mechanically ventilated patients with marked diaphragm myofiber atrophy?
q.e: In the human study Chang cites, 18 to 69 hours of complete diaphragmatic inactivity during mechanical ventilation was associated with marked diaphragm myofiber atrophy. (Chang 4th ed., p. 94)

q.q: Because a patient in the control mode depends completely on the ventilator, which alarms are most critical for alerting the caregiver to interrupted ventilation?
o: Low exhaled volume and low inspiratory pressure alarms
High tidal volume and inverse I:E ratio indicator alarms
High respiratory rate and high oxygen concentration alarms
High PEEP baseline and elevated gas temperature alarms
q.e: In the control mode, the low exhaled volume alarm and the low inspiratory pressure alarm are essential to detect circuit disconnection or interrupted ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 94)

q.q: In volume control with patient triggering disabled, each mandatory breath is ____-triggered.
q.e: The preset frequency determines when each breath starts. Inspiration normally ends when the preset tidal volume has been delivered, but reaching the high pressure limit can end it earlier. (Chang 4th ed., p. 94)

q.q: A patient on assist/control ventilation has a preset control rate of 10/min (every 6 sec) and a stable assist rate of 12/min (every 5 sec). How many time-triggered control breaths will be delivered?
q.e: Because the patient triggers assisted breaths every 5 seconds—shorter than the 6-second control interval—no time-triggered breaths are delivered unless the patient's rate drops below 10/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 95)

q.q: ____ is defined as any ventilator mode that provides all of the work of breathing.
q.e: Assist/control is commonly used initially to provide full ventilatory support, defined as any mode in which the ventilator performs all of the work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 95)

q.q: In the assist/control mode, the backup control frequency is typically set 2 to 4/min less than the patient's assist rate, or at a minimum of what frequency?
q.e: The generally accepted minimum control rate in AC mode is 2 to 4 breaths/min below the patient's assist frequency, or at least 8 to 10/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 95)

q.q: Once trigger sensitivity is set appropriately in AC mode, how much inspiratory flow should the ventilator supply to minimize the patient’s work of breathing?
o: Enough to meet or exceed the patient’s inspiratory flow demand
A flow based on the backup respiratory rate regardless of patient demand
Just below the patient’s inspiratory flow demand
A flow matched to the patient’s mean expiratory flow on the preceding breath
q.e: AC mode keeps patient work of breathing very low provided trigger sensitivity is appropriate and delivered inspiratory flow meets or exceeds patient demand. (Chang 4th ed., p. 96)

q.q: A patient with a respiratory center injury on AC mode (preset VT 12 mL/kg) assists at 25/min and develops hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis. What is the safest corrective action?
o: Switch to a mode such as SIMV that limits excessive minute volume
Add long segments of mechanical deadspace tubing to the circuit
Increase the preset mandatory tidal volume to slow the drive down
Decrease trigger sensitivity until no patient effort triggers flow
q.e: Alveolar hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis) is the primary hazard of AC when central drive is high; switching to a mode like SIMV is considered safer than adding mechanical deadspace. (Chang 4th ed., p. 96)

q.q: In conventional volume-cycled assist/control ventilation, what normally ends inspiration, and what safety limit can end it early?
o: Preset tidal volume delivery or the high pressure limit
Drop in spontaneous minute volume or demand valve closure
Completion of a neural diaphragm signal or pause interval
Decay of peak flow to 25% or opening of the release valve
q.e: Delivery of the preset tidal volume normally ends inspiration. If airway pressure reaches the high pressure limit first, inspiration can end before the full volume is delivered. (Chang 4th ed., p. 96)

q.q: In intermittent mandatory ventilation (IMV), setting appropriate ____ reduces the risk of barotrauma if random breath stacking occurs.
q.e: Because unsynchronized IMV mandatory breaths can stack atop spontaneous breaths and elevate lung volume and pressure, appropriate high pressure limits reduce barotrauma risk. (Chang 4th ed., p. 97)

q.q: With an SIMV mandatory rate of 10/min and a 0.5-second synchronization window, how long after the start of one mandatory breath does the window for the next mandatory breath open?
q.e: With a 6-second mandatory cycle and a 0.5-second synchronization window, the ventilator becomes sensitive to a patient effort for an assisted mandatory breath at 5.5 seconds. (Chang 4th ed., p. 98)

q.q: Compared with assist/control, why does SIMV tend to have a lower mean airway pressure?
o: Its spontaneous breaths have a lower peak inspiratory pressure and inspiratory time
Its mandatory breaths have a higher peak flow and shorter cycle time
Its mandatory breaths are pressure-limited rather than volume-cycled
Its spontaneous breaths have a higher tidal volume and inspiratory time
q.e: Mean airway pressure is related to PIP and inspiratory time; spontaneous SIMV breaths have a lower PIP and inspiratory time, so SIMV tends to have a lower mean airway pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 99)

q.q: In the SIMV mode, humidified gas for spontaneous breaths taken between mandatory breaths is typically supplied by a patient-triggered ____.
q.e: Between mandatory SIMV breaths, a pressure- or flow-triggered demand valve supplies gas at the selected FIO2 while the patient's effort determines spontaneous rate and volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 99)

q.q: Whereas positive pressure breaths hyperinflate upper lung zones, spontaneous breathing during SIMV distributes tidal volume more evenly and reduces ____.
q.e: Pulmonary perfusion favors gravity-dependent lower lung zones; spontaneous breaths in SIMV distribute ventilation more evenly than positive pressure breaths, reducing upper-zone alveolar deadspace. (Chang 4th ed., p. 99)

q.q: Along with respiratory frequency and PEEP, mean airway pressure is directly related to ____.
o: peak inspiratory pressure and inspiratory time
endotracheal cuff pressure and circuit bias flow
trigger sensitivity and expiratory pause duration
q.e: Mean airway pressure is directly related to peak inspiratory pressure, inspiratory time, respiratory frequency, and PEEP; lower peak pressure and I-time on spontaneous breaths reduce mPaw in SIMV. (Chang 4th ed., p. 99)

q.q: Without pressure support, the primary disadvantage of SIMV is weaning the mandatory rate too rapidly, causing high spontaneous work of breathing, ____, and weaning failure.
q.e: Decreasing the SIMV mandatory frequency too rapidly imposes an excessive spontaneous workload that can lead to respiratory muscle fatigue and weaning failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 100)

q.q: A patient receives conventional volume-controlled SIMV with unassisted spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths. Which pairing describes mandatory breath cycling and control of spontaneous tidal volume?
o: Volume-cycled mandatory breath; patient controls spontaneous tidal volume
Volume-cycled mandatory breath; ventilator presets spontaneous tidal volume
Flow-cycled mandatory breath; patient controls spontaneous tidal volume
Flow-cycled mandatory breath; ventilator presets spontaneous tidal volume
q.e: In this setup, delivery of the preset tidal volume normally ends a mandatory breath. Between mandatory breaths, the patient determines the rate and volume of unassisted spontaneous breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 100)

q.q: A patient on SIMV has a mandatory frequency of 4/min with a mandatory tidal volume of 800 mL and a spontaneous minute volume of 6 L/min. What is the total minute volume?
q.e: Ventilator-delivered minute volume is 4 × 0.8 L = 3.2 L/min; total minute volume is that plus the spontaneous 6 L/min, or 9.2 L/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 101)

q.q: A patient in the final stages of SIMV weaning with MMV (mandatory V̇E 3.2 L/min, spontaneous V̇E 6 L/min, preset MMV 8.0 L/min) suddenly becomes apneic. How do most MMV-equipped ventilators respond?
o: Automatically increase the SIMV mandatory frequency
Switch immediately to continuous positive airway pressure
Automatically double the preset mandatory tidal volume
Open the exhalation valve and sound the high-rate alarm
q.e: On most ventilators, MMV operates within SIMV to prevent hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis; when total minute volume drops below the preset minimum, the ventilator automatically increases the SIMV mandatory rate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 101)

q.q: A distressed patient on MMV breathes rapidly with very small tidal volumes while keeping total minute ventilation above the preset minimum. Why is this breathing pattern dangerous?
o: Total minute ventilation stays above the MMV threshold while alveolar minute ventilation falls.
Measured minute volume drops to zero and triggers continuous apnea mode.
Rapid shallow breaths lock the demand valve and stack mandatory breaths.
MMV rapidly increases mandatory breaths and causes severe alkalosis.
q.e: A rapid spontaneous rate with low tidal volume can satisfy the total minute volume threshold—preventing MMV from activating—while increasing deadspace ventilation and lowering alveolar minute volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 101)

q.q: To guard against unrecognized rapid shallow breathing during MMV, where should the clinician set the high respiratory frequency alarm?
o: Approximately 20 to 25/min above baseline spontaneous rate
Exactly equal to the preset SIMV mandatory breath rate
q.e: Setting the high frequency alarm about 10 breaths/min above the patient's baseline spontaneous rate alerts the clinician if tachypneic deadspace breathing develops during MMV. (Chang 4th ed., p. 101)

q.q: As an exception to most ventilators, selecting MMV on the ____ places the patient in a pure pressure support mode with no mandatory breaths.
q.e: Selecting MMV on the Hamilton Veolar places the patient in pure pressure support ventilation without mandatory breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 101)

q.q: How does the Hamilton Veolar respond in MMV when the patient's actual minute volume drops below the preset minimal minute volume?
o: It automatically increases the pressure support level
It automatically increases the mandatory breath rate
It switches from flow cycling to constant-flow volume control
It increases baseline PEEP in 5 cm H2O steps until V̇E rises
q.e: Whereas most ventilators increase mandatory frequency in MMV, the Hamilton Veolar automatically increases the pressure support level until the preset minimum minute volume is achieved. (Chang 4th ed., p. 102)

q.q: When PSV is added to SIMV, Chang reports a significant decrease in the patient’s ____, probably because breathing requires less work.
q.e: Adding PSV to SIMV reduces oxygen consumption. Chang identifies the lower work of spontaneous breathing as the likely explanation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 102)

q.q: A patient receives a pressure support plateau of 30 cm H2O above 5 cm H2O of PEEP. What peak inspiratory pressure is reached?
q.e: A pressure support level of 30 cm H2O added to a PEEP baseline of 5 cm H2O produces a peak inspiratory pressure of 35 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 102)

q.q: A pressure-supported breath is patient-triggered, pressure-limited, and ____.
q.e: A pressure-supported breath is initiated by the patient, limited to the preset pressure support level, and cycled to expiration when inspiratory flow falls to a minimal threshold. (Chang 4th ed., p. 103)

q.q: During pressure support ventilation, servo control of the demand valve typically produces a ____ flow pattern that cycles at a minimal flow such as 5 L/min or 25% of peak flow.
q.e: PSV rapidly pressurizes the airway to the preset plateau and maintains it with a steeply descending tapered flow waveform until flow drops to a threshold such as 5 L/min or 25% of peak flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 103)

q.q: When PSV is applied in the SIMV mode, pressure support assists spontaneous breaths and is ____ during mandatory breaths.
q.e: In SIMV, pressure support operates only during the patient's spontaneous breaths and is not active during mandatory mechanical breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 103)

q.q: When spontaneous respiratory frequency is the endpoint for titrating PSV during SIMV weaning, Chang gives ____ as the usual upper limit of the target rate.
q.e: Proper PSV titration endpoints include achieving a spontaneous tidal volume of 10 to 15 mL/kg, reducing spontaneous frequency to 25/min or less, or overcoming endotracheal tube resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 103)

q.q: On ventilators not equipped with automated mechanics displays, which formula estimates airway resistance?
o: (Peak Inspiratory Pressure − Plateau Pressure) / Mean Flow
(Plateau Pressure − Baseline PEEP) / Delivered Tidal Volume
(Peak Inspiratory Pressure + Plateau Pressure) × Mean Flow
(Peak Inspiratory Pressure − Baseline PEEP) × Minute Flow
q.e: Airway resistance is estimated by subtracting plateau pressure from peak inspiratory pressure and dividing the difference by mean inspiratory flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 103)

q.q: When adaptive support ventilation is set to 100% minute volume, what baseline minute ventilation per kilogram does Chang specify for an adult?
q.e: ASV uses a baseline minute ventilation of 100 mL/min/kg for adults and 200 mL/min/kg for children. The therapist selects a target from 20% to 200% of the applicable baseline. (Chang 4th ed., p. 104)

q.q: At a given flow-cycling threshold, the duration of a pressure-supported breath depends on the patient’s ____.
o: peak expiratory flow on the previous breath
interval between the previous two inspiratory efforts
q.e: At a given cycling threshold, the patient’s spontaneous inspiratory flow demand determines how long the pressure-supported breath lasts. The ventilator cycles to expiration when inspiratory flow falls to its preset threshold. (Chang 4th ed., p. 104)

q.q: Adaptive support ventilation (ASV) uses the ____ to calculate the optimal respiratory frequency that corresponds with the lowest work of breathing.
q.e: ASV measures dynamic compliance and expiratory time constant and applies the Otis Equation to select the optimal frequency yielding the lowest total work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 104)

q.q: In adaptive support ventilation (ASV), what predetermined baseline minute ventilation settings (adjustable from 20% to 200%) are used for adults and children?
o: 100 mL/min/kg for adults and 200 mL/min/kg for children
150 mL/min/kg for adults and 300 mL/min/kg for children
200 mL/min/kg for adults and 100 mL/min/kg for children
75 mL/min/kg for adults and 150 mL/min/kg for pediatrics
q.e: ASV uses predetermined baseline minute ventilation settings of 100 mL/min/kg for adults and 200 mL/min/kg for children, and the therapist selects a percentage from 20% to 200% alongside body weight. (Chang 4th ed., p. 104)

q.q: Once target minute ventilation is set in ASV, the ventilator uses test breaths to measure ____.
o: system compliance, airway resistance, and intrinsic PEEP
vital capacity, maximum inspiratory force, and cuff volume
alveolar oxygen tension, shunt fraction, and cardiac index
diaphragmatic EMG, esophageal pressure, and cuff leakage
q.e: ASV delivers test breaths to measure system compliance, airway resistance, and any intrinsic PEEP before selecting frequency, inspiratory time, I:E ratio, and high pressure limit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 104)

q.q: When ASV calculates required tidal volume as alveolar volume plus deadspace volume, what deadspace estimate per kilogram of body weight does it add?
q.e: As a patient triggers ASV, mandatory breaths decrease and pressure support increases until calculated tidal volume equals alveolar volume plus 2.2 mL/kg of deadspace volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 105)

q.q: PAV supplies 80% of the pressure needed to overcome elastance. If elastance is 40 cm H2O/L, how much elastic-assist pressure does the ventilator provide at 1 L above baseline volume?
q.e: The elastic pressure at 1 L is 40 cm H2O/L × 1 L = 40 cm H2O. The ventilator supplies 80% of that elastic pressure, or 32 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 105)

q.q: During proportional assist ventilation, ____ applies pressure to meet the patient's inspiratory flow demand and reduce the effort needed to overcome airflow resistance.
q.e: PAV operates in assist breaths only as either flow assist (FA), which meets inspiratory flow demand to overcome airflow resistance, or volume assist (VA), which meets volume demand. (Chang 4th ed., p. 105)

q.q: A patient receiving proportional assist ventilation (PAV) via positive feedback control has a sudden improvement in lung elastance and airway resistance. What hazard may result?
o: Excessive pressure causing overdistension, air trapping, and barotrauma
Premature opening of the CPAP release valve during spontaneous inhalation
Immediate drop in airway pressure causing acute hypoventilation and apnea
Automatic switch to time-triggered volume control with fixed square flow
q.e: When elastance or airflow resistance suddenly improves, the positive-feedback pressure delivered by PAV may become too high, leading to overdistension, increased air trapping, and barotrauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 106)

q.q: Which pairing correctly identifies the type of breath delivered in proportional assist ventilation (PAV) and its cycling endpoint?
o: Assisted breath ending when the patient’s volume or flow demand is met
Assisted breath ending when a preset inspiratory time elapses
Time-triggered breath ending when a preset inspiratory pressure is reached
Time-triggered breath ending when the patient’s volume or flow demand is met
q.e: PAV provides pressure during assisted breaths and ends inspiration when the patient’s volume or flow demand has been met. (Chang 4th ed., p. 106)

q.q: In volume-assured pressure support (VAPS), which is similar to pressure augmentation on the Bear 1000, the therapist must preset the ____.
o: desired minimum tidal volume and pressure support level
inspiratory release time and baseline CPAP pressure
percent minute volume and patient ideal body weight
oscillation amplitude, bias flow, and mean airway pressure
q.e: VAPS combines PSV with volume-assisted cycles to assure a stable tidal volume in irregular breathing patterns, requiring the clinician to preset the minimum tidal volume and pressure support level. (Chang 4th ed., p. 106)

q.q: During VAPS in a patient with airflow obstruction, why can failure to reach the preset tidal volume during the pressure-limited portion of a breath cause air trapping?
o: Constant-flow delivery continues until the target volume is reached, leaving less time for expiration
Baseline PEEP rises automatically to deliver the missing volume during expiration
The backup rate increases immediately, shortening the next expiratory interval
Pressure-limited delivery stops early, leaving the exhalation valve closed until the next breath
q.e: When delivered volume in VAPS is less than preset tidal volume, the ventilator transitions from pressure-limited to constant-flow volume-limited delivery, prolonging inspiratory time and risking air trapping in obstructed patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 107)

q.q: In the Siemens 300 ventilator, PRVC (called AutoFlow on the Dräger Evita XL) is active only during ____, whereas in other ventilators it is also active in SIMV.
q.e: On the Siemens 300, Chang identifies CMV as the mode in which PRVC is available. Other ventilators also offer this type of dual control during SIMV. (Chang 4th ed., p. 107)

q.q: In Chang’s Chapter 4 example, when PRVC lowers inspiratory flow as resistance rises, it ____ to deliver the target tidal volume.
q.e: In this example, a longer inspiratory time compensates for the lower flow so the target volume can be delivered. (Chang 4th ed., p. 108)

q.q: In Automode on the Siemens 300A (combining PRVC and volume support), what apnea durations trigger time-triggered PRVC breaths in adult, pediatric, and neonatal modes, respectively?
q.e: Automode delivers time-triggered PRVC breaths after prolonged apnea of 12 seconds in adults, 8 seconds in pediatrics, and 5 seconds in neonates, and switches to volume support after two consecutive patient-triggered breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 108)

q.q: A patient receiving adaptive pressure control (APC) develops hypoxia and pain, strongly increasing spontaneous inspiratory effort. Why can this increase the patient's work of breathing?
o: APC reduces inflation pressure when inspiratory effort increases
APC increases baseline PEEP and causes severe alveolar air trapping
APC switches to time-cycled apnea backup and blocks patient flow
APC locks the exhalation valve closed during inspiratory demand
q.e: APC cannot distinguish improved lung compliance from increased patient effort, so rising inspiratory effort lowers the ventilator's variable inflation pressure and increases work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 108)

q.q: In volume control plus (VC+) on the Puritan Bennett 840, spontaneous breathing or coughing during mandatory inspiration is accommodated by an ____ that vents excess pressure.
q.e: After a single decelerating-flow test breath measures compliance to adjust target pressure for (Set VT − Delivered VT), VC+ uses an active exhalation valve to vent excess pressure and maintain synchrony. (Chang 4th ed., p. 109)

q.q: In volume support (VS), a mode commonly used when weaning from anesthesia, the clinician presets the ____ but not the inspiratory time or mandatory frequency.
q.e: In VS, the clinician sets the target tidal volume. The patient determines breath timing, and the ventilator reduces pressure support as spontaneous tidal volume increases during recovery from anesthesia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 109)

q.q: In pressure-controlled ventilation (PCV) for severe ARDS with high peak pressures, inverted I:E ratios as high as ____ have been reported with successful outcomes.
q.e: An inverse I:E ratio means that inspiration lasts longer than expiration. In severe ARDS, Chang reports successful use of pressure-controlled ventilation with ratios as high as 4:1. (Chang 4th ed., p. 110)

q.q: In airway pressure release ventilation (APRV), using a high-flow CPAP circuit modified with a release valve, how long does the patient spend at the low pressure level?
q.e: APRV allows unrestricted spontaneous breathing on a high-flow CPAP circuit with a time-triggered release valve, spending most of the cycle at Phigh and less than 1.5 seconds at Plow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 111)

q.q: Unlike APRV, in biphasic positive airway pressure (Biphasic PAP) the patient spends more time at the ____.
q.e: Like APRV, Biphasic PAP uses time-triggered, time-cycled transitions between two baseline pressures with unrestricted spontaneous breathing, except the patient spends more time at the low pressure level. (Chang 4th ed., p. 112)

q.q: Whereas conventional mechanical ventilation uses an I:E ratio of about 1:1.5 to 1:3, what inverse I:E ratio range is used in ARDS to raise mean airway pressure?
q.e: Inverse ratio ventilation extends inspiratory time to an I:E ratio between 2:1 and 4:1, achieving oxygenation with lower PIP and PEEP but higher mean airway pressure and auto-PEEP than conventional ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 113)

q.q: Another potential hazard of inverse ratio ventilation is a higher rate of ____ induced by increased alveolar pressure, which may induce or worsen pulmonary edema.
q.e: Elevated alveolar pressure during IRV can increase transvascular fluid flow or flooding, potentially causing or worsening pulmonary edema; agitated IRV patients may also require sedation and neuromuscular blockade. (Chang 4th ed., p. 114)

q.q: In studies of patients with ARDS switched from conventional positive pressure ventilation with PEEP to PC-IRV, which two parameters were observed to decrease?
o: Peak airway pressure and PEEP requirement
Mean airway pressure and central venous pressure
Mean airway pressure and intrinsic PEEP
q.e: The studies summarized by Chang reported lower peak airway pressure and a lower requirement for applied PEEP. Mean airway pressure, central venous pressure, and intrinsic PEEP increased. (Chang 4th ed., p. 114)

q.q: Which option identifies all phases of airflow during which automatic tube compensation offsets artificial-airway resistance, according to Chang?
o: During the zero-flow end-inspiratory and end-expiratory holds
From the onset of expiratory flow to the end of exhalation
q.e: ATC (called tubing compensation on the PB840) can be applied in all modes and delivers compensating pressure during both inspiration and expiration based on tube resistance and patient flow demand. (Chang 4th ed., p. 115)

q.q: In neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA), bipolar electrodes on a disposable EAdi catheter positioned in the ____ at the level of the diaphragm detect electrical activity.
q.e: In NAVA (used in adults, children, and neonates, including spinal cord injury), bipolar electrodes on an esophageal catheter at the level of the diaphragm detect phrenic-nerve-driven diaphragm activity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 115)

q.q: Which set lists the six primary ventilator settings in high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV)?
o: Amplitude, frequency, mPaw, % inspiration, bias flow, and FIO2
VT, rate, PEEP, peak flow, TI, and FIO2
Target volume, elastance gain, flow-cycle threshold, CPAP, I:E ratio, and FIO2
Pressure support, EPAP, IPAP, backup rate, trigger sensitivity, and PEEP
q.e: HFOV (approved by the FDA for neonates in 1991, children in 1995, and adults in 2001) has no tidal volume setting; its primary controls are amplitude (delta P), frequency, mean airway pressure, percent inspiration, bias flow, and FIO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 115)

q.q: During high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV), the piston pump oscillates at frequencies from 3 Hz to 15 Hz, which equals how many breaths per minute?
q.e: HFOV delivers a constant bias flow while its piston pump oscillates at 3 to 15 Hz (180 to 900 breaths/min), and adults are sedated to prevent deep spontaneous breaths that trigger alarms. (Chang 4th ed., p. 116)

q.q: Besides decreasing oscillation frequency, which set consists entirely of adjustments that can each increase ventilation during HFOV?
o: Increase amplitude, lengthen inspiration, or increase bias flow with a cuff leak
Decrease amplitude, lengthen inspiration, or decrease bias flow with a cuff leak
Increase amplitude, shorten inspiration, or decrease bias flow with a cuff leak
Decrease amplitude, shorten inspiration, or increase bias flow with a cuff leak
q.e: In HFOV, ventilation is increased by decreasing oscillation frequency or by increasing oscillation amplitude, inspiratory time, or bias flow (with an intentional cuff leak). (Chang 4th ed., p. 116)

q.q: During high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV), oxygenation to the patient can be increased by raising the FIO2 or increasing the ____.
q.e: In HFOV, patient oxygenation is improved by increasing either the mean airway pressure or the FIO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 116)

q.q: Besides relieving upper airway obstruction and facilitating bag-mask ventilation, an oropharyngeal airway may be used as a ____ in intubated patients.
q.e: An oropharyngeal airway relieves upper airway obstruction when head tilt-chin lift or jaw thrust maneuvers fail, facilitates bag-mask ventilation, and can serve as a bite block in intubated patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 126)

q.q: An awake patient in respiratory distress needs upper airway assistance. Why should an oropharyngeal airway be used only in sedated or unconscious patients?
o: It may trigger the gag reflex, vomiting, and aspiration
It may compress the cricoid cartilage and slow heart rate
It may seal the esophagus and cause stomach distention
It may fracture the cribriform plate during insertion
q.e: An oropharyngeal airway should only be used in sedated or unconscious patients because inserting it in a conscious patient may trigger the gag reflex, vomiting, and pulmonary aspiration of stomach contents. (Chang 4th ed., p. 126)

q.q: How does the Cath-Guide Guedel oropharyngeal airway differ structurally from the common Guedel airway?
o: It has three internal channels rather than one large internal channel
It has one large internal channel rather than three narrow channels
It has a removable wire stylet extending past a fenestrated distal tip
It has an inflatable pharyngeal cuff positioned above the curved tip
q.e: The common Guedel oropharyngeal airway has one large internal channel, whereas the Cath-Guide Guedel airway has three internal channels. (Chang 4th ed., p. 127)

q.q: What are the infant and medium-adult sizes for a Berman oropharyngeal airway?
q.e: Berman airway sizes range from 43 mm (infant) to 110 mm (extra-large adult) with 90 mm for a medium adult, whereas Guedel sizes range from 55 mm to 120 mm with 100 mm for a medium adult. (Chang 4th ed., p. 127)

q.q: When sizing an oropharyngeal airway from the mouth center to the jaw angle or from the mouth corner to the earlobe, choosing an airway that is too large may push the ____ against the larynx.
q.e: Oropharyngeal airway size is estimated from the center of the mouth or central incisors to the angle of the jaw or from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe; an airway that is too large may push the epiglottis against the larynx, whereas one too small fails to move the tongue from the soft palate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 127)

q.q: After opening a supine patient's mouth with the scissors technique, an oropharyngeal airway inserted upside down initially faces the ____ before being turned 180° into position.
q.e: With the patient supine and the mouth opened via the scissors technique, an upside-down oropharyngeal airway is inserted facing the hard palate and rotated 180° until the flange rests on the lips or teeth and the distal tip rests at the base of the tongue; if gagging occurs, it is removed immediately. (Chang 4th ed., p. 128)

q.q: A conscious trauma patient with an intact gag reflex and an unstable mandibular fracture requires an upper airway adjunct. Which device is indicated?
q.e: A nasopharyngeal airway can be used in patients with an intact gag reflex, unstable fractures of the mandible, lockjaw, or oral trauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 129)

q.q: Using Chang’s height-based guidance, which nasopharyngeal airway size is recommended for a short female patient?
q.e: Final nasopharyngeal airway sizing should rely on height and clinical condition rather than anecdotal nares or little-finger methods; the recommended sizes are 6 (pin 1 cm from flange) for a short female, 6 for an average female, 7 for an average male, and 8 for a tall male. (Chang 4th ed., p. 129)

q.q: Chang gives ____ as the maximum ideal distance between the distal end of a nasopharyngeal airway and the epiglottis.
q.e: An ideally sized nasopharyngeal airway positions the distal end within 1 cm of the epiglottis; an overly short tube fails to separate the soft palate from the posterior pharynx, and an overly long tube enters the larynx or vallecula. (Chang 4th ed., p. 129)

q.q: With the patient sitting or in semi-Fowler position, advance the lubricated nasopharyngeal airway ____.
q.e: After inspecting the nares and placing the patient in a sitting or semi-Fowler position, a water-soluble lubricated nasopharyngeal airway is gently rotated parallel to the nasal floor rather than upward toward the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. (Chang 4th ed., p. 129)

q.q: Common complications of a nasopharyngeal airway include outward displacement, mucosal damage, and bleeding, while two reported cases involved ____.
q.e: Outward movement is more common than inward migration with a nasopharyngeal airway; soft tissue damage of the nasal mucosa and bleeding are common complications, and two cases of basilar skull fracture have been reported. (Chang 4th ed., p. 130)

q.q: An esophageal obturator airway has an open proximal end, ventilation holes near its midsection, an inflatable distal cuff, and a ____.
q.e: Inserted into the esophagus, an EOA has a proximal opening, small mid-section holes, a large distal cuff that prevents gastric air entry and regurgitation, and a blind (closed) distal end without an opening. (Chang 4th ed., p. 130)

q.q: With what volume of air is the cuff of an esophageal obturator airway initially inflated to check for cuff integrity and leaks prior to insertion?
q.e: Before insertion, the EOA cuff is checked for leaks with 20 to 30 mL of air and then deflated; verifying esophageal placement prior to re-inflation prevents asphyxia and tracheal damage from misplaced tracheal inflation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 131)

q.q: A patient ventilated temporarily with an esophageal obturator airway requires transition to an endotracheal tube for positive pressure ventilation. How should intubation proceed?
o: Intubate with the EOA in place and secure the ET tube before removal
Thread a flexible bougie through the EOA distal tip into the trachea
Leave the EOA in place and attach the ventilator circuit to its mask
Deflate and pull the EOA first so the laryngeal inlet is unobstructed
q.e: Because the EOA is temporary and not designed for positive pressure ventilation, endotracheal intubation is performed with the EOA in place, bilateral breath sounds are verified, and the ET tube is secured before removing the EOA with suction ready. (Chang 4th ed., p. 131)

q.q: Which option gives both of Chang’s exact pediatric cutoffs for avoiding an esophageal obturator airway and correctly states whether one or both cutoffs must be met?
o: Age under 16 years or height under 5 ft
Age under 12 years or height under 4 ft
Age under 16 years and height under 5 ft
Age under 12 years and height under 4 ft
q.e: Either cutoff is sufficient. Chang advises against EOA use in children under 16 years of age or under 5 ft tall. (Chang 4th ed., p. 132)

q.q: Unlike an esophageal obturator airway, an esophageal gastric tube airway has a patent distal end that permits a gastric tube to relieve ____.
q.e: The EGTA has an open distal end allowing passage of a gastric tube to aspirate stomach air and contents and relieve gastric distention, while ventilation is delivered through the ventilation port of its two-port mask. (Chang 4th ed., p. 132)

q.q: Which combination of features characterizes the esophageal gastric tube airway (EGTA) rather than the esophageal obturator airway (EOA)?
o: No ventilation holes along the tube and two ports on the mask
Ventilation holes along the tube and a blind distal tube tip
Tracheal placement with two cuffs and a single mask connector
Ventilation holes along the tube and a single port on the mask
q.e: The EGTA has no ventilation holes along the tube, a patent distal end, and two mask ports (ventilation and gastric tube), whereas the EOA has ventilation holes along the tube, a blind distal end, and one mask port. (Chang 4th ed., p. 133)

q.q: The original reusable LMA-Classic, whose cushioned mask seals over the laryngeal opening, is latex-free and made primarily of ____.
q.e: Invented by Archie Brain and reusable up to 40 times, the original LMA-Classic is latex-free, constructed primarily of medical-grade silicone rubber, and seals over the laryngeal opening without entering the larynx or trachea. (Chang 4th ed., p. 133)

q.q: During resuscitation, in which patient and clinical situation is a laryngeal mask airway specifically indicated?
o: Profoundly unconscious patient with absent reflexes when intubation fails
Semiconscious trauma patient with intact gag reflexes and oral laceration
Awake asthmatic patient with bronchospasm needing high inflation pressure
Alert neonate with mild grunting responding adequately to blow-by oxygen
q.e: The LMA is indicated for resuscitation in profoundly unconscious patients with absent glossopharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes when tracheal intubation fails or is precluded by lack of expertise or equipment, including neonatal 'cannot intubate' or 'cannot ventilate' situations. (Chang 4th ed., p. 134)

q.q: An unconscious patient with a known hiatal hernia who has not fasted needs emergency ventilation. Why is a laryngeal mask airway contraindicated?
o: It does not protect the airway from regurgitation and aspiration
It blocks pharyngeal drainage and causes mucosal ulceration
It enters the upper esophagus and worsens hiatal herniation
It stimulates laryngeal receptors when stomach pH is acidic
q.e: Because the LMA does not protect the airway from regurgitation and aspiration, it should not be used in unfasted patients or those with hiatal hernia, nor in patients who are not profoundly unconscious or have severe oropharyngeal trauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 134)

q.q: Citing a study that reported only 27% success, Chang generally advises against using a laryngeal mask airway as a conduit for ____.
q.e: One study reported 27% success with emergency resuscitation drugs given through an LMA. Chang describes this route as an emergency option when venous access or an endotracheal tube is not readily available. (Chang 4th ed., p. 135)

q.q: While size 4 fits most adult females and size 5 fits most adult males, a ____ provides a better pharyngeal seal than an overinflated smaller laryngeal mask airway.
o: larger LMA with less air in its cuff
larger mask inflated to maximum cuff volume
smaller mask with less air in its cuff
smaller mask inflated to maximum cuff volume
q.e: Size 4 is recommended for most adult females and size 5 for most adult males; a larger LMA with less air in the cuff provides a better seal, and although standard cuff pressure is 60 cm H2O, adjusting to the minimal effective volume lowers pharyngeal pressure and sore throat. (Chang 4th ed., p. 135)

q.q: Compared with an endotracheal tube, what effects does Chang report for an LMA on work of breathing and the hemodynamic response during surgery?
o: Lower work of breathing and a smaller hemodynamic response
Higher work of breathing and a larger hemodynamic response
Lower work of breathing and a larger hemodynamic response
Higher work of breathing and a smaller hemodynamic response
q.e: Compared with an endotracheal tube, the LMA provides lower work of breathing, less hemodynamic response during surgery, less airway reaction, shorter hospital stay, and complete survey of the larynx and trachea before thoracotomy. (Chang 4th ed., p. 135)

q.q: Which laryngeal mask airway (LMA) size and maximum cuff volume are recommended for a child weighing 15 kg?
q.e: LMA size 2 is used for infants and children between 10 and 20 kg, with a maximum cuff volume of 10 mL. (Chang 4th ed., p. 136)

q.q: Which laryngeal mask airway size and maximum cuff volume are recommended for an 80-kg adult?
q.e: A size 5 LMA with a 40 mL maximum cuff volume is recommended for adults weighing 70 to 100 kg, compared with size 4 (30 mL) for 50 to 70 kg and size 6 (50 mL) for adults over 100 kg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 136)

q.q: Once the patient no longer needs the LMA for ventilation or oxygenation, which pair consists entirely of states Chang identifies as suitable for removal?
q.e: An LMA is inserted blindly without a laryngoscope along the hard palate and may be removed safely while the patient is either anesthetized or awake once upper airway support is no longer required. (Chang 4th ed., p. 136)

q.q: After advancing a laryngeal mask airway until definite resistance is felt at the base of the hypopharynx, cuff inflation should occur ____ so the mask seats optimally.
q.e: During standard LMA insertion, once the mask reaches definite resistance at the base of the hypopharynx and the index finger is withdrawn, inflating the cuff without holding the tube allows the mask to seat itself optimally. (Chang 4th ed., p. 137)

q.q: Up to what peak inspiratory pressure can most standard laryngeal mask airways maintain a seal during positive pressure ventilation, and up to what pressure can an LMA-ProSeal?
q.e: Most LMAs provide a seal during positive pressure ventilation up to 20 cm H2O (up to 30 cm H2O with the LMA-ProSeal); if higher pressures are anticipated from low compliance or high resistance, an endotracheal tube should replace the LMA. (Chang 4th ed., p. 138)

q.q: During extended anesthesia with a reusable laryngeal mask airway, diffusion of ____ through the silicone cuff can raise cuff volume and pressure above 60 cm H2O.
q.e: Nitrous oxide can diffuse into the silicone cuff, increasing its volume and pressure. Chang recommends checking cuff pressure periodically and maintaining it at 60 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 138)

q.q: What is the only recommended sterilization method and upper temperature limit for a reusable laryngeal mask airway?
q.e: Steam autoclaving is the only recommended sterilization method for reusable LMAs; steam autoclaving usually operates at 250°F (121°C) and up to 275°F (135°C) for reusable LMAs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 138)

q.q: What are the material and inflation volume of the proximal pharyngeal cuff and distal cuff on an esophageal-tracheal combitube (ETC)?
o: 100 mL proximal latex cuff and 15 mL distal PVC cuff
15 mL proximal PVC cuff and 100 mL distal latex cuff
40 mL proximal silicone cuff and 10 mL distal PVC cuff
60 mL proximal latex cuff and 30 mL distal rubber cuff
q.e: The esophageal-tracheal combitube has a 15-mm proximal connector and two cuffs: a 100 mL proximal latex pharyngeal cuff and a 15 mL PVC cuff near the distal end. (Chang 4th ed., p. 139)

q.q: During blind intubation without visual aid, an esophageal-tracheal combitube is properly positioned once the ____ lie opposite the front teeth, after which both cuffs are inflated.
q.e: Blind intubation places an airway without visual aid or direct vision; the ETC reaches proper insertion depth when the black rings lie opposite the front teeth, and both cuffs are inflated immediately. (Chang 4th ed., p. 139)

q.q: After placement of an esophageal-tracheal combitube, ventilation is poor through both lumen 1 and lumen 2. How should a suspected cuff leak be addressed first?
o: Inflate the proximal cuff with more air and retry lumen 1
Advance the tube 5 cm deeper and add air to the distal cuff
Deflate the proximal cuff completely and ventilate lumen 2
Insert a suction catheter down lumen 1 to relieve pressure
q.e: Poor ventilation with both lumens 1 and 2 of an ETC suggests a cuff leak, which may be corrected by adding more air to the proximal cuff and retrying lumen 1 before preoxygenating and repeating insertion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 140)

q.q: Air leak complications of the esophageal-tracheal combitube—including subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and pneumoperitoneum—appear to be caused by ____.
q.e: Esophageal laceration was the suspected cause of the reported subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and pneumoperitoneum after ETC insertion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 140)

q.q: Why is a left-sided double-lumen endobronchial tube used more commonly than a right-sided tube for independent lung ventilation?
o: The right upper lobe bronchus arises only about 2 cm from the carina
The left main bronchus takes a straighter course from the trachea than the right
The left upper lobe orifice sits directly adjacent to the tracheal wall
The right mainstem bronchus is too narrow to accept a bronchial cuff
q.e: Used for lung isolation, thoracic surgery, and bronchopleural or bronchocutaneous fistulas, a left-sided DLT is preferred because the adult right upper lobe bronchus is only about 2 cm from the carina and easily occluded by a right-sided tube. (Chang 4th ed., p. 141)

q.q: How does Chang describe the relationship between DLT size and complications?
o: Most complications are associated with using small tubes
Complications occur at similar rates across tube sizes
Most complications are associated with using large tubes
Complications are associated with tube length alone
q.e: It is essential to use the largest DLT appropriate for the patient since most complications associated with DLTs result from using small tubes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 142)

q.q: When the bronchi are not visible on a PA chest radiograph, the diameter of the left bronchus for selecting a double-lumen endobronchial tube may be estimated as ____ of the tracheal diameter.
q.e: Choosing the largest appropriate DLT minimizes complications; on a PA chest radiograph (where the air bronchogram is enlarged by 10%), left bronchus diameter may be estimated as 68% of the tracheal diameter when bronchi are not visible. (Chang 4th ed., p. 142)

q.q: Which adult left-sided double-lumen endobronchial tube size should be selected when measured tracheal width is 16.1 to 18 mm?
q.e: Adult DLTs range from 35 to 41 Fr (with 28 and 32 Fr for small children); guidelines assign 35 Fr for tracheal width <15 mm, 37 Fr for 15.1–16 mm, 39 Fr for 16.1–18 mm, and 41 Fr for >18 mm. (Chang 4th ed., p. 142)

q.q: To minimize airway trauma during insertion of a double-lumen endobronchial tube, a guiding stylet must be removed as soon as the tube passes the ____.
q.e: Remove the guiding stylet as soon as the DLT tip passes the vocal cords to minimize airway trauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 142)

q.q: If a left-sided double-lumen endobronchial tube inadvertently enters the right bronchus, left bronchial entry is facilitated by rotating the tube and turning the head 90° so the chin rests on the ____.
q.e: If the left-sided DLT enters the right bronchus, turn the head 90° so the chin rests on the right shoulder and rotate the tube so its bronchial tip points laterally to the left. (Chang 4th ed., p. 143)

q.q: Which factor is associated with airway rupture, the most severe injury caused by double-lumen endobronchial tubes?
o: Moving the tube with both cuffs inflated or using a small PVC tube
Deflating both cuffs prior to repositioning the endobronchial lumen
Using the largest appropriate PVC tube with deflated cuffs on motion
Inflating the bronchial cuff slowly while avoiding nitrous oxide gas
q.e: Airway rupture is the most severe DLT injury and occurs more often with large or medium red rubber DLTs and small PVC DLTs; Chang also lists direct trauma (such as moving the tube with both cuffs inflated or carinal hook damage), cuff overinflation (including nitrous oxide distention), and preexisting airway pathology. (Chang 4th ed., p. 143)

q.q: When nitrous oxide is used with a double-lumen endobronchial tube, Chang specifies ____ as the upper limit that bronchial cuff pressure must stay below.
q.e: Safe DLT management includes choosing the largest appropriate PVC DLT, inflating the bronchial cuff with a 3-mL syringe, keeping bronchial cuff pressure <30 cm H2O when nitrous oxide is used, and deflating the bronchial cuff when lung isolation is not needed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 144)

sections.title: Ch 6 · Airway Management in Mechanical Ventilation

q.q: Two common artificial airways used in conjunction with mechanical ventilators are the ____ tubes.
q.e: In mechanical ventilation, the endotracheal (ET) tube and the tracheostomy tube are the two common artificial airways linking the ventilator and patient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 151)

q.q: According to the estimate cited by Chang, approximately how many patients undergo endotracheal intubation annually?
q.e: It is estimated that 15 million patients undergo endotracheal intubation each year. (Chang 4th ed., p. 152)

q.q: The surgical procedure that creates an airway opening by cutting into the trachea is called ____.
q.e: Tracheotomy is the surgical procedure that creates an opening at the trachea, whereas a tracheostomy tube is the artificial airway inserted through that opening. (Chang 4th ed., p. 152)

q.q: An adult tracheostomy tube often includes a disposable ____ that may be replaced as required to maintain airway patency.
q.e: Adult tracheostomy tubes may feature a disposable inner cannula that is replaced as needed to keep the tube patent. (Chang 4th ed., p. 152)

q.q: Compared with an endotracheal tube of the same internal diameter, the shorter tracheostomy tube reduces ____.
q.e: Because a tracheostomy tube is much shorter and enters the trachea directly, it has a lower mechanical deadspace volume than an endotracheal tube. (Chang 4th ed., p. 153)

q.q: When full recovery is expected, which duration does Chang explicitly give as an example of brief artificial-airway use favoring an endotracheal tube?
q.e: An endotracheal tube is generally chosen when full recovery is expected and an artificial airway is needed for a brief period such as 10 days or less. (Chang 4th ed., p. 153)

q.q: A patient arrives in the emergency department with facial burns, smoke inhalation, and vocal cord edema. Intubating this patient addresses which primary indication for an artificial airway?
q.e: Epiglottitis, facial burns with smoke inhalation, and vocal cord edema are examples of intubating for relief of airway obstruction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 153)

q.q: An ICU patient experiencing seizures has a spiral stainless-steel wire-reinforced endotracheal tube in place and must undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). What step must be taken before the MRI?
o: Replace it with a regular endotracheal tube
Secure the tube tightly with a neck harness
Deflate the cuff and leave the pilot port open
Insert a plastic stylet to stabilize the wire
q.e: Wire-reinforced endotracheal tubes contain stainless steel metal and must be replaced with a regular ET tube before any MRI procedure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 154)

q.q: Passing a larger endotracheal tube via the oral route reduces airflow resistance and lowers the ____ airway pressures.
q.e: Chang states that a larger ET tube, which lowers airflow resistance, lowers the peak, plateau, and mean airway pressures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 154)

q.q: Which of the following clinical conditions favors the oral route of intubation over the nasal route?
o: Severe trismus with limited jaw opening.
Short neck with limited oral access.
q.e: The oral route is preferred in CPR, apnea, nasal or midfacial trauma, nasopharyngeal obstruction, basilar skull fracture, epiglottitis, and anticipated fiberoptic bronchoscopy. (Chang 4th ed., p. 154)

q.q: Use of an endotracheal tube with an evacuation port for continuous subglottic secretion aspiration delays the early onset of ____.
q.e: Continuous aspiration of subglottic secretions via an evacuation lumen delays early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia and helps prevent nosocomial pneumonia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 155)

q.q: In which of the following conditions is the nasal route of intubation preferred over the oral route?
q.e: Nasal intubation provides lower airway access when oral entry is restricted, such as in trismus (lockjaw), oral trauma or deformities, mandible fracture, and short neck. (Chang 4th ed., p. 155)

q.q: Of the complications that can occur with an ET tube in place, Chang specifically associates ____ with use of the nasal route.
q.e: Nasal intubation is harder to perform, requires a smaller tube, and carries the risk of developing sinusitis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 155)

q.q: For long-term mechanical ventilation, what minimum duration of prior endotracheal intubation does Chang cite when describing replacement with a tracheostomy tube?
q.e: In patients requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation, a tracheostomy tube replaces an endotracheal tube that has been in place for 21 days or longer. (Chang 4th ed., p. 155)

q.q: On a talking tracheostomy tube with an inflated cuff, the external air or oxygen line is set from ____ so gas passes through the vocal cords when the thumb port is occluded.
q.e: Talking tracheostomy tubes use an external gas source set at 4 to 6 L/min; occluding the thumb port directs gas across the vocal cords for whispered speech. (Chang 4th ed., p. 155)

q.q: When a Bivona Fome-Cuf is used without the auto-control airway connector, how should the pilot port be managed to let the foam cuff self-inflate?
o: The pilot port is left open to room air so the foam self-inflates.
Withdraw air through the pilot port and then cap it.
Cap the pilot port before the foam expands.
Connect the pilot port to continuous low-pressure suction.
q.e: A silicone foam cuff does not use syringe inflation; leaving the red wing pilot port open to room air (or attached to an auto-control airway connector) lets the foam self-inflate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 156)

q.q: A ____ can be left in place between treatments to maintain a tracheal stoma and permit direct suctioning. In an emergency, it can be exchanged for a traditional tracheostomy tube.
q.e: A tracheostomy button maintains the stoma temporarily or permanently, allows direct tracheal suctioning, and permits emergency tracheostomy tube reinsertion without repeat surgery. (Chang 4th ed., p. 156)

q.q: The ____ is a preintubation assessment method that evaluates the degree of difficulty in oral intubation from Class 1 to Class 4.
q.e: The Mallampati classification evaluates anticipated intubation difficulty based on pharyngeal structures visible when a seated patient opens the mouth wide and protrudes the tongue. (Chang 4th ed., p. 156)

q.q: During a preintubation airway exam with the patient seated, mouth wide open, and tongue protruded, only the soft palate is visible. Which Mallampati class and action are indicated?
q.e: Visibility of the soft palate only defines Mallampati Class 4 (the most difficult airway class), for which anesthesia consultation should be sought. (Chang 4th ed., p. 157)

q.q: Which of the following items are classified as optional—rather than minimum—supplies for endotracheal intubation?
o: Stylet, topical anesthetic, and Magill forceps
q.e: Minimum intubation supplies are the handle, blade, ET tube, 10-mL syringe, water-soluble lubricant, tape, and stethoscope; stylet, topical anesthetic, and Magill forceps are optional. (Chang 4th ed., p. 157)

q.q: A ____ is an instrument used to displace the tongue and soft tissues and visualize the larynx and vocal cords during intubation.
q.e: The laryngoscope consists of a battery-containing handle and an illuminated blade used to displace the tongue and soft tissues so the vocal cords can be seen. (Chang 4th ed., p. 157)

q.q: A straight laryngoscope blade directly lifts the tongue and epiglottis, whereas a curved blade placed in the vallecula directly lifts ____.
q.e: The curved blade directly lifts the tongue and indirectly elevates the epiglottis. The straight blade passes beneath the epiglottis and lifts it directly. (Chang 4th ed., p. 158)

q.q: During standard direct laryngoscopy, how does Chang assign the operator’s hands?
o: Left hand holds the handle; right hand advances the tube.
The dominant hand holds the handle regardless of side.
The hand holding the handle changes when the blade passes the tongue.
Right hand holds the handle; left hand advances the tube.
q.e: All standard laryngoscope blades are designed for right-hand intubation, so the laryngoscope handle must be held in the left hand. (Chang 4th ed., p. 158)

q.q: Straight and curved laryngoscope blades range from ____ for small premature infants up to size 4 for large adults.
q.e: Laryngoscope blades range from size 00 for small premature neonates to size 4 for large adults, with size 3 intended for most adults. (Chang 4th ed., p. 158)

q.q: The tip of a curved Macintosh laryngoscope blade rests in the ____, the anatomical area between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis.
q.e: The vallecula lies between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis and serves as the anatomical landmark for positioning a curved Macintosh blade. (Chang 4th ed., p. 158)

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes proper technique with a straight (Miller) blade from that with a curved (Macintosh) blade?
o: The epiglottis is not visible when a straight blade is used correctly.
The straight blade rests in the vallecula and lifts the tongue.
The curved blade directly lifts beneath the epiglottis to hide it.
Both blades conceal the epiglottis behind the blade flange in use.
q.e: A straight blade passes beneath and directly lifts the epiglottis, obscuring it from view. A curved blade rests in the vallecula and lifts the tongue, indirectly elevating the epiglottis, which may remain visible. (Chang 4th ed., p. 158)

q.q: For a larynx made rigid by scarring or trauma, Chang favors a blade that exposes the cords by ____.
o: lifting the epiglottis directly with its tip
elevating the epiglottis indirectly from the vallecula
depressing the epiglottis toward the glottis
q.e: Chang favors a straight blade for a larynx made rigid by scarring or trauma. Its tip passes beneath the epiglottis and lifts it directly to expose the vocal cords. A curved blade lifts the epiglottis indirectly from the vallecula. (Chang 4th ed., p. 159)

q.q: Which endotracheal tube internal diameters are generally recommended for oral intubation of an adult female and an adult male, respectively?
o: 7.0 or 7.5 mm for a female; 7.5 or 8.0 mm for a male
6.5 or 7.0 mm for a female; 8.5 or 9.0 mm for a male
6.0 or 6.5 mm for a female; 6.5 or 7.0 mm for a male
8.0 or 8.5 mm for a female; 8.5 or 9.0 mm for a male
q.e: For oral intubation, an adult female generally receives a 7.0 or 7.5 mm ID endotracheal tube and an adult male receives a 7.5 or 8.0 mm ID tube. (Chang 4th ed., p. 160)

q.q: When an endotracheal tube is selected for nasal intubation, how should its internal diameter compare with the size chosen for the oral route?
q.e: Endotracheal tubes used for nasal intubation should be 0.5 mm to 1.0 mm smaller than the size selected for oral intubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 160)

q.q: A lengthwise ____ line along the body of an endotracheal tube is impenetrable to X-rays and appears as a light area on a chest radiograph.
q.e: A radiopaque strip runs lengthwise down the endotracheal tube and appears light on chest radiographs to confirm tube depth. (Chang 4th ed., p. 160)

q.q: The ____ on the proximal end of an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube is used with a 10-mL or larger syringe to regulate and indicate air volume in the cuff.
q.e: The pilot balloon is connected to the distal cuff and allows a 10-mL or larger syringe to adjust and monitor cuff air volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 160)

q.q: Before intubation, a ____ lubricant should be applied to the distal end of the endotracheal tube.
q.e: A water-soluble lubricant facilitates endotracheal tube insertion, whereas petroleum or oil-based lubricants cause adverse reactions in the airways and lung parenchyma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 161)

q.q: Which guideline applies when using a flexible wire stylet for endotracheal intubation?
o: It is never used in nasal intubation and must not protrude past the ET tube tip.
It is required for blind nasal intubation to stiffen the distal ET tube curve.
Its distal end should extend 1 cm past the ET tube tip to part the vocal cords.
Its proximal end is kept straight so the wire can advance deeper if needed.
q.e: A stylet is optional for oral intubation and is never used in nasal intubation; its tip must remain inside the ET tube (with the proximal end bent) to prevent tracheal trauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 161)

q.q: During direct-vision nasal intubation, once the tube enters the pharynx, ____ are used with the laryngoscope blade to guide the endotracheal tube into the trachea.
q.e: Magill forceps are specialized angled forceps used alongside direct laryngoscopy to grasp and direct a nasally inserted ET tube through the vocal cords. (Chang 4th ed., p. 161)

q.q: What is the estimated ET tube size for a neonate weighing 1,500 grams?
q.e: A 3.0 mm ID tube is estimated for neonates weighing 1000 to 2000 grams. (Chang 4th ed., p. 162)

q.q: Compared with direct laryngoscopy, what is an advantage of intubating with an optical stylet?
o: Less hemodynamic variability, less trauma, and fewer failed difficult airways
Shorter routine intubation time with similar hemodynamic variability
Shorter intubation time with a similar rate of difficult-airway failure
Less need for preoxygenation because the stylet maintains oxygenation during insertion
q.e: Compared with direct laryngoscopy, the optical stylet provides equivalent intubation time with less hemodynamic variability, less trauma and sore throat, and fewer failed difficult airway intubations. (Chang 4th ed., p. 162)

q.q: Using the endotracheal tube size formula for children aged 2 to 12 years, which tube internal diameter is estimated for an 8-year-old child?
q.e: For children 2 to 12 years old, estimated endotracheal tube size is 4.5 + (age / 4) mm ID; for an 8-year-old, 4.5 + (8 / 4) = 6.5 mm ID. (Chang 4th ed., p. 162)

q.q: What is the maximum recommended duration for a single intubation attempt before stopping to prevent hypoxia and arrhythmias?
q.e: If an intubation attempt is unsuccessful after 30 seconds, the tube and blade must be removed immediately because attempts exceeding 30 seconds may cause hypoxia and arrhythmias. (Chang 4th ed., p. 162)

q.q: After an unsuccessful intubation attempt, which SpO₂ does Chang give as an example of satisfactory recovery during bag-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen?
q.e: Chang describes ventilating with 100% oxygen for at least 30 seconds or until SpO2 returns to a satisfactory level, such as greater than 95%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 163)

q.q: In alert, cooperative, spontaneously breathing patients, ____ nasal intubation may be performed by slowly advancing the tube during inspiratory efforts while listening for airflow.
q.e: Blind nasal intubation is performed in alert, spontaneously breathing patients by advancing the tube through a nostril on inspiration while listening for air movement through the tube. (Chang 4th ed., p. 163)

q.q: Which endotracheal tube distance markings guide initial depth for nasal intubation in adult females and adult males, respectively?
o: 26 cm for females and 28 cm for males
20 cm for females and 22 cm for males
28 cm for females and 30 cm for males
22 cm for females and 24 cm for males
q.e: Proper initial depth for a nasal endotracheal tube in adults is guided by the 26-cm mark for females and the 28-cm mark for males. (Chang 4th ed., p. 163)

q.q: The head-tilt ____ position for endotracheal intubation is achieved by tilting the forehead back slightly and moving the mandible anteriorly.
q.e: Chang describes the sniffing position as a slight backward tilt of the forehead with anterior movement of the mandible. (Chang 4th ed., p. 164)

q.q: For adults undergoing oral intubation, the centimeter marking on the endotracheal tube should initially be placed at the lips or incisors at ____.
q.e: During adult oral intubation, the endotracheal tube is initially positioned at 21 to 23 cm (commonly 22 cm) at the lips or incisors before chest radiograph confirmation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 164)

q.q: Which combination of findings supports successful endotracheal intubation?
o: Rising SpO2, bilateral breath sounds, and detection of CO2
Falling SpO2, gurgling over the epigastrium, and no CO2
Rising SpO2, absent left-sided breath sounds, and no CO2
Patient phonation, epigastric distention, and stable SpO2
q.e: Rising SpO2, bilateral breath sounds, airflow, condensation on the ET tube, and detection of CO2 are signs of successful ET intubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 165)

q.q: Immediately after endotracheal intubation and cuff inflation, ____ is not possible because the tube bypasses the vocal cords.
q.e: Because an inflated endotracheal tube bypasses the vocal cords and prevents airflow across them, loss of speech (phonation) is an expected sign of tracheal placement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 165)

q.q: In the step-by-step nasal intubation procedure, what is done immediately after spraying oxymetazoline and 4% topical lidocaine into the nares?
o: Insert a 32 French soft nasal trumpet prelubricated with 2% lidocaine jelly.
Advance a stylet-stiffened endotracheal tube rapidly during exhalation.
Insert a 14 French rigid suction catheter coated with petroleum ointment.
Flush both nasal passages with 10 mL of sterile isotonic saline solution.
q.e: Before inserting the nasal ET tube, the nares are sprayed with oxymetazoline and 4% lidocaine, followed by a 32 French soft nasal trumpet prelubricated with 2% lidocaine jelly. (Chang 4th ed., p. 166)

q.q: When attached to a properly placed endotracheal tube, a chemical CO2 detector changes color from ____ because expired air from the lungs contains about 5% CO2.
q.e: A change from purple to yellow indicates CO2 in exhaled gas and supports tracheal placement. Assess it together with bilateral breath sounds and the patient’s other clinical signs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 166)

q.q: During oral intubation with a straight blade, the vocal cords are visible, but the endotracheal tube cannot be advanced because it hits the light bulb on the right side of the blade. What should the practitioner do?
o: Rotate the blade slightly counterclockwise to move the light bulb aside.
Pivot the laryngoscope handle backward against the patient's upper teeth.
Advance the straight blade deeper into the esophagus and lift anteriorly.
Withdraw the endotracheal tube and switch to a larger diameter tube.
q.e: When the light bulb on the right side of a straight blade blocks the ET tube, rotating the blade slightly counterclockwise (top of handle to the left) moves the bulb out of the path. (Chang 4th ed., p. 167)
