q.q: With an adult's endotracheal tube tip properly placed 1.5 inches above the carina in neutral head position, how do head and neck flexion and extension move the tube?
o: Flexion can move the tip about 2 cm downward, and extension can move it about 2 cm upward.
About 2 cm downward with both flexion and extension.
About 2 cm upward with both flexion and extension.
About 2 cm upward with flexion and downward with extension.
q.e: Flexion can advance the tip toward the carina, and extension can withdraw it. Chang gives approximately 2 cm as the possible displacement in either direction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 167)

q.q: In the absence of obvious lung pathology such as atelectasis, uneven bilateral breath sounds after intubation may suggest ____.
q.e: Without obvious lung pathology, unilateral breath sounds suggest main-stem intubation, and uneven bilateral sounds can suggest borderline main-stem placement. Check tip depth on the chest radiograph. (Chang 4th ed., p. 167)

q.q: After an emergency intubation, a compressed self-inflating esophageal detection bulb is connected to the tube and reinflates within 10 seconds, yet SpO2 continues to drop. Which condition can cause a false-negative bulb test when the tube is actually in the esophagus?
o: The stomach is already full of air
The tube tip rests above the carina
q.e: Normally the self-inflating bulb stays collapsed in the esophagus and reinflates within 10 seconds in the trachea, but a false negative can occur if the tube is in the esophagus and the stomach is full of air. (Chang 4th ed., p. 168)

q.q: In which clinical situation is rapid sequence intubation (RSI) contraindicated?
o: The patient sustains adequate ventilation and oxygenation spontaneously.
The patient exhibits hemodynamic instability and a breathing rate of 36/min.
The patient has severe brain injury with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7.
The patient develops severe hypoxemia with a PaO2/FIO2 ratio of 180 mm Hg.
q.e: Rapid sequence intubation should not be performed if a patient can maintain adequate ventilation and oxygenation while breathing spontaneously, or if the provider is unfamiliar with RSI. (Chang 4th ed., p. 168)

q.q: Common pre-RSI medications for adults include ____ (0.3 mg/kg) for sedation and induction and 100 mg (1 to 1.5 mg/kg) of succinylcholine for paralysis.
q.e: Chang gives etomidate as 20 mg IV or 0.3 mg/kg IV. If succinylcholine is needed for paralysis, the listed dose is 100 mg or 1–1.5 mg/kg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 169)

q.q: During rapid sequence intubation, ____ (Sellick's maneuver) may be applied to close off the esophagus and minimize aspiration.
q.e: Cricoid pressure (Sellick's maneuver) compresses the esophagus behind the cricoid cartilage to minimize aspiration, though excessive pressure can obstruct the airway itself. (Chang 4th ed., p. 169)

q.q: If ongoing paralysis and sedation are desired after adult rapid sequence intubation, which intravenous drug and dosage regimen is suggested?
o: Vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg, diazepam 5 to 10 mg, and fentanyl 200 mcg
Succinylcholine 0.1 mg/kg, etomidate 10 mg, and fentanyl 500 mcg
Vecuronium 0.3 mg/kg, diazepam 1 to 2 mg, and lidocaine 200 mcg
Vecuronium 1.5 mg/kg, diazepam 20 mg, and fentanyl 50 to 100 mcg
q.e: For post-RSI maintenance paralysis, anxiolysis, and analgesia in adults, vecuronium bromide 0.1 mg/kg, diazepam 5 to 10 mg, and fentanyl 200 mcg IV are recommended. (Chang 4th ed., p. 169)

q.q: For rapid sequence intubation, which threshold criteria define severe brain injury, severe hypoxemia, and abnormal respiratory frequency?
o: GCS ≤ 8, PaO2/FIO2 < 250 mm Hg, and rate < 10 or > 30/min
GCS ≤ 10, PaO2/FIO2 < 200 mm Hg, and rate < 8 or > 35/min
GCS ≤ 6, PaO2/FIO2 < 150 mm Hg, and rate < 6 or > 40/min
GCS ≤ 12, PaO2/FIO2 < 300 mm Hg, and rate < 12 or > 24/min
q.e: Indications for RSI include inability to maintain a patent airway, Glasgow Coma Scale of 8 or less, PaO2/FIO2 ratio below 250 mm Hg, spontaneous rate < 10/min or > 30/min, and hemodynamic instability. (Chang 4th ed., p. 169)

q.q: A patient with extensive crush injury, rhabdomyolysis, and hyperkalemia requires rapid sequence intubation. According to the RSI practice guideline, which agent is contraindicated?
q.e: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in hyperkalemia, penetrating eye injuries, spinal cord injury, CVA, burns, crush injury, rhabdomyolysis, and history of malignant hyperthermia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 170)

q.q: In the rapid sequence intubation practice guideline, ____ is administered prior to etomidate for patients with a closed head injury.
q.e: For patients with a closed head injury undergoing rapid sequence intubation, the practice guideline includes pretreatment with lidocaine 100 mg IV push. (Chang 4th ed., p. 170)

q.q: Estimated tracheal capillary perfusion pressure is in the range of ____, above which cuff pressure can cause mucosal ischemia and necrosis.
q.e: Tracheal capillary perfusion pressure is estimated at 25 to 35 mm Hg; lateral wall cuff pressures exceeding this range risk mucosal ischemia and tissue necrosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 171)

q.q: Normally, endotracheal cuff pressure is kept at 25 mm Hg or less. If a mechanically ventilated patient becomes hypotensive, how should cuff pressure be managed?
o: Keep cuff pressure even lower to compensate for reduced capillary blood flow.
Deflate the cuff for 15 minutes at hourly intervals until shock resolves.
Maintain cuff pressure at exactly 25 mm Hg regardless of blood pressure.
Increase cuff pressure to 35 mm Hg to prevent aspiration during hypotension.
q.e: ET cuff pressure should normally be 25 mm Hg or less, and in hypotensive patients it must be kept even lower because systemic hypotension reduces tracheal capillary perfusion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 172)

q.q: The ____ is obtained by inflating the endotracheal cuff slowly to the point where no air leak is heard at end-inspiration.
q.e: Minimal occlusion volume is achieved by slowly inflating the cuff just until no leak is audible over the trachea at end-inspiration, when tracheal diameter is maximal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 173)

q.q: The ____ is performed by inflating the cuff until the leak stops and then slowly removing a small amount of air until a slight leak is heard at end-inspiration.
q.e: In the minimal leak technique, the cuff is inflated until air leak ceases and then slightly deflated until a small audible leak returns at end-inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 173)

q.q: For an ET tube with an 8-mm internal diameter, what suction catheter size does Chang’s equation Fr = (mm × 3) / 2 yield?
q.e: Multiplying the 8-mm ET tube size by 3 and dividing by 2 yields a 12 Fr suction catheter, keeping the catheter outer diameter at no more than 50% of the ET tube internal diameter. (Chang 4th ed., p. 174)

q.q: Adult endotracheal suction vacuum should be kept between 70 and 150 mm Hg, with optimal secretion removal and minimal tracheal damage occurring at:
q.e: While adult suction vacuum may range from 70 to 150 mm Hg, suction effectiveness is optimal at 100 mm Hg, and higher pressures increase tracheal wall trauma without removing more secretions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 174)

q.q: Chang lists suction durations of ____ for adults and up to 5 seconds for pediatric patients, with preoxygenation to reduce the risk of hypoxemia.
q.e: Chang lists 10–15 seconds for adults and up to 5 seconds for pediatric patients. Preoxygenation with 100% oxygen and limiting suction duration may help avoid suction-induced hypoxemia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 174)

q.q: A ventilated patient has copious tracheal secretions. A ____ suction system allows repeated suctioning through the ET tube while the ventilator circuit stays connected.
q.e: A closed in-line suction system is useful for copious secretions because it permits suctioning without disconnecting the circuit, preserving PEEP and oxygenation settings. (Chang 4th ed., p. 174)

q.q: For safety reasons, the person using an ET tube changer must be ____.
o: proficient in intubation and experienced in airway management
certified in bronchoscopy and trained in airway surgery
credentialed in anesthesia and trained in conscious sedation
trained in tracheostomy care and experienced in cuff management
q.e: Tube changers can cause lateral wall laceration, bronchial perforation with pneumothorax, loss of airway, and hypoxemia, so the user must be proficient in intubation and experienced in airway management. (Chang 4th ed., p. 175)

q.q: Adult endotracheal tubes with a small dorsal lumen above the cuff drain subglottic secretions using a vacuum pressure of ____.
q.e: Subglottic secretion drainage through the dorsal lumen above the cuff uses a low vacuum pressure of 20 mm Hg or less, and a blocked lumen can be cleared with a small injection of air. (Chang 4th ed., p. 175)

q.q: Routine instillation of saline during endotracheal suctioning is not recommended because it may dislodge ____ into the lower airway.
q.e: Routine saline instillation before suctioning is not recommended because saline may dislodge bacteria into the lower airway. (Chang 4th ed., p. 175)

q.q: When replacing an endotracheal tube over a flexible tube changer, what is the most crucial step to prevent esophageal placement, main-stem intubation, or lung laceration?
o: Stabilizing the tube changer throughout the entire exchange procedure
Keeping the endotracheal cuff inflated while withdrawing the old tube
Flushing the existing endotracheal tube with 10 mL of normal saline
Advancing the tube changer 3 cm beyond the distal tip of the ET tube
q.e: Initially insert the changer until its tip lies near the distal end of the existing ET tube without protruding beyond it. Hold the changer at that depth while withdrawing the old tube and advancing the replacement over it. (Chang 4th ed., p. 175)

q.q: According to the open endotracheal suctioning procedure, what should the practitioner do immediately after advancing the catheter with the sterile hand until resistance is met?
o: Withdraw the catheter slightly before applying suction and rotating.
Flush 5 mL of sterile water down the suction catheter lumen directly.
Push the catheter 1 cm further to enter the right main-stem bronchus.
Apply continuous suction for 5 seconds at the carina before pulling.
q.e: Once resistance is met, the catheter is withdrawn slightly before activating suction to avoid suctioning the tracheal wall and minimize mucosal trauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 176)

q.q: Contraindications for using a speaking valve include laryngeal stenosis, ____, and severe tracheal stenosis.
q.e: Laryngeal stenosis, vocal cord paralysis, and severe tracheal stenosis obstruct exhaled airflow around the tube and are contraindications to speaking valve use. (Chang 4th ed., p. 177)

q.q: A patient has a cuffless fenestrated tracheostomy tube with a nonfenestrated inner cannula in place. Before attaching a one-way speaking valve, what should the therapist do to open the expiratory pathway through the fenestrations?
o: Open the fenestrations by removing a nonfenestrated inner cannula.
Exchange the inner cannula for a clean nonfenestrated one.
Leave the inner cannula locked in place for the valve trial.
Place a decannulation plug in the outer hub.
q.e: Before placing a speaking valve on a fenestrated tracheostomy tube, the fenestrations must be opened by removing any nonfenestrated inner cannula or inserting a fenestrated inner cannula. (Chang 4th ed., p. 178)

q.q: When a speaking valve is used in mechanically ventilated patients, the resulting air leak may require periodic adjustments of the ____.
o: tidal volume, PEEP, and alarm settings
inspiratory time, flow pattern, and cycling threshold
inspiratory pause, peak flow, and FIO2
backup rate, trigger sensitivity, and rise time
q.e: Because air leaks out the upper airway when a speaking valve is used during positive pressure ventilation, periodic adjustments to tidal volume, PEEP, and ventilator alarms may be needed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 178)

q.q: After breathing spontaneously for 3 minutes, an intubated adult has a spontaneous respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min and an average tidal volume of 0.40 L. What is the rapid shallow breathing index, and what does it predict?
q.e: The rapid shallow breathing index (f/VT) equals spontaneous rate divided by tidal volume in liters (20 / 0.40 = 50/min/L); a value below 100/min/L is highly predictive of successful extubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 179)

q.q: In the general criteria for extubation, acceptable arterial blood gases should be achieved at what FIO2 and spontaneous minute ventilation thresholds?
o: FIO2 less than 40% and minute ventilation less than 10 L/min
FIO2 less than 60% and minute ventilation greater than 12 L/min
FIO2 of 50% to 60% and minute ventilation of 12 to 15 L/min
FIO2 greater than 50% and minute ventilation greater than 15 L/min
q.e: General blood gas criteria for extubation include acceptable blood gases on an FIO2 below 40% with spontaneous minute ventilation under 10 L/min and a PaO2/FIO2 ratio above 250 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 180)

q.q: In Chang’s clinical predictor model for reintubation after unplanned extubation, the exact cutoff above which SIMV or AC frequency counts as unfavorable is ____.
q.e: Unfavorable predictor 1 is SIMV or AC frequency > 6/min, meaning the patient is dependent on the ventilator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 181)

q.q: Unplanned extubation accounts for 8% to 10% of ICU extubations, and for patients who self-extubate an endotracheal tube, about ____ of them do not need to be reintubated.
q.e: Approximately 50% of ICU patients who self-extubate their endotracheal tube maintain adequate ventilation and do not require reintubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 181)

q.q: In the seven-factor clinical predictor model used after unplanned extubation, what is the minimum number of unfavorable predictors that indicates the need for reintubation?
q.e: After unplanned extubation, the presence of four or more unfavorable predictors favors reintubation, whereas three or fewer predictors indicates no need for reintubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 181)

q.q: When grouping endotracheal airway complications by timing, which set of complications occurs immediately after extubation rather than late following extubation?
o: Aspiration, laryngospasm, hoarseness, and laryngeal or subglottic edema
Laryngeal stenosis, tracheal dilation, and chronic vocal cord paralysis
Esophageal intubation, dental trauma, and vagally induced bradycardia
Tube kinking, sinusitis, pressure sores, and obstruction by secretions
q.e: Aspiration, laryngospasm, hoarseness, and laryngeal/subglottic edema occur immediately after extubation, whereas laryngeal or tracheal stenosis and vocal cord paralysis are later complications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 182)

q.q: Once the ET tube is properly placed, its centimeter distance marking should be noted on the ____ as a quick reference point.
q.e: The distance marking should be noted on the ventilator flow sheet; it is a quick reference but not a substitute for routine assessment of tube position. (Chang 4th ed., p. 183)

q.q: The ____, or tenth cranial nerve, has laryngeal branches adjoining the upper trachea that can cause bradycardia when stimulated during intubation or suctioning.
q.e: The vagus (tenth cranial) nerve supplies superior and recurrent laryngeal branches near the upper trachea; mechanical stimulation by an ET tube or suction catheter can induce bradycardia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 183)

q.q: The ASA Task Force on the Management of the Difficult Airway recommends a limit of ____ intubation attempts to minimize patient injury.
q.e: Chang reports a three-attempt limit. The chapter associates prolonged or repeated attempts with hypoxia and possible arrhythmias. (Chang 4th ed., p. 183)

q.q: Because extubation during the semiconscious excitement stage can trigger laryngospasm, Chang recommends extubating when the patient is deeply anesthetized or, preferably, ____.
q.e: Stimulation of the vocal cords during the excitement stage can cause reflex spasm. Chang identifies fully awake as the preferred state for extubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 183)

q.q: Shortly after extubation, an adult develops mild inspiratory stridor from laryngeal and subglottic edema. Along with cool aerosol therapy, which nebulized regimen is helpful initially?
o: 0.25 to 0.5 mL of 2.25% racemic epinephrine in 5 mL of saline
1.0 to 2.0 mL of 2% oxymetazoline in 5 mL of normal saline
2.0 to 4.0 mL of 4% topical lidocaine in 5 mL of sterile water
0.5 to 1.0 mL of 20% acetylcysteine in 5 mL of normal saline
q.e: Minor postextubation stridor from laryngospasm or laryngeal/subglottic edema is initially treated with cool aerosol and 0.25 to 0.5 mL of 2.25% racemic epinephrine in 5 mL of saline. (Chang 4th ed., p. 184)

q.q: Giving ____ at 0.15 mg/kg may help prevent worsening postextubation laryngeal and subglottic edema.
q.e: Chang states that dexamethasone at 0.15 mg/kg may help prevent worsening postextubation laryngeal and subglottic edema. (Chang 4th ed., p. 184)

q.q: In addition to managing airflow obstruction in sleep apnea and acute respiratory failure, NPPV has been used successfully to reduce ____ in gross obesity.
q.e: NPPV provides assisted ventilation without an artificial airway and has been used successfully to reduce respiratory workload in gross obesity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 193)

q.q: Disadvantages of negative pressure ventilators such as iron lungs include upper airway obstruction and ____.
o: lack of access for patient care
q.e: Negative pressure ventilators are associated with upper airway obstruction and lack of access for patient care, whereas tracheal injury, VAP, and barotrauma are disadvantages of positive pressure ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 194)

q.q: During NPPV, the IPAP level is similar to ____ in traditional mechanical ventilation and directly affects tidal volume and minute ventilation.
q.e: IPAP is analogous to peak airway pressure in traditional mechanical ventilation, and raising IPAP produces a larger tidal volume and minute ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 194)

q.q: By what two mechanisms does expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) benefit patients receiving NPPV?
o: Increasing functional residual capacity and splinting open the upper airway
Elevating peak inspiratory airflow and enhancing mucociliary clearance
Lowering alveolar surface tension and stimulating central breathing drive
Augmenting spontaneous tidal volume and reducing anatomical dead space
q.e: EPAP improves oxygenation by increasing functional residual capacity (FRC) and relieves upper airway obstruction through its splinting action. (Chang 4th ed., p. 194)

q.q: When arterial blood gas measurements are unavailable during NPPV, ____ may be used as noninvasive alternatives to titrate IPAP and EPAP levels.
q.e: Although PaO2 and PaCO2 from arterial blood gases are standard titration endpoints, pulse oximetry (SpO2) and capnography (PETCO2) can be used alternatively to titrate IPAP and EPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 194)

q.q: In NPPV terminology, ____ refers to a positive pressure plateau used to augment spontaneous tidal volume.
q.e: Chang defines Pressure Support (PS) as a positive pressure plateau used to augment spontaneous tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 195)

q.q: In noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, EPAP functions as PEEP rather than CPAP when ____.
q.e: EPAP is used as PEEP when IPAP > EPAP (with mechanical breaths) and acts as CPAP when IPAP = EPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 195)

q.q: A patient with progressive hypoventilation and fatigue of the respiratory muscles experiences frequent apneas during sleep. Why is CPAP contraindicated for this patient?
o: CPAP depends on spontaneous effort and cannot deliver a breath during apnea.
CPAP is indicated exclusively for apneas resulting from neuromuscular disorders.
CPAP cannot deliver airway pressure high enough to splint open the upper airway.
CPAP requires an artificial airway before treating nocturnal oxygen desaturation.
q.e: CPAP depends on spontaneous effort. As the respiratory muscles fatigue and ventilation falls, CPAP cannot supply a mechanical breath during apnea. (Chang 4th ed., p. 196)

q.q: When loss of neurologic breathing effort is the sole cause of an apnea during sleep, Chang classifies the event as ____ sleep apnea.
q.e: Sleep apnea may be caused by airflow obstruction (obstructive), loss of neurologic breathing effort (central), or a combination of both (mixed). (Chang 4th ed., p. 196)

q.q: During nocturnal polysomnography, a patient sleeps for a total of 6 hours and has 150 apneas during sleep. What is the apnea index in events per hour of sleep?
q.e: The apnea index (respiratory disturbance index) equals the average number of apneas per hour of sleep during a test (150 / 6 = 25). (Chang 4th ed., p. 196)

q.q: Hypopnea is defined as a reduction in airflow lasting 10 or more seconds that falls at least ____ below an estimated baseline amplitude.
q.e: Hypopnea is a reduction in airflow for 10 or more seconds that is at least 50% below an estimated baseline amplitude, usually accompanied by oxygen desaturation or pulse alteration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 196)

q.q: The ____ describes the average number of pulse oximeter oxygen desaturations of 4% or more from baseline in each hour of sleep during a test.
q.e: The desaturation index quantifies the average number of oxygen desaturations of 4% or more from baseline per hour of sleep as measured by pulse oximetry. (Chang 4th ed., p. 196)

q.q: Compared with the general middle-aged adult population, the incidence of obstructive sleep apnea among morbidly obese patients is ____ higher.
q.e: OSA affects 2% to 4% of middle-aged adults (4% to 9% of men and 1% to 2% of women), while its incidence among morbidly obese patients is 12 to 30 times higher. (Chang 4th ed., p. 196)

q.q: Which group of findings represents the major clinical signs and symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea?
o: Snoring, daytime sleepiness, restless sleep, morning fatigue, and headaches
Stridor, orthopnea, productive cough, digital clubbing, and chest tightness
Bradypnea, central cyanosis, pedal edema, jugular distention, and hoarseness
Wheezing, nocturnal hemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats, and pleuritic pain
q.e: The major clinical signs and symptoms of OSA are snoring, daytime sleepiness, restless sleep, morning fatigue, and headaches. (Chang 4th ed., p. 196)

q.q: When bilevel PAP is used as an adjunct to provide mechanical ventilation, its two major indications are acute respiratory failure and ____.
o: central sleep apnea with normal PaCO2
q.e: The two major indications for bilevel PAP are acute respiratory failure and acute hypercapnic exacerbations of COPD. (Chang 4th ed., p. 197)

q.q: A patient being assessed for bilevel PAP has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.31, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, and PaO2 50 mm Hg. How does the textbook characterize these typical blood gas criteria for acute respiratory failure?
o: Partially compensated respiratory acidosis with moderate hypoxemia
Partially compensated metabolic alkalosis with refractory hypoxemia
Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis with mild arterial hypoxemia
Fully compensated metabolic acidosis with severe arterial hypoxemia
q.e: Typical blood gas criteria indicating acute respiratory failure show partially compensated respiratory acidosis with moderate hypoxemia (e.g., pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 50 mm Hg, PO2 < 55 mm Hg). (Chang 4th ed., p. 197)

q.q: In patients with hypoxemic respiratory failure, refractory hypoxemia is suggested when the PaO2/FIO2 (P/F) index falls below the threshold of ____.
q.e: A PaO2/FIO2 (P/F) index of less than 250 mm Hg suggests refractory hypoxemia, meaning PaO2 fails to respond to a high FIO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 197)

q.q: In patients with ____, CPAP or bilevel PAP ventilation has been found to reduce the need for subsequent mechanical ventilation.
q.e: CPAP or bilevel PAP reduces the need for subsequent invasive mechanical ventilation in patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. (Chang 4th ed., p. 197)

q.q: A patient in acute respiratory distress continues to deteriorate despite NPPV and now requires invasive support. Continuing NPPV may worsen the outcome by delaying ____.
o: endotracheal intubation and initiation of mechanical ventilation
humidification delivery and clearance of oral secretions
oxygenation titration and upper airway splinting therapy
arterial blood gas sampling and pulse oximetry verification
q.e: When NPPV fails to stabilize the patient and invasive support is indicated, delaying endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation may worsen the outcome. (Chang 4th ed., p. 197)

q.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV)?
q.e: Contraindications to NPPV include apnea, inability to handle secretions, facial trauma, and claustrophobia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 198)

q.q: A common error when fitting a nasal mask for NPPV is selecting a mask that is ____.
q.e: Chang identifies selecting a nasal mask that is too large as a common error, and recommends letting the patient try different sizes for maximal comfort and minimal leakage. (Chang 4th ed., p. 198)

q.q: A patient receiving bilevel PAP via a nasal mask develops a significant gas leak through the mouth that compromises ventilation. Which action should the respiratory therapist consider?
o: Changing to a nasal pillows unit
q.e: While a minor leak is acceptable with a nasal mask, an oronasal mask should be considered when the mouth leak is significant or when ventilation is the primary indication for NPPV. (Chang 4th ed., p. 198)

q.q: Which pair describes a gas-delivery problem and a nasal symptom commonly encountered with a nasal mask during NPPV?
o: Gas leaks and nasal dryness or drainage
q.e: Comfort and patient compliance are advantages of the nasal mask, and gas leaks and nasal dryness or drainage are disadvantages. (Chang 4th ed., p. 199)

q.q: If ventilator flow stops because of a power or gas supply failure, which components of an oronasal mask open a path to room air?
q.e: Because an oronasal mask covers both the nose and mouth, anti-asphyxia valves provide a safety opening if ventilator failure or power or gas disconnection occurs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 200)

q.q: For noninvasive ventilation, the two advantages of an oronasal mask are a good seal and ____.
q.e: A good seal and more effective ventilation are the advantages of the oronasal mask; claustrophobia is one of its disadvantages. (Chang 4th ed., p. 201)

q.q: Because nasal pillows operate within a lower pressure range of approximately ____, they are not as effective as larger nasal or oronasal masks during bilevel PAP.
q.e: Nasal pillows have a lower pressure range (e.g., 3 to 20 cm H2O), making them less effective than a larger nasal or oronasal mask in bilevel PAP mode. (Chang 4th ed., p. 201)

q.q: A patient using nasal pillows for CPAP complains of nasal congestion, nosebleeds, and a dry mouth. What should the respiratory therapist recommend to minimize these side effects?
o: A humidifier or saline nasal spray
A shorter ramp duration at bedtime
A tighter side strap and wing knob
A higher CPAP setting by 2 cm H2O
q.e: Common complaints with nasal pillows include nasal congestion, nosebleed, and dry or sore mouth, which can be minimized by using a humidifier or saline nasal spray. (Chang 4th ed., p. 201)

q.q: When significant gas leaks occur through the mouth during nasal pillows therapy, a ____ to close the mouth or an oronasal mask should be considered.
q.e: A chin strap helps keep the mouth closed when significant gas leakage occurs through the mouth during nasal pillows therapy. Chang also suggests considering an oronasal mask. (Chang 4th ed., p. 201)

q.q: An edentulous patient who breathes through the mouth and experiences claustrophobia requires NPPV. Which interface is ideal for this patient?
q.e: Because a full-face mask covers the nose bridge and mouth without direct contact, it is ideal for claustrophobic patients, mouth breathers, and patients without teeth or with facial abnormalities. (Chang 4th ed., p. 203)

q.q: After initiating CPAP at 4 cm H2O during polysomnography, the CPAP level is fine-tuned using ____.
o: pulse oximetry readings and number of apnea episodes
end-tidal CO2 tracings and peak inspiratory pressures
arterial pH measurements and spontaneous tidal volume
spirometric flow loops and baseline heart rate values
q.e: CPAP is started at 4 cm H2O and then fine-tuned using pulse oximetry readings and the number of apnea episodes observed during polysomnography. (Chang 4th ed., p. 203)

q.q: In which patient is unattended autotitration of CPAP contraindicated?
o: A patient with central sleep apnea and cardiac failure
A patient whose snoring triggers inspiratory flow sensors
A patient with uncomplicated obstructive sleep apnea
A patient who completed medical screening and education
q.e: Central sleep apnea and cardiac failure are each reasons Chang gives to avoid unattended CPAP autotitration. The chapter describes uncontrolled asthma, epilepsy, angina, fluid or electrolyte disturbances, nocturnal myoclonus, and other parasomnias as potential contraindications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 204)

q.q: In Chang’s example of the CPAP Ramp feature, what upper limit is given for the time taken to reach the prescribed pressure?
q.e: Chang gives up to 45 minutes as an example of a ramp interval for patients who have difficulty tolerating the immediate onset of prescribed pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 204)

q.q: During C-Flex™ CPAP therapy, expiratory pressure is reduced proportional to expiratory airflow, and the preset CPAP level is restored ____.
o: prior to the end of expiration and start of inspiration
after three consecutive breaths without snoring
halfway through the following spontaneous inspiration
immediately when peak expiratory airflow is detected
q.e: C-Flex™ provides breath-to-breath expiratory pressure relief proportional to expiratory flow across three levels (1, 2, 3) and restores the preset CPAP level prior to the end of expiration and start of inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 204)

q.q: When initiating bilevel PAP to support acute respiratory failure, common initial settings are an EPAP of 4 to 5 cm H2O and an IPAP of ____.
q.e: Although 8/4 cm H2O is a typical starting point, common initial bilevel PAP pressure settings range from 8 to 12 cm H2O for IPAP and 4 to 5 cm H2O for EPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 204)

q.q: To soften airflow and improve comfort during bilevel PAP, Bi-Flex™ provides pressure relief at ____.
o: the end of inhalation and the start of exhalation
the midpoint of inhalation and throughout exhalation
the end of exhalation and throughout inhalation
the start of inhalation and the end of exhalation
q.e: Bi-Flex™ provides pressure relief at the end of inhalation and the start of exhalation across three patient-adjustable levels (1, 2, 3), with level 3 providing the highest relief. (Chang 4th ed., p. 205)

q.q: In Chang’s spontaneous/timed bilevel titration protocol, IPAP maximum time is set 0.15 to 0.25 seconds longer than the patient’s actual inspiratory time. What percentage of the respiratory cycle is the upper limit?
q.e: In this spontaneous/timed protocol, IPAP maximum time should exceed actual inspiratory time by 0.15 to 0.25 seconds while remaining at or below 50% of the respiratory cycle. (Chang 4th ed., p. 205)

q.q: During titration of bilevel PAP in spontaneous/timed mode, a patient exhibits poor synchronization with the ventilator. What should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Check for leaks or alter IPAP maximum time
Switch from spontaneous/timed mode to CPAP
Increase IPAP in 4 cm H2O increments quickly
Add supplemental oxygen and lower the EPAP
q.e: The titration protocol instructs the clinician to check for leaks or alter IPAP maximum time to improve synchronization if poor synchronization occurs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 205)

q.q: During NPPV monitoring, which findings indicate that a patient's condition is deteriorating and may require endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation?
o: Accessory muscle use, vital sign changes, respiratory distress, or hypoxia
Normal heart rate, improved PaCO2, restful sleep, or slight claustrophobia
Mild nasal dryness, minor mask leakage, lower IPAP, or morning headaches
Stable SpO2, decreased respiratory rate, calm breathing, or mild snoring
q.e: Close monitoring is essential during NPPV; use of accessory muscles, changes in vital signs, and signs of respiratory distress or hypoxia indicate deterioration and possible need for intubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 206)

q.q: Mechanical ventilation alone does not ____ leading to the need for ventilator support, functioning instead as a support system until weaning is possible.
o: treat or reverse the underlying pathology
q.e: Mechanical ventilation is a supportive measure rather than a cure; it does not treat or reverse the underlying pathology, but supports the patient until the pathological condition reverses. (Chang 4th ed., p. 213)

q.q: Mechanical ventilation is indicated when a patient cannot maintain spontaneous ventilation to provide adequate ____.
o: cardiac output or systemic blood pressure
q.e: Mechanical ventilation is indicated whenever spontaneous ventilation is insufficient to maintain adequate oxygenation or carbon dioxide removal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 214)

q.q: In a patient with COPD, mechanical ventilatory support is indicated by an acute increase in PaCO2 above the patient's normal baseline accompanied by ____.
q.e: Because COPD patients may have a chronically elevated baseline PaCO2, acute ventilatory failure in COPD is identified by an acute rise above baseline PaCO2 accompanied by a decompensating respiratory acidosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 214)

q.q: Which arterial oxygenation range represents mild to moderate hypoxemia that does not by itself indicate acute ventilatory failure or the need for ventilatory support?
o: PaO2 50 to 60 mm Hg or SaO2 85% to 90%
PaO2 80 to 100 mm Hg or SaO2 95% to 99%
PaO2 below 40 mm Hg or SaO2 below 75%
PaO2 below 30 mm Hg or SaO2 below 60%
q.e: Mild to moderate hypoxemia (PaO2 of 50 to 60 mm Hg or SaO2 of 85% to 90%) does not by itself indicate acute ventilatory failure if the patient maintains adequate ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 214)

q.q: Which specific target falls under the mechanical ventilation goal of avoiding complications?
o: Reduce the metabolic oxygen cost of breathing
q.e: Protecting the lung and airway and preventing disuse respiratory muscle dystrophy are the specific targets under the goal of avoiding complications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 214)

q.q: A patient without chronic lung disease arrives in the emergency department with severe bradypnea. Which arterial blood gas result meets the criteria for acute ventilatory failure?
q.e: Acute ventilatory failure is defined as a PaCO2 greater than 50 mm Hg (higher for COPD patients) accompanied by an arterial pH less than 7.30. (Chang 4th ed., p. 215)

q.q: At the beginning of impending ventilatory failure, the PaCO2 value may be ____ because minute ventilation increases to compensate for gas exchange deficiencies.
q.e: Early in impending ventilatory failure, increased minute ventilation compensates for gas exchange deficits so PaCO2 may be normal or low before respiratory muscle fatigue causes hypercapnia and acidosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 215)

q.q: What SaO2 cutoff does Chang pair with PaO2 <40 mm Hg when defining severe hypoxemia?
q.e: PaO2 <40 mm Hg, SaO2 <75%, and reduced P/F ratios (≤300 mm Hg for ALI, ≤200 mm Hg for ARDS) are examples of severe hypoxemia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 215)

q.q: Because the work of breathing is carried out entirely by the respiratory system, assessment of impending ventilatory failure relies solely on ____.
o: measurements related to the lung functions
serial serum bicarbonate and renal panels
q.e: Impending ventilatory failure develops when metabolic needs impose excessive work of breathing, so its assessment relies on lung function measurements (VT, f, VE, VC, and MIP). (Chang 4th ed., p. 216)

q.q: Which combination of spontaneous tidal volume and respiratory frequency suggests impending ventilatory failure?
o: VT 10 to 12 mL/kg and f 10 to 12/min
VT 8 to 10 mL/kg and f 20 to 25/min
VT 6 to 8 mL/kg and f 12 to 16/min
q.e: A spontaneous VT below 3 to 5 mL/kg and a frequency above 30/min suggest impending ventilatory failure, particularly when breathing is labored or irregular. (Chang 4th ed., p. 216)

q.q: When an elevated spontaneous minute volume (>10 L/min) results from an increased frequency and a decreased tidal volume, it leads to a larger percentage of ____.
q.e: Rapid, shallow breathing that raises minute volume above 10 L/min increases the fraction of deadspace (wasted) ventilation, elevating oxygen cost of breathing and CO2 production. (Chang 4th ed., p. 217)

q.q: If a patient cannot perform a vital capacity maneuver, the patient must generate an MIP more negative than which cutoff within 20 seconds for Chang to assume a vital capacity of 15 mL/kg?
q.e: Chang states that patients who can generate an MIP stronger than −25 cm H2O (more negative, i.e., a greater inspiratory effort) within 20 seconds can be assumed to have a vital capacity of 15 mL/kg. The −20 cm H2O value is a different threshold, used for impending ventilatory failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 217)

q.q: During MIP measurement with a T-piece and a unidirectional valve that permits exhalation only, consecutive forced inspiratory maneuvers are performed from the ____ level.
q.e: Attaching a unidirectional exhalation-only valve to the T-piece lets the patient exhale between efforts so subsequent MIP maneuvers are performed from residual volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 217)

q.q: A tiring neuromuscular patient exhibits tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, and accessory muscle use. Which MIP (negative inspiratory force) is weaker (less negative) than the −20 cm H2O threshold and so indicates impending ventilatory failure?
q.e: An MIP (negative inspiratory force) less negative than −20 cm H2O (such as −12 cm H2O), along with clinical distress signs like tachycardia, hypertension, and diaphoresis, indicates impending ventilatory failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 217)

q.q: Which patient's oxygenation status meets the chapter's definition of severe hypoxemia?
o: PaO2 of 54 mm Hg while breathing 60% oxygen
PaO2 of 55 mm Hg while receiving room air (21%)
PaO2 of 46 mm Hg while breathing 28% oxygen
PaO2 of 64 mm Hg while breathing 50% oxygen
q.e: Severe hypoxemia is defined as a PaO2 less than 60 mm Hg on 50% or more oxygen, or a PaO2 less than 40 mm Hg at any FIO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 218)

q.q: While a patient breathes 100% oxygen, every 50-mm Hg difference in P(A-a)O2 approximates how much intrapulmonary shunt?
q.e: Normal P(A-a)O2 on 21% oxygen is less than 4 mm Hg per 10 years of age, and on 100% oxygen every 50-mm Hg difference in P(A-a)O2 approximates 2% shunt. (Chang 4th ed., p. 218)

q.q: According to the chapter's key-term definition of P(A-a)O2, a gradient exceeding the ____ threshold while on 100% oxygen indicates severe hypoxemia or intrapulmonary shunting.
q.e: P(A-a)O2 is the difference between PAO2 and PaO2; a gradient over 450 mm Hg on 100% oxygen indicates severe hypoxemia or intrapulmonary shunting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 218)

q.q: In the simplified alveolar air equation PAO2 = (PB − PH2O) × FIO2 − (PaCO2/R) at 37°C, what standard values are used for PH2O and R?
q.e: At 37°C, water vapor pressure (PH2O) is 47 mm Hg and the respiratory quotient (R) is estimated to be 0.8 (allowing PaCO2/0.8 to be written as PaCO2 × 1.25). (Chang 4th ed., p. 218)

q.q: A patient with acute onset of bilateral infiltrates and a PCWP of 14 mm Hg has a PaO2 of 120 mm Hg on an FIO2 of 0.50. How is this condition classified?
o: ALI, because the P/F ratio is 240 mm Hg (≤300 mm Hg)
ARDS, because the P/F ratio is 60 mm Hg (≤200 mm Hg)
Normal oxygenation, because PaO2 exceeds 100 mm Hg
ARDS, because the P/F ratio is 240 mm Hg (≤300 mm Hg)
q.e: ALI and ARDS share acute onset, bilateral infiltrates, and PCWP ≤18 mm Hg, and are separated by the P/F ratio: 120 / 0.50 = 240 mm Hg, which meets the ≤300 mm Hg threshold for ALI rather than ≤200 mm Hg for ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 218)

q.q: When evaluating acute bilateral infiltrates for ALI or ARDS, a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) of ≤18 mm Hg is used to rule out ____.
q.e: A normal PCWP of ≤18 mm Hg rules out pulmonary edema or bilateral infiltrates caused by cardiogenic pulmonary edema when diagnosing ALI or ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 218)

q.q: Positive pressure mechanical ventilation is absolutely contraindicated in ____ unless a functional chest tube is placed to relieve pleural pressure.
q.e: Untreated tension pneumothorax is an absolute contraindication to positive pressure ventilation; a functional chest tube must be in place before applying any positive airway pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 218)

q.q: Medical futility is a relative contraindication to mechanical ventilation; Schneiderman and colleagues suggested intervention may be futile if physicians concluded it was useless in the last ____.
q.e: Relative contraindications include a patient's informed request, medical futility, and reducing pain and suffering; Schneiderman et al. suggested futility when intervention was useless in the last 100 similar cases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 219)

q.q: Head injury and smoke inhalation are clinical examples of prophylactic ventilatory support primarily intended to ____.
q.e: Prolonged shock, head injury, and smoke inhalation are grouped under prophylactic ventilatory support to reduce the risk of pulmonary complications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 219)

q.q: Under what condition does synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation (SIMV) provide full ventilatory support?
o: No spontaneous breaths occur between mechanical breaths at a rate ≥12/min
Mandatory frequency is set at 6 to 8/min with pressure support of 8 cm H2O
Spontaneous tidal volumes are augmented with 5 cm H2O of baseline PEEP
The patient breathes spontaneously at 20/min between mandatory breaths
q.e: Full ventilatory support assumes essentially all work of breathing; SIMV provides full support if the patient does not breathe spontaneously between mechanical breaths and the mandatory rate is ≥12/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 220)

q.q: Partial ventilatory support modes such as BiPAP and PSV provide less than the total work of breathing and are inappropriate initially for patients with ____.
q.e: Partial ventilatory support provides less than the total amount of work of breathing and is commonly used for weaning, making it inappropriate as initial therapy for ventilatory failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 220)

q.q: When volume-controlled and pressure-controlled ventilation are combined in a dual control mode, the patient receives mandatory breaths that are ____.
q.e: A dual control mode regulates two control variables via independent feedback loops; combining VCV and PCV delivers mandatory breaths that are volume-targeted, pressure-limited, and time-cycled. (Chang 4th ed., p. 220)

q.q: Which set of factors contributes to the development of auto-PEEP during mechanical ventilation?
o: High ventilator frequency, inadequate inspiratory flow, and air trapping
Low tidal volume, a long expiratory time, and a decelerating flow
Low ventilator frequency, high inspiratory flow, and a short I time
High FIO2, low PEEP, and a constant flow pattern
q.e: High ventilator frequency, inadequate inspiratory flow, and air trapping contribute to the development of auto-PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 221)

q.q: The initial ventilator frequency is usually set between 10 and 12/min, whereas frequencies at or above what rate are associated with auto-PEEP and should be avoided?
q.e: Initial ventilator frequency is typically set at 10 to 12/min, while frequencies of 20/min or higher (along with inadequate inspiratory flow and air trapping) contribute to auto-PEEP and should be avoided. (Chang 4th ed., p. 221)

q.q: An adult female has a body surface area (BSA) of 1.6 m² and a set tidal volume of 0.56 L. Using the BSA formulas, what are her estimated minute volume and initial ventilator frequency?
q.e: Estimated minute volume is 3.5 × BSA for females (3.5 × 1.6 = 5.6 L/min, versus 4.0 × BSA for males), and dividing by the 0.56 L tidal volume gives an initial frequency of 10/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 221)

q.q: When elevated CO2 production or increased physiologic deadspace requires a higher minute volume, it is usually better to increase ____ because raising tidal volume increases airway pressures.
q.e: Ventilator frequency is the primary control to regulate PaCO2; raising frequency increases minute ventilation without producing the higher airway pressures caused by increasing tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 221)

q.q: After placing a patient on a ventilator, arterial blood gases should be obtained within ____ after stabilization to assess ventilation and oxygenation.
q.e: Arterial blood gases should be drawn within 15 to 30 minutes after the patient has stabilized on the ventilator so frequency and FIO2 can be adjusted appropriately. (Chang 4th ed., p. 221)

q.q: Low tidal volume ventilation (as low as 6 mL/kg PBW) is used in ARDS to minimize airway pressures and barotrauma, but it may cause which complication?
o: Reduced work of breathing and hyperoxemia
Decreased oxygen cost of breathing and alkalemia
q.e: Although low tidal volumes (permissive hypercapnia) reduce airway pressures and barotrauma in ARDS, they can cause acute hypercapnia, increased deadspace ventilation and work of breathing, dyspnea, severe acidosis, and atelectasis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 222)

q.q: Decreasing the initial tidal volume by ____ in patients with COPD reduces expiratory time requirements and helps prevent air trapping.
q.e: COPD patients have reduced expiratory flow from loss of alveolar elastic recoil; reducing tidal volume by 100 to 200 mL (or increasing inspiratory flow) allows more time for exhalation and helps prevent air trapping. (Chang 4th ed., p. 222)

q.q: Using the predicted body weight formula for males, PBW (lb) = 106 + [6 × (height in inches − 60)], what is the PBW in kilograms for an adult male who is 68 inches tall?
q.e: Initial tidal volume is usually set at 10 to 12 mL/kg PBW; for a 68-inch male, PBW = 106 + [6 × (68 − 60)] = 154 lb, and dividing by 2.2 yields 70 kg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 222)

q.q: Expansion of the ventilator circuits during inspiration creates ____, a small 'lost' volume of gas that never reaches the patient yet is recorded in the expired tidal volume.
q.e: Delivered tidal volume is lower than set tidal volume due to circuit leaks, cuff leaks, and circuit compressible volume—gas lost to tubing expansion during inspiration that still registers in expired volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 222)

q.q: What level of gas leakage is defined as significant and requires identifying and correcting the cause rather than compensating with a larger tidal volume?
q.e: Minor gas leaks can be compensated by increasing set tidal volume, but significant gas leakage (>5% of ventilator tidal volume) requires finding and correcting the leak. (Chang 4th ed., p. 223)

q.q: Pressure support ventilation (PSV) augments a patient's spontaneous breathing effort by reducing ____ caused by the artificial airway, ventilator circuit, and secretions.
q.e: Pressure support is applied in spontaneous-breathing modes (such as SIMV) to overcome airflow resistance imposed by the endotracheal tube, circuit, and airway secretions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 223)

q.q: Emphysema and pneumonectomy are examples of conditions that may require lower tidal volumes because of ____, respectively.
o: increased lung compliance and decreased lung volumes
increased airway pressure need and alveolar recruitment
decreased lung compliance and increased airway resistance
decreased chest wall compliance and pulmonary shunting
q.e: Emphysema increases lung compliance, and pneumonectomy reduces available lung volume. Chang lists both as reasons a lower tidal volume may be appropriate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 223)

q.q: During pressure support weaning, PS is reduced by 2 to 4 cm H2O increments as tolerated, and extubation can be considered once PS reaches ____ with no respiratory distress.
q.e: For a spontaneous breathing trial, PS is titrated to a spontaneous frequency of 20 to 25/min or a VT of 8 to 10 mL/kg PBW, then reduced by 2 to 4 cm H2O increments as tolerated. Extubation can be considered when PS reaches 5 to 8 cm H2O for 2 hours with no signs of respiratory distress. (Chang 4th ed., p. 224)

q.q: During Y-occlusion testing of the ventilator circuit, expired volume is 120 mL at 40 cm H2O. On the ventilator, PIP is 45 cm H2O and PEEP is 10 cm H2O. What is the circuit compressible volume?
q.e: The circuit compression factor is 120 mL / 40 cm H2O = 3 mL/cm H2O; multiplying by (PIP − PEEP), or 3 × (45 − 10) cm H2O, gives a circuit compressible volume of 105 mL. (Chang 4th ed., p. 224)

q.q: Although initial FIO2 may be set at 100% for severe hypoxemia, after stabilization of the patient the FIO2 is best kept ____ to avoid oxygen-induced lung injuries.
q.e: Patients with severe hypoxemia or cardiopulmonary instability (post-resuscitation, smoke inhalation, ARDS) may start on 100% oxygen, but after stabilization FIO2 is best kept below 50% to prevent oxygen toxicity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 224)

q.q: A patient with normal cardiopulmonary function is being intubated following a drug overdose. What initial FIO2 is suggested, and what PaO2 range should be maintained?
o: 40%, maintaining PaO2 of 80 to 100 mm Hg
21%, maintaining PaO2 of 60 to 75 mm Hg
100%, maintaining PaO2 of 110 to 140 mm Hg
60%, maintaining PaO2 of 50 to 60 mm Hg
q.e: For mild hypoxemia or normal cardiopulmonary function (such as drug overdose or uncomplicated postoperative recovery), initial FIO2 may be set at 40% or prior FIO2 and adjusted to maintain PaO2 at 80 to 100 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 225)

q.q: What initial PEEP setting is recommended before adjusting based on blood gases, FIO2 requirement, PEEP tolerance, and cardiovascular responses?
q.e: PEEP increases functional residual capacity to treat refractory hypoxemia; the initial PEEP level is set at 5 cm H2O and titrated according to oxygenation and cardiovascular tolerance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 225)

q.q: Air trapping during mechanical ventilation may be checked by occluding the ____ at the end of exhalation; auto-PEEP is present if end-expiratory pressure stays above baseline.
o: expiratory port of the ventilator circuit
unidirectional valve at residual lung volume
inspiratory limb at peak inspiratory flow
q.e: Occluding the expiratory port at end-exhalation reveals auto-PEEP when pressure fails to return to baseline (0 cm H2O or set PEEP), a finding also visible on the pressure-time waveform. (Chang 4th ed., p. 225)

q.q: Although the normal mechanical ventilation I:E ratio is 1:2 to 1:4, an inverse I:E ratio should not be used as the initial setting because reverse I:E ventilation has ____.
q.e: Inverse I:E ratios may be tried for refractory hypoxemia in low-compliance ARDS only after traditional strategies fail, because reverse I:E ratios carry inherent cardiovascular complications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 225)

q.q: A patient's minute volume is 10 L/min and the desired I:E ratio is 1:3. After calculating the minimum required flow rate, what flow setting adds the usual 10 L/min margin?
q.e: Minimum flow equals Minute Volume × Sum of I:E Ratio = 10 × (1 + 3) = 40 L/min, and flow is usually set 10 L/min higher (50 L/min) to accommodate changing minute volume demands. (Chang 4th ed., p. 226)

q.q: With tidal volume and frequency fixed, decreasing inspiratory flow lengthens inspiration and shortens expiration. When I:E is written as 1:x, the value of x ____.
q.e: x equals expiratory time divided by inspiratory time. Shorter expiration and longer inspiration therefore decrease x. (Chang 4th ed., p. 226)

q.q: With inspiratory flow and respiratory frequency fixed, decreasing tidal volume shortens inspiration and lengthens expiration. When I:E is written as 1:x, this produces ____ in x.
q.e: The breath cycle has the same duration. Less time is needed to deliver the smaller VT, leaving more time for expiration and increasing x. (Chang 4th ed., p. 226)

q.q: During constant-flow volume ventilation, tidal volume and inspiratory flow stay fixed, with no inspiratory pause. If frequency increases, what happens to inspiratory time, expiratory time, and x in I:E = 1:x?
o: Inspiratory time stays the same, expiratory time shortens, and x decreases.
Inspiratory time lengthens, expiratory time stays the same, and x decreases.
Inspiratory time stays the same, expiratory time lengthens, and x increases.
Inspiratory time shortens, expiratory time lengthens, and x increases.
q.e: At fixed VT and flow, delivery takes the same time. Increasing frequency shortens the total cycle, leaving less time for expiration and decreasing x. (Chang 4th ed., p. 226)

q.q: At a ventilator frequency of 12/min, what inspiratory time (I time) is needed to achieve a desired I:E ratio of 1:3?
q.e: At f = 12/min, each breath lasts 60 / 12 = 5.0 sec; multiplying 5.0 sec by [1 / (1 + 3)] gives an inspiratory time of 1.25 sec (and when I time % is preset instead, the ventilator auto-adjusts flow rate). (Chang 4th ed., p. 227)

q.q: Among the constant, accelerating, sine, and decelerating inspiratory flow waveforms, which pattern may reduce peak inspiratory pressure, mean airway pressure, physiologic deadspace, and PaCO2 in patients with COPD?
q.e: Of the constant, accelerating, sine, and decelerating waveforms, decelerating flow may reduce PIP, mean airway pressures, physiologic deadspace, and PaCO2 in COPD patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 228)

q.q: What percent inspiratory time (I time %) corresponds to an inverse I:E ratio of 2:1?
q.e: At an I:E ratio of 2:1, inspiration occupies two of the three equal parts of the breath cycle. Inspiratory time is therefore 2 ÷ 3 × 100% = 66.7%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 228)

q.q: Before calculating airway resistance (Pressure/Flow), the ventilator should be switched to a ____ because it is the only waveform in which peak flow equals mean inspiratory flow.
q.e: Airway resistance calculations require mean inspiratory flow, and the constant (square wave) flow pattern is the only flow pattern in which peak flow equals mean inspiratory flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 229)

q.q: To detect system leaks or circuit disconnection, the low exhaled volume alarm should be set at about ____ than the expired mechanical tidal volume.
q.e: Basic battery-backed ventilator alarms include the low exhaled volume alarm, which should be set about 100 mL below the expired mechanical tidal volume to detect leaks or disconnection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 229)

q.q: How far above and below the observed peak inspiratory pressure should the high and low inspiratory pressure alarms be set?
q.e: The low inspiratory pressure alarm is set 10 to 15 cm H2O below observed PIP to detect leaks or disconnection, and the high inspiratory pressure limit is set 10 to 15 cm H2O above observed PIP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 229)

q.q: Once the high inspiratory pressure limit alarm is triggered by airflow obstruction, inspiration is immediately ____ and the ventilator enters the expiratory cycle.
q.e: When secretions, coughing, tube kinking, bronchospasm, or reduced compliance push PIP to the high pressure limit, inspiration is immediately terminated and the ventilator cycles to expiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 230)

q.q: What initial settings are recommended for the apnea alarm time delay and the high frequency alarm?
o: 30- to 45-sec time delay; 20/min over observed rate
q.e: The apnea alarm is set with a 15- to 20-second time delay (shorter at higher rates), and the high frequency alarm is set at 10/min over the observed frequency. (Chang 4th ed., p. 230)

q.q: The high and low FIO2 alarms should be set ____ above and below the analyzed FIO2 (for example, at 50% and 40% when FIO2 is 45%).
q.e: High and low FIO2 alarms are set 5% to 10% over and below the analyzed FIO2, such as 50% and 40% for an analyzed FIO2 of 45%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 230)

q.q: Among the hazards and complications of mechanical ventilation, nosocomial pneumonia caused by cross-contamination is classified as related to ____.
q.e: Nosocomial pneumonia (from cross-contamination), inappropriate ventilator settings, and communication misadventures are grouped as complications related to medical professionals. (Chang 4th ed., p. 231)

q.q: In a Joint Commission review of 23 deaths and coma injuries associated with long-term mechanical ventilation, 65% were related to ____.
o: malfunction or misuse of ventilator alarms
oxygen toxicity from prolonged high FIO2
q.e: Sixty-five percent of the reviewed ventilator-related deaths and coma injuries involved alarms that were turned off, set improperly, untested, absent for certain disconnections, or answered late. (Chang 4th ed., p. 232)

q.q: What airway pressure thresholds define a high risk of inducing barotrauma for PIP, plateau pressure, mean airway pressure (mPaw), and PEEP, respectively?
q.e: Barotrauma risk is high when PIP >50 cm H2O, plateau pressure >35 cm H2O, mPaw >30 cm H2O, and PEEP >10 cm H2O, though uneven ventilation to low-resistance, high-compliance zones can cause injury at lower pressures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 232)

q.q: When positive pressure ventilation elevates CVP and reduces venous return slightly, a competent cardiovascular system compensates via cardiac baroreceptor-mediated ____.
o: increased heart rate and arterial vasoconstriction
pulmonary venodilation and decreased stroke volume
bronchial smooth muscle relaxation and diuresis
decreased heart rate and peripheral arterial dilation
q.e: Positive airway pressure raises pleural pressure and CVP, narrowing the gradient for venous return to the right atrium; cardiac baroreceptors compensate by increasing heart rate and causing arterial vasoconstriction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 233)

q.q: Which combination of compliance abnormalities transmits a given positive airway pressure most strongly into the pleural space, worsening the drop in venous return and cardiac output?
o: High lung compliance (COPD) and low chest wall compliance (chest burns)
Decreased lung compliance (ARDS) and high chest wall compliance (normal)
Low lung compliance (fibrosis) and normal chest wall compliance
Normal lung compliance and increased thoracic cage compliance
q.e: More compliant lungs (as in COPD) transmit airway pressure into the pleural space more readily than stiff lungs, while low chest wall compliance (tight chest bandages or extensive chest wall burns) has the opposite effect and further elevates pleural pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 233)

q.q: When inadequate oxygen delivery threatens the brain or myocardium, the primary goal of prophylactic ventilatory support is to ____.
q.e: Hypoxic brain and hypoxia of heart muscles are categorized under prophylactic ventilatory support aimed at reducing hypoxia of major body organs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 234)

q.q: When initial ventilator settings use a constant flow pattern, switching to other flow patterns is guided by achieving ____.
o: lower peak inspiratory pressure and better gas distribution
higher peak inspiratory pressure and shorter expiratory time
automatic compensation for circuit compressible gas volume
preset inspiratory time percentage and constant I:E ratios
q.e: Constant is the initial flow pattern; other flow patterns may be used for a lower peak inspiratory pressure (on the manometer) and better gas distribution (by breath sounds). (Chang 4th ed., p. 235)

q.q: Which of the following is one of the four primary reasons for monitoring a mechanically ventilated patient continuously?
o: Establishing baseline values as a reference point
Eliminating the need for routine bedside auscultation
Reversing the underlying pulmonary disease directly
Replacing arterial blood gas analysis in acute failure
q.e: Continuous monitoring establishes baseline measurements for the initial treatment plan and future reference, documents trends, guides changes to treatment plans, and provides high-limit and low-limit safety alarms. (Chang 4th ed., p. 242)

q.q: Whereas hypoxemia refers to a deficiency of oxygen in the blood, ____ is defined as a deficiency of oxygen in the tissues.
q.e: Hypoxemia is a deficiency of oxygen in the blood (low PaO2), whereas hypoxia is a deficiency of oxygen in the tissues. (Chang 4th ed., p. 243)

q.q: What is the normal resting heart rate range for an adult patient?
q.e: Normal adult heart rate is between 60 and 100/min; tachycardia in adults is higher than 100/min and bradycardia is lower than 60/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 243)

q.q: During endotracheal suctioning, arterial oxygen desaturation can occur in as little as how many seconds?
q.e: Because arterial desaturation can occur in as little as 5 sec during endotracheal suctioning, preoxygenation is often necessary to minimize desaturation and arrhythmias. (Chang 4th ed., p. 243)

q.q: During endotracheal suctioning of a mechanically ventilated adult, the heart rate drops below 60/min due to vagal stimulation. What action should the therapist take immediately?
o: Complete the pass and reduce suction vacuum
Instill normal saline and silence the alarm
Withdraw the endotracheal tube by two centimeters
q.e: When arrhythmia or bradycardia occurs during endotracheal suctioning, suctioning must be stopped immediately and 100% oxygen provided to the patient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 243)

q.q: For continuous blood pressure monitoring in the critically ill patient, the most common insertion site for an indwelling arterial catheter is the ____ artery.
q.e: Continuous arterial blood pressure monitoring is most commonly performed via the radial artery, although the brachial, femoral, popliteal, and dorsalis pedis arteries are alternative sites. (Chang 4th ed., p. 243)

q.q: Which condition is recognized as a cause of bradycardia rather than tachycardia?
o: Acute blood loss with compensatory sympathetic activation
q.e: Causes of bradycardia include drug reaction to morphine sulfate, hypothermia, heart block, abnormal SA node function, inadequate coronary blood flow, and vagal stimulation during suctioning, whereas epinephrine causes tachycardia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 244)

q.q: When hypotension occurs during mechanical ventilation, it is often associated with excessive ____, peak inspiratory pressure, and lung volume.
q.e: Hypotension is a complication of positive pressure ventilation or PEEP and is often associated with excessive intrathoracic pressure, peak inspiratory pressure, and lung volume reducing venous return. (Chang 4th ed., p. 244)

q.q: Polycythemia may lead to hypertension during mechanical ventilation because of ____.
q.e: Polycythemia (increased blood viscosity), fluid overload, stress, anxiety, pain, congestive heart failure, and cardiovascular disease are causes of hypertension, whereas decreased venous return and absolute or relative hypovolemia cause hypotension. (Chang 4th ed., p. 244)

q.q: What is the normal spontaneous respiratory frequency for an adult?
q.e: The normal spontaneous respiratory frequency for adults is 10 to 16 breaths per minute. (Chang 4th ed., p. 244)

q.q: Hyperthermia causes a lower oxygen saturation at any PaO2, whereas hypothermia lowers a person's ____.
q.e: Hypothermia lowers a person's basal metabolic rate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 245)

q.q: In normal individuals, the maximum respiratory response to hypoxia occurs when the PaO2 drops below what cutoff value?
q.e: In normal individuals, maximum respiratory response to hypoxia occurs below a PaO2 of 50 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 245)

q.q: When tachypnea and ____ are observed together in a ventilator patient, successful weaning from mechanical ventilation is not likely.
q.e: Rapid, shallow breathing (tachypnea combined with low tidal volume) is a reliable sign of ventilatory insufficiency and makes successful weaning unlikely. (Chang 4th ed., p. 245)

q.q: Continuous noninvasive acoustic respiratory monitoring measures breathing frequency using an adhesive sensor with an integrated acoustic transducer applied to the patient's ____.
q.e: Masimo Rainbow Acoustic Monitoring measures respiratory frequency continuously via an adhesive acoustic sensor applied to the patient's neck and is useful in postanesthesia settings and partial ventilatory support. (Chang 4th ed., p. 245)

q.q: Hyperthermia shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, causing a ____ at any PaO2 while promoting oxygen unloading to the tissues.
q.e: Hyperthermia shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, producing a lower oxygen saturation at any PaO2 because elevated temperature promotes oxygen unloading from hemoglobin to tissues. (Chang 4th ed., p. 245)

q.q: In nonextreme hypothermic conditions, blood gas temperature correction is unnecessary provided the uncorrected PaO2 remains above what cutoff value?
q.e: Whereas extreme hypothermia causes blood gases analyzed at body temperature to read higher than actual PaO2 and PaCO2, temperature correction in nonextreme hypothermia is unnecessary if the uncorrected PaO2 is above 60 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 245)

q.q: Excessive cooling of the phrenic nerve during coronary artery bypass surgery may cause temporary ____.
q.e: Excessive cooling of the phrenic nerve during coronary artery bypass (CAB) surgery can cause temporary paralysis of the hemidiaphragms that may take months to resolve. (Chang 4th ed., p. 246)

q.q: Which pair of conditions is associated with hypothermia rather than hyperthermia?
o: Coronary bypass surgery and head injury
Acute leukemia and elevated metabolic rate
Acute tissue necrosis and systemic infection
q.e: Hypothermia may be induced during coronary bypass surgery and in selected patients with head trauma. Chang associates infection, tissue necrosis, leukemia, and increased metabolic rate with hyperthermia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 246)

q.q: During chest inspection of a mechanically ventilated patient, the therapist notes asymmetrical chest movement with the trachea and mediastinum shifted toward the opposite unaffected side. Which condition best explains these findings?
q.e: In tension pneumothorax, the trachea and mediastinum shift to the opposite unaffected side, whereas in atelectasis they shift toward the affected side. (Chang 4th ed., p. 246)

q.q: When dysynchronous motion of the chest and abdomen is noted in a ventilated patient, the patient should be evaluated for ____ or underlying pathology.
q.e: Dysynchronous motion between the chest and abdomen during mechanical ventilation warrants evaluation for diaphragmatic fatigue or underlying pathology. (Chang 4th ed., p. 247)

q.q: With the examiner's hands placed on opposite sides of the thorax and thumbs touching, chest expansion is symmetrical when the hands ____ during a deep breath.
o: move apart in equal distance from midline
remain fixed together over the xiphoid tip
shift laterally toward the right hemithorax
lift sequentially from the base to the apex
q.e: Chest expansion is symmetrical when the patient takes a deep breath and the examiner's hands move apart an equal distance from the midline. (Chang 4th ed., p. 247)

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient develops pulmonary edema. On inspiration, the therapist hears brief, discontinuous popping sounds. Which breath sound is present?
q.e: Inspiratory crackles are associated with lung consolidation and pulmonary edema, coarse crackles with excessive secretions, wheezes with airway narrowing, and diminished or absent sounds with airway obstruction, atelectasis, main-stem intubation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax. (Chang 4th ed., p. 248)

q.q: Using a side-to-side technique of chest auscultation from left to right allows comparison of the ____ between the left and right lungs.
q.e: Assessing breath sounds with a left-to-right (side-to-side) stethoscope technique allows the therapist to compare the quantity of breath sounds between the left and right lungs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 248)

q.q: When auscultating over the trachea at the cuff site, a cuff leak is present if distinct air movement can be heard ____.
o: toward the end of a mechanical breath
at the end of passive exhalation
q.e: Placing the stethoscope diaphragm over the trachea at the cuff's location detects a leaking cuff when distinct air movement is heard toward the end of a mechanical breath. (Chang 4th ed., p. 249)

q.q: On a normal chest radiograph, air-filled structures such as the trachea and lung parenchyma appear ____ because air does not absorb X-rays.
q.e: Air-filled structures such as the trachea and lung parenchyma appear dark-shaded due to overexposure of the negative film because air does not absorb X-rays, whereas tissues and bones absorb X-rays and appear almost white. (Chang 4th ed., p. 251)

q.q: A lateral chest radiograph is used with a PA radiograph to verify lesion location because abnormalities in the LUL lingula segments and the ____ segment are indistinguishable on a PA view alone.
q.e: A lateral chest radiograph is used alongside the PA radiograph to verify the exact location of pulmonary abnormalities, such as distinguishing lesions in the LUL lingula segments (#5) from those in the LLL superior segment (#11). (Chang 4th ed., p. 251)

q.q: On a chest radiograph, a blunted costophrenic angle suggests ____ such as pleural effusion, hemothorax, or empyema.
o: accumulation of fluid in pleural space
jagged fracture of the thoracic rib cage
rotation of the patient during exposure
q.e: Whereas normal right and left costophrenic angles are sharply pointed, a blunted costophrenic angle suggests fluid accumulation in the pleural space (pleural effusion, hemothorax, or empyema). (Chang 4th ed., p. 252)

q.q: What percentage of the distance between the right and left costophrenic angles does Chang use as the cutoff for an enlarged cardiac shadow measured along the diaphragm?
q.e: Normally the cardiac shadow along the diaphragm line is less than 50% of the distance between the right and left costophrenic angles; exceeding 50% suggests a congestive heart. (Chang 4th ed., p. 252)

q.q: When K+ is included in the anion gap calculation (Na+ + K+ − Cl− − HCO3−), the normal range is ____.
q.e: The anion gap is 10 to 14 mEq/L when K+ is excluded and 15 to 20 mEq/L when K+ is included in the calculation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 253)

q.q: In addition to reducing cardiac output and renal perfusion, mechanical ventilation reduces urine output through an increase in antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and a reduction of ____.
q.e: Positive pressure ventilation decreases urine output and causes fluid retention both by decreasing renal perfusion and by increasing antidiuretic hormone (ADH) while reducing atrial natriuretic factor (ANF). (Chang 4th ed., p. 253)

q.q: Normal adult urine output is 50 to 60 mL/hour, whereas oliguria indicative of fluid deficiency is present when urine output falls below ____.
q.e: Normal urine output is 50 to 60 mL/hour, and a urine output below 20 mL/hour (or 400 mL in 24 hours or 160 mL in 8 hours) indicates fluid deficiency. (Chang 4th ed., p. 253)

q.q: A ventilated patient has a serum Na+ of 140 mEq/L, Cl− of 104 mEq/L, and HCO3− of 24 mEq/L. What is the calculated anion gap (excluding K+) and its interpretation?
o: 12 mEq/L, which is within the normal 10 to 14 mEq/L range
60 mEq/L, which exceeds the normal 15 to 20 mEq/L range
36 mEq/L, which exceeds the normal 10 to 14 mEq/L range
12 mEq/L, which falls below the normal 15 to 20 mEq/L range
q.e: Excluding K+, the anion gap equals Na+ − Cl− − HCO3− (140 − 104 − 24 = 12 mEq/L), which is within the normal range of 10 to 14 mEq/L (15 to 20 mEq/L when K+ is included). (Chang 4th ed., p. 253)

q.q: Whereas metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap is usually caused by a loss of base, metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap is usually due to ____.
q.e: Metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis) results from base loss, whereas an increased anion gap indicates increased fixed acids from renal failure, diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or salicylate/alcohol poisoning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 254)

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient with metabolic acidosis develops compensatory hyperventilation and a low PaCO2. What occurs if the therapist mistakenly reduces the ventilator frequency in response to the low PaCO2?
o: Persistent hyperventilation and higher work of breathing will ensue
Sudden hypoventilation and uncompensated metabolic alkalosis will result
Immediate closure of peripheral chemoreceptors and apnea will be induced
Excessive renal excretion of bicarbonate ions will rapidly accelerate
q.e: In metabolic acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation, the underlying acidosis must be treated and ventilator frequency must not be reduced, or persistent hyperventilation and worsening work of breathing will continue. (Chang 4th ed., p. 254)

q.q: Why should serum potassium (K+) levels be monitored closely in patients being weaned from mechanical ventilation?
o: Severe K+ depletion causes metabolic alkalosis and hypoventilation
Low K+ shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve and triggers severe tachypnea
Mild K+ elevation induces diaphragmatic paralysis and acute apnea
Severe K+ depletion causes metabolic acidosis and hyperventilation
q.e: Severe potassium depletion can lead to metabolic alkalosis and compensatory hypoventilation, prolonging the weaning process by requiring continued ventilatory support. (Chang 4th ed., p. 254)

q.q: Which serum electrolyte concentration is within the normal reference range?
q.e: Normal serum electrolyte ranges are Na+ 138 to 142 mEq/L, Cl− 101 to 105 mEq/L (103 mEq/L), K+ 3 to 5 mEq/L, and HCO3− 23 to 27 mEq/L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 254)

q.q: Which set of adult arterial blood gas values falls completely within normal ranges?
o: pH 7.40, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, PaO2 90 mm Hg
pH 7.49, PaCO2 29 mm Hg, PaO2 96 mm Hg
pH 7.30, PaCO2 50 mm Hg, PaO2 85 mm Hg
pH 7.38, PaCO2 42 mm Hg, PaO2 65 mm Hg
q.e: Normal adult arterial blood gas ranges are pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mm Hg, and PaO2 80 to 100 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 255)

q.q: In weaning assessment, what minute ventilation criterion defines excessive work of breathing associated with poor weaning outcomes?
q.e: Prolonged increases in the work of breathing can cause respiratory muscle fatigue, and a minute ventilation in excess of 10 L/min is often associated with poor weaning outcomes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 255)

q.q: A decrease in PaO2 accompanied by little or no increase in the P(A-a)O2 gradient is probably due to ____, which can be confirmed by an elevated PaCO2.
q.e: Whereas decreased PaO2 with an increased P(A-a)O2 indicates diffusion defect, V/Q mismatch, or shunt, a decreased PaO2 with little or no increase in P(A-a)O2 points to hypoventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 256)

q.q: When calculating PAO2 with the simplified alveolar air equation, under what FIO2 condition may the respiratory quotient R (0.8) be deleted from the equation?
q.e: In the simplified alveolar air equation, PH2O is generally 47 mm Hg at 37°C and the respiratory quotient R (estimated at 0.8) may be deleted when the FIO2 is greater than 60%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 256)

q.q: An adult patient with a PaO2 of 52 mm Hg is classified as having ____.
q.e: PaO2 values of 80 to 100 mm Hg are normal, 60 to 79 mm Hg is mild hypoxemia, 40 to 59 mm Hg is moderate hypoxemia, and below 40 mm Hg is severe hypoxemia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 256)

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient receiving an FIO2 of 0.30 has a PaO2 of 72 mm Hg and a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) of 14 mm Hg. Based on the PaO2/FIO2 ratio, which condition is indicated?
q.e: The PaO2/FIO2 ratio is 72 / 0.30 = 240 mm Hg; with PCWP below 18 mm Hg, a PaO2/FIO2 of 300 mm Hg or less indicates acute lung injury (ALI), whereas 200 mm Hg or less indicates ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 256)

q.q: When a patient breathes 100% oxygen, every 50 mm Hg difference in P(A-a)O2 approximates how much intrapulmonary shunt?
q.e: On 100% oxygen, each 50 mm Hg difference in P(A-a)O2 approximates 2% intrapulmonary shunt. (Chang 4th ed., p. 256)

q.q: Which oxygenation index finding indicates hypoxemia?
o: PaO2/PAO2 below 75% while on an FIO2 of 40%
Room-air P(A-a)O2 of 12 mm Hg in a 50-year-old
PaO2/PAO2 of 82% while on an FIO2 of 35%
PaO2 of 88 mm Hg while breathing room air
q.e: At an FIO2 of 30% or higher, a PaO2/PAO2 ratio below 75% indicates hypoxemia, whereas on room air the P(A-a)O2 should be less than 4 mm Hg for every 10 years of age. (Chang 4th ed., p. 256)

q.q: In ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, a high V/Q ratio is related to deadspace ventilation, whereas a low V/Q ratio is associated with ____.
q.e: Ventilation/perfusion mismatch involves an abnormal distribution of ventilation and blood flow in which high V/Q relates to deadspace ventilation and low V/Q is associated with intrapulmonary shunting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 257)

q.q: Because shunted blood does not contact ventilated alveoli, ____ in conjunction with oxygen is usually required to correct hypoxemia caused by intrapulmonary shunting.
q.e: Hypoxemia caused by intrapulmonary shunting responds poorly to high oxygen concentrations alone, so PEEP in conjunction with oxygen is usually required. (Chang 4th ed., p. 257)

q.q: Decreased alveolar surface area causing an irreversible diffusion defect is seen in ____ due to destruction of lung tissues.
q.e: Diffusion defects arise from a low oxygen pressure gradient, increased alveolar-capillary thickness (as in pneumonia or edema), or irreversible decreased alveolar surface area as seen in emphysema. (Chang 4th ed., p. 257)

q.q: Because values reflect an isolated measurement in time, arterial blood gas measurements are generally a ____ of respiratory failure rather than an early warning sign.
q.e: Arterial blood gases can be affected by air bubbles, excess heparin, or faulty handling, reflect only an isolated point in time, and serve generally as a late indicator of respiratory failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 257)

q.q: A pulse oximeter estimates arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) noninvasively by ____ through a pulsating vascular bed.
q.e: A pulse oximeter estimates SpO2 by emitting dual wavelengths of light through a pulsating vascular field while also measuring pulse rate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 258)

q.q: While assessing a critically ill patient, the therapist notes an SpO2 reading of 93% accompanied by an active low perfusion alarm and a pulse rate that differs markedly from the cardiac monitor. What should the therapist do?
o: Refrain from using or reporting the SpO2 reading
Record the SpO2 value and reduce the FIO2 setting
Document the SpO2 after silencing the active alarm
Average the oximeter pulse rate with the ECG rate
q.e: Pulse discrepancies indicate low perfusion or motion artifact, and an SpO2 reading must not be used or reported when a concurrent low perfusion alarm is present. (Chang 4th ed., p. 258)

q.q: How does the accuracy of pulse oximetry change as a patient's SaO2 falls below 95%?
o: SpO2 becomes less accurate and may overestimate oxygenation
SpO2 becomes more accurate and may underestimate oxygenation
SpO2 stays equally accurate across the whole SaO2 range
SpO2 becomes less accurate and tends to underestimate SaO2
q.e: SpO2 correlates well with SaO2 when SaO2 is 95% or greater; it becomes less accurate as SaO2 decreases, and overestimation of oxygenation status may result. (Chang 4th ed., p. 259)

q.q: To assure a PaO2 above 60 mm Hg in a ventilator-dependent patient during FIO2 weaning, the SpO2 should be kept above what minimum value?
