q.e: Maintaining SpO2 above 92% assures oxygenation in ventilator-dependent patients because an SpO2 above 92% correlates with a PaO2 above 60 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 259)

q.q: Comparing pulse oximetry (SpO2) with blood gas oxygen saturation helps verify ABG accuracy by ruling out ____.
q.e: Pulse oximetry is used to monitor oxygenation status, titrate FIO2, and verify ABG accuracy by comparing oxygen saturation readings to rule out a venous sample. (Chang 4th ed., p. 259)

q.q: Blue, green, or black nail polish can produce a falsely low SpO2 reading, which may be addressed by placing the pulse oximeter probe ____.
q.e: Sunlight, intravascular dyes, and blue, green, or black nail polish can cause falsely low SpO2 readings; if a patient is wearing nail polish, the oximeter probe may be placed sideways. (Chang 4th ed., p. 259)

q.q: Which factor does Chang identify as a possible cause of a pulse oximeter reading higher than the actual SaO2?
o: Ambient exposure to bright direct sunlight
q.e: Dyshemoglobins and low perfusion may cause SpO2 to overestimate SaO2. Chang groups sunlight, nail polish, fluorescent light, and intravenous dyes among potential causes of falsely low readings. (Chang 4th ed., p. 260)

q.q: Calculated from respiratory variations in the pulse oximeter plethysmographic waveform amplitude, the pleth variability index (PVI) has been used to predict ____ in mechanically ventilated patients during general anesthesia.
q.e: Integrated pulse CO-oximetry measures SpHb, SpOC, SpCO, SpMet, PI, and PVI; PVI calculates respiratory variations in plethysmographic waveform amplitude to predict fluid responsiveness during general anesthesia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 260)

q.q: On an integrated pulse CO-oximeter, the perfusion index (PI) ranges from 0.02% to 20% and is influenced primarily by ____ rather than by the level of oxygenation.
o: the amount of blood at the monitoring site
the level of arterial carbon dioxide tension
the peak inspiratory pressure of the breath
q.e: Perfusion index (PI) assesses pulse strength from 0.02% to 20% (selecting the site with the highest PI) and is influenced primarily by the amount of blood at the monitoring site, not blood oxygenation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 260)

q.q: Compared with a sidestream capnograph, what is a primary disadvantage of a mainstream capnography sensor?
o: Added weight on the endotracheal tube and extra circuit deadspace
Frequent occlusion of a narrow sampling line by aspirated secretions
Longer display lag time caused by aspirating gas into the unit
Inability to function when water condensation forms in tubing
q.e: Mainstream CO2 sensors offer fast response times and are unaffected by water condensation, but they add weight to the endotracheal tube and deadspace to the circuit, whereas sidestream tubes can occlude with water and secretions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 261)

q.q: On a normal capnogram measured by infrared absorption, phase III reflects exhalation of alveolar gas, and the end of this ____ represents the end-tidal PCO2 (PetCO2).
q.e: During exhalation on a capnogram, phase I represents CO2-free anatomic deadspace gas, phase II reflects mixing of deadspace and alveolar gas, and the end of the phase III alveolar plateau is the PetCO2, which estimates PaCO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 261)

q.q: During cardiopulmonary resuscitation of an intubated patient, capnography is monitored on a trend screen. Which capnographic change indicates that external chest compressions are effective?
o: A resultant rise in PetCO2 values
Flattening of phase II into baseline zero
A sudden drop of PetCO2 values to zero
q.e: Cardiac arrest causes a sudden drop in PetCO2 from inadequate lung perfusion, whereas effective external chest compressions are reflected by a resultant rise in PetCO2 on the trend screen. (Chang 4th ed., p. 263)

q.q: In normal individuals under ideal conditions, what is the approximate P(a-et)CO2 gradient between PaCO2 and PetCO2?
q.e: Under ideal conditions, PaCO2 is about 2 mm Hg higher than PetCO2, producing a normal P(a-et)CO2 gradient of about 2 mm Hg (with 5 mm Hg considered acceptable in critically ill patients). (Chang 4th ed., p. 264)

q.q: A disposable plastic pH-sensitive ETCO2 detector attached to an endotracheal tube senses CO2 changes to quickly differentiate ____.
q.e: Attaching a low-cost disposable pH-sensitive CO2 detector to the endotracheal tube allows clinicians to quickly differentiate tracheal from esophageal intubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 264)

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient develops a pulmonary embolism, causing PetCO2 to fall while the P(a-et)CO2 gradient increases. How should the therapist interpret the decreased PetCO2?
o: Increased physiologic deadspace rather than improved ventilation
Excessive minute ventilation requiring added mechanical deadspace
Improved alveolar ventilation warranting a lower ventilator rate
Reduced metabolic CO2 production from acute tissue hyperperfusion
q.e: Conditions that reduce perfusion or increase deadspace—such as pulmonary embolism, hypotension, or high intrathoracic pressure—lower PetCO2 and widen the P(a-et)CO2 gradient without improving ventilation, so ventilator frequency must not be lowered. (Chang 4th ed., p. 264)

q.q: For transcutaneous PO2 monitoring, a heating element keeps the skin at a constant temperature, such as ____, to provide adequate blood flow to the skin.
q.e: A heating element provides a constant skin temperature (e.g., 44ºC) for adequate skin blood flow during PtcO2 monitoring. (Chang 4th ed., p. 265)

q.q: Transcutaneous blood gas monitoring measures PO2 through the skin by means of a heated miniature ____ electrode.
q.e: Transcutaneous blood gas monitoring uses a heated (e.g., 44°C) miniature Clark electrode (combined platinum and silver) for PO2 and a Severinghaus electrode for PCO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 265)

q.q: For most infants, what is the clinical optimal range for transcutaneous PO2 (PtcO2)?
q.e: In neonates PtcO2 closely approximates PaO2 (unlike adults, whose thicker skin yields lower PtcO2 readings), and the optimal clinical PtcO2 range for most infants is 50 to 70 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 265)

q.q: Which factors affect the accuracy of the transcutaneous PO2 (PtcO2) electrode?
o: Skin edema, hypothermia, and capillary perfusion status
Skin pigment, fever, and hemoglobin level
Skin edema, hyperthermia, and carboxyhemoglobin level
Nail polish, motion artifact, and ambient light
q.e: Accuracy of the PtcO2 electrode is affected by skin edema, hypothermia, and capillary perfusion status; it is also less accurate above 80 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 266)

q.q: In studies of severe head injury, maintaining the CPP above 70 mm Hg was associated with what reduction in mortality?
q.e: In studies involving severe head injuries, a 35% reduction in mortality was achieved when CPP was maintained above 70 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 266)

q.q: Transcutaneous PCO2 (PtcCO2) values are usually higher than arterial PaCO2 values because heating the underlying tissues causes ____.
q.e: Heating the skin (40°C to 42°C in neonates, 44°C standard, maximum 45°C) increases local metabolic CO2 production—and shock or low perfusion further accumulates tissue CO2—causing PtcCO2 to read higher than PaCO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 266)

q.q: In patients with head injury and impaired cerebral autoregulation, mortality increases by approximately what percentage for each 10 mm Hg drop in cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)?
q.e: The critical CPP threshold is 70 to 80 mm Hg; mortality increases about 20% for each 10 mm Hg drop in CPP, whereas maintaining CPP above 70 mm Hg achieved a 35% mortality reduction in severe head injury studies. (Chang 4th ed., p. 266)

q.q: A mechanically ventilated head trauma patient has a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 88 mm Hg and an intracranial pressure (ICP) of 16 mm Hg. What is the patient's cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)?
q.e: Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure (CPP = MAP − ICP = 88 − 16 = 72 mm Hg), and a higher CPP may be maintained by raising MAP or lowering ICP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 267)

q.q: What is the normal intracranial pressure (ICP) range, which in clinical practice is generally controlled below 20 mm Hg?
q.e: Normal intracranial pressure (ICP) is 8 to 12 mm Hg, and in clinical practice ICP is usually controlled below 20 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 267)

q.q: In severe brain injury without hemorrhage, MAP is managed initially with adequate fluid balance followed by norepinephrine or dopamine to avoid ____, which contributes to cerebral ischemia and mortality.
q.e: In the absence of hemorrhage, MAP is maintained first by adequate fluid balance and then with vasopressors such as norepinephrine or dopamine so that systemic hypotension (SBP <90 mm Hg) is avoided. (Chang 4th ed., p. 267)

q.q: In its most basic sense, hemodynamic monitoring measures the ____ in vessels or heart chambers during systole and diastole.
q.e: The pressure measurement spans both contraction and relaxation. Monitoring can also supply cardiac output and mixed venous oxygen saturation in critically ill patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 276)

q.q: In a closed, liquid-filled catheter system, pressure exerted at one point can be measured accurately at any other point ____.
q.e: A noncompressible liquid transmits pressure equally, and keeping points at the same level prevents gravity from altering the reading. (Chang 4th ed., p. 276)

q.q: Which term describes the resistance of the vessels into which a ventricle ejects blood?
q.e: Preload describes end-diastolic muscle fiber stretch. Afterload describes the vascular resistance to ejection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 276)

q.q: Between the catheter and the amplifier, the transducer converts fluid pressure into ____.
q.e: The monitor displays the electronic signal derived from catheter pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 277)

q.q: Which multipliers convert mm Hg to kPa and kPa to mm Hg, respectively?
q.e: The forward conversion uses 0.133 and the reverse conversion uses 7.501. The reference zero is atmospheric pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 277)

q.q: With the pulmonary artery catheter tip in position, its proximal opening can still measure ____.
q.e: The proximal opening measures right atrial pressure, also called CVP. Invasive monitoring carries risks of infection, dysrhythmia, bleeding, and vessel trauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 277)

q.q: A radial arterial line is planned. Which test checks the hand’s collateral blood supply before puncture?
q.e: The Allen test confirms ulnar collateral flow before radial access. Brachial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis arteries are alternative sites. (Chang 4th ed., p. 278)

q.q: Which bedside task can be performed through the same radial catheter used for continuous blood pressure monitoring?
o: Collect an arterial blood gas sample
Infuse fluid into the right atrium
Collect a mixed venous blood sample
q.e: An arterial waveform helps confirm placement. The line gives direct systemic pressure measurements and access for arterial blood sampling. (Chang 4th ed., p. 278)

q.q: Which hemodynamic catheter can provide cardiac pacing as well as cardiac output measurement?
q.e: The pulmonary artery catheter can measure cardiac output and mixed venous oxygen saturation and provide pacing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 278)

q.q: Which systemic systolic and diastolic pressure ranges are usual in most adults, in mm Hg?
q.e: Normal adult arterial pressure is 100–140 mm Hg systolic and 60–90 mm Hg diastolic. (Chang 4th ed., p. 279)

q.q: An arterial tracing peaks at 126 mm Hg and reaches 72 mm Hg at end diastole. What is the calculated MAP?
q.e: MAP is the sum of systolic pressure and twice diastolic pressure, divided by three. Diastole lasts about twice as long as systole. (Chang 4th ed., p. 279)

q.q: The chapter gives ____ as the minimum MAP needed for adequate tissue perfusion.
q.e: The minimum mean arterial pressure given for tissue perfusion is 60 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 279)

q.q: Which interval on a systemic arterial tracing reflects the rapid pressure rise during ventricular ejection?
q.e: The systolic upstroke runs from C to A. The downslope reflects declining pressure, with semilunar valve closure producing the notch. (Chang 4th ed., p. 279)

q.q: A rise in the volume ejected per contraction can leave arterial pressure unchanged if ____ falls sufficiently.
q.e: Arterial pressure depends on stroke volume and vascular resistance. Opposing changes can offset each other. (Chang 4th ed., p. 279)

q.q: Which interval represents normal systolic minus diastolic arterial pressure?
q.e: Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure. Values above 40 are wide and values below 30 are narrow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 280)

q.q: Bradycardia can widen pulse pressure because it allows more time for ____.
q.e: Longer runoff lowers diastolic pressure. Hypervolemia, arteriosclerosis, and heart block also appear among causes of wide pulse pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 280)

q.q: Which condition causes a narrow pulse pressure through increased (high) vascular compliance?
q.e: Septic shock narrows pulse pressure through high vascular compliance, congestive heart failure through low stroke volume, and tachycardia through reduced diastolic runoff time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 280)

q.q: In older patients, a 10 mm Hg rise in pulse pressure increases the risk of major cardiovascular complications and mortality by about ____.
q.e: The chapter reports an approximately 20% rise in risk for that pulse pressure increment. (Chang 4th ed., p. 280)

q.q: Blood backs up into an arterial pressure line. Which finding best explains the direction of flow?
o: Flush bag pressure below arterial pressure
Catheter tip pressed against the vessel wall
Air bubbles in the transducer tubing
q.e: Blood backs up when arterial pressure exceeds flush pressure. Air bubbles and loose connections dampen the signal, while clot or wall obstruction interferes with it. (Chang 4th ed., p. 281)

q.q: A transducer and catheter positioned above the measurement site yield a reading that is ____.
q.e: Positioning them above the site lowers the reading. Positioning them below the site raises it. (Chang 4th ed., p. 281)

q.q: A central venous catheter measures filling pressure in the ____ and helps assess systemic fluid status.
q.e: The tip lies in the superior vena cava near the right atrium or in the atrium itself. CVP often reflects left heart changes late. (Chang 4th ed., p. 281)

q.q: Which pair of veins does Chang name as common insertion sites for a central venous catheter in the section on central venous pressure monitoring?
q.e: Central venous catheters are commonly inserted through the subclavian vein or the internal jugular vein. (Chang 4th ed., p. 282)

q.q: On simultaneous ECG and CVP recordings, the right atrial pressure upstroke associated with atrial contraction follows the ____.
q.e: The electrical event precedes the pressure response. The c wave occurs within the QRS complex and the v wave appears at the T wave. (Chang 4th ed., p. 283)

q.q: Which event produces the y downslope of a normal CVP waveform?
o: Rapid filling of the right ventricle
q.e: Ventricular relaxation and rapid filling from the right atrium produce the y downslope. Right atrial relaxation produces the x downslope. (Chang 4th ed., p. 283)

q.q: A patient with tricuspid stenosis has increased resistance to right ventricular filling. Which CVP finding is expected?
q.e: Increased filling resistance raises the a wave. Weak or absent atrial activity can abolish it, while tricuspid incompetence raises the v wave. (Chang 4th ed., p. 283)

q.q: Besides infection and bleeding, insertion of a central venous catheter carries a risk of ____.
q.e: Pneumothorax is one of the three insertion complications listed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 283)

q.q: Which pair gives the normal mean pressures in the vena cava and right atrium, respectively?
q.e: The vena cava range is 0–6 mm Hg. Right atrial readings are slightly higher at 2–7 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 284)

q.q: At constant MAP, rising CVP reduces the pressure gradient driving ____.
q.e: Less blood returns to the right heart as the MAP-to-CVP gradient falls. Increased CVP can accompany positive pressure ventilation or right ventricular failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 284)

q.q: Which condition lowers CVP by causing relative (rather than absolute) hypovolemia?
q.e: Shock and vasodilation cause relative hypovolemia, whereas blood loss and dehydration cause absolute hypovolemia. Increased pulmonary resistance, hypervolemia, and right heart failure can raise CVP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 284)

q.q: On a typical 110-cm, three-lumen pulmonary artery catheter, how far behind the tip is the proximal injectate port?
q.e: The proximal port lies about 30 cm behind the distal opening and rests in the right atrium. External markings indicate 10-cm intervals. (Chang 4th ed., p. 285)

q.q: After the balloon is inflated in the right atrium, ____ carries the catheter toward a smaller pulmonary artery branch.
q.e: Blood flow directs the balloon through the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery. Balloon-related complications include pulmonary hemorrhage and infarction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 285)

q.q: Between wedge pressure measurements, the balloon stays ____ so the monitor displays the PAP tracing.
q.e: Balloon inflation is momentary for a wedge reading. The usual PAP waveform has systolic and diastolic phases and a dicrotic notch at semilunar valve closure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 286)

q.q: Which systolic and diastolic ranges describe normal pulmonary arterial pressure?
q.e: Systolic PAP approximates right ventricular systolic pressure. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance or flow can raise the systolic component. (Chang 4th ed., p. 286)

q.q: Which set gives the chapter’s pulmonary hypertension cutoffs for systolic PAP, resting mean PAP, and exertional mean PAP, respectively?
q.e: The systolic criterion is above 35 mm Hg. The mean pressure criterion is above 25 at rest or above 30 during exertion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 287)

q.q: Increasing PEEP can raise PAP when distended alveoli compress the ____.
q.e: Alveolar overdistension compresses adjacent capillaries and raises capillary and arterial pressures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 287)

q.q: During advancement of a pulmonary artery catheter from the right atrium, which pressure waveform is recorded immediately before the pulmonary arterial waveform?
q.e: The successive recordings are right atrial, right ventricular, pulmonary arterial, and wedge pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 287)

q.q: An unstable patient’s PAP falls during positive pressure ventilation. Which change explains the fall?
q.e: Reduced venous return lowers right ventricular output and pulmonary arterial blood volume. The overall PAP response varies with ventilator pressures, compliance, and hemodynamic status. (Chang 4th ed., p. 288)

q.q: Which condition raises PAP through increased pulmonary blood flow?
q.e: A left-to-right shunt and hypervolemia increase flow. Embolism and hypoxic vasoconstriction increase resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 288)

q.q: For consistent wedge pressure readings during spontaneous or mechanical ventilation, measure PCWP at ____.
q.e: End-expiration is used in both groups. Wedge pressure reflects left ventricular preload. (Chang 4th ed., p. 289)

q.q: What range of air volumes does the chapter give for obtaining a wedge tracing, depending on balloon size?
q.e: The balloon is inflated slowly with 0.75–1.5 mL and deflated as soon as PCWP is obtained. (Chang 4th ed., p. 289)

q.q: On the wedge waveform, the small c wave sometimes seen on the x downslope accompanies ____.
q.e: The a wave reflects atrial contraction and the x downslope the subsequent pressure fall. The v wave accompanies ventricular contraction and passive atrial filling, and the y downslope follows mitral opening. (Chang 4th ed., p. 289)

q.q: A wedge tracing shows a prominent v wave as blood flows back into the left atrium during ventricular contraction. Which lesion fits?
q.e: Mitral insufficiency raises the v wave. Increased resistance to ventricular filling, as in mitral stenosis, can raise the a wave. (Chang 4th ed., p. 290)

q.q: Which range is normal for pulmonary capillary wedge pressure?
q.e: Normal PCWP is 8–12 mm Hg. Chang lists hypervolemia and balloon overwedging among causes of an increased reading. (Chang 4th ed., p. 290)

q.q: A patient has pulmonary edema, a PCWP of 18 mm Hg, and a near-normal PAP. Which explanation fits this pattern?
q.e: Pulmonary edema with a PCWP of at least 18 mm Hg and near-normal PAP suggests left ventricular failure. Edema associated with increased permeability or acute pulmonary hypertension typically has a normal PCWP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 290)

q.q: When checking wedge position by pressure gradient, diastolic PAP is normally ____ the average PCWP.
q.e: Forceful inspiration can lower measured diastolic PAP and mitral disease can elevate PCWP. A dampened tracing alone may mimic a wedge tracing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 291)

q.q: Compared with systemic arterial blood, which minimum PO₂ and PCO₂ differences support a properly wedged distal sample?
o: PO₂ 19 mm Hg higher, PCO₂ 11 mm Hg lower
PO₂ 11 mm Hg lower, PCO₂ 19 mm Hg higher
PO₂ 19 mm Hg lower, PCO₂ 11 mm Hg higher
PO₂ 11 mm Hg higher, PCO₂ 19 mm Hg lower
q.e: Wedging excludes shunted venous blood from the sample. Up to 40 mL of waste blood may be needed, making sampling difficult in hypovolemia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 291)

q.q: With catheter oximetry, saturation at a proper wedge position should be about ____ the reading with the balloon deflated.
q.e: The saturation gradient provides another way to verify wedging. (Chang 4th ed., p. 291)

q.q: For bolus thermodilution, 10 mL of iced or room-temperature D5W is injected into the ____.
q.e: The tip thermistor detects the temperature change. Continuous thermodilution uses a heated strip, and normal adult cardiac output is 4–8 L/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 291)

q.q: The wedged position of a pulmonary artery catheter may be confirmed by which of the following?
q.e: Wedge position may be confirmed by the PAP diastolic–PCWP gradient, the postcapillary–mixed venous PO2 gradient, and the postcapillary–mixed venous O2 saturation gradient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 291)

q.q: The normal cardiac index is ____.
q.e: The normal adult cardiac output is 4 to 8 L/min and the normal cardiac index is 2.5 to 3.5 L/min/m2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 291)

q.q: An adult has a cardiac output of 6 L/min and a body surface area of 2 m². Which cardiac index should be reported?
q.e: Cardiac index is output divided by body surface area. This result is within the normal range of 2.5–3.5 L/min/m². (Chang 4th ed., p. 292)

q.q: Which pressure falls when right-sided heart failure causes pulmonary hypoperfusion?
q.e: PAP reflects right ventricular afterload and can fall with reduced pulmonary perfusion. Systemic arterial pressure reflects left ventricular afterload. (Chang 4th ed., p. 292)

q.q: Which range is normal for resistance in the arterial system receiving left ventricular output?
q.e: Normal systemic vascular resistance is 800–1,500 dyn·s/cm⁵. (Chang 4th ed., p. 292)

q.q: Cardiac output is 6,000 mL/min, heart rate is 75/min, and body surface area is 2 m². What is the stroke volume index?
q.e: Dividing output by heart rate gives 80 mL/beat. Dividing by surface area gives 40 mL/beat/m². (Chang 4th ed., p. 293)

q.q: The three determinants of stroke volume are preload, afterload, and ____.
q.e: Contractility is pumping strength and may increase with improved blood volume or positive inotropic drugs. Shock can reduce preload, and downstream obstruction can increase afterload. (Chang 4th ed., p. 293)

q.q: Which expression gives oxygen consumption indexed to body size?
q.e: Oxygen consumption per minute is blood flow times the arterial–mixed venous oxygen content difference. The index divides that product by body surface area. (Chang 4th ed., p. 293)

q.q: Mean PAP is 17 mm Hg, PCWP is 10 mm Hg, and cardiac output is 4 L/min. What is the PVR?
q.e: PVR equals (PAP − PCWP) × 80 divided by cardiac output. The result of 140 is within the stated normal range of 50–150 dyn·s/cm⁵. (Chang 4th ed., p. 293)

q.q: At a MAP of 84 mm Hg, RAP of 4 mm Hg, and cardiac output of 5 L/min, what is the SVR?
q.e: Subtract RAP from MAP, multiply by 80, and divide by cardiac output. Systemic hypertension can elevate SVR. (Chang 4th ed., p. 293)

q.q: When oxygen delivery and consumption are balanced, mixed venous oxygen saturation averages ____.
q.e: Balanced oxygen delivery and consumption yield an SvO₂ of 68%–77% with an average of 75%, while the fiberoptic catheter measures accurately across the clinical range of 50%–80%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 294)

q.q: A febrile patient’s SvO₂ falls to 60% as oxygen consumption rises. What response does this value suggest?
o: Inability of tissues to utilize oxygen
q.e: At 50%–70%, extraction compensates for increased consumption or reduced delivery. Low cardiac output, anemia, and hypoxic hypoxia reduce delivery. (Chang 4th ed., p. 294)

q.q: Which SvO₂ range does the chapter associate specifically with severe lactic acidosis as venous oxygen reserves fall?
q.e: Lactic acidosis becomes evident at 30%–50% and is commonly severe at 25%–30%. The chapter associates levels below 25% with cellular death. (Chang 4th ed., p. 294)

q.q: An unexpectedly high SvO₂ can occur when the pulmonary artery catheter tip is ____ and senses blood from a high ventilation/perfusion region.
q.e: Wedging obstructs forward mixed venous flow. Analgesics, sedation, full ventilatory support, and hypothermia can also raise SvO₂ by reducing consumption. (Chang 4th ed., p. 294)

q.q: Which plasma lactate cutoffs suggest significant cyanide exposure after smoke inhalation and suspected pure cyanide poisoning, respectively?
q.e: Cyanide impairs aerobic metabolism, so SvO₂ can rise despite tissue hypoxia. The chapter gives different lactate cutoffs for the two exposures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 294)

q.q: Which pair of conditions can raise SvO₂ by impairing tissue oxygen utilization?
q.e: Sepsis and cyanide poisoning impair oxygen utilization. Hypothermia, postanesthesia, and pharmacologic paralysis raise SvO₂ by reducing oxygen consumption. (Chang 4th ed., p. 295)

q.q: Pulse contour analysis uses patient data and the area under the ____ to estimate stroke volume.
q.e: Pulse contour analysis requires an arterial catheter and accounts for vascular compliance. Multiplying stroke volume or its index by heart rate yields output or cardiac index. (Chang 4th ed., p. 295)

q.q: Which procedure provides the dilution measurement for the LiDCO system?
o: Inject venous lithium chloride and measure arterial lithium
Inject central venous saline and measure arterial temperature
Inject peripheral venous saline and measure atrial temperature
Inject arterial lithium chloride and measure venous lithium
q.e: LiDCO measures arterial lithium after peripheral venous injection, while PiCCO measures arterial temperature after central venous cold saline injection. Both require repeat measurements after changes in patient condition or administration of fluid or vasoactive drugs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 296)

q.q: How often does FLOTRAC update the data displayed as a continuous value on the Vigileo monitor?
q.e: FLOTRAC uses a peripheral arterial transducer without separate output calibration. A PreSep fiberoptic line can add central venous saturation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 296)

q.q: To estimate cardiac output by esophageal Doppler, multiply the outflow time–velocity integral by ____.
o: body surface area and stroke volume
body surface area and heart rate
q.e: Doppler shift gives blood flow velocity. Accurate continuous bedside measurement requires a skilled operator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 296)

q.q: Which set names the three major types of noninvasive hemodynamic monitoring described in the chapter?
o: Transesophageal echocardiography, carbon dioxide elimination, and impedance cardiography
Transesophageal echocardiography, thermodilution, and arterial pressure monitoring
Pulmonary artery catheter, carbon dioxide elimination, and impedance cardiography
Central venous catheter, pulse contour analysis, and thermodilution
q.e: The three major noninvasive methods are transesophageal echocardiography, carbon dioxide elimination (V̇CO2), and impedance cardiography (ICG). (Chang 4th ed., p. 296)

q.q: Transesophageal echocardiography calculates cardiac output from blood flow velocity by recording the ____.
o: change in exhaled CO2 during rebreathing
temperature change of an injected solution
q.e: Transesophageal echocardiography can calculate cardiac output from blood flow velocity measured by recording the Doppler shift of ultrasound. (Chang 4th ed., p. 296)

q.q: In transesophageal echocardiography, the Doppler transducer in the esophagus indirectly measures blood flow velocity in the ____.
q.e: A Doppler transducer in the esophagus indirectly measures blood flow velocity in the descending aorta to calculate cardiac output and other hemodynamic data. (Chang 4th ed., p. 296)

q.q: For esophageal Doppler monitoring, the midthoracic probe is rotated to face the ____.
q.e: The probe enters via the mouth or nose and detects the aortic flow signal from the esophagus. (Chang 4th ed., p. 297)

q.q: During brief partial rebreathing, the NICO₂ system estimates output from changes in ____.
q.e: NICO₂ uses flow, airway pressure, and CO₂ sensors to calculate CO₂ elimination. End-tidal CO₂ replaces arterial and mixed venous blood sampling. (Chang 4th ed., p. 297)

q.q: Which calculation gives cardiac output by the original oxygen-based Fick method?
o: O₂ consumption divided by the arterial–mixed venous O₂ content difference
CO₂ elimination divided by the arterial–mixed venous O₂ content difference
O₂ consumption multiplied by the arterial–mixed venous O₂ content difference
CO₂ elimination multiplied by the arterial–mixed venous O₂ content difference
q.e: The original Fick calculation uses oxygen consumption and the oxygen content difference. NICO₂ uses CO₂ elimination in place of oxygen consumption. (Chang 4th ed., p. 297)

q.q: The IQ impedance cardiography system identifies aortic valve opening and closing to measure ____.
q.e: ICG is also called thoracic electrical bioimpedance. Other devices use ensemble averaging of the QRS and dZ/dt or digital processing with R-wave detection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 297)

q.q: In an eight-electrode ICG setup, the four inner electrodes ____ while the outer electrodes transmit current.
q.e: The outer electrodes supply high-frequency, low-amplitude current. Thoracic impedance varies with blood flow in the ascending aorta through the cardiac cycle. (Chang 4th ed., p. 298)

q.q: Which factor affects the reliability of bolus thermodilution measurements?
q.e: Reliability also depends on the computation constant, injectate volume and temperature, injection technique, and averaging strategy. (Chang 4th ed., p. 298)

q.q: Which pair of hemodynamic values is unavailable from ICG?
o: Wedge pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance
Cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance
Thoracic fluid content and heart rate
Stroke volume index and cardiac index
q.e: ICG provides systemic resistance, contractility, and fluid status. It cannot supply PAP, wedge pressure, PVR, or indexed PVR. (Chang 4th ed., p. 299)

q.q: Among hemodynamic parameters provided by impedance cardiography, the interval from ventricular electrical stimulation to aortic valve opening is the ____.
q.e: The pre-ejection period ends when the aortic valve opens. Left ventricular (LV) ejection time runs from valve opening to closure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 299)

q.q: Which impedance cardiography index measures how rapidly aortic blood velocity increases just after the aortic valve opens?
q.e: The acceleration index describes the early increase in aortic blood velocity after the valve opens. The velocity index describes the peak velocity reached. (Chang 4th ed., p. 299)

q.q: In patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension, what correlations were reported for ICG cardiac output versus Fick and versus thermodilution, respectively?
q.e: The study reported 0.84 for comparison with Fick and 0.80 for comparison with thermodilution. (Chang 4th ed., p. 300)

q.q: Above what heart rate does the chapter specifically list tachycardia as a possible source of ICG error?
q.e: Other sources of error include misplaced electrodes, abnormal habitus or cardiac anatomy, pacemakers, arrhythmias, cardiac or aortic surgery, abnormal hematocrit, and pleural effusion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 300)

q.q: A subacute care team uses ICG to assess the response to a cardiovascular drug dose change. Which measurements does the chapter identify for this purpose?
o: Thoracic fluid status, stroke volume, and cardiac output
Thoracic fluid status, wedge pressure, and cardiac output
Thoracic fluid status, stroke volume, and pulmonary artery pressure
Wedge pressure, stroke volume, and cardiac output
q.e: ICG permits continuous noninvasive assessment of responses to fluids and drugs, including outside the hospital. It also reduces costs and risks associated with invasive monitoring. (Chang 4th ed., p. 300)

q.q: Ventilator graphics allow the therapist to observe patient–ventilator interactions in ____.
q.e: Ventilator graphics allow the therapist to observe patient–ventilator interactions in real time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 309)

q.q: When should the therapist compare waveforms to assess a ventilator adjustment?
o: At the next scheduled blood gas draw
At the start of the next spontaneous breathing trial
At the end of the ventilator day
q.e: Graphics obtained before and after an adjustment allow the therapist to assess its effects. (Chang 4th ed., p. 310)

q.q: In the chapter’s waveform notation, CLT stands for ____.
q.e: In the chapter’s waveform notation, CLT stands for static lung-thorax compliance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 310)

q.q: In pressure control, the descending inspiratory flow trace may show a concave decay depending on lung mechanics and ____.
q.e: In pressure control, the descending inspiratory flow trace may show a concave decay depending on lung mechanics and patient effort. (Chang 4th ed., p. 311)

q.q: Slowing the rise to peak flow for comfort can give a constant flow waveform a ____ initial contour.
q.e: Slowing the rise to peak flow for comfort can give a constant flow waveform a convex initial contour. (Chang 4th ed., p. 311)

q.q: Which pair of inspiratory flow patterns offers a fast rise to peak flow for assisted breaths?
q.e: Constant and descending ramp flow reach peak flow rapidly to meet patient demand. (Chang 4th ed., p. 311)

q.q: A true descending ramp differs from a ramp with a preset residual flow because the true ramp ends at ____.
q.e: A true descending ramp differs from a ramp with a preset residual flow because the true ramp ends at zero flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 311)

q.q: A heavily sedated patient makes no inspiratory effort. Which change may improve gas distribution to poorly ventilated regions?
o: Slow the rise to peak flow
Shorten the rise to peak flow
q.e: Slower flow may reduce resistance and improve distribution to poorly ventilated lung regions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 312)

q.q: During a patient-triggered breath, setting initial flow above demand may compensate for valve opening time and the time needed for gas to ____.
q.e: During a patient-triggered breath, setting initial flow above demand may compensate for valve opening time and the time needed for gas to accelerate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 312)

q.q: Approximately how many flow or pressure measurements per second are digitized for the waveform display described in the chapter?
q.e: The display uses approximately 30 to 50 measurements each second to produce smoother traces. (Chang 4th ed., p. 313)

q.q: From peak expiratory flow toward baseline, normal passive expiration produces a ____ pattern.
q.e: From peak expiratory flow toward baseline, normal passive expiration produces a convex exponential decay pattern. (Chang 4th ed., p. 313)

q.q: Which interval represents a passive expiratory pause on a flow-time trace?
o: From return to zero flow until the next breath
From peak exhaled flow until flow reaches zero
From peak inspiratory flow until cycling
From onset of inspiration until flow peaks
q.e: The expiratory pause follows the return of expiratory flow to baseline and ends with the next breath. (Chang 4th ed., p. 313)

q.q: Because gas compresses and circuit tubing expands during inflation, flow measured at the ventilator outlet can ____ flow reaching the carina.
q.e: Because gas compresses and circuit tubing expands during inflation, flow measured at the ventilator outlet can exceed flow reaching the carina. (Chang 4th ed., p. 314)

q.q: Under passive conditions, constant inspiratory flow produces a pressure-time waveform shaped like a ____.
q.e: Under passive conditions, constant inspiratory flow produces a pressure-time waveform shaped like a step ascending ramp. (Chang 4th ed., p. 314)

q.q: Without volume compensation, what compressible volume loss is common in a disposable adult circuit?
q.e: Tubing expansion and gas compression account for a typical loss of 2 to 3 mL per cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 314)

q.q: The initial pressure step before the linear rise during constant flow primarily reflects resistance in the ____.
q.e: The initial pressure step before the linear rise during constant flow primarily reflects resistance in the circuit and endotracheal tube. (Chang 4th ed., p. 314)

q.q: Initial flow rises slowly during a volume-controlled breath. If the delivery time cannot be extended, which adjustment can recover the initial volume deficit?
q.e: A higher peak flow can replace the volume lost during the initial delay. (Chang 4th ed., p. 315)

q.q: For a rectangular inspiratory flow trace, tidal volume equals constant flow multiplied by ____.
q.e: For a rectangular inspiratory flow trace, tidal volume equals constant flow multiplied by inspiratory time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 315)

q.q: On a flow-time waveform, the area under the expiratory curve (area b) is less than the area under the inspiratory curve (area a). This suggests ____.
q.e: Area a (inspired volume) should equal area b (expired volume); if area b is less than area a, air leak or air trapping may be present. (Chang 4th ed., p. 315)

q.q: At a constant flow of 60 L/min, how much volume enters during each 0.25-second interval?
q.e: At 1 L/s, each quarter second of delivery adds 0.25 L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 316)

q.q: During the 0.5-second end-inspiratory hold, gas volume is maintained because ____.
o: the expiratory valve is open and the inspiratory valve is closed
the inspiratory valve is open and the expiratory valve is closed
q.e: During the 0.5-second end-inspiratory hold, gas volume is maintained because both ventilator valves are closed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 316)

q.q: During inspiration with flow, airway opening pressure is the sum of alveolar pressure and ____.
q.e: During inspiration with flow, airway opening pressure is the sum of alveolar pressure and transairway pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 317)

q.q: Which calculation gives circuit and airway resistance during constant-flow ventilation?
o: Divide PIP minus plateau pressure by flow
Divide tidal volume by the plateau pressure
Divide PIP plus plateau pressure by flow
Multiply plateau pressure by tidal volume
q.e: At constant flow, the difference between peak and plateau pressure is the flow-resistive pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 317)

q.q: During an end-inspiratory pause, the pressure attributable to airflow resistance ____.
q.e: During an end-inspiratory pause, the pressure attributable to airflow resistance dissipates immediately. (Chang 4th ed., p. 317)

q.q: A controlled breath has a 1-second inspiration and a 3-second expiration. What mandatory rate does this timing produce?
q.e: The 4-second total cycle time gives 15 breaths per minute and an I:E ratio of 1:3. (Chang 4th ed., p. 318)

q.q: In volume-controlled ventilation, flow and volume are controlled while ____ varies with compliance and resistance.
q.e: In volume-controlled ventilation, flow and volume are controlled while pressure varies with compliance and resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 318)

q.q: Which feature distinguishes a time-triggered controlled breath from a pressure-triggered assist breath?
o: Absence of a negative trigger deflection
Presence of a descending expiratory flow trace
Presence of a square inspiratory flow trace
Absence of a positive inspiratory pressure
q.e: A controlled breath begins without the negative triggering pressure seen with a patient effort. (Chang 4th ed., p. 318)

q.q: When a patient triggers a second CMV breath before the timed breath is due, the interval cut short is ____.
o: the first breath’s volume delivery period
q.e: When a patient triggers a second CMV breath before the timed breath is due, the interval cut short is expiratory time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 319)

q.q: During optimal assisted CMV with volume control, what fraction of the normal ventilatory workload do patients commonly perform?
q.e: Patients commonly perform one-third to one-half of the normal workload during optimal assisted breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 319)

q.q: With set tidal volume and average flow unchanged, inspiratory time during assisted VCV equals ____.
o: total cycle time divided by VT
q.e: With set tidal volume and average flow unchanged, inspiratory time during assisted VCV equals VT divided by average flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 319)

q.q: How much variability in airway opening pressure is described as unremarkable when a patient expands the thorax in synchrony with the ventilator?
q.e: Synchronous inspiratory effort can lower airway opening pressure by 2 to 3 cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 319)

q.q: PEEP is 10 cm H₂O and pressure sensitivity is set 2 cm H₂O below baseline. At what circuit pressure should the assisted breath trigger?
q.e: With PEEP compensation, a drop of 2 cm H₂O from 10 cm H₂O reaches the trigger at 8 cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 320)

q.q: At constant inspiratory flow and unchanged compliance, the PAO and PALV traces rise in parallel while PTA ____.
q.e: At constant inspiratory flow and unchanged compliance, the PAO and PALV traces rise in parallel while PTA remains constant. (Chang 4th ed., p. 320)

q.q: With constant flow and stable static compliance, volume and alveolar pressure both rise ____ as inspiration progresses.
q.e: With constant flow and stable static compliance, volume and alveolar pressure both rise linearly as inspiration progresses. (Chang 4th ed., p. 321)

q.q: At 50 L/min constant flow, which sequence gives cumulative volumes at 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 and 1.00 seconds, respectively?
q.e: Each quarter second adds approximately 0.208 L, giving 0.833 L after four intervals. (Chang 4th ed., p. 322)

q.q: At 50 L/min constant flow for 1 second, how does the volume in the fourth quarter compare with that in the first quarter?
o: The fourth quarter delivers twice as much
The fourth quarter delivers half as much
q.e: Equal time intervals at constant flow deliver equal volumes, even as cumulative volume rises. (Chang 4th ed., p. 322)

q.q: When peak alveolar pressure and PEEP are known, static compliance equals VT divided by ____.
q.e: When peak alveolar pressure and PEEP are known, static compliance equals VT divided by peak PALV minus PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 323)

q.q: At a CLT of 0.04166 L/cm H₂O and PEEP of 10 cm H₂O, which PALV values correspond to delivered volumes of 0.2083, 0.4166, 0.6249 and 0.8333 L?
q.e: Dividing each accumulated volume by compliance and adding PEEP gives successive alveolar pressures of 15, 20, 25 and 30 cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 323)

q.q: Which set of breath types can appear together in SIMV?
q.e: SIMV permits controlled, spontaneous and assist breaths without overlapping mechanical and spontaneous breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 323)

q.q: No patient effort occurs during the synchronization window in SIMV. Which breath follows?
q.e: A timed mandatory breath is delivered when the synchronization window passes without patient effort. (Chang 4th ed., p. 324)

q.q: In relaxed, synchronous spontaneous breathing during SIMV, the inspiratory flow trace approximates a ____.
q.e: In relaxed, synchronous spontaneous breathing during SIMV, the inspiratory flow trace approximates a sine wave. (Chang 4th ed., p. 324)

q.q: During a spontaneous breath on a ventilator, which of the following determines flow, volume, and inspiratory and expiratory times?
q.e: The ventilator supplies the flow demanded by the patient during spontaneous ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 324)

q.q: All breaths on a tracing are spontaneous, pressure stays near 5 cm H₂O during inspiration and rises briefly during exhalation. Which mode fits?
q.e: CPAP maintains a positive baseline during spontaneous breathing, with a brief positive pressure excursion possible during expiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 325)

q.q: During inspiration on demand CPAP, pressure maintained near baseline indicates that ____.
q.e: During inspiration on demand CPAP, pressure maintained near baseline indicates that flow meets patient demand. (Chang 4th ed., p. 325)

q.q: On demand CPAP set at 5 cm H₂O, inspiratory flow begins when circuit pressure drops to 4 cm H₂O. What pressure sensitivity relative to baseline does this represent?
q.e: A drop from the 5 cm H₂O CPAP baseline to 4 cm H₂O represents a trigger sensitivity of 1 cm H₂O below CPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 325)

q.q: As gas passes through circuit bends and components of different diameters, the resulting flow can become ____.
q.e: As gas passes through circuit bends and components of different diameters, the resulting flow can become turbulent. (Chang 4th ed., p. 326)

q.q: During constant flow VCV, an increase in flow rate causes which change?
o: Higher PIP and PTA, with peak PALV unchanged
Lower PIP and PTA, with peak PALV unchanged
Higher peak PALV and PTA, with PIP unchanged
Higher PIP and peak PALV, with PTA unchanged
q.e: An increase in flow rate raises airflow resistance and therefore PIP and PTA; peak alveolar (plateau) pressure is not affected by changes in flow rate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 326)

q.q: A therapist doubles constant inspiratory flow while preserving tidal volume and compliance. How does the time needed to reach peak PALV change?
q.e: Doubling the flow shortens inspiration by half while peak alveolar pressure remains unchanged. (Chang 4th ed., p. 327)

q.q: When turbulent flow through the circuit increases, circuit pressure rises ____.
q.e: When turbulent flow through the circuit increases, circuit pressure rises exponentially. (Chang 4th ed., p. 327)

q.q: During constant flow VCV, a decrease in lung-thorax compliance causes which change?
o: Higher PALV and PIP, with PTA unchanged
Lower PALV and PIP, with PTA unchanged
Higher PTA and PALV, with PIP unchanged
Higher PTA and PIP, with PALV unchanged
q.e: A decrease in lung-thorax compliance increases PALV and PIP, while transairway pressure (PTA) is not affected by changes in compliance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 327)

q.q: A 1,000-mL breath requires 40 cm H₂O of alveolar distending pressure instead of 20 cm H₂O. What is the new CLT?
q.e: Doubling the pressure needed for the same volume halves compliance from 50 to 25 mL/cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 328)

q.q: For a linearly descending flow ramp, the average inspiratory flow equals ____.
o: half the sum of peak and end-flow
the sum of peak flow and average flow
half the difference between peak and end-flow
the difference between peak flow and end-flow
q.e: For a linearly descending flow ramp, the average inspiratory flow equals half the sum of peak and end-flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 329)

q.q: A constant flow of 40 L/min delivers 0.67 L in 1 second. What initial flow will deliver this volume in 1 second with a true descending ramp?
q.e: For a ramp ending at zero, an 80 L/min peak gives the same average flow as constant flow at 40 L/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 329)

q.q: On a ventilator that sets inspiratory time as a percentage, which other quantity determines inspiratory time in seconds?
q.e: Inspiratory time in seconds depends on total cycle time and the percentage allotted to inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 329)

q.q: Which end-flow does the chapter specify for the Puritan Bennett 840 descending ramp?
q.e: The Puritan Bennett 840 descending ramp ends at 5 L/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 329)

q.q: A flow-limited ventilator delivers a true descending ramp starting at 40 L/min. How long does it need to deliver approximately 0.67 L?
q.e: At the same peak flow, the ramp has half the average flow of the constant waveform and takes 2 seconds. (Chang 4th ed., p. 330)

q.q: Compared with the linear pressure rise during constant flow, pressure during descending ramp flow tends to ____.
q.e: Compared with the linear pressure rise during constant flow, pressure during descending ramp flow tends to square off. (Chang 4th ed., p. 330)

q.q: A passive patient receives a descending ramp that reaches zero flow just before cycling. Which pressure can be read directly at that instant?
q.e: Flow-resistive pressure reaches zero, so end-inspiratory airway pressure equals peak alveolar pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 330)

q.q: During a true descending ramp starting at 80 L/min, initial flow-resistive pressure is 40 cm H₂O and peak alveolar pressure at zero end-flow is 20 cm H₂O. The highest airway pressure occurs at ____.
o: the end of the expiratory pause
q.e: In this example, the fall in flow-resistive pressure offsets the rise in alveolar pressure throughout inspiration. Their sum, the airway opening pressure, is highest at the start of the ramp. (Chang 4th ed., p. 330)

q.q: During a true descending ramp, the amount of gas delivered in each successive equal interval ____.
q.e: During a true descending ramp, the amount of gas delivered in each successive equal interval decreases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 331)

q.q: A true descending ramp delivers 0.67 L. How much enters the lungs in the first half of inspiration?
q.e: The first half of inspiration accounts for 75% of the tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 331)

q.q: A true descending ramp starts at 80 L/min and ends at zero after 1 second. Which end-flow belongs in the calculation for the first half-second alone?
q.e: At the midpoint of the ramp, flow is 40 L/min. This is the end-flow for the first half of inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 332)

q.q: At equal VT and inspiratory time, mean alveolar pressure with a descending ramp is ____ that with constant flow.
q.e: At equal VT and inspiratory time, mean alveolar pressure with a descending ramp is higher than that with constant flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 332)

q.q: Why might oxygenation improve when a descending ramp replaces constant flow at the same VT and inspiratory time?
o: Alveoli stay more distended through inspiration
Alveoli receive most volume late in inspiration
Peak inspiratory flow occurs closer to expiration
q.e: With more volume delivered early, alveoli are more distended over inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 332)

q.q: For a 0.67-L tidal volume delivered at constant flow, what fraction and volume enter during the first half of inspiration?
q.e: Constant flow delivers half the tidal volume in half the inspiratory time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 332)

q.q: As total PALV rises during descending ramp ventilation, its slope progressively decreases, giving the PALV curve a ____ contour.
q.e: As total PALV rises during descending ramp ventilation, its slope progressively decreases, giving the PALV curve a convex contour. (Chang 4th ed., p. 333)

q.q: With circuit and lung mechanics unchanged, peak descending ramp flow is reduced while inspiratory time is held fixed. What happens to initial flow-resistive pressure?
q.e: Reducing peak flow lowers initial PTA and decreases the volume delivered over the same time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 333)

q.q: A Hamilton-style 50% descending ramp starts at 100 L/min. At what flow will it end?
q.e: A 50% ramp ends at half its initial peak flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 334)

q.q: If inspiratory flow is still 5 L/min when a descending ramp ends, end-inspiratory PAO lies ____ PALV.
q.e: Residual flow creates a small flow-resistive pressure above alveolar pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 334)

q.q: A true descending ramp peaks at 60 L/min and lasts 1 second. Which volumes enter during its first and second halves, respectively?
q.e: The ramp delivers 0.5 L in all, with three quarters entering in the first half. (Chang 4th ed., p. 335)

q.q: In a zero-PEEP example, 0.5 L produces a peak PALV of 40 cm H₂O. What is static compliance?
q.e: Dividing 500 mL by 40 cm H₂O gives 12.5 mL/cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 335)

q.q: A true descending ramp produces a peak PALV of 40 cm H₂O from a zero baseline. If compliance stays constant, what is PALV halfway through inspiration?
q.e: At the midpoint, 75% of the volume has entered and PALV has reached 75% of its peak. (Chang 4th ed., p. 335)

q.q: When true ramp duration doubles at the same peak flow, the initial flow-resistive pressure ____.
q.e: When true ramp duration doubles at the same peak flow, the initial flow-resistive pressure stays the same. (Chang 4th ed., p. 336)

q.q: During pressure-triggered assist/control ventilation, an inspiratory effort lowers airway pressure to the trigger threshold before each of the first two breaths. The next two breaths begin when the preset interval expires without an inspiratory effort. Who initiates the first pair and the next pair?
q.e: Patient effort reaches the pressure-trigger threshold for each of the first two breaths. The ventilator initiates the next two when the preset interval expires. (Chang 4th ed., p. 336)

q.q: In pressure-controlled CMV, the ventilator sustains the targeted pressure for a preset ____.
q.e: In pressure-controlled CMV, the ventilator sustains the targeted pressure for a preset inspiratory time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 337)

q.q: A pressure-controlled breath starts every 2 seconds. What frequency does this represent?
q.e: Frequency is 60 seconds divided by the time between successive inspirations. (Chang 4th ed., p. 337)

q.q: Which statement describes breath initiation during pressure-controlled CMV?
o: Either time or patient effort can trigger a breath
A timed trigger requires a simultaneous patient effort
Patient effort initiates expiration and the timer initiates inspiration
A fall in delivered tidal volume triggers the next breath
q.e: Either the ventilator or the patient can initiate a pressure-controlled breath. (Chang 4th ed., p. 337)

q.q: An air-hungry patient triggers PCV breaths with different flow patterns. Which measurement should remain at the target despite these changes?
q.e: The ventilator varies flow to sustain the targeted pressure, so tidal volume can fluctuate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 338)

q.q: In inverse ratio pressure-controlled ventilation, inspiratory time is ____ expiratory time.
q.e: In inverse ratio pressure-controlled ventilation, inspiratory time is longer than expiratory time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 338)

q.q: For which condition does the chapter describe using inverse ratio pressure-controlled ventilation?
q.e: The chapter describes inverse ratio PCV in severe hypoxemia and lung injury. (Chang 4th ed., p. 339)

q.q: When inspiratory flow ceases early during IRPCV, the ventilator holds gas in the lungs by curtailing flow and closing the ____.
q.e: When inspiratory flow ceases early during IRPCV, the ventilator holds gas in the lungs by curtailing flow and closing the expiratory valve. (Chang 4th ed., p. 339)

q.q: To calculate compliance during a no-flow period in PCV, subtract ____ from PIP before dividing expired VT by the pressure difference.
q.e: To calculate compliance during a no-flow period in PCV, subtract total PEEP from PIP before dividing expired VT by the pressure difference. (Chang 4th ed., p. 339)

q.q: Incomplete exhalation develops during PCV. Which consequence of the trapped gas should the therapist expect?
o: Higher FRC and lower delivered VT
Lower FRC and higher delivered VT
Lower FRC and lower delivered VT
Higher FRC and higher delivered VT
q.e: Trapped gas increases functional residual capacity, and auto-PEEP reduces the volume delivered at the set pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 339)

q.q: In IRPCV, the patient is often sedated and paralyzed to ____.
q.e: IRPCV offers an unnatural, uncomfortable breathing pattern, so the patient is often sedated and paralyzed to prevent patient-ventilator dyssynchrony. (Chang 4th ed., p. 339)

q.q: A relaxed patient breathing synchronously on PSV typically produces a square pressure trace and a ____ inspiratory flow trace.
q.e: A relaxed patient breathing synchronously on PSV typically produces a square pressure trace and a concave inspiratory flow trace. (Chang 4th ed., p. 340)

q.q: The chapter favors ____ over deliberately allowing auto-PEEP during inverse ratio ventilation.
q.e: The chapter favors external PEEP over deliberately allowing auto-PEEP during inverse ratio ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 340)

q.q: What is the intended oxygenation benefit of titrating inverse inspiratory time while monitoring for gas trapping?
o: Raise mean PALV at a lower peak PALV
Raise peak PALV at a lower mean PALV
Reduce both mean PALV and expiratory time
Reduce mean PALV and raise intrinsic PEEP
q.e: Increasing inspiratory time without trapping gas can raise mean alveolar pressure while limiting peak pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 340)

q.q: In the pressure support example with a 25% cycling criterion, expiration starts when flow falls to one quarter of ____.
q.e: In the pressure support example with a 25% cycling criterion, expiration starts when flow falls to one quarter of peak inspiratory flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 340)

q.q: The ventilator’s rise time percent describes the fraction of the inspiratory cycle needed to reach ____.
q.e: The ventilator’s rise time percent describes the fraction of the inspiratory cycle needed to reach peak flow and target pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 341)

q.q: A patient on PSV develops a pressure spike at the start of inspiration that overshoots the target. Which adjustment may improve comfort?
o: Slow the rise to peak flow
q.e: An excessively rapid rise can overshoot the pressure target and increase discomfort and work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 341)

q.q: At a sufficiently high level of pressure support, which effort may still be required when the rest of the breath is nearly passive?
q.e: High pressure support can unload nearly all patient effort after triggering. (Chang 4th ed., p. 341)

q.q: During PSV, the flow, volume, and inspiratory time are under the ____ control.
q.e: During PSV the patient controls the flow, volume, and inspiratory time; a faster initial rise to peak flow (short rise time) reaches the preset pressure support level sooner. (Chang 4th ed., p. 341)

q.q: In the combined SIMV plus PSV tracing with square mandatory flow, the breaths between the mandatory and assisted volume breaths receive ____.
q.e: In the combined SIMV plus PSV tracing with square mandatory flow, the breaths between the mandatory and assisted volume breaths receive pressure support. (Chang 4th ed., p. 342)

q.q: In Chang’s SIMV plus PSV example, the SIMV breaths use a descending ramp from 80 L/min to an end-flow of 5 L/min. When does airway pressure peak during those breaths?
q.e: The high initial flow produces a large resistive pressure at the start of the ramp, when airway pressure reaches its peak in this example. (Chang 4th ed., p. 343)

q.q: Whereas volume delivery is sustained during volume-controlled CMV, the quantity sustained in pressure-controlled ventilation as mechanics change is the ____.
q.e: Whereas volume delivery is sustained during volume-controlled CMV, the quantity sustained in pressure-controlled ventilation as mechanics change is the pressure target. (Chang 4th ed., p. 343)

q.q: With PCV pressure, compliance and effort unchanged, the initial flow falls and exhalation takes longer. Which change best explains both findings?
q.e: Greater resistance allows the target pressure to be reached at lower flow and reduces average expiratory flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 344)

q.q: When compliance alone falls during PCV, initial inspiratory flow is preserved because resistance and the initial ____ have not changed.
q.e: When compliance alone falls during PCV, initial inspiratory flow is preserved because resistance and the initial driving pressure have not changed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 344)

q.q: During PCV, initial flow is unchanged but decays more steeply as compliance falls. Which change explains the lower VT at the same inspiratory time?
q.e: A steeper fall after the same peak reduces the area under the inspiratory flow curve and therefore tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 345)

q.q: During mechanical ventilation, both disuse of the respiratory muscles and excessive work of breathing can delay ____.
q.e: During mechanical ventilation, both disuse of the respiratory muscles and excessive work of breathing can delay weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 345)

q.q: Which group of changes accompanies patient–ventilator dyssynchrony?
o: Increased oxygen consumption, minute ventilation and myocardial work
Decreased oxygen consumption, minute ventilation and myocardial work
Decreased oxygen consumption with increased myocardial work and ventilation
Increased oxygen consumption with decreased myocardial work and ventilation
q.e: Dyssynchrony increases work of breathing, oxygen consumption, minute ventilation and myocardial work. (Chang 4th ed., p. 345)

q.q: For a pressure-triggered breath, ventilator response time begins when the sensitivity threshold is reached and ends when ____.
q.e: For a pressure-triggered breath, ventilator response time begins when the sensitivity threshold is reached and ends when flow begins. (Chang 4th ed., p. 346)

q.q: A patient with weak ventilatory drive struggles to trigger at −3 cm H₂O. Which pressure sensitivity setting would ease triggering?
q.e: The less negative threshold requires less effort from a patient with weak drive. (Chang 4th ed., p. 346)

q.q: During the negative pressure deflection before positive pressure is recorded, circuit gas is ____.
q.e: During the negative pressure deflection before positive pressure is recorded, circuit gas is decompressed and recompressed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 346)

q.q: What approximate alveolar pressure accompanies normal spontaneous inspiration in the chapter’s comparison with pressure triggering?
q.e: During normal spontaneous inspiration, gas flows into expanding alveoli at an alveolar pressure of approximately −1 cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 346)

q.q: A ventilator reading of −2 cm H₂O during triggering can underestimate how negative the patient’s ____ pressure has become.
q.e: A ventilator reading of −2 cm H₂O during triggering can underestimate how negative the patient’s intrathoracic pressure has become. (Chang 4th ed., p. 347)

q.q: What respiratory frequency criterion accompanies agitation as an early sign of increased work of breathing in the chapter?
q.e: An early sign is tachypnea above 20/min together with agitation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 347)

q.q: Which finding tends to appear late as respiratory muscle fatigue progresses?
o: Blood gas evidence of respiratory failure
Agitation with a rising respiratory rate
q.e: Blood gas abnormalities may appear only after earlier physical signs of increased work. (Chang 4th ed., p. 347)

q.q: Which set lists signs of patient-ventilator dyssynchrony described in the chapter?
o: Tachypnea, agitation, and use of accessory respiratory muscles
Bradypnea, sedation, and decreased work of breathing
q.e: Signs of dyssynchrony include tachypnea, agitation, use of accessory respiratory muscles, active expiration, paradoxical breathing, and respiratory alternans. (Chang 4th ed., p. 347)

q.q: During constant-flow assistance, the initial pressure step nearly disappears as the patient draws gas almost as fast as it arrives. Which adjustment addresses the initial demand?
q.e: Increasing flow above the patient’s initial demand restores ventilator assistance and the pressure pattern. (Chang 4th ed., p. 348)

q.q: A volume-controlled breath begins with a normal pressure rise, but pressure falls just as the ventilator cycles. What is the patient still demanding?
q.e: The late pressure drop indicates that the ventilator cycles before the patient’s volume demand has been met. (Chang 4th ed., p. 348)

q.q: If adjustments to flow, volume and sensitivity fail to restore synchrony during VCV, the chapter describes changing to ____.
q.e: If adjustments to flow, volume and sensitivity fail to restore synchrony during VCV, the chapter describes changing to pressure-controlled ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 349)

q.q: Which factors can produce erratic breathing that a ventilator has difficulty matching?
o: Pain, neurologic damage and psychologic stress
Low circuit compliance and a slow rise time
Constant flow and a long expiratory pause
Reduced circuit resistance and a stable plateau
q.e: Pain, neurologic damage and psychologic stress can produce erratic breathing and may necessitate periods of sedation for rest. (Chang 4th ed., p. 349)

q.q: During an end-inspiratory hold, airway pressure rises above its relaxed plateau. Which respiratory effort accounts for the rise?
q.e: Expiratory effort during the hold can raise pressure above the relaxed plateau. (Chang 4th ed., p. 350)

q.q: Patient-ventilator dyssynchrony with a rising airway pressure during the pause time may occur when the patient ____.
o: continues to inspire during the pause
has a small leak in the circuit
q.e: Rising airway pressure during the pause may occur when the patient moves, talks, coughs, or expires; decreasing pressure suggests a small circuit leak or continued inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 350)

q.q: During an end-inspiratory hold, continued inspiratory effort can lower the measured pressure by expanding the thorax and ____ gas.
q.e: During an end-inspiratory hold, continued inspiratory effort can lower the measured pressure by expanding the thorax and decompressing gas. (Chang 4th ed., p. 351)

q.q: A relaxed patient’s airway pressure drifts downward during an inspiratory hold. Which circuit condition can cause this?
q.e: A leak can lower pressure during a pause and distort the static mechanics measurement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 351)

q.q: In the chapter’s description of static mechanics measurement, which PaCO₂ approximates the apneic threshold?
q.e: The chapter describes a 10% to 15% increase in minute ventilation to reduce PaCO₂ toward about 32 mm Hg and suppress effort during measurement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 351)

q.q: On a pressure-time waveform with an end-inspiratory pause, a decreasing airway pressure during the pause may occur when ____.
o: there is a small circuit leak or the patient continues to inspire
the patient actively expires during the pause
the patient coughs or talks during the pause
q.e: Dyssynchrony with decreasing airway pressure may occur with a small leak in the ventilator circuit or when the patient continues to inspire during the pause time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 351)

q.q: On PSV, a high inspiratory flow that stays nearly square and ends abruptly indicates ____.
q.e: A nearly square flow trace with abrupt cycling can reflect sustained inspiratory demand at the set support level. (Chang 4th ed., p. 352)

q.q: A distressed patient on PSV has forceful triggering, incomplete expiration and failure to sustain the support pressure. Which change does the chapter suggest for this example?
o: Increase pressure support to 15–20 cm H₂O
Reduce trigger sensitivity to −5 cm H₂O
Reduce pressure support to 3–5 cm H₂O
q.e: In this example, increasing pressure support may better meet demand and reduce work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 352)

q.q: With an 8-mm internal-diameter tube and humidifier at 60 L/min, what circuit resistance does the chapter describe as typical?
q.e: The circuit contribution can be subtracted from the measured resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 352)

q.q: In the severe obstruction example, which reported expiratory flow time accompanies low peak and average expiratory flow?
q.e: An expiratory flow time longer than 5 seconds accompanies severely elevated resistance in this example. (Chang 4th ed., p. 352)

q.q: At high PIP, an early sharp expiratory flow spike can represent decompression of gas previously compressed in the ____.
q.e: At high PIP, an early sharp expiratory flow spike can represent decompression of gas previously compressed in the ventilator circuit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 353)

q.q: A patient with exacerbated bronchitis has high PIP but a low expiratory circuit pressure. Why does the measured expiratory pressure fall?
o: Gas flows slowly through narrowed airways
Gas moves more rapidly through the circuit
Alveolar recoil drives a higher peak flow
A larger volume leaves during early expiration
q.e: Slow expiratory flow generates less flow-resistive pressure in the circuit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 353)

q.q: Which controlled rate and VT does the chapter describe for severe obstruction when limiting auto-PEEP?
q.e: The chapter describes low rates and low tidal volumes for a temporarily controlled patient with severe auto-PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 354)

q.q: In emphysema, loss of elastic recoil reduces the alveolar pressure that drives ____.
q.e: In emphysema, loss of elastic recoil reduces the alveolar pressure that drives expiratory flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 354)

q.q: In the example of diminished recoil, peak expiratory flow develops slowly and has a ____ contour.
q.e: In the example of diminished recoil, peak expiratory flow develops slowly and has a rounded contour. (Chang 4th ed., p. 355)

q.q: At unchanged flow and resistance, a patient with ARDS develops a higher PIP without a change in the initial resistive step. Which pressure accounts for the rise?
q.e: Reduced compliance raises the alveolar pressure required for inflation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 355)

q.q: With resistance unchanged, loss of lung-thorax compliance speeds lung emptying and ____ expiratory time.
q.e: With resistance unchanged, loss of lung-thorax compliance speeds lung emptying and shortens expiratory time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 355)

q.q: When expiratory flow abruptly slows toward zero and expiratory pressure falls with it, the patient may be attempting to ____ during expiration.
q.e: When expiratory flow abruptly slows toward zero and expiratory pressure falls with it, the patient may be attempting to inspire during expiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 356)

q.q: Several volume traces end above baseline. A later breath expires more volume than was inspired and crosses below baseline. What explains the larger expired breath?
o: A sustained increase in inspiratory flow
Progressive loss through a circuit leak
q.e: Trapped gas released on a later breath can make the expired volume exceed that breath’s inspired volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 356)

q.q: With hyperinflation, an ineffective inspiratory effort can slow expiratory flow without creating enough negative PAO to ____.
q.e: With hyperinflation, an ineffective inspiratory effort can slow expiratory flow without creating enough negative PAO to trigger a breath. (Chang 4th ed., p. 357)

q.q: During obstructed expiration, which event could cause expiratory flow and pressure to rise suddenly together?
q.e: Active expiration or transient relief of obstruction can increase both flow and expiratory pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 357)

q.q: The ventilator count appears too low during weaning assessment. Which bedside observation can be correlated with interruptions in expiratory flow?
o: Palpate the abdomen for respiratory efforts
Compare inspiratory and expiratory valve size
Measure the plateau after each timed breath
q.e: Palpation and observation during waveform monitoring can reveal efforts missed by the ventilator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 357)

q.q: A mismatch between the displayed pressure trigger and the set sensitivity can indicate a sticking inspiratory valve or ____.
q.e: A mismatch between the displayed pressure trigger and the set sensitivity can indicate a sticking inspiratory valve or a miscalibrated sensitivity threshold. (Chang 4th ed., p. 357)

q.q: During VCV, inspiratory flow is unchanged, expired volume persistently fails to reach baseline and PIP falls. What best explains this combination?
q.e: A leak reduces the volume reaching the lungs, lowering PIP and expired volume despite the same inspiratory flow pattern. (Chang 4th ed., p. 358)

q.q: A leak in a circuit with PEEP can generate extra mechanical breaths when circuit pressure falls to the ____.
q.e: A leak-induced pressure drop can trigger rapid breaths without patient effort. (Chang 4th ed., p. 359)

q.q: On a conventionally displayed pressure-volume loop (unlike the Servo 300 display), which variables are read from the horizontal and vertical axes, respectively?
q.e: Standard pressure-volume loops in the chapter plot airway opening pressure horizontally (x-axis) and volume vertically (y-axis), whereas some ventilators such as the Servo 300 reverse those axes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 359)

q.q: A control breath on the pressure-volume loop begins without ____ to initiate the mechanical breath.
q.e: A control breath on the pressure-volume loop begins without negative pressure to initiate the mechanical breath. (Chang 4th ed., p. 360)

q.q: On a loop with volume plotted vertically and pressure horizontally, inflation shifts down and to the right. Which change is illustrated?
q.e: The shift toward the pressure axis indicates that more pressure is needed to inflate the less compliant system. (Chang 4th ed., p. 360)

q.q: On a ventilator that plots pressure vertically and volume horizontally, reduced compliance moves the loop ____.
q.e: On a ventilator that plots pressure vertically and volume horizontally, reduced compliance moves the loop up and to the left. (Chang 4th ed., p. 361)

q.q: At constant volume and flow, PIP rises from 30 to 40 cm H₂O and peak PALV from 25 to 35 cm H₂O. What happens to the resistive gradient?
q.e: Both pressures rise together as compliance falls, preserving their difference. (Chang 4th ed., p. 361)

q.q: Which pressure-volume finding favors increased airflow resistance at constant flow and volume?
o: A wider resistive gradient with stable PALV
An unchanged resistive gradient with rising PALV
A narrower resistive gradient with rising PALV
An unchanged resistive gradient with falling PALV
q.e: Increased resistance raises transairway pressure during inspiration and expiration while alveolar pressure remains unchanged. (Chang 4th ed., p. 361)

q.q: An alternative to using the inspiratory inflection point is to set PEEP above the ____ on the expiratory limb.
q.e: An alternative to using the inspiratory inflection point is to set PEEP above the closing alveolar pressure on the expiratory limb. (Chang 4th ed., p. 362)

q.q: In a homogeneous lung, the initial point of inflection marks a change from low compliance to ____.
q.e: In a homogeneous lung, the initial point of inflection marks a change from low compliance to improved compliance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 362)

q.q: In the historical approach using a clearly identified initial inflection point, how far above that pressure was PEEP suggested to prevent closure?
q.e: Some studies suggested setting PEEP about 2 cm H₂O above the initial inflection point. The chapter notes that the usefulness of this approach is disputed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 362)

q.q: Why does the chapter caution against applying a single initial inflection point to ARDS lungs?
o: Lung units differ in compliance and opening pressure
Lung units share a common opening pressure
Lung recoil is uniform throughout inspiration
The expiratory limb has no closing pressure
q.e: The initial inflection point described for homogeneous lungs does not apply to heterogeneous ARDS lungs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 362)

q.q: Repeated opening and closing of alveoli during mechanical ventilation can cause ____ of lung parenchyma.
q.e: Repeated opening and closing of alveoli during mechanical ventilation can cause shearing of lung parenchyma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 362)

q.q: After bronchodilation improves expiratory flow during constant-flow VCV, the inspiratory limb retains its flow level because that flow is ____.
q.e: After bronchodilation improves expiratory flow during constant-flow VCV, the inspiratory limb retains its flow level because that flow is set by the ventilator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 363)

q.q: The historically described “duckbill” at the top of a pressure-volume loop reflects late loss of compliance from alveolar ____.
q.e: The historically described “duckbill” at the top of a pressure-volume loop reflects late loss of compliance from alveolar hyperdistention. (Chang 4th ed., p. 363)

q.q: In the historical duckbill interpretation, which change was made until the abnormal upper loop shape disappeared?
q.e: Tidal volume was reduced until the duckbill disappeared. The chapter describes the accuracy of this upper inflection point as uncertain. (Chang 4th ed., p. 363)

q.q: On a conventionally displayed ventilator flow-volume loop, the horizontal axis represents ____.
q.e: On the illustrated flow-volume loop, the horizontal axis represents volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 363)

q.q: Two flow-volume loops are superimposed before and after bronchodilator therapy. Which change in the expiratory limb supports reduced airflow resistance?
q.e: A greater peak expiratory flow magnitude is consistent with reduced resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 364)

q.q: To compare waveform contours before and after therapy, the therapist can ____ the saved baseline tracings.
o: swap the pressure and flow scales of
q.e: To compare waveform contours before and after therapy, the therapist can superimpose follow-up tracings on the saved baseline tracings. (Chang 4th ed., p. 364)

q.q: Which pair of settings, when increased as indicated, markedly improves oxygenation while ventilation may stay the same or decrease?
q.e: Increasing FIO2 or PEEP primarily improves oxygenation. Increasing frequency, tidal volume, pressure support, or the pressure gradient primarily improves ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 375)

q.q: In a patient with COPD, the reference PaCO2 for judging hypoventilation is the value ____.
o: at the onset of an exacerbation
at the start of oxygen therapy
q.e: The usual PaCO2 range is 35–45 mm Hg. The discharge baseline for a patient with COPD is generally about 50 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 376)

q.q: The first priority for improving ventilation is to increase the ____.
q.e: Increase ventilator frequency first, spontaneous VT second, and ventilator VT third. The chapter advises a rate ceiling of 20/min because auto-PEEP may occur at or above that frequency. (Chang 4th ed., p. 376)

q.q: Gas in the endotracheal tube or ventilator circuit that does not participate in gas exchange constitutes ____.
q.e: Low-compliance tubing, appropriate ET tube length, and tracheotomy reduce mechanical deadspace. High frequency jet or oscillatory ventilation follows deadspace reduction in the priority table. (Chang 4th ed., p. 376)

q.q: At 12 breaths/min, PaCO2 is 60 mm Hg. With tidal volume and deadspace unchanged, which rate is predicted to yield a PaCO2 of 45 mm Hg?
q.e: Multiply the original rate by the original PaCO2 and divide by the desired PaCO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 377)

q.q: When spontaneous breathing becomes rapid and shallow, unchanged anatomic deadspace occupies ____ of each tidal volume.
