q.e: Minute ventilation is the sum of ventilator VT times ventilator rate and spontaneous VT times spontaneous rate. With rapid, shallow breaths, anatomic deadspace stays the same as spontaneous VT falls, increasing VD/VT. (Chang 4th ed., p. 377)

q.q: What initial pressure support range does the chapter give when starting PSV for a patient whose respiratory muscles cannot maintain prolonged spontaneous ventilation?
q.e: For a patient whose respiratory muscles cannot sustain spontaneous ventilation, Chang gives an initial pressure support of 10–15 cm H₂O, titrated to the desired spontaneous tidal volume. When the aim is to offset circuit and endotracheal tube resistance, Chang describes titrating support below 10 cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 377)

q.q: During spontaneous breathing, pressure support above 20 cm H2O produces a pattern resembling ____.
q.e: PSV acts only during spontaneous breaths and increases spontaneous VT and minute ventilation. Levels below 10 cm H2O are used to offset circuit and tube resistance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 378)

q.q: Which change is attributed to an inadequately small ventilator tidal volume?
q.e: Excessive VT increases injury risk, whereas inadequate VT can cause hypoventilation and atelectasis. Increasing VT is reserved for a rate that already exceeds the patient's ideal pattern and I:E ratio. (Chang 4th ed., p. 378)

q.q: What tidal volume range does the chapter associate with permissive hypercapnia?
q.e: Reducing VT lowers peak inspiratory pressure but can produce CO2 retention and acidosis. Plateau pressure estimates average peak alveolar pressure and may be kept at or below 35 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 379)

q.q: In permissive hypercapnia, the nonbicarbonate buffer that indirectly decreases CO2 and raises bicarbonate is ____.
q.e: Tromethamine directly lowers hydrogen ion concentration. Renal compensation or buffering can restore pH to 7.35–7.45. (Chang 4th ed., p. 379)

q.q: Which product gives the chapter's dose calculation for 0.3 M tromethamine?
o: Body weight in kg × base deficit in mEq/L
Base deficit in mEq/L × respiratory rate per minute
Plasma bicarbonate in mEq/L × tidal volume in liters
q.e: The dose calculation uses body weight and base deficit. Adverse effects include transient hypoglycemia, respiratory depression, and hemorrhagic hepatic necrosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 379)

q.q: CO2 retention during low-volume ventilation can cause acidosis that increases ____.
q.e: Other complications include intracranial hypertension, central nervous dysfunction, weakness, and cardiovascular impairment. With normalization of pH, the chapter describes use in status asthmaticus and ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 379)

q.q: Oxygenation depends on a balance among ventilation, diffusion, and ____.
q.e: Supplemental oxygen increases the alveolar-capillary oxygen pressure gradient and readily corrects hypoxemia from uncomplicated V/Q mismatch. (Chang 4th ed., p. 380)

q.q: In the stepwise strategy for improving oxygenation, which priority comes after improving ventilation and reducing deadspace and immediately before maintaining normal hemoglobin?
q.e: Circulatory measures include fluid replacement for hypovolemia, vasopressors for shock, and cardiac drugs for congestive heart failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 380)

q.q: In the prioritized oxygenation strategies, the mode listed after CPAP and immediately before PEEP titration is ____.
q.e: After PEEP, the table lists inverse ratio ventilation, then prone positioning, then consideration of ECMO, high frequency ventilation, or hyperbaric oxygenation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 380)

q.q: Without significant shunt or deadspace abnormalities, the desired PaO2 is 80 mm Hg and the a/A ratio is 0.40. What FIO2 does the chapter's estimate predict?
q.e: Divide desired PaO2 by the prechange arterial/alveolar ratio to obtain needed PAO2. Add 50 and divide by 713 to estimate FIO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 381)

q.q: When elevated PaCO2 accompanies hypoxemia from hypoventilation, the chapter calls for ____.
q.e: Improving ventilation may partially correct the hypoxemia. Shunt-related refractory hypoxemia may require oxygen with CPAP or PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 381)

q.q: Which FIO2 cutoff and maximum duration of high-FIO2 exposure does the chapter specify to limit oxygen toxicity?
o: FIO2 below 60%, high FIO2 for less than 24 hours
FIO2 below 50%, high FIO2 for less than 48 hours
FIO2 below 80%, high FIO2 for less than 12 hours
FIO2 below 70%, high FIO2 for less than 36 hours
q.e: The chapter targets PaO2 around 80 mm Hg, lower in COPD. Exposure to 100% oxygen may cause complications within 12–24 hours, including ciliary impairment, lung damage, respiratory distress syndrome, and fibrosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 381)

q.q: When ventilation exceeds perfusion, alveolar deadspace can be reduced by improving ____.
q.e: Alveolar ventilation can be improved by reducing anatomic, mechanical, or alveolar deadspace. PaCO2 is the best indicator of ventilatory status. (Chang 4th ed., p. 382)

q.q: A patient in shock has relative hypovolemia from loss of venous tone. Why does the chapter advise caution with fluid replacement?
o: Volume overload may follow recovery of vascular tone.
Alveolar deadspace rises as pulmonary flow recovers.
Hemoglobin loses oxygen as vascular tone recovers.
Myocardial function falls as deadspace decreases.
q.e: Restoration of venous tone can lead to overload after fluid replacement, while vasopressors can provide rapid relief during shock. When congestive heart failure causes hypoperfusion, improving myocardial function may correct it. (Chang 4th ed., p. 382)

q.q: The chapter calls for reporting anemia with arterial blood gases when hemoglobin falls below ____.
q.e: PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen, while hemoglobin carries more than 98% of blood oxygen. CO-oximetry evaluates hemoglobin and arterial oxygen content. (Chang 4th ed., p. 382)

q.q: A steadily rising PaCO2 during CPAP suggests that the patient is ____.
q.e: CPAP requires sustainable spontaneous ventilation. CPAP and PEEP increase functional residual capacity, and PEEP can accompany mechanical breaths without spontaneous breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 383)

q.q: At PEEP levels of 0, 5, 8, 10, and 12 cm H2O, compliance measures 26, 33, 37, 43, and 41 mL/cm H2O. Which level is optimal in this trial?
q.e: The corresponding PaO2 values are 43, 67, 77, 83, and 79 mm Hg. Optimal PEEP is the lowest level giving the best indicator value without significant cardiopulmonary complications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 383)

q.q: For a stable patient at minimal risk of PEEP complications, the text advises lowering FIO2 to ____ before decreasing PEEP.
q.e: The weaning table starts with FIO2 at 40% or 50%, then reduces PEEP by 2–3 cm H2O to about 3 cm H2O. It calls for PaO2 above 60 mm Hg or SpO2 above 90% and observation for hypoxia or increased work after discontinuation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 384)

q.q: Inverse ratio ventilation can prolong inspiration by lowering inspiratory flow or by lengthening ____.
o: the time spent at end expiration
q.e: Longer inspiration expands collapsed alveoli, overcomes noncompliant tissue, and allows more diffusion time. The rise in mean airway pressure can impair cardiovascular function. (Chang 4th ed., p. 384)

q.q: Which population does the chapter identify as having considerable success with ECMO for severe refractory hypoxemia?
q.e: The chapter identifies infants as the group with considerable success and reports no adult oxygenation advantage over conventional ventilation with PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 385)

q.q: An adult receiving HFOV remains hypercapnic despite an increase in amplitude. Which frequency adjustment increases tidal volume?
o: Lower frequency by 1 Hz every 30 minutes to 3 Hz.
Raise frequency by 2 Hz every 10 minutes to 12 Hz.
Lower frequency by 2 Hz every 10 minutes to 1 Hz.
Raise frequency by 1 Hz every 30 minutes to 8 Hz.
q.e: Higher amplitude or lower frequency treats hypoventilation during HFOV. For rising PaCO2 with pH above 7.2, amplitude can be increased by 10 cm H2O every 30 minutes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 385)

q.q: In the chapter's adult HFOV procedure, which mean airway pressure maneuver is described for severe hypoxia?
q.e: Mean pressure can subsequently rise by 3–5 cm H2O every 30 minutes. Oxygenation may initially worsen, and a chest radiograph is obtained within four hours to assess lung volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 385)

q.q: When initiating adult HFOV, the suggested mean airway pressure exceeds the previous conventional mean by ____.
q.e: Start frequency at 5–6 Hz, inspiratory time at 33%, and FIO2 at 100%, with inspiratory time up to 50% if ventilation remains inadequate. As oxygenation improves, wean FIO2 to 40% before reducing mean pressure by 2–3 cm H2O at a time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 385)

q.q: During initiation of adult HFOV, power starts at ____ and is increased rapidly to produce chest wiggle.
q.e: Power ranges from 1 to 10 and controls oscillation amplitude. Chest wiggle extends from shoulder to midthigh. (Chang 4th ed., p. 386)

q.q: After switching from HFOV to pressure control at 20–25/min, I:E 1:1, and PEEP 12 cm H2O, what delivered VT is targeted?
q.e: The chapter describes reducing mean pressure every 4–6 hours to 22–24 cm H2O before switching. During pressure control, plateau and mean airway pressures are kept below 35 and 20 cm H2O, respectively. (Chang 4th ed., p. 386)

q.q: The ABG is pH 7.43, PaCO2 50 mm Hg, and HCO3− 32 mEq/L. Which acid-base condition fits these values?
q.e: The table contrasts this result with compensated respiratory acidosis at 7.38/52/30 and primary respiratory acidosis at 7.31/53/26. Increasing support during compensation for metabolic alkalosis can further compromise spontaneous breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 387)

q.q: Reducing ventilator frequency while the patient is hyperventilating to compensate for metabolic acidosis risks ____.
q.e: The metabolic cause must be treated. Lowering the rate leaves the patient to sustain compensatory ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 387)

q.q: For persistent respiratory alkalosis, additional deadspace tubing is sometimes placed between the ET tube and the ____.
o: inspiratory flow sensor at the ventilator
q.e: Additional deadspace in this location may partially correct persistent respiratory alkalosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 387)

q.q: A patient's pH is 7.37, PaCO2 is 25 mm Hg, and HCO3− is 14 mEq/L. Which interpretation is correct?
q.e: A near-normal acidic pH with low HCO3− and low PaCO2 indicates compensated metabolic acidosis. By contrast, 7.42/27/17 represents compensated respiratory alkalosis and 7.51/30/23 primary respiratory alkalosis; clinical presentation helps distinguish the conditions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 388)

q.q: A patient with COPD may hyperventilate and appear to have partially compensated metabolic alkalosis when ventilator settings are improper or when ____ develops.
q.e: Acute hypoxia, improper settings, and metabolic acidosis can drive hyperventilation. If hypoxia persists, reducing ventilator rate can leave the patient hyperventilating until the muscles fatigue. (Chang 4th ed., p. 388)

q.q: During a premature weaning attempt, a tiring patient develops pH 7.30, PaCO2 50 mm Hg, and HCO3− 24 mEq/L. Which response addresses the cause?
o: Continue weaning at a lower rate.
q.e: Acute respiratory acidosis may reflect respiratory muscle fatigue or excessive sedation. Blood gases must be interpreted alongside clinical signs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 389)

q.q: Renal failure, diabetic ketoacidosis, and lactic acidosis are major causes of ____.
q.e: Hypokalemia is a major cause of metabolic alkalosis. Primary metabolic disorders are treated by correcting their causes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 389)

q.q: The low expired volume limit is 400 mL. Exhaled volume falls to 390 mL and the low pressure alarm sounds. Which finding indicates loss of circuit pressure?
o: Failure of the source gas supply
q.e: Loss of circuit pressure commonly lowers both pressure and delivered volume. System pressure loss, premature termination of inspiration, and inappropriate settings are other categories to check. (Chang 4th ed., p. 390)

q.q: A ventilator set with its low pressure limit above the patient's peak inspiratory pressure will signal ____.
q.e: A low pressure limit above PIP and a low tidal volume limit above VT are examples of inappropriate alarm settings. (Chang 4th ed., p. 390)

q.q: Which group triggers high pressure through decreased lung or chest wall compliance?
o: Water in the circuit, cuff herniation, and coughing
Kinked tubing, a mucus plug, and biting
q.e: Tension pneumothorax also decreases compliance. The high pressure alarm sounds when circuit pressure reaches or exceeds its set limit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 391)

q.q: A high frequency alarm compares the preset limit with the ____.
q.e: Tachypnea and autotriggering from excessive sensitivity can drive total frequency above the alarm limit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 391)

q.q: Very small patient movements trigger repeated ventilator breaths when the trigger is ____.
o: set for a high backup rate
q.e: Autotriggering raises total frequency. Persistent tachypnea shortens expiration, raises mean airway pressure, and alters ventilation/perfusion, so its cause requires investigation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 392)

q.q: An apnea alarm sounds and the ventilator enters backup ventilation. Which connection should the therapist check first for the most frequent trigger?
q.e: A disconnected circuit prevents sensing of respiratory effort. Respiratory depressants, paralysis, respiratory center dysfunction, and muscle fatigue can also trigger the alarm. (Chang 4th ed., p. 392)

q.q: When measured PEEP falls below its low alarm limit, the usual explanation is ____.
q.e: Low PEEP reflects failure to hold pressure. Air trapping, long inspiration, or short expiration can instead produce auto-PEEP and a high PEEP alarm. (Chang 4th ed., p. 392)

q.q: To measure intrinsic PEEP accurately in a sedated or paralyzed patient, occlude the expiratory port ____.
q.e: Auto-PEEP may be seen on a pressure-time waveform. Distal airway pressure can reach 15 cm H2O despite zero pressure at the proximal manometer. (Chang 4th ed., p. 393)

q.q: For small-airway trapping that persists after setting changes, the chapter keeps therapeutic PEEP below what percentage of measured auto-PEEP?
q.e: Reduce VT or rate, increase inspiratory flow to lengthen expiration, or relieve obstruction. Therapeutic PEEP for this purpose is excluded in fixed large-airway obstruction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 393)

q.q: With intrinsic PEEP of 6 cm H2O, external PEEP of 5 cm H2O, and a trigger 2 cm H2O below external PEEP, what pressure change triggers a breath?
q.e: The figure gives a gradient of 2 cm H2O without auto-PEEP, 8 with auto-PEEP alone, and 3 after applying external PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 394)

q.q: At a peak pressure of 40 cm H2O, how much set VT is held in tubing with compliance of 3 mL/cm H2O?
q.e: Compressible volume equals circuit compliance times pressure. At the same pressure, a circuit with compliance of 5 mL/cm H2O holds 200 mL. (Chang 4th ed., p. 395)

q.q: A heated-wire circuit and an inline water trap address the common threat to circuit patency posed by ____.
q.e: Gas from a heated humidifier cools on its way to the patient. Water then collects in the tubing and can obstruct airflow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 395)

q.q: What output does the chapter report for a heat and moisture exchanger?
q.e: The HME absorbs heat and moisture during expiration on a surface impregnated with CaCl2 or AlCl2 and returns them during inspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 395)

q.q: Which patient finding meets a stated contraindication to HME use?
q.e: Contraindications include minute volume above 10 L/min, temperature below 32°C, copious thick secretions, and need for aerosolized medications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 396)

q.q: When a metered-dose inhaler is used with an HME, place the inhaler ____.
o: between the HME and circuit Y
q.e: The inhaler is placed on the patient side of the exchanger. (Chang 4th ed., p. 396)

q.q: With the humidifier temperature probe in the inspiratory limb near the patient, what distal temperature is targeted?
q.e: Temperature and water content determine water vapor saturation. The distal reading guides the humidifier setting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 397)

q.q: In the studies cited in the chapter, the optimal interval for ventilator circuit change was ____.
q.e: The chapter also advises changing humidifier or HME circuits when visibly soiled. Weekly changes saved labor and cost without increasing nosocomial infection compared with more frequent changes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 397)

q.q: Retained mucus halves the effective airway radius. By what factor must driving pressure rise to maintain the same flow?
q.e: Driving pressure varies inversely with the fourth power of radius at constant flow. The chapter emphasizes appropriate tube diameter, adequate humidification, and prompt secretion removal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 397)

q.q: Preoxygenation and closed inline suction help limit suction-induced hypoxia; total suction time should be no more than ____.
q.e: Closed suction maintains FIO2 and PEEP without circuit disconnection. Weekly catheter changes showed no significant increase in VAP compared with daily changes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 398)

q.q: Which practice does the chapter describe as lacking support for thinning secretions or stimulating a cough?
o: Instilling saline directly into the airway
Providing humidity through a heated circuit
Providing humidity with an artificial nose
q.e: Direct saline instillation has been implicated in lower-airway contamination. The chapter calls for aseptic equipment handling and sterile suction technique. (Chang 4th ed., p. 398)

q.q: Which incidence and fatality ranges does the chapter report for ventilator-associated pneumonia, respectively?
q.e: VAP is lung parenchymal infection related to events during mechanical ventilation. Potential sources include the oropharynx, caregivers' hands, respiratory equipment, ET and nasogastric tubes, and manual ventilation bags. (Chang 4th ed., p. 399)

q.q: Along with handwashing, closed suction, and continuous-feed humidification, the chapter recommends head-of-bed elevation to ____ for VAP prevention.
q.e: The chapter also recommends changing circuits when visibly soiled. Early microbiologic examination helps guide antibiotic selection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 399)

q.q: On Gram stain, bacteria such as Pseudomonas take up ____.
q.e: Gram-positive bacteria retain purple gentian violet. Culture and sensitivity grows organisms and tests their response to antimicrobial drugs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 399)

q.q: Which test pairing matches the suspected infections in the chapter?
q.e: Gram staining rapidly identifies a general bacterial category. Empiric therapy can start before pathogen confirmation when the presentation suggests a likely organism. (Chang 4th ed., p. 400)

q.q: On the sputum collecting tube, the lower outlet connects to the ____.
q.e: The upper outlet connects to vacuum and the lower outlet to the suction catheter. After collection, the free end of the rubber tubing is placed on the upper arm to seal the specimen. (Chang 4th ed., p. 400)

q.q: The term for antibiotic treatment begun on clinical grounds before confirmation of the pathogen is ____.
q.e: The presentation may suggest a likely organism before a Gram stain or culture and sensitivity study is obtained. (Chang 4th ed., p. 400)

q.q: Extracellular fluid (ECF) in the plasma and interstitial space is mainly affected by the ____ concentration in the plasma.
q.e: ECF is fluid in the plasma and interstitial space (20% of body weight ) and is mainly affected by plasma sodium concentration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 400)

q.q: Which distribution expresses plasma, interstitial fluid, and intracellular fluid as percentages of body weight, respectively?
q.e: Water accounts for about 60% of body weight. Plasma and interstitial fluid form the extracellular compartment. (Chang 4th ed., p. 401)

q.q: The chapter uses an hourly urine output below ____ as a criterion for oliguria.
q.e: The chapter also lists 400 mL in 24 hours or 160 mL in eight hours as cutoffs. Inadequate intake, excessive loss, or fluid shifts into cells and tissues can produce ECF deficit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 401)

q.q: A patient has a bounding pulse, an accentuated pulmonic P2, pulmonary edema, and increased urine output. Which disturbance fits this pattern?
q.e: ECF deficit can instead cause diminished sensorium or coma, tachycardia, hypotension, cold extremities, weak pulses, and oliguria or anuria. (Chang 4th ed., p. 401)

q.q: The replacement fluid recommended because its composition resembles extracellular fluid is ____.
q.e: Physiologic 0.9% saline is an alternative. A falling heart rate and rising blood pressure and urine output indicate improvement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 402)

q.q: Furosemide has increased a patient's urine output. Which finding best indicates that ECF excess itself has improved?
q.e: Reduction in pulse intensity and disappearance of the accentuated pulmonic P2 also indicate improvement. Fluid restriction or furosemide may be used, with electrolyte monitoring during diuresis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 402)

q.q: For ECF excess, the chapter cautions against mannitol because before diuresis it can ____.
q.e: Pulmonary edema is a common manifestation of excessive ECF. Mannitol may expand plasma volume before inducing diuresis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 402)

q.q: Which normal anion gap ranges correspond to calculations with and without potassium, respectively?
q.e: The anion gap is the difference between the selected plasma cations and anions. Sodium predominates in ECF and potassium in ICF. (Chang 4th ed., p. 402)

q.q: After fluid replacement for an ECF deficit, which set of changes indicates improvement?
o: Decreased heart rate, increased blood pressure and urine output
Increased heart rate, increased blood pressure and decreased urine output
Increased heart rate, decreased blood pressure and urine output
Decreased heart rate, decreased blood pressure and urine output
q.e: A decrease in heart rate and an increase in blood pressure and urine output are signs of improvement in ECF deficit after fluid replacement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 402)

q.q: Which expression gives the anion gap when potassium is included?
q.e: The calculation adds sodium and potassium and subtracts chloride and bicarbonate. The alternative calculation omits potassium. (Chang 4th ed., p. 403)

q.q: What are the normal mean plasma concentrations of sodium, chloride, potassium, and bicarbonate, respectively, in mEq/L?
q.e: The listed intervals are 138–142 for sodium, 101–105 for chloride, 3–5 for potassium, and 23–27 for bicarbonate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 403)

q.q: What are the normal mean plasma concentrations of calcium, magnesium, and protein, respectively, in mEq/L?
q.e: The listed intervals are 4.5–5.5 for calcium, 1.5–2.5 for magnesium, and 14–18 for protein. (Chang 4th ed., p. 403)

q.q: What are the normal mean plasma concentrations of phosphate, sulfate, and organic acids, respectively, in mEq/L?
q.e: The intervals are 1.5–2.5 for phosphate, 0.8–1.2 for sulfate, and 3.5–4.5 for organic acids. Total cations and total anions each measure 151 mEq/L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 403)

q.q: Of the major sodium and potassium disturbances, watery diarrhea with loss of reflexes and increased intracranial pressure points to ____.
q.e: Hyponatremia can produce oliguria to anuria. Hypernatremia can produce weakness, delirium, tachycardia, severe hypotension, and oliguria. (Chang 4th ed., p. 403)

q.q: For hyponatremia associated with hypovolemia, which saline regimen does the chapter describe?
q.e: Hyponatremia commonly accompanies ECF deficit. Sodium-free fluid can enter brain and kidney cells by osmosis and cause edema. (Chang 4th ed., p. 404)

q.q: After prolonged IV fluid administration with sufficient sodium but no dextrose, hypernatremia usually reflects ____.
q.e: The chapter describes reversal with water supplemented with dextrose. (Chang 4th ed., p. 404)

q.q: The chapter uses potassium chloride to replace potassium because hypokalemia commonly coexists with ____.
q.e: Losses with vomiting, diuretics, trauma, or infection and inadequate replacement during prolonged IV infusion can cause potassium deficiency. Replacement may be oral or by slow IV infusion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 404)

q.q: Which ECG change is seen in mild hyperkalemia but not in hypokalemia?
q.e: Hypokalemia produces a flattened T wave and depressed ST segment, while mild hyperkalemia produces an elevated T wave and depressed ST segment; ST depression occurs in both. Hyperkalemia increases neuromuscular conduction and bowel activity and can progress to arrhythmias or cardiac arrest, while hypokalemia reduces muscle and bowel activity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 404)

q.q: Which hourly dose, 24-hour dose, and drip concentration are the upper limits for IV potassium replacement stated in the chapter?
q.e: The chapter favors oral replacement. Its IV precautions require urine output of at least 40–50 mL/hour and dilution of KCl because undiluted KCl can cause arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. (Chang 4th ed., p. 405)

q.q: Hyperkalemia with renal failure and urine output below 200–300 mL/day results from ____.
q.e: Improving kidney function addresses this form of hyperkalemia. The chapter identifies emergency hemodialysis for life-threatening hyperkalemia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 405)

q.q: Which intervention for acute hyperkalemia is described as antagonizing cardiac toxicity in a patient who is not receiving digitalis?
q.e: Bicarbonate, insulin, and glucose promote cellular potassium uptake. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate and, with normal renal function, furosemide promote elimination. (Chang 4th ed., p. 405)

q.q: In an undernourished patient with severe hypoalbuminemia, interstitial and pulmonary edema follow a fall in ____.
q.e: Fluid shifts into interstitial tissue and eventually the alveoli. Undernutrition also depletes diaphragmatic glycogen and protein, contributing to fatigue, hypercapnia, and inability to wean. (Chang 4th ed., p. 405)

q.q: Which complication is listed for overfeeding but is absent from the undernutrition list?
q.e: Overfeeding increases oxygen consumption, CO2 production, and work of breathing. Undernutrition can impair wound healing, pulmonary function, and cell-mediated immunity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 406)

q.q: In patients with limited pulmonary reserve, a high-calorie enteric feeding can increase oxygen consumption and CO2 production enough to cause ____.
q.e: High-calorie enteric feeding can increase respiratory quotient. Respiratory acidosis has also been reported within hours of starting intravenous total parenteral nutrition. (Chang 4th ed., p. 406)

q.q: How much energy does 1 g of hydrous dextrose provide compared with 1 g of fat emulsion?
q.e: The chapter assigns 3.4 kcal per gram to hydrous dextrose and 9.1 kcal per gram to fat emulsion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 406)

q.q: The specified minimum fat contribution in the chapter's fat-based diet is ____ of total kilocalories.
q.e: This concentrated energy source suits fluid restriction and can reduce CO2 production and ventilatory requirements. In a COPD study, 28% carbohydrate and 55% fat were associated with 22% improvements in FVC and FEV1. (Chang 4th ed., p. 407)

q.q: The minimum energy needed for basic metabolism is called ____.
q.e: Harris-Benedict estimates energy expenditure, while metabolic testing measures it. TEE accounts for activity and stress as well as resting needs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 407)

q.q: Below which serum phosphate cutoff does the chapter describe reduced tissue ATP and possible confusion, weakness, heart failure, or respiratory failure?
q.e: Reported hypophosphatemia frequencies are about 30% in ICU admissions, 65–80% with sepsis, 75% with major trauma, and 21.5% with COPD. (Chang 4th ed., p. 407)

q.q: For weight W in kg, height H in cm, and age A in years, which Harris-Benedict expression estimates resting kcal/day for men?
q.e: The corresponding equation for women is 655 + 9.6W + 1.85H − 4.7A. (Chang 4th ed., p. 408)

q.q: A bedbound patient with major sepsis has an estimated REE of 1,500 kcal/day. Which expression gives the estimated daily TEE?
q.e: The activity multiplier is 1.2 in bed or 1.3 out of bed. Stress multipliers are 1.20 for minor operation, 1.35 for skeletal trauma, 1.60 for major sepsis, and 2.10 for severe thermal burn. (Chang 4th ed., p. 408)

q.q: The volume-selection section gives a plateau pressure target of less than ____ for volume-targeted ventilation in ALI or ARDS.
q.e: Plateau pressure reflects the condition of the lung parenchyma. Select the lowest VT that meets minimal ventilation and oxygenation needs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 409)

q.q: An air leak into the pleural space caused by excessive lung pressure or volume is termed ____.
q.e: The chapter also uses the term volutrauma. Conventional tidal volumes can exacerbate lung injury in ALI or ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 409)

q.q: Which cluster of complications can follow low tidal volume ventilation?
q.e: Other listed complications are increased work of breathing and severe acidosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 409)

q.q: Turning an ARDS patient face down can improve compliance and oxygenation while reducing ____.
q.e: Prone positioning can improve alveolar inflation and gas distribution. As more perfused alveoli receive ventilation, intrapulmonary shunting decreases and oxygenation can improve. (Chang 4th ed., p. 409)

q.q: Which expression gives the oxygen index used to assess a supine ARDS patient for prone positioning?
q.e: The chapter gives a rising OI above 30% during supine mechanical ventilation as the primary indication. It reports rapid oxygenation improvement without increased survival. (Chang 4th ed., p. 410)

q.q: A patient with ARDS has a rising oxygen index. Which finding is a contraindication to turning the patient prone?
q.e: Other contraindications are raised intracranial pressure, hemodynamic instability, recent thoracic or abdominal surgery, flail chest, and intolerance of the position. (Chang 4th ed., p. 410)

q.q: After one hour prone, a patient's oxygen index improves from 40 to 30. How does the chapter classify this response?
q.e: After one hour of stabilization, the procedure identifies an improvement of at least 20% from baseline as beneficial. (Chang 4th ed., p. 410)

q.q: For more stable improvement in pediatric oxygen index, the specific duration cutoff Chang says a prone session should exceed is ____.
q.e: Adult duration depends on response and tolerance. A pediatric period over 12 hours is described for more stable improvement in oxygen index. (Chang 4th ed., p. 410)

q.q: After prone positioning, decreased movement or sensation in the arm and shoulder suggests ____.
q.e: Other complications include accidental extubation, instability, pressure wounds, and residual obstructive or restrictive lung defects. (Chang 4th ed., p. 410)

q.q: What supplemental gas flow does TGI deliver through a small catheter ending near the distal ET tube?
q.e: Oxygen or air exits just above the carina. Continuous delivery during inspiration and expiration can dry secretions, damage mucosa, increase delivered VT, produce auto-PEEP, and increase triggering effort. (Chang 4th ed., p. 410)

q.q: According to the chapter, prone positioning in patients with acute respiratory failure or ARDS ____.
o: improves oxygenation rapidly but does not increase survival
increases survival but does not improve oxygenation
improves oxygenation slowly and increases survival
does not change oxygenation or survival
q.e: Prone positioning improves oxygenation parameters rapidly but does not increase the survival rate of patients with acute respiratory failure or ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 410)

q.q: With phasic TGI, the gas that fills the ET tube for the next inspiration contains approximately ____ CO2.
q.e: Expired gas left in the tube during conventional ventilation contains about 4% CO2. TGI flushes it out during expiration and reduces rebreathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 411)

q.q: In ventilated newborns receiving TGI, what reduction in minute ventilation may be possible while maintaining the same PaCO2?
q.e: TGI reduces instrumental deadspace, improves CO2 clearance, and lowers the pressure and VT requirements. At unchanged minute ventilation, PaCO2 may fall. (Chang 4th ed., p. 411)

q.q: Providing comfort and facilitating ____ are the two primary purposes of drug therapy during mechanical ventilation.
q.e: Drug therapy supports patient comfort, airway management, and mechanical ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 421)

q.q: A ventilated patient develops wheezing, hypoxemia, and agitation. Which pressure change further suggests airway narrowing?
q.e: Increasing peak inspiratory pressure accompanies other signs of airway distress. Accumulated secretions and mechanical irritation are possible causes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 422)

q.q: At the terminal axon of a parasympathetic fiber, the transmitter that elicits a cholinergic response is ____.
q.e: Parasympathetic fibers release acetylcholine at their terminals. Stimulation of this branch causes bronchoconstriction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 422)

q.q: Which pair of drugs stimulates sympathetic receptors in the airways to produce bronchodilation?
q.e: Albuterol and formoterol are sympathomimetic bronchodilators that stimulate beta-2 receptors. (Chang 4th ed., p. 423)

q.q: Parasympatholytic bronchodilators produce a relative increase in sympathetic activity by ____ the cholinergic response.
q.e: Interference with cholinergic activity shifts the balance toward sympathetic activity and bronchodilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 424)

q.q: An increase in cardiac contractility and rate reflects stimulation of ____ receptors.
q.e: Beta-1 stimulation has positive inotropic and chronotropic effects. Beta-2 stimulation produces bronchodilation and peripheral vasodilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 424)

q.q: Vasoconstriction and pupillary constriction are associated with stimulation of ____ receptors.
q.e: Alpha-1 stimulation constricts vessels and pupils. Alpha-2 stimulation decreases gastrointestinal activity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 424)

q.q: Which property limits the use of epinephrine and other catecholamines by the enteral route?
q.e: COMT and MAO rapidly degrade catecholamines. These drugs have rapid onset, bind nonspecifically, and are ineffective enterally. (Chang 4th ed., p. 424)

q.q: Compared with catecholamines, catecholamine derivatives generally produce ____ bronchodilation because COMT and MAO degrade them more slowly.
q.e: The derivatives have more specific beta-2 binding, prolonged bronchodilation, and fewer cardiac adverse effects. Skeletal muscle tremors and palpitations can still occur. (Chang 4th ed., p. 425)

q.q: Racemic epinephrine is given by nebulizer at 0.25–0.5 mL QID using which solution concentration?
q.e: Racemic epinephrine is nebulized as a 2.25% solution at 0.25–0.5 mL QID; epinephrine (1%) and isoproterenol (0.5%) use the same volume and frequency but different concentrations. (Chang 4th ed., p. 425)

q.q: Bitolterol MDI is dosed at two puffs every 4–6 hours. What is the pirbuterol MDI dose at the same interval?
q.e: Bitolterol is listed at two puffs and pirbuterol at one to two puffs every four to six hours. (Chang 4th ed., p. 425)

q.q: Which nebulizer preparation is the usual dose of metaproterenol?
q.e: Metaproterenol is given as 0.3 mL of 5% solution by nebulizer TID or QID, or two to three MDI puffs every four hours. (Chang 4th ed., p. 425)

q.q: What nebulized dose of levalbuterol (Xopenex) is given TID or QID?
q.e: The levalbuterol dose is 0.63–1.25 mg TID or QID. (Chang 4th ed., p. 425)

q.q: Which QID terbutaline inhaler regimen is recommended?
q.e: Terbutaline is dosed as a single dry-powder (DPI) puff or two metered-dose (MDI) puffs QID. (Chang 4th ed., p. 425)

q.q: Salmeterol is given as two puffs BID. What BID nebulizer dose is used for arformoterol as an alternative long-acting agent?
q.e: Arformoterol tartrate is listed at 15 mcg by nebulizer twice daily. (Chang 4th ed., p. 425)

q.q: Loss of receptors from the cell surface during regular beta-agonist therapy contributes to ____.
q.e: Loss of surface receptors and failure of cell function can reduce responsiveness. Combined agonist and corticosteroid use can rarely cause sudden paradoxical bronchospasm. (Chang 4th ed., p. 426)

q.q: Acetylcholine binding to muscarinic receptors in the larger airways increases bronchial tone and ____.
q.e: Muscarinic stimulation increases tone and secretion. Atropine blocks these responses and is also used for symptomatic bradycardia and preoperative drying of secretions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 426)

q.q: Which anticholinergic is listed at 18 mcg once daily via HandiHaler?
q.e: Tiotropium is given by dry-powder inhaler. Nebulized atropine is listed at 0.3–0.5 mL up to four times daily. (Chang 4th ed., p. 426)

q.q: Which nebulized volumes are listed for 0.025% ipratropium and 0.02% glycopyrrolate, respectively?
q.e: Chang lists 1–2 mL for ipratropium and 5 mL for glycopyrrolate. Ipratropium is also listed at one to two MDI puffs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 426)

q.q: A ventilated patient develops hallucinations after inhaling an anticholinergic. Which drug readily crosses the blood-brain barrier?
q.e: Atropine can produce hallucinations or confusion. Inhaled ipratropium and glycopyrrolate are poorly absorbed systemically. (Chang 4th ed., p. 427)

q.q: In the chapter’s Combivent MDI regimen, albuterol is combined with ____ for two puffs QID.
q.e: Ipratropium supplements a rapid-acting beta agonist. Alone, it is unsuitable for initial treatment when an immediate response is required. (Chang 4th ed., p. 427)

q.q: In patients who retain CO₂, xanthines heighten central CO₂ sensitivity and enhance ____.
q.e: The stronger diaphragm and heightened respiratory drive improve ventilation. Theophylline also inhibits phosphodiesterase, which normally inactivates cyclic AMP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 427)

q.q: Besides inhibiting phosphodiesterase and increasing catecholamine release, theophylline may act as an ____ antagonist.
q.e: Blocking adenosine receptors may reduce histamine release. PDE inhibition increases cyclic AMP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 428)

q.q: Which serum theophylline result falls in the chapter’s severe toxicity category associated with seizures and gastric bleeding?
q.e: Severe toxicity occurs above 40 mcg/mL. The therapeutic range is 5–15 mcg/mL, and mild to moderate toxicity occurs at 20–30 mcg/mL. (Chang 4th ed., p. 428)

q.q: A paralyzed patient receiving theophylline develops heart failure. Why is close serum monitoring important?
q.e: Heart failure reduces liver perfusion, and early toxicity such as nausea or abdominal pain may go unreported during paralysis. Smoking increases clearance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 428)

q.q: Unlike the 100% anhydrous theophylline preparation, water-soluble IV aminophylline contains ____ theophylline.
q.e: Chang lists IV aminophylline as 78–86% theophylline. (Chang 4th ed., p. 428)

q.q: Corticosteroids act at the target cell nucleus to block inflammatory mediators and require about ____ to take effect.
q.e: These adrenal cortex hormones reduce inflammation without directly dilating bronchi. Their onset makes them unsuitable as sole therapy during an acute asthma attack. (Chang 4th ed., p. 429)

q.q: Which two-puff corticosteroid MDI regimen is listed three to four times daily rather than twice daily?
q.e: Chang lists two puffs twice daily for the other three agents. Hoarseness and oral candidiasis are common adverse effects of inhaled corticosteroids. (Chang 4th ed., p. 429)

q.q: Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy can produce ____.
q.e: Systemic steroids also increase susceptibility to opportunistic infections. They may be used for bronchospasm when traditional bronchodilators fail. (Chang 4th ed., p. 430)

q.q: Which systemic corticosteroids are listed for both oral and IV administration?
q.e: Of the five drugs, hydrocortisone and dexamethasone have both routes listed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 430)

q.q: To improve ventilator-circuit MDI delivery, synchronize actuation with ____.
o: the end of the inspiratory pause
the end of peak inspiratory flow
q.e: A delay of 1–1.5 seconds can reduce delivery. A tidal volume of at least 500 mL, longer inspiration, slower flow, and a spacer improve delivery. (Chang 4th ed., p. 430)

q.q: Which circuit accessory used with an MDI on the inspiratory limb delivers inhaled medication to the lungs more efficiently than a right-angle MDI port?
q.e: Studies show that an MDI with a spacer delivers inhaled medication to the lungs more efficiently than a right-angle MDI port. (Chang 4th ed., p. 430)

q.q: During controlled ventilation with an inverse I:E ratio, paralysis can improve ____ and increase chest wall compliance.
q.e: Paralysis relaxes respiratory muscles, reduces agitation, and promotes synchrony. It can also prevent hypoxemia from increased breathing work and reduce intracranial pressure caused by excessive movement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 431)

q.q: A patient is motionless after neuromuscular blockade. Why are a sedative and an opioid still indicated?
q.e: A neuromuscular blocker leaves perception and pain intact, so comfort requires sedation and analgesia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 432)

q.q: At the motor nerve terminal, ____ store acetylcholine before its release into the synaptic cleft.
q.e: Motor nerve terminals contain vesicles that store acetylcholine until nerve impulses trigger its release into the synaptic cleft, where some is broken down by acetylcholinesterase and the rest diffuses to the end plate to trigger contraction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 432)

q.q: The brief uncoordinated contraction marking the onset of depolarizing blockade is called ____.
q.e: Succinylcholine sustains depolarization. Abnormal or deficient plasma pseudocholinesterase can prolong its action and necessitate hours of ventilatory support. (Chang 4th ed., p. 433)

q.q: Neostigmine and pyridostigmine reverse competitive blockade by allowing ____ levels to rise at the motor end plate.
q.e: Nondepolarizing agents compete with acetylcholine at the motor end plate. Anticholinesterases increase acetylcholine and reverse this block. (Chang 4th ed., p. 433)

q.q: Which muscles are affected earliest as pharmacologic blockade progresses?
q.e: Rapidly contracting muscles are affected before the extremities, trunk, and diaphragm. (Chang 4th ed., p. 433)

q.q: There is no antidote for depolarizing agents; however, succinylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed by ____.
q.e: There is no antidote for depolarizing agents, but succinylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase (PCHE). (Chang 4th ed., p. 433)

q.q: The effects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents are antagonized by ____.
q.e: Nondepolarizing (competitive) agents are antagonized by anticholinesterase agents such as pyridostigmine and neostigmine, which allow ACh levels to rise. (Chang 4th ed., p. 433)

q.q: Which blocker is preferred in organ failure because it undergoes self-destruction?
q.e: Organ failure can reduce clearance and prolong paralysis. Atracurium does not rely on organ metabolism or excretion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 434)

q.q: High concentrations of aminoglycosides can potentiate competitive blockade by ____ acetylcholine release.
q.e: Calcium promotes acetylcholine release and contraction. Several antibiotics inhibit release, and beta blockers, procainamide, quinidine, calcium channel blockers, and nitroglycerin may also potentiate competitive blockade. (Chang 4th ed., p. 434)

q.q: What are the initial dose and onset of action for pancuronium?
q.e: Pancuronium is given at 0.07 mg/kg with a 5–7 minute onset and long duration. Vecuronium is given at 0.05 mg/kg with a 4–6 minute onset and intermediate duration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 434)

q.q: Which neuromuscular blocking agent has an initial dose of 0.3 mg/kg, onset in 3–4 minutes, and short duration?
q.e: Rocuronium has an initial dose of 0.3 mg/kg, onset in 3–4 minutes, short duration, and hepatic metabolism. Atracurium is given at 0.4–0.5 mg/kg (onset 4–5 minutes), succinylcholine at 0.3–1.1 mg/kg (onset 1 minute), and pancuronium at 0.07 mg/kg (onset 5–7 minutes, long duration). (Chang 4th ed., p. 434)

q.q: Which of the following is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase?
q.e: Succinylcholine (Anectine, Quelicin) is the depolarizing agent; its drug clearance is metabolism by plasma cholinesterase. Pancuronium is metabolized by the liver. (Chang 4th ed., p. 434)

q.q: An example of a steroidal-based neuromuscular blocking (paralyzing) agent is ____.
q.e: Pipecuronium illustrates the steroidal structure of a neuromuscular blocker. (Chang 4th ed., p. 435)

q.q: A rise in magnesium inhibits muscle contraction by reducing membrane sensitivity and ____ release.
q.e: High magnesium potentiates both classes of blockers. Low calcium also potentiates nondepolarizing agents. (Chang 4th ed., p. 435)

q.q: At rest, sodium is more concentrated outside the muscle cell, while ____ is more concentrated inside.
q.e: In a resting muscle cell, potassium concentration is higher inside the cell than outside. Sodium has the opposite gradient, with a higher concentration outside the cell. (Chang 4th ed., p. 435)

q.q: A patient becomes hypokalemic after diuresis. What happens to the effects of nondepolarizing and depolarizing agents, respectively?
q.e: An acute fall in extracellular potassium hyperpolarizes the membrane and increases resistance to depolarization. (Chang 4th ed., p. 435)

q.q: Which electrolyte change enhances neuromuscular blockade with nondepolarizing agents?
q.e: A decrease in Ca++ or an increase in Mg++ enhances neuromuscular blockade with nondepolarizing agents. (Chang 4th ed., p. 435)

q.q: Acidemia ____ neuromuscular blockade, while alkalemia has the opposite effect.
q.e: Acidemia intensifies blockade and alkalemia diminishes it. (Chang 4th ed., p. 436)

q.q: Which complication makes apnea, disconnect, low exhaled volume, heart rate, and low SpO₂ alarms particularly important during paralysis?
q.e: Apnea is the most immediate life-threatening effect of both classes of blockers. (Chang 4th ed., p. 436)

q.q: Bronchospasm, flushing, and hypotension after atracurium may reflect the release of ____.
q.e: Succinylcholine and atracurium can provoke bronchospasm and hypotension through histamine release. (Chang 4th ed., p. 436)

q.q: Exhaled CO₂ rises rapidly during succinylcholine and volatile anesthetic administration. Which drug does the chapter identify for malignant hyperthermia?
q.e: Capnography offers the fastest detection of the CO₂ rise. Dantrolene is the preferred treatment. (Chang 4th ed., p. 437)

q.q: A peripheral nerve stimulator delivers four stimuli in two seconds. Which frequency produces this train?
q.e: Stimuli are spaced 0.5 seconds apart. One or two twitches are a common titration target, while three generally correspond to about 80% blockade. (Chang 4th ed., p. 437)

q.q: Which neuromuscular blocking agent is “not likely” to cause histamine release and has minimal cardiovascular impairment?
q.e: Vecuronium has this profile. Rocuronium is minimal in both categories, atracurium is moderate/minimal, pancuronium is minimal/moderate, and succinylcholine is moderate/moderate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 437)

q.q: For train-of-four monitoring in the upper extremity, the chapter identifies the superficial ____ nerve as a commonly used site for electrode placement.
q.e: The ulnar, facial, and posterior tibial nerves are commonly used for train-of-four monitoring because they are superficial and easy to locate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 437)

q.q: Which PaO₂ and PaCO₂ satisfy the listed arterial blood gas criteria for blockade reversal in a patient without chronic CO₂ retention?
q.e: The table specifies PaO₂ above 80 and PaCO₂ below 45 mm Hg. A slightly higher PaCO₂ is acceptable with chronic retention. (Chang 4th ed., p. 438)

q.q: Which pair of measurements meets the chapter’s inspiratory pressure and vital capacity criteria for blockade reversal?
q.e: The criteria include an MIP at least as strong as −25 cm H₂O and VC over 900 mL. Hand grip, a five-second head lift, and sustained tongue protrusion also help assess recovery. (Chang 4th ed., p. 438)

q.q: A calm patient with reduced anxiety and indifference to the surroundings illustrates the altered state called ____.
q.e: Neurolepsis includes calming and indifference. Analgesia relieves pain, anesthesia diminishes bodily sensation, and sedation diminishes awareness. (Chang 4th ed., p. 439)

q.q: Which injected sedative-hypnotic is singled out for its combined analgesic and sedative properties?
q.e: Ketamine provides both analgesia and sedation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 439)

q.q: Benzodiazepines facilitate GABA-mediated opening of ____ channels, making neurons more resistant to repeated depolarization.
q.e: Increased chloride conductance hyperpolarizes neurons. Benzodiazepines facilitate this inhibitory action, producing sedation, amnesia, anticonvulsant effects, and anxiolysis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 440)

q.q: An unstable patient needs a benzodiazepine for bronchoscopy. Which route is preferred in critical illness?
q.e: Gastrointestinal absorption may be unreliable. Intramuscular administration has a slower onset and can be painful. (Chang 4th ed., p. 440)

q.q: The benzodiazepine that is most lipid soluble and distributes rapidly across the blood-brain barrier is ____.
q.e: Midazolam is the most lipophilic. Lorazepam and midazolam are both rapidly and completely absorbed intramuscularly. (Chang 4th ed., p. 440)

q.q: After hepatic metabolism, active and inactive benzodiazepine metabolites are excreted mainly in the ____.
q.e: Benzodiazepines undergo liver metabolism and their metabolites leave primarily in urine. Dose-dependent CNS effects include confusion, ataxia, dizziness, and amnesia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 441)

q.q: A prolonged benzodiazepine infusion is stopped abruptly. The patient becomes hypertensive, sweaty, and tachycardic. Which complication best explains the change?
q.e: Benzodiazepine withdrawal can cause severe anxiety, tachycardia, diaphoresis, hypertension, and occasionally seizures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 441)

q.q: Adding an opioid to parenteral benzodiazepine therapy can produce additive respiratory depression and a further fall in ____.
q.e: Benzodiazepines can reduce arterial pressure, stroke volume, cardiac output, and systemic vascular resistance. Elderly patients and those with COPD are particularly susceptible to respiratory depression. (Chang 4th ed., p. 441)

q.q: For prolonged benzodiazepine sedation, a bolus may be followed by ____ to maintain patient comfort.
q.e: Intermittent IV boluses suit short periods of sedation. An IV bolus is also appropriate for an uncomfortable procedure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 442)

q.q: Which sequence describes Ramsay levels I, II, and III in ascending order?
o: Agitated, tranquil, responds only to commands
Agitated, responds only to commands, tranquil
Tranquil, agitated, responds only to commands
Responds only to commands, tranquil, agitated
q.e: Level I is anxious and agitated, level II cooperative and oriented, and level III responsive only to verbal commands. (Chang 4th ed., p. 442)

q.q: A sleeping patient responds sluggishly to stimulation. Which Ramsay score applies?
q.e: Level IV indicates a brisk response to light stimulation, level V a sluggish response, and level VI no response. (Chang 4th ed., p. 442)

q.q: In a paralyzed patient who cannot follow Ramsay commands, lacrimation, diaphoresis, hypertension, and tachycardia suggest ____.
q.e: These autonomic signs can signal pain or insufficient sedation when motor responses cannot be assessed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 442)

q.q: What initial IV dose range is used for diazepam (Valium) for sedation?
q.e: Initial IV sedation doses are 2.5–10 mg for diazepam, 0.5–2 mg for lorazepam, and 1–5 mg for midazolam; diazepam and midazolam have fast onsets, whereas lorazepam has intermediate onset and duration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 442)

q.q: An opioid that activates one opiate receptor while blocking another is classified as a(n) ____.
q.e: Full agonists produce a maximal cellular response. Many agonist-antagonists stimulate sigma receptors and can produce delirium as the dose increases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 443)

q.q: Which pain-related response accounts for reduced tidal volume, respiratory rate, and minute ventilation?
q.e: Splinting reduces ventilation. Autonomic activation raises blood pressure and heart rate, while immobility contributes to gastrointestinal dysfunction and thromboembolism. (Chang 4th ed., p. 443)

q.q: Which sequence matches the CNS effects of mu, kappa, and sigma opioid receptor activation?
q.e: Mu activation is associated with sedation, kappa with hypnosis, and sigma with delirium. Mu and kappa activation reduce pain sensation, pupil size, and respiratory rate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 444)

q.q: Which opioid drug blocks all three opiate receptor classes?
q.e: Naloxone can reverse narcotic respiratory depression and allow severe pain to return. Morphine and fentanyl are agonists, while butorphanol and pentazocine are agonist-antagonists. (Chang 4th ed., p. 444)

q.q: Opioids decrease tidal volume and breathing frequency through agonist activity at ____ receptors in the brain stem.
q.e: Opioid suppression of deep breathing can produce atelectasis. The chapter describes an automatic ventilator sigh as a preventive measure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 444)

q.q: Ventilation becomes difficult because the chest wall turns rigid during induction of anesthesia with an opioid. Which drug is most often associated with this effect?
q.e: Severe opioid-induced chest wall rigidity may require intubation, ventilation, and paralysis. Risk is greater with large doses, renal failure, or advanced age. (Chang 4th ed., p. 445)

q.q: A hepatic metabolite associated with convulsions after meperidine is ____.
q.e: Convulsions are most common with normeperidine, and naloxone does not reverse meperidine-induced convulsions. Opioid myoclonus may respond to dose reduction, a different opioid, or a benzodiazepine. (Chang 4th ed., p. 445)

q.q: Along with direct vasodilation, which cardiovascular effect does Chang list as a primary adverse effect of narcotic analgesics that can contribute to hypotension?
q.e: Opioids can slow the heart rate through vagal stimulation. The slower rate can lower cardiac output and contribute to hypotension alongside direct vasodilation and histamine release. (Chang 4th ed., p. 445)

q.q: Regular cathartic therapy during opioid use addresses ____ because tolerance to this effect develops slowly, if at all.
q.e: Cathartics promote bowel movements. Other gastrointestinal effects of opioids include delayed gastric emptying and nausea. (Chang 4th ed., p. 446)

q.q: An opioid-treated patient reports nausea chiefly when turning the head. Which mechanism best fits this timing?
q.e: Head movement points to a vestibular mechanism. Reduced gastric motility causes postprandial nausea, while trigger-zone stimulation tends to cause continuous nausea. (Chang 4th ed., p. 446)

q.q: The need for progressively larger opioid doses to maintain the same pain relief is called ____.
q.e: Physical dependence produces withdrawal after abrupt cessation or an antagonist. Psychological dependence involves drug seeking and use for purposes other than pain relief. (Chang 4th ed., p. 446)

q.q: A ventilated patient cannot report pain but guards the incision and grimaces. Which additional finding supports inadequate pain control?
q.e: The chapter lists tachycardia in the absence of hypoxemia, blood pressure changes, dilated pupils, sweating, grimacing, restlessness, and guarding. (Chang 4th ed., p. 447)

q.q: When discussing barbiturates for elevated intracranial pressure, what normal ICP range does the chapter give?
q.e: The text gives 8–12 mm Hg as normal and a value below 20 mm Hg in clinical practice. Seizure control is another application. (Chang 4th ed., p. 447)

q.q: What hypnotic duration is listed for the ultrashort-acting barbiturates thiopental and methohexital?
q.e: Thiopental and methohexital are listed at 0.2 hour, pentobarbital at 1–4 hours, amobarbital at 2–8 hours, and phenobarbital at 4–12 hours. (Chang 4th ed., p. 447)

q.q: Expressed as multiples of the hypnotic dose, what are the approximate anesthetic and lethal barbiturate doses, respectively?
q.e: The anesthetic dose is about three times and the lethal dose about six times the hypnotic dose. (Chang 4th ed., p. 447)

q.q: Barbiturate-induced coma lowers cerebral oxygen consumption, leading through autoregulation to a decrease in ____.
q.e: Lower cerebral flow reduces intracranial pressure. High doses of barbiturates may directly activate chloride channels independently of the GABA receptor complex. (Chang 4th ed., p. 448)

q.q: Which hemodynamic change contributes to barbiturate-induced hypotension in a patient with poor cardiac function?
q.e: Venous pooling, tachycardia, and depressed contractility contribute to hypotension. Barbiturates also blunt responses to hypoxia and hypercapnia and reduce respiratory rate and tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 448)

q.q: Barbiturates may weaken the effects of other hepatically metabolized drugs by ____ their clearance.
q.e: Barbiturates enhance liver metabolism of other drugs. They lack analgesic action and can paradoxically heighten pain intensity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 448)

q.q: After a rapid IV propofol bolus of 1–2.5 mg/kg, within what time is hypnosis produced?
q.e: The listed onset is within 40 seconds. The maintenance infusion is 0.05–0.2 mg/kg/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 449)

q.q: Green or red-brown urine during propofol administration may be due to ____.
q.e: Propofol metabolites can discolor urine. Other reported reactions include apnea, bradycardia, airway spasm, hypotension, and infusion-site pain. (Chang 4th ed., p. 449)

q.q: The soybean oil in a propofol infusion contributes dietary fat, so the chapter recommends monitoring serum ____.
q.e: Other calorie sources may need adjustment. The fat emulsion supports microbial growth, making aseptic administration essential. (Chang 4th ed., p. 449)

q.q: At sedative doses of propofol, a painful procedure may require additional ____ because propofol’s analgesic effect occurs at general anesthetic doses.
q.e: Adding an opioid can cause additive hypotension. Reducing the infusion rate gradually helps avoid abrupt awakening in pain or disorientation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 449)

q.q: An intubated patient becomes delirious; fever, renal failure, and several current medications are possible contributors. Which initial approach is recommended?
q.e: Potential causes include fever, renal or hepatic failure, thyroid disorders, and medications. Reorientation, explanation, and written or hand signals can help. (Chang 4th ed., p. 450)

q.q: Haloperidol helps calm a delirious ventilated patient by blocking central ____ receptors.
q.e: Haloperidol is preferably given intravenously in critical care. Blockade in the chemoreceptor trigger zone may also prevent nausea and vomiting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 450)

q.q: A patient develops neck twisting and jaw spasm after haloperidol. Which adverse effect do these findings suggest?
q.e: Extrapyramidal reactions include torticollis, laryngeal dystonia, trismus, and opisthotonus. These reactions occur less often with IV administration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 451)

q.q: After haloperidol, hyperthermia, altered consciousness, diaphoresis, and labile blood pressure suggest ____.
q.e: This rare, life-threatening reaction can occur after a single dose. QT prolongation and torsade de pointes are separate hazards of haloperidol. (Chang 4th ed., p. 451)

q.q: Which regimen does the chapter describe for an extremely agitated, delirious patient requiring critical care?
q.e: A benzodiazepine, an opioid, and haloperidol may be needed together while the team searches for reversible causes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 451)

q.q: Dexmedetomidine produces sedation and anxiolysis through receptors in the ____, and analgesia through receptors in the spinal cord.
q.e: This alpha-2 agonist provides sedation and analgesia without significant respiratory depression. Its infusion can continue through extubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 451)

q.q: What maximum dexmedetomidine infusion duration does the chapter attribute to the manufacturer?
q.e: The manufacturer’s recommendation is 24 hours. The chapter distinguishes this from trial experience extending to five days. (Chang 4th ed., p. 451)

q.q: The manufacturer recommends dexmedetomidine infusion not exceed 24 hours, but randomized trials have shown efficacy and safety for up to ____ of continuous use.
q.e: Although the manufacturer recommends no more than 24 hours of infusion, trials comparing it to midazolam and lorazepam showed efficacy and safety for up to 5 days. (Chang 4th ed., p. 451)

q.q: A patient receiving dexmedetomidine develops persistent hypotension and bradycardia. Which infusion change does the chapter describe?
q.e: Bradycardia, hypotension, and sinus arrest are potential adverse reactions. Mild hypotension may respond to IV fluids, leg elevation, or vasopressors. (Chang 4th ed., p. 452)

q.q: Endothelial cells synthesize nitric oxide from the amino acid ____.
q.e: Nitric oxide increases cGMP, which lowers smooth muscle calcium and dilates vessels. Rapid inactivation by hemoglobin limits systemic hypotension. (Chang 4th ed., p. 452)

q.q: In a newborn with persistent pulmonary hypertension, inhaled nitric oxide improves oxygenation by preferentially dilating vessels serving ____ alveoli.
q.e: Redistribution of blood toward gas-exchanging units reduces pulmonary vascular resistance and improves V/Q matching. The chapter also describes use in pediatric hypoxemic respiratory failure and ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 452)

q.q: Which nitrogen dioxide reading exceeds the chapter’s threshold for cell damage, hemorrhage, and pulmonary edema?
q.e: Nitric oxide combines with oxygen to form NO₂. The chapter describes potential injury above 10 ppm NO₂. (Chang 4th ed., p. 452)

q.q: Deficiency of methemoglobin reductase during nitric oxide therapy predisposes the patient to ____.
q.e: Methemoglobin contains ferric iron and cannot transport oxygen. The amount present depends on NO administration and enzymatic elimination. (Chang 4th ed., p. 453)

q.q: Which by-products of nitric oxide therapy can cause interstitial pneumonitis?
q.e: Nitric and nitrous acids can inflame the lung. Other potential NO effects include inhibition of platelet aggregation and a negative inotropic effect. (Chang 4th ed., p. 453)

q.q: The chapter describes supply cylinders containing 800 or 2,200 ppm NO. Which gas makes up the balance?
q.e: The system needs a source of NO and inline monitoring of NO and NO₂. The cylinders use nitrogen as the inert balance gas. (Chang 4th ed., p. 453)

q.q: When hypoxic vasoconstriction reduces perfusion to both obstructed and unobstructed airways, inhaled nitric oxide ____.
o: improves perfusion and restores a normal V/Q ratio in the unobstructed airway
reduces perfusion and creates a high V/Q ratio in the unobstructed airway
improves perfusion and restores a normal V/Q ratio in the obstructed airway
reduces perfusion and creates a high V/Q ratio in the obstructed airway
q.e: The unobstructed airway initially has high V/Q because perfusion is reduced. Inhaled NO dilates pulmonary vessels serving ventilated alveoli. (Chang 4th ed., p. 453)

q.q: Which gases does the INOvent continuously monitor while delivering a stable NO concentration across ventilator modes?
q.e: The system monitors NO, NO₂, and O₂ and integrates with a manual resuscitator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 454)

q.q: A patient has central cyanosis of the trunk and limbs but otherwise feels well. Which methemoglobin level is most consistent with these findings?
q.e: At 10–20%, central cyanosis is usually otherwise asymptomatic. At 20–45%, CNS depression can cause headache, dizziness, fatigue, lethargy, or syncope. (Chang 4th ed., p. 454)

q.q: Which methemoglobin concentration is associated with coma, arrhythmia, shock, and convulsion?
q.e: Coma, arrhythmia, shock, and convulsion occur at methemoglobin levels of 45–55%, and concentrations above 70% carry a high risk of death. (Chang 4th ed., p. 454)

sections.title: Ch 14 · Procedures Related to Mechanical Ventilation

q.q: A thoracostomy tube removes air or fluid by connecting the drainage system to the ____.
q.e: The chest tube connects the pleural space to the drainage system. (Chang 4th ed., p. 462)

q.q: Which cutoff defines a large pneumothorax in the chapter’s indications for chest tube placement?
q.e: A pneumothorax greater than 25% is listed alongside hemothorax and pleural effusion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 463)

q.q: Blockage of lymphatic drainage can cause fluid to accumulate in the pleural space as a ____.
q.e: The chapter links lymphatic blockage to chylothorax, intra-abdominal infection to empyema, and thoracic trauma to hemothorax. (Chang 4th ed., p. 463)

q.q: A symptomatic patient needs pleural drainage, but the skin over the insertion site is infected. How does the chapter classify this finding?
q.e: Infection at the entry site and conditions predisposing to severe bleeding are relative contraindications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 463)

q.q: In contrast to laceration or insertion-site hemorrhage during tube placement, a complication that may develop later is ____.
q.e: Infection may appear as a late complication of chest tube placement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 463)

q.q: Which sequence gives the suggested chest tube sizes for a large adult, a teen, a child, and a neonate, respectively, in French?
q.e: The suggested size decreases from 36–40 Fr in large adults to 12–14 Fr in neonates. (Chang 4th ed., p. 463)

q.q: A 16–20 Fr tube may suffice for an adult pneumothorax because ____ is less likely when draining air.
q.e: Blood can clot in the tube. Larger tubes are selected for hemothorax or thick fluid such as empyema. (Chang 4th ed., p. 463)

q.q: For blood or other pleural fluid, which tube size is the chapter’s nominal recommendation within the 28–40 Fr range?
q.e: A 36 Fr tube is recommended to reduce clotting. For pneumothorax, a 16–20 Fr tube is generally placed anteriorly at the second or third interspace. (Chang 4th ed., p. 463)

q.q: Chest tubes may be placed at the second intercostal space along the anterior midclavicular line or at the fifth intercostal space along the midaxillary line. What material is each site intended to drain, respectively?
q.e: The anterior site relieves pneumothorax. The lateral fifth interspace drains pleural fluid. (Chang 4th ed., p. 464)

q.q: The structures at risk if the tube enters just below a rib include the intercostal nerves and the ____.
q.e: The incision passes above the rib because the vessels and intercostal nerves lie below it. (Chang 4th ed., p. 464)

q.q: In operative tube thoracostomy, after blunt dissection and digital inspection, the operator guides the tube with a finger and a ____.
q.e: A hemostat or Kelly clamp holds the tube for finger-guided insertion. Digital inspection guards against placement between parietal pleura and chest wall. (Chang 4th ed., p. 465)

q.q: Before advancing the tube over the trocar, how far should the assembled tube and trocar enter the chest?
q.e: Deeper insertion risks lung puncture. The tube is clamped before complete trocar withdrawal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 465)

q.q: When taping the clear flange that joins the chest tube to the Creech tubing, leave it visible to check for ____.
q.e: Clots may lodge in the narrow flange, so tape should permit inspection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 465)

q.q: A kink in the chest tube can hinder lung re-expansion by ____.
q.e: A kink reduces suction. Fluid can also flow back into the pleural space, creating a risk of infection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 466)

q.q: A one-chamber unit starts with 100 mL of sterile water. What is the specified initial submersion depth of the long tube?
q.e: The submerged long tube provides a one-way water seal. The short tube vents pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 466)

q.q: As drainage accumulates in a one-chamber system, spontaneous breathing becomes more difficult because ____.
o: the long tube is submerged more deeply
the air vent draws a stronger vacuum
the long tube rises above the water
the volume of sterile water evaporates
q.e: The work of spontaneous breathing is proportional to the depth of submersion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 466)

q.q: Pleural drainage increases in chamber 1 of a two-chamber system. What effect does this have on the water-seal depth and spontaneous work of breathing?
q.e: Chamber 1 collects the fluid, leaving the long tube in chamber 2 submerged to the same depth. (Chang 4th ed., p. 467)

q.q: Bubbling from the long tube of a one-chamber unit has ceased. Possible explanations are obstruction or ____.
q.e: Some bubbling is normal while pleural air remains. Its absence can mean obstruction or complete evacuation of air. (Chang 4th ed., p. 467)

q.q: Chamber 3 bubbles slowly under wall vacuum. If water evaporates from this chamber, what happens to the suction applied to the pleural space?
o: It decreases as vent-tube depth falls
It increases as vent-tube depth falls
It rises with the rate of bubbling
It stays fixed at the wall setting
q.e: Slow, constant bubbling is normal. Vent-tube depth determines suction, so evaporated water must be replaced. (Chang 4th ed., p. 468)

q.q: Which range of suction levels does the chapter recommend for a three-chamber chest drain?
q.e: A 15-cm water column gives −15 cm H₂O, within the recommended range. (Chang 4th ed., p. 468)

q.q: In a chest drainage unit, if blocked suction tubing causes excessive pressure, the pressure relief valve on the water-seal cap ____.
q.e: The valve stays closed under normal suction and opens to protect the chest tube and pleural space from excessive pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 468)

q.q: Drainage holes that were previously inside the chest have become visible. Which action does the chapter specify?
o: Clamp the tube until bubbling stops
q.e: Visible holes indicate that the tube has come out too far and needs assessment for repositioning or reinsertion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 469)

q.q: If the tube comes completely out of the patient, immediately cover the incision with ____.
q.e: Apply an occlusive dressing such as Vaseline gauze, notify the physician, and monitor for respiratory distress. (Chang 4th ed., p. 469)

q.q: When replacing a disconnected drainage unit, what maximum clamping time does the chapter specify?
q.e: Clamp the chest tube for reconnection to a new unit and limit the clamp time to one minute. (Chang 4th ed., p. 469)

q.q: The water seal normally fluctuates with breathing. Marked bubbling in this chamber suggests pleural air or ____.
q.e: Check the patient and apparatus for the source of the air. Overfilling the suction chamber increases suction and underfilling reduces it. (Chang 4th ed., p. 469)

q.q: Which 24-hour pleural drainage cutoff does the chapter give for considering tube removal when output has slowed?
q.e: Drainage may have stopped or fallen below 100 mL over 24 hours. Another indication is resolution of pneumothorax with no further air leak. (Chang 4th ed., p. 469)

q.q: After tube removal during a Valsalva maneuver and application of petrolatum gauze, when is follow-up chest radiography performed?
q.e: The interval allows lung re-expansion, and the radiograph checks for recurrent pneumothorax. (Chang 4th ed., p. 469)

q.q: During stretcher transfer, which arrangement maintains pleural drainage and limits the risk of tension pneumothorax?
o: Drain below chest, water seal connected, tube open
Drain above chest, tube open to room air
Drain below chest, water seal connected, tube clamped
Drain above chest, water seal connected, tube open
q.e: Keep the drain below the chest, protect it from tipping or dropping, and keep the tube unobstructed and connected to a functional water seal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 470)

q.q: The insertion tube of a fiberoptic bronchoscope transmits light and images through ____.
o: a bundle of insulated copper wires
q.e: Coated glass fibers permit direct visual examination for diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 470)

q.q: Which use of bronchoscopy is diagnostic?
o: Staging a lung tumor before surgery
Draining an abscess through the airway
q.e: Diagnostic uses include evaluating tumors, obstruction, hemoptysis, infection, interstitial disease, and vocal cord paralysis, as well as collecting specimens. (Chang 4th ed., p. 470)

q.q: During transport of a patient with a chest tube, the drainage system must be ____.
o: kept lower than the patient's chest, with the tube not clamped
kept level with the patient's chest, with the tube clamped
kept higher than the patient's chest, with the tube not clamped
kept lower than the patient's chest, with the tube clamped
q.e: During transport, the drainage system must be kept lower than the patient's chest and the chest tube must not be clamped or occluded. (Chang 4th ed., p. 470)

q.q: Which of the following is listed as a general indication for therapeutic bronchoscopy?
o: Removal of retained secretions, mucus plugs, or polyps
Assessment of chest tube position, suction, or drainage
Measurement of airway resistance, compliance, or dead space
Evaluation of airway tumors, obstruction, or vocal cords
q.e: General indications for therapeutic bronchoscopy begin with removal of retained secretions, mucus plugs, or polyps; evaluation of tumors is an example of diagnostic bronchoscopy. (Chang 4th ed., p. 470)

q.q: For cytological brushing of a solitary peripheral lesion, the final approach to the target is guided by ____.
q.e: Tomography or bronchography identifies the related bronchi. X-ray monitoring guides the brush or forceps to the lesion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 471)

q.q: For bronchoalveolar lavage, the operator wedges the tip in a segmental or subsegmental bronchus and retrieves cells by flushing with ____.
q.e: The recovered saline contains cells for examination. Washing larger bronchi is called bronchial lavage. (Chang 4th ed., p. 471)

q.q: After bronchoscopic identification of the bleeding bronchus, how is the patient positioned to protect the other lung?
q.e: The patient lies on the bleeding side to protect the contralateral lung. Local thrombin can provide hemostasis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 471)

q.q: After thoracic surgery, bronchial toilet assists a patient who cannot expectorate by ____.
q.e: Aspiration through the flexible bronchoscope clears retained sputum after thoracic procedures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 471)

q.q: Which instrument does the chapter specify for removal of a large airway foreign object?
q.e: Flexible bronchoscopes can remove many foreign bodies using grasping forceps. The chapter specifies a rigid bronchoscope for large objects. (Chang 4th ed., p. 472)

q.q: During bronchoscopic electrosurgery, incision and coagulation result from ____.
q.e: Electrosurgical current generates heat that evaporates cells. (Chang 4th ed., p. 472)

q.q: For the Olympus BF-XT40 bronchoscope, which pair gives the maximum upward and downward angulation, respectively?
q.e: The example instrument bends up 180° and down 130°. (Chang 4th ed., p. 472)

q.q: Which aerosol lidocaine preparation is used 30–90 minutes before bronchoscopy?
q.e: Aerosol lidocaine reduces mucosal irritation from the insertion tube. (Chang 4th ed., p. 473)

q.q: To reduce vagal response, oral secretions, and bronchospasm before bronchoscopy, the premedication given is ____.
q.e: Atropine is given intramuscularly before bronchoscopy for these effects. (Chang 4th ed., p. 473)

q.q: Which morphine sulfate regimen does the chapter list for pain relief and cough suppression before bronchoscopy?
q.e: Chang lists 1.5–10 mg intramuscularly before the procedure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 473)

q.q: What IV bolus and oral doses, respectively, are used for diazepam sedation during bronchoscopy?
q.e: Diazepam provides sedation before or during bronchoscopy. Midazolam with fentanyl or fospropofol disodium can also be used for sedation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 473)

q.q: What upper oxygen flow does the chapter describe during bronchoscopy for a spontaneously breathing patient without an artificial airway?
q.e: Oxygen may be given at up to 6 L/min, with pulse oximetry used to assess saturation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 473)

q.q: After testing the bronchoscope and before introducing it through the nare, mouth, or artificial airway, coat its distal end with ____.
q.e: For oral insertion the chapter describes a bite block. Once above the carina, the operator directs the scope into the intended bronchi and segments. (Chang 4th ed., p. 473)

q.q: As the bronchovideoscope follows the airway into the lung, the normal structures viewed are the ____.
q.e: Through the bronchovideoscope, the normal bronchi and their segments are viewed as the scope advances into the lung. (Chang 4th ed., p. 474)

q.q: During bronchoscopy through an endotracheal tube, two common changes are hypoxia and ____.
q.e: A minor adaptor leak may require more tidal volume. The pressure limit may need adjustment for the larger volume and the scope inside the tube. (Chang 4th ed., p. 475)

q.q: A visible lesion is sampled with biopsy forceps passed through the channel outlet. The retrieved tissue is placed in ____.
q.e: Forceps biopsy yields tissue for analysis in formalin. Suctioned secretions are collected in a sterile sputum trap. (Chang 4th ed., p. 475)

q.q: During transbronchial lung biopsy, the opened forceps are advanced on maximal inhalation and closed after the patient ____.
q.e: Maximal exhalation compresses lung tissue around the forceps before closure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 475)

q.q: A lesion lies beyond the bronchial wall with no visible lesion in the lumen. Which method obtains a sample by puncturing the wall and applying suction?
o: Forceps biopsy within direct visual range
Bronchoalveolar lavage of the involved segment
q.e: The needle passes through the wall. Aspiration is applied with movement at the target, and a syringe expels the retrieved specimen. (Chang 4th ed., p. 476)

q.q: For bronchial cytology, loosened mucosal cells adhere to a small brush that is withdrawn into its ____ before removal.
q.e: A shielded brush collects cells for a slide or for pathologic testing of the removed brush. (Chang 4th ed., p. 476)

q.q: Which feature of bronchoscopy can cross-contaminate healthy lung segments within the same patient?
o: Using the same scope in successive segments
Lubricating the distal tip before insertion
Applying intermittent suction at a single site
q.e: Both the scope and the lavage fluid can transfer contamination from infected to healthy lung segments. (Chang 4th ed., p. 476)

q.q: Retained lavage fluid, hypoventilation from premedication, pooled secretions, and excessive suctioning may produce V/Q mismatch and ____.
q.e: Supplemental oxygen treats the associated desaturation. The chapter states it can usually be discontinued four hours after bronchoscopy. (Chang 4th ed., p. 476)

q.q: For substantial biopsy-site bleeding, the chapter describes mixing 1 mL of 1:1000 epinephrine with 9 mL of normal saline. In what portions is the mixture given?
q.e: Minor bleeding may respond to saline lavage. The chapter describes diluted epinephrine in 2-mL portions for substantial bleeding. (Chang 4th ed., p. 476)
