q.q: A bleeding bronchus is too wide to wedge with the bronchoscope tip. What size Fogarty balloon catheter does the chapter describe for this situation?
q.e: When the scope cannot wedge the site, a 6-Fr balloon-tipped Fogarty catheter is an alternative. (Chang 4th ed., p. 476)

q.q: After a peripheral bronchoscopic biopsy during mechanical ventilation, a patient becomes cyanotic despite high oxygen, tachycardic, and diaphoretic with a thready pulse. Which complication requires a chest tube?
q.e: Lung puncture under mechanical ventilation can produce tension pneumothorax. A complete chest tube setup belongs with the bronchoscopy supplies. (Chang 4th ed., p. 477)

q.q: The two most common complications during and after bronchoscopy are ____.
q.e: Oxygen, topical anesthesia, and intermittent suction help minimize hypoxemia and arrhythmias. Continuous pulse oximetry is used in recovery. (Chang 4th ed., p. 477)

q.q: What minimum duration does the chapter give for monitoring vital signs during recovery after bronchoscopy, with continued monitoring until stable?
q.e: Monitor vital signs for at least two hours or until stable. Withhold food and drink until the gag reflex returns. (Chang 4th ed., p. 477)

q.q: For delicate bronchoscope parts that cannot tolerate steam autoclaving, the chapter describes sterilization with ____.
q.e: The chapter specifies sterilization for parts contacting mucosa and for scopes used in patients with tuberculosis or hepatitis B. (Chang 4th ed., p. 477)

q.q: In the cited survey of more than 24,000 bronchoscopies, what percentage had major complications?
q.e: The reported major complication rate was 0.08%. The chapter gives mortality of 0.1%–0.2%, mostly secondary to hemorrhage and pneumothorax. (Chang 4th ed., p. 477)

q.q: Which indication for interhospital transfer differs from the usual reason for moving a ventilated patient within a hospital?
o: Specialized burn care available only at the destination
A CT scan in the hospital’s diagnostic imaging suite
A scheduled MRI in the hospital’s radiology department
A procedure using stationary equipment on another floor
q.e: Intrahospital transport usually allows diagnostic testing. Interhospital transport commonly provides access to tertiary care such as burn care or a third-level nursery. (Chang 4th ed., p. 478)

q.q: A trained team can maintain airway control, ventilation, oxygenation, and monitoring during transfer. Which remaining finding contraindicates departure?
q.e: An unstable or deteriorating hemodynamic state contraindicates transport. Inadequate respiratory support, monitoring, or trained personnel are also contraindications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 478)

q.q: A transport ventilator must be capable of operation without an electrical connection or ____.
q.e: The defining feature is operation independent of piped gas and an electrical connection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 478)

q.q: Which syringe does the transport inventory pair with the cuff manometer under airway management?
q.e: The inventory lists a cuff manometer and 10-mL syringe alongside intubation supplies, airway adjuncts, bags and masks, and suction devices. (Chang 4th ed., p. 479)

q.q: Which distance range is appropriate for both ground ambulance and helicopter transport of a ventilated patient?
q.e: Road and traffic conditions limit ground travel. Helicopters avoid those constraints but are noisy and require a landing pad at both facilities. (Chang 4th ed., p. 479)

q.q: Which transport distance range is suited to propeller-driven aircraft?
q.e: These aircraft can be faster than helicopters when landing sites are nearby. Unpressurized cabins reduce inspired oxygen pressure and relative humidity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 479)

q.q: For jet transport over 200 miles, which cabin pressure altitude is associated with a variable delivered tidal volume?
q.e: Low or changing cabin pressure can vary delivered tidal volume. Jets can cover intercontinental distances. (Chang 4th ed., p. 479)

q.q: During intrahospital transfer, a transport ventilator is preferred because manual bagging can cause provider fatigue, irregular tidal volumes and rates, and ____.
q.e: The chapter allows that a bag and oxygen may suffice for short support, for example under 30 minutes, but favors a transport ventilator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 480)

q.q: A pressure-control transport ventilator continues to reach the set pressure as airflow resistance increases. Which displayed value needs particular attention?
q.e: Expired volume can fall with increasing resistance or decreasing compliance. The chapter calls for close monitoring of expired volume in pressure control. (Chang 4th ed., p. 480)

q.q: When ground trips to and from airfields add substantial time, the team should choose the mode of travel using the ____.
q.e: Time spent reaching the aircraft and then the receiving facility counts toward total transport time. (Chang 4th ed., p. 480)

q.q: Before interhospital transport of a mechanically ventilated patient, the team must obtain ____.
q.e: A written physician order is required before transport. (Chang 4th ed., p. 480)

q.q: A one-way transfer is estimated to require 450 L of oxygen. What minimum amount should the team carry to allow for delay?
q.e: The chapter calls for at least twice the one-way requirement, so 2 × 450 L = 900 L. E cylinders should be full and accompanied by a wrench. (Chang 4th ed., p. 481)

q.q: Which record should the team maintain throughout transfer while assessing hemodynamics, oxygenation, and ventilation?
o: A log of monitoring data, adverse reactions, and interventions
A summary of departures from ordered ventilator settings
A list of intended settings and estimated arrival times
A record of equipment calibration and battery changes
q.e: The team monitors the patient throughout transport and logs observations, adverse reactions, and interventions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 481)

q.q: On arrival, after the patient stabilizes, the receiving ventilator is set to the ____.
o: pretransport settings with appropriate alarm limits
transport settings with pressure alarms disabled
initial factory settings with default alarm limits
lowest support settings tolerated during transfer
q.e: Check and document endotracheal tube position and function, restore pretransport settings, give verbal handoff, and file the written record. (Chang 4th ed., p. 481)

q.q: A ventilated patient is going to MRI. Which oxygen cylinder material does the chapter specify for this environment?
q.e: Steel cylinders present a projectile hazard. Equipment approaching the scanner must resist its magnetic field. (Chang 4th ed., p. 481)

q.q: In the event of a delay, the oxygen content for transporting a ventilated patient should be at least ____ the volume needed for a one-way transport.
q.e: In case of delay, the oxygen supply should be at least twice the volume needed for a one-way transport. (Chang 4th ed., p. 481)

q.q: PEEP is lost intermittently despite an unchanged setting on a manual resuscitation bag during transport. Which correction addresses an inaccurate bag PEEP valve?
o: Increase the oxygen flow to the bag
Reduce the volume of each manual breath
q.e: An inaccurate manual-bag PEEP valve can cause loss of PEEP or CPAP; the recommended correction is to use a transport ventilator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 482)

q.q: If equipment failure interrupts mechanical ventilation during patient transport, the immediate alternative is ____.
q.e: Provide manual ventilation with oxygen for equipment failure. A battery-capable ventilator and portable compressed oxygen address loss of power or gas. (Chang 4th ed., p. 482)

q.q: During stretcher transfer, the team reduces the risk of extubation or loss of vascular access by coordinating ____.
o: movement of the patient and equipment
q.e: Moving the patient without accounting for equipment and supplies can pull out the airway or vascular lines. (Chang 4th ed., p. 482)

q.q: What is the appropriate response to hypoxia at altitude in an unpressurized aircraft during patient transport?
o: Monitor ventilation and SpO₂, increase FIO₂, and use a pressurized aircraft
Monitor airway pressure, reduce FIO₂, and switch to manual ventilation
Monitor pulse and blood pressure, reduce FIO₂, and continue at altitude
Monitor exhaled volume, lower PEEP, and continue in the same aircraft
q.e: This hypoxia is caused by hypobaric conditions at altitude; remedies are increased inspired oxygen and aircraft pressurization. (Chang 4th ed., p. 482)

sections.title: Ch 15 · Critical Care Issues in Mechanical Ventilation

q.q: Prolonged ventilation can injure noncompliant lung units when they repeatedly undergo ____.
q.e: Repetitive recruitment and derecruitment contribute to ventilator-induced lung injury. (Chang 4th ed., p. 490)

q.q: When peak transalveolar pressure was 30 cm H₂O in a model of mixed lung compliance, what stress developed at the boundary between normal and collapsed units?
q.e: Compliant units can overdistend beside intermittently recruited units. Boundary stress reached 140 cm H₂O in the cited study. (Chang 4th ed., p. 491)

q.q: In the chapter’s classification, the frontal chest radiograph in both acute lung injury (ALI) and ARDS shows ____.
q.e: Both conditions have acute onset and bilateral infiltrates on the frontal film. (Chang 4th ed., p. 491)

q.q: Which wedge-pressure criterion does the chapter use to exclude a cardiac cause when classifying ALI and ARDS?
q.e: The criterion is PCWP ≤18 mm Hg when measured, or no clinical evidence of left atrial hypertension. (Chang 4th ed., p. 491)

q.q: An acutely ill patient meets the radiographic and wedge-pressure criteria for ALI and ARDS. With a PaO₂/FIO₂ of 250 mm Hg, which classification applies under the chapter’s oxygenation thresholds?
q.e: The limits are ≤300 mm Hg for ALI and ≤200 mm Hg for ARDS at any PEEP. Hypoventilation can also lower the ratio. (Chang 4th ed., p. 492)

q.q: After direct epithelial injury activates alveolar macrophages, edema, fibrin, and neutrophilic aggregates may accumulate in the ____.
q.e: Direct injury can fill alveoli with edema, fibrin, collagen, neutrophilic aggregates, or blood. (Chang 4th ed., p. 492)

q.q: When inflammatory mediators reach the lungs from an extrapulmonary focus, their first target is the ____.
q.e: Indirect injury increases endothelial permeability, producing microvascular congestion and interstitial edema with relative sparing of the air spaces. (Chang 4th ed., p. 492)

q.q: Which group consists entirely of direct causes of lung injury associated with ARDS?
o: Pneumonia, sepsis, transfusion of blood products
Fat embolism, drug overdose, cardiopulmonary bypass
q.e: Direct causes include aspiration, near drowning, contusion, pneumonia, toxin inhalation, and fat embolism. Indirect causes include sepsis, severe trauma, pancreatitis, bypass, transfusion, and drug overdose. (Chang 4th ed., p. 492)

q.q: As ARDS progresses, worsening shunt and V/Q mismatch are accompanied by a falling ____.
q.e: Worsening V/Q mismatch and intrapulmonary shunting progressively lower the PaO₂/FIO₂ ratio as ARDS advances, whereas deadspace ventilation, oxygen demand, and work of breathing all increase. (Chang 4th ed., p. 493)

q.q: Most patients who progress to diffuse alveolar infiltrates and respiratory failure do so within what interval after ARDS symptoms begin?
q.e: Most patients develop diffuse alveolar infiltrates and respiratory failure within 48 hours of symptom onset. (Chang 4th ed., p. 493)

q.q: In the exudative phase of ARDS, diffuse interstitial infiltrates typically progress to ____.
q.e: The opacities are typically bilateral. Reticular opacities suggest interstitial fibrosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 493)

q.q: A patient has bilateral pulmonary edema. Which finding favors ARDS as its cause?
q.e: PCWP should be normal in ARDS. Cardiomegaly, pleural effusions, and vascular redistribution are often absent. (Chang 4th ed., p. 493)

q.q: In the chapter’s general lung-protection guidance, what are the respective upper limits for PIP, plateau pressure, mean airway pressure, and PEEP, in cm H₂O?
q.e: The chapter gives these general limits for reducing barotrauma and identifies a stricter ARDSNet plateau limit of <30 cm H₂O. Thresholds require adjustment for coexisting conditions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 494)

q.q: A ventilated COPD patient has air trapping. After reducing tidal volume, which flow adjustment allows more time for exhalation?
q.e: Increasing peak inspiratory flow lengthens expiratory time. COPD patients are susceptible to overdistention, air trapping, and auto-PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 494)

q.q: With low tidal volume ventilation, deadspace ventilation increases while ____ decreases.
q.e: Low tidal volume decreases alveolar ventilation. Complications include acute hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis, dyspnea, increased work of breathing, and atelectasis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 494)

q.q: During permissive hypercapnia with tidal volumes of 4–7 mL/kg, the chapter allows PaCO₂ to rise above ____.
q.e: Permissive hypercapnia uses low tidal volume and accepts PaCO₂ above 50 mm Hg to limit airway pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 494)

q.q: When initiating permissive hypercapnia, tidal volume is titrated until PIP approaches the previous ____.
q.e: Plateau pressure estimates average peak alveolar pressure. Using the previous plateau as the new PIP target helps avoid overdistention. (Chang 4th ed., p. 495)

q.q: Which buffer does the chapter prefer for acidosis during permissive hypercapnia?
q.e: Tromethamine directly lowers hydrogen ion concentration and indirectly lowers carbon dioxide. Elevated PaCO₂ and acidosis can impair CNS and cardiovascular function, raise ICP and pulmonary vascular resistance, and cause weakness. (Chang 4th ed., p. 495)

q.q: When PEEP lowers cardiac output, the expected renal response includes ____.
q.e: PEEP can reduce venous return, cardiac output, and systemic oxygen delivery. Renal insufficiency, oliguria, and sodium and water retention may follow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 495)

q.q: For volume-controlled assist/control ventilation in ARDS, which tidal volume and saturation targets are recommended together?
o: VT as low as 4 mL/kg predicted weight, saturation 88–95%
VT as low as 4 mL/kg measured weight, saturation 90–98%
VT as low as 6 mL/kg measured weight, saturation 90–98%
VT as low as 6 mL/kg predicted weight, saturation 88–95%
q.e: VT can be reduced to 4 mL/kg predicted body weight to keep plateau pressure <30 cm H₂O. The saturation target is 88–95%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 496)

q.q: Under the ARDSNet initial FIO₂/PEEP combinations, for FIO₂ settings of 30%, 40%, 50%, and 60%, respectively, which sequence gives the corresponding PEEP settings (cm H₂O)?
q.e: The lower four FIO₂ settings pair with PEEP of 5, 5–8, 8–10, and 10 cm H₂O, respectively. (Chang 4th ed., p. 496)

q.q: In the FIO₂/PEEP combination scale used for ARDS oxygenation, which PEEP sequence (cm H₂O) pairs with FIO₂ settings of 70%, 80%, 90%, and 100%, respectively?
q.e: The upper four FIO₂ settings pair with PEEP of 10–14, 14, 16–18, and 20–24 cm H₂O, respectively. (Chang 4th ed., p. 496)

q.q: Which patient does the chapter identify as most likely to benefit from a recruitment maneuver?
q.e: Recruitment is reserved for severe edema with risk of death from refractory hypoxemia. Existing barotrauma, unstable hemodynamics, blebs or bullae, and elevated ICP are contraindications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 496)

q.q: Prone positioning at a 15–30° Trendelenberg angle brings most of the lower lobes uppermost and ____ their opening pressure.
q.e: Prone positioning lowers lower-lobe opening pressure, enhances ventilation distribution, and reduces the transpulmonary pressure gradient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 496)

q.q: Which supine patient meets the chapter’s PEEP and FIO₂ criteria for prone positioning to maintain a saturation of 90%?
q.e: The described candidates require PEEP >10 cm H₂O and FIO₂ ≥60% to maintain supine saturation ≥90%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 496)

q.q: Before the initial recruitment maneuver, spontaneous effort is suppressed by sedation and 100% oxygen is applied for ____.
q.e: Vital signs are monitored and supported. The protocol continues sedation, uses 100% oxygen for 20 minutes, and specifies inline suction without disconnecting the patient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 497)

q.q: Which combination of CPAP and maximum duration is specified for initial recruitment on 100% oxygen?
q.e: The initial maneuver uses CPAP 40 cm H₂O for up to 40 seconds. The final maneuver again uses 100% oxygen and CPAP 40 cm H₂O for 40 seconds. (Chang 4th ed., p. 497)

q.q: During recruitment, which observation meets a stopping criterion if the other vital signs remain stable?
o: Mean arterial pressure 65 mm Hg at baseline
q.e: Stopping criteria include SpO₂ <88%, HR >140 or <60/min, MAP <60 mm Hg or a deviation >20% from baseline, and arrhythmia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 497)

q.q: Immediately after initial recruitment, what inspiratory pressure above PEEP and what PEEP are specified for pressure-controlled ventilation?
q.e: These settings produce a peak pressure of 35 cm H₂O. A 20% rise in PaO₂ permits progression, and the maneuver may be repeated up to three times if this rise is absent. (Chang 4th ed., p. 497)

q.q: After recruitment, FIO₂ is decreased in steps of 5–20% until SpO₂ stabilizes at ____.
q.e: The maneuver specifies a stable saturation of 90–94% before PEEP titration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 497)

q.q: During decremental recruitment, PEEP falls from 14 to 12 cm H₂O and SpO₂ first falls below 90%. Which PEEP is used after final recruitment?
q.e: PEEP is reduced by 2 cm H₂O every 15–20 minutes. The preceding PEEP is optimal and is paired with the previously titrated FIO₂ after final recruitment. (Chang 4th ed., p. 497)

q.q: Ventilator-associated pneumonia is a newly acquired infection of the ____ in an intubated patient receiving mechanical ventilation.
q.e: VAP affects the lung parenchyma. The chapter reports that it affects 10–25% of mechanically ventilated patients and accounts for about 25% of ICU-acquired infections. (Chang 4th ed., p. 497)

q.q: What sequence describes VAP incidence during the first five ventilator days, the next five days, and thereafter?
q.e: Risk peaks immediately after intubation and declines over time. Reported VAP mortality is 33–50%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 498)

q.q: Which group of findings increases susceptibility to VAP?
o: Malnutrition, immune suppression, and depressed consciousness
Malnutrition, preserved immunity, and improved consciousness
Adequate nutrition, brief ventilation, and young age
Adequate nutrition, preserved immunity, and brief ventilation
q.e: Additional risks include prolonged ventilation, advanced age, and preexisting lung disease. Incidence is higher in trauma, neurosurgical, and burn units. (Chang 4th ed., p. 498)

q.q: New or progressive infiltrates plus two findings among fever, abnormal leukocyte count, and purulent secretions had a reported sensitivity and specificity for VAP of ____, respectively.
q.e: Either leukocytosis or leukopenia qualifies as an abnormal count. Infiltrates plus two clinical findings had 69% sensitivity and 75% specificity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 498)

q.q: For VAP onset after intubation and initiation of mechanical ventilation, which sequence matches predominant microbes in the first 48 hours, at 3–7 days, and after 7 days?
o: Upper airway flora, gram-negative bacilli, S. aureus including MRSA
Upper airway flora, S. aureus including MRSA, gram-negative bacilli
S. aureus including MRSA, gram-negative bacilli, upper airway flora
Gram-negative bacilli, upper airway flora, S. aureus including MRSA
q.e: Upper airway flora predominate first, followed by gram-negative bacilli such as Pseudomonas at 3–7 days and S. aureus including MRSA after 7 days. (Chang 4th ed., p. 498)

q.q: The modified CPIS initially uses the first ____ variables, before Gram stain or culture results are incorporated.
q.e: Baseline modified CPIS sums the first five variables (tracheal secretions, chest X-ray infiltrates, temperature, leukocyte count, and PaO₂/FIO₂) before the sixth variable (microbiology) is available. A score >6 at baseline or after incorporating microbiology suggests pneumonia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 499)

q.q: A ventilated patient has abundant purulent tracheal secretions and a localized infiltrate. What CPIS subtotal comes from these two findings?
q.e: Rare, abundant, and abundant purulent secretions score 0, 1, and 2. Absent, diffuse, and localized infiltrates likewise score 0, 1, and 2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 499)

q.q: Which temperature sequence represents 0, 1, and 2 modified CPIS points, respectively?
q.e: The listed bands are 36.5–38.4 °C for 0, 38.5–38.9 °C for 1, and <36 or >39 °C for 2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 499)

q.q: With a leukocyte count outside 4–11 thousand/mm³, the finding that raises the leukocyte component of CPIS from 1 to 2 is ____.
q.e: The reference range earns 0 points. An abnormal count earns 1 point, or 2 with >500 bands. (Chang 4th ed., p. 499)

q.q: Which patient meets the abnormal oxygenation criterion in the modified CPIS?
q.e: The abnormal criterion is a ratio <240 mm Hg without ARDS. A ratio >240 mm Hg or the presence of ARDS belongs in the zero-point category. (Chang 4th ed., p. 499)

q.q: When ventilator-associated pneumonia is suspected, the modified CPIS approach calls for PAL or BAL specimens for Gram stain and culture ____ empiric antibiotics.
q.e: Microbiology distinguishes positive from negative specimens. The table calls for sampling before therapy and describes suctioned sputum as suboptimal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 499)

q.q: In the prevention bundle that reduced VAP by 95% over three years, circuits were changed weekly and inline suction devices and HME filters were changed every ____.
q.e: The bundle also used proper cuff pressure, suction of pooled subglottic secretions, and single-use saline vials when lavage was indicated. (Chang 4th ed., p. 499)

q.q: For subglottic secretion drainage, the endotracheal tube’s separate dorsal lumen opens ____.
q.e: The lumen allows suction of secretions pooled above the cuff. (Chang 4th ed., p. 499)

q.q: Which VAP prevention measure does the chapter describe as the simplest and most cost-effective?
q.e: Hand hygiene before and after contact reduces nosocomial infection. Oral care and sterile suctioning limit lower-airway pathogen exposure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 500)

q.q: To reduce aspiration and VAP, the head of the bed should be elevated to ____ when clinically appropriate.
q.e: Severe hypotension and a postneurosurgical state are examples of contraindications. Tapered cuffs and subglottic drainage also target aspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 500)

q.q: As a method to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia by limiting contamination from condensate or secretions during handling, the ventilator circuit should be changed when it is ____.
o: used for a scheduled sedation hold
used for the first suction procedure
q.e: Changing a visibly soiled or malfunctioning circuit limits exposure during circuit changes. Noninvasive mask ventilation avoids direct pathogen access to the lower tract. (Chang 4th ed., p. 500)

q.q: To prevent VAP, how long is the daily sedation vacation intended to permit weaning assessment and early extubation?
q.e: The scheduled hold is 6–8 hours daily. Early weaning reduces lower-airway pathogen exposure and ventilator-induced injury. (Chang 4th ed., p. 500)

q.q: An oral feeding tube is favored for VAP prevention because nasal feeding tubes may cause ____, a condition associated with VAP.
q.e: The oral route avoids the nasal feeding tube’s association with sinusitis. Silver or antimicrobial tube coatings provide protection against some pathogens. (Chang 4th ed., p. 500)

q.q: VAP develops while a patient is already receiving antibiotics. How should the initial replacement regimen be chosen according to the chapter?
o: Use broad coverage from different classes
Continue the current drugs until day seven
Use broad coverage from the same classes
q.e: The chapter favors empiric coverage of multidrug-resistant pathogens and a change of class because resistance to current drugs is likely. Local organisms and resistance patterns guide selection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 501)

q.q: After empiric therapy for suspected VAP begins, the modified CPIS should be reassessed by ____.
q.e: Score changes guide continuation, selection, or discontinuation. Quantitative culture and sensitivity results guide pathogen-specific therapy and dosage. (Chang 4th ed., p. 501)

q.q: Severe oxygen deprivation that damages neurons in the brain and spinal cord is termed ____.
q.e: HIE can result from inadequate ventilation or oxygenation, inadequate perfusion, or reduced cerebral perfusion pressure. The term applies beyond the newborn period. (Chang 4th ed., p. 501)

q.q: What share of total body weight and energy use does the brain represent, respectively?
q.e: The brain has only small astrocyte glycogen stores. Fatty acids do not cross its capillaries, so it depends on circulating glucose and oxygen. (Chang 4th ed., p. 502)

q.q: With complete loss of cerebral circulation, neuronal oxygen is depleted within ____, whereas glucose and ATP stores are lost within about five minutes of anoxia.
q.e: Loss of oxygen stores is associated with unconsciousness. Continued anoxia depletes glucose and ATP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 502)

q.q: After energy depletion causes sodium-potassium pump failure and neuronal depolarization, excess ____ enters the synaptic cleft.
q.e: Chang links glutamate release to calcium entry, catabolic enzyme activation, and increased nitric oxide production. Passive chloride and sodium entry can cause osmotic edema. (Chang 4th ed., p. 502)

q.q: A patient has a MAP of 92 mm Hg and an ICP of 16 mm Hg. What is the calculated cerebral perfusion pressure?
q.e: CPP equals MAP minus ICP. It is the pressure needed to deliver blood, oxygen, and metabolites to the brain. (Chang 4th ed., p. 503)

q.q: Mild HIE may cause poor judgment and coordination, whereas severe cerebral oxygen deprivation may cause ____.
q.e: The chapter distinguishes seizures and coma in severe deprivation from attention, judgment, and coordination deficits in mild cases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 503)

q.q: For each 10 mm Hg decrease in CPP, how much does the chapter report mortality increases?
q.e: Mortality increases by about 20% for each 10 mm Hg drop in CPP. The chapter places the critical CPP range at 70–80 mm Hg and notes a 35% mortality reduction in severe head injury studies when CPP was maintained above 70 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 503)

q.q: What therapeutic hypothermia range does the chapter describe for lowering oxygen utilization after cardiac arrest?
q.e: The chapter describes 32–34 °C after cardiac arrest. Restoration of heart function through advanced cardiac life support is the primary goal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 504)

q.q: In septic shock, vasodilation can lower MAP and CPP by producing ____.
q.e: Blood loss produces absolute hypovolemia. With ICP fixed, a fall in MAP lowers CPP, and raising MAP increases CPP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 504)

q.q: A hypotensive patient has no hemorrhage. Which sequence does the chapter describe for supporting MAP?
o: Restore fluid balance, then use a vasopressor if needed
Reduce systolic pressure, then reassess fluid balance
Start dopamine, then restrict fluid intake
Lower ICP first, then reduce circulating volume
q.e: Adequate fluid balance comes first, followed if needed by norepinephrine or dopamine. Early systolic pressure <90 mm Hg is associated with worse outcomes after severe brain injury. (Chang 4th ed., p. 504)

q.q: For HIE due to carbon monoxide poisoning, which therapy increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of plasma?
q.e: Hyperbaric oxygen is particularly useful with dysfunctional hemoglobin. Other HIE management focuses on ventilation, perfusion, and seizure control, with cooling used to reduce oxygen consumption. (Chang 4th ed., p. 505)

q.q: In adults older than 65 years, the leading cause of death and disability from TBI is ____.
q.e: Vehicle crashes cause most deaths and injuries in young people. Most TBI patients are younger than 35, and the male-to-female ratio is about 2:1. (Chang 4th ed., p. 505)

q.q: Which values describe the usual ICP range and the upper clinical normal value, respectively?
q.e: ICP above 20 mm Hg reduces CPP. A CPP below 70 mm Hg can cause cerebral hypoxia, ischemia, and death. (Chang 4th ed., p. 505)

q.q: The adult skull holds about 1,500 mL, of which brain tissue normally occupies ____.
q.e: Blood and cerebrospinal fluid account for about 10% and 3%, respectively. Rapid expansion within the rigid skull raises ICP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 505)

q.q: After the initial impact of TBI, swelling and a subsequent fall in cerebral perfusion are features of ____ injury.
q.e: Secondary neurological injury is the leading cause of in-hospital death following primary TBI. Systemic hypotension further lowers MAP and CPP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 505)

q.q: The clinical normal range for cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is ____.
q.e: The clinical normal range for CPP is 70–80 mm Hg; a suboptimal CPP (<70 mm Hg) can cause cerebral hypoxia or ischemia and death. (Chang 4th ed., p. 505)

q.q: A patient falls onto concrete. The skull stops, but the brain continues moving and strikes the skull. Which mechanism explains the injury?
q.e: A stationary object abruptly stops the skull in deceleration injury. A direct blow moves the skull in acceleration injury, while rotation can shear axons. (Chang 4th ed., p. 506)

q.q: In transtentorial herniation, a mass above the tentorium displaces the ____ downward through the tentorial notch.
q.e: The uncus is the medial temporal lobe. Its displacement can compress the brainstem and third cranial nerve. (Chang 4th ed., p. 506)

q.q: After TBI, a patient develops a single dilated pupil. In transtentorial herniation, which pupillary pattern occurs in about 80% of cases?
q.e: Third-nerve compression suppresses parasympathetic input to the eye. A unilateral dilated pupil or unilateral posturing calls for immediate surgical evaluation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 506)

q.q: Which sequence gives the chapter’s GCS ranges for mild, moderate, and severe TBI?
q.e: The chapter classifies 13–14 as mild, 9–12 as moderate, and 3–8 as severe. (Chang 4th ed., p. 506)

q.q: Which management goal accounts for airway protection, eucapnic ventilation, oxygenation, and blood-pressure support in severe TBI?
q.e: The goal is to prevent further neuronal loss. Systolic pressure should exceed 90 mm Hg, and CT can identify epidural or subdural hematoma and guide surgical decisions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 507)

q.q: A patient with traumatic brain injury briefly rouses to stimulation but is unaware of the surroundings, cannot perform a task, and returns to inactivity when left alone. Which level of impairment does this describe?
q.e: An obtunded patient briefly rouses but lacks awareness and cannot perform tasks. In lethargy, awareness persists, and in cloudy consciousness, short-term memory is impaired while long-term memory remains intact. (Chang 4th ed., p. 507)

q.q: A patient who cannot communicate clearly but can be aroused by painful stimulation matches the chapter’s description of ____.
q.e: Stupor permits arousal by pain. Coma entails no response to vigorous stimulation, and brain death is irreversible cessation of whole-brain function documented by EEG. (Chang 4th ed., p. 507)

q.q: Sedation helps control ICP during ventilation for severe TBI by preventing coughing and ____.
q.e: Coughing and dyssynchrony tend to increase ICP. The chapter advises avoiding or minimizing endotracheal suctioning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 508)

q.q: An infant opens the eyes to a shout. Which adult response earns the same GCS eye-opening score?
q.e: An infant opening the eyes to a shout and an adult opening them to verbal command both score 3. Spontaneous opening scores 4, opening in response to pain scores 2, and no eye opening scores 1. (Chang 4th ed., p. 508)

q.q: Which progression of adult GCS motor findings earns 6, 5, and 4 points, respectively?
o: Obeys command, localizes pain, withdraws in flexion
Withdraws in flexion, localizes pain, obeys command
Obeys command, withdraws in flexion, localizes pain
Localizes pain, obeys command, withdraws in flexion
q.e: Command following scores 6, localization scores 5, and flexion withdrawal scores 4. No motor response scores 1. (Chang 4th ed., p. 508)

q.q: Arms flexed inward on the chest with clenched fists, extended legs, and inward-turned feet indicate ____ posturing.
q.e: Abnormal flexion scores 3 on the motor scale. Decerebrate extension, with the head arched back and arms extended, scores 2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 508)

q.q: Which verbal responses earn 4 GCS points in an adult, a 3-year-old, and a 1-year-old, respectively?
o: Oriented conversation, appropriate words, appropriate crying
q.e: The verbal scale is age-specific. The three groups receive 5 for oriented conversation, appropriate words, or appropriate crying, respectively, and 1 for no response. (Chang 4th ed., p. 508)

q.q: What range of GCS scores does the chapter report for an intubated patient?
q.e: Verbal response cannot be assessed during intubation. The reported range is 2T–10T, with T designating intubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 508)

q.q: In traumatic brain injury, further lowering PaCO₂ below 26 mm Hg produces little additional reduction in ____.
q.e: The chapter describes 26 torr as the lower PaCO₂ limit during the first 24 hours of ventilation for TBI. Below it, there is no additional benefit for ICP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 509)

q.q: For minimal cerebral oxygenation after TBI, what lower targets does the chapter specify for PaO₂ and SaO₂, respectively?
q.e: Arterial oxygen saturation should be monitored, with PaO₂ above 60 mm Hg and SaO₂ above 90%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 509)

q.q: During weaning, the work of breathing shifts from the ventilator to the ____.
q.e: Weaning transfers the work of breathing from the ventilator to the patient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 517)

q.q: A patient has recovered normal cardiopulmonary function after one day of ventilation for a drug overdose. Which approach may this patient tolerate?
q.e: Patients ventilated for no more than 1 to 2 days who regain normal cardiopulmonary function may tolerate abrupt termination. Longer ventilation generally calls for a more gradual, individualized withdrawal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 517)

q.q: At what time after extubation does the chapter assess absence of ventilatory support to define weaning success?
q.e: The chapter defines weaning success as absence of ventilatory support 48 hours after extubation. It lists supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, PSV and CPAP as possible ways to support spontaneous ventilation and oxygenation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 518)

q.q: An extubated patient who still needs ventilatory support through a nasal mask is classified as ____.
q.e: Weaning in progress describes continued noninvasive ventilation after extubation. Noninvasive ventilation is mechanical ventilation without an artificial airway. (Chang 4th ed., p. 518)

q.q: A patient passes an SBT but needs reintubation 30 hours after extubation. How is the weaning attempt classified?
q.e: Either a failed SBT or reintubation within 48 hours of extubation meets the chapter’s definition of weaning failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 518)

q.q: In the six-study review, what percentage of patients who passed the initial SBT required reintubation?
q.e: The review reported that 79% passed the initial SBT and the overall weaning success rate was 68.8%. Among patients who passed the initial trial, 13% required reintubation, and a separate study found that 15% of ventilated patients needed more than 7 days to wean successfully. (Chang 4th ed., p. 518)

q.q: Compared with surgical patients, medical patients with coexisting or chronic problems generally need ____ to complete weaning.
q.e: The chapter notes that medical patients often have coexisting problems and generally take longer to complete weaning than surgical patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 518)

q.q: Before a weaning attempt, the patient should have recovered from the acute phase of the illness and be able to assume ____.
q.e: Initial assessment checks whether the patient has recovered from the acute disease or injury and can sustain spontaneous breathing. The chapter also flags ventilation for more than 72 hours and upper airway disorders as factors that can affect the outcome. (Chang 4th ed., p. 519)

q.q: Conditions that may hinder weaning are grouped as patient/pathophysiologic, cardiac/circulatory, and dietary/acid-base/electrolyte. Which pair correctly categorizes anemia and caloric deficit?
q.e: Fever, infection, renal failure, sepsis and sleep deprivation are patient factors. Circulatory factors include arrhythmias, high or low blood pressure or cardiac output, fluid imbalance, anemia and dysfunctional hemoglobins, while the dietary category includes caloric, acid-base and electrolyte disturbances. (Chang 4th ed., p. 519)

q.q: Among common clinical weaning criteria, the patient should have an adequate cough and an absence of ____.
q.e: The clinical criteria include resolution of the acute disease phase, an adequate cough, absence of excessive secretions and cardiovascular and hemodynamic stability. (Chang 4th ed., p. 520)

q.q: Which set reproduces the common ventilatory weaning criteria thresholds? Assume normal pH and satisfactory blood gases.
o: PaCO₂ <50 mm Hg, VC >10 mL/kg, VT >5 mL/kg, f <35/min, f/VT <100 breaths/min/L, minute ventilation <10 L
PaCO₂ <45 mm Hg, VC >10 mL/kg, VT >5 mL/kg, f <30/min, f/VT <100 breaths/min/L, minute ventilation <12 L
PaCO₂ <50 mm Hg, VC >5 mL/kg, VT >10 mL/kg, f <35/min, f/VT <105 breaths/min/L, minute ventilation <10 L
PaCO₂ <55 mm Hg, VC >12 mL/kg, VT >6 mL/kg, f <40/min, f/VT <105 breaths/min/L, minute ventilation <8 L
q.e: Common weaning criteria include SBT tolerance of 20 to 30 minutes, PaCO₂ <50 mm Hg with normal pH and minute ventilation <10 L with satisfactory blood gases. Other thresholds are VC >10 mL/kg, VT >5 mL/kg, f <35/min and f/VT <100 breaths/min/L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 520)

q.q: As a weaning criterion at an FIO₂ of up to 0.40, which PaO₂ cutoffs apply without PEEP and with PEEP below 8 cm H₂O, respectively?
q.e: Adequate oxygenation for weaning is PaO₂ >60 mm Hg without PEEP and >100 mm Hg with PEEP below 8 cm H₂O, at FIO₂ up to 0.4. The SaO₂ cutoff at the same FIO₂ is >90%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 520)

q.q: Which PaCO₂ and pH ranges does the chapter give for patients with normal lung function?
q.e: Normal lung function is associated with PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg and pH 7.35–7.45. In COPD, a higher PaCO₂ and a lower pH may be acceptable depending on baseline values. (Chang 4th ed., p. 521)

q.q: Before measuring spontaneous tidal volume and vital capacity in a patient on full support, allow about ____ of spontaneous breathing under close observation.
q.e: The equilibration period allows the measured effort to reflect the patient’s respiratory requirement. The chapter also gives 3 minutes before measuring spontaneous frequency and explains that a rapid, shallow pattern raises deadspace ventilation and impairs gas exchange. (Chang 4th ed., p. 521)

q.q: Poor effort or difficulty following instructions can make the measured vital capacity ____ the patient’s actual vital capacity.
q.e: The vital capacity maneuver depends on effort and cooperation. Teaching and coaching help obtain accurate measurements. (Chang 4th ed., p. 521)

q.q: In the chapter’s example of acceptable blood gases during weaning in a patient with COPD, a pH near 7.35 is paired with a PaCO₂ of approximately ____.
q.e: Chang’s example pairs a PaCO₂ around 50 mm Hg with a pH near 7.35. For an individual patient with COPD, interpret both values against the patient’s stable baseline before ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 521)

q.q: A minute ventilation above 10 L/min needed to normalize PaCO₂ suggests that spontaneous work of breathing is ____.
q.e: The chapter associates a minute ventilation below 10 L/min with successful weaning when PaCO₂ is normal. A higher requirement to normalize PaCO₂ implies excessive work. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: Which condition can raise minute ventilation requirements by increasing carbon dioxide production?
q.e: The chapter links extensive burns, fever and carbohydrate overfeeding to increased carbon dioxide production. It also lists increased alveolar deadspace and metabolic acidosis as causes of excessive minute ventilation requirements. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: Alveolar deadspace increases when alveolar ventilation ____ alveolar perfusion.
q.e: The chapter associates increased deadspace with V/Q >0.8. It gives alveolar overventilation and pulmonary underperfusion as mechanisms. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: An anemic patient has a reassuring PaO₂ and SpO₂ during a readiness check. Which measurements does the chapter advise using to make oxygenation decisions?
q.e: For anemia or dysfunctional hemoglobins, the chapter advises measuring arterial oxygen content and arterial oxygen saturation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: Which SpO₂ range does the chapter suggest aiming for when using pulse oximetry to monitor oxygenation during weaning?
q.e: The chapter suggests keeping SpO₂ in the mid-90s to allow for measurement error. In critical care, SpO₂ readings are described as accurate within 2% to 4% of SaO₂. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: The minimum P/F criterion that suggests acceptable physiologic shunt is ____.
q.e: The chapter gives PaO₂/FIO₂ ≥150 mm Hg as the threshold that suggests acceptable physiologic shunt. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: For a successful weaning outcome, the patient's minute ventilation should be less than ____ with acceptable blood gases.
q.e: For a successful weaning outcome, minute ventilation should be less than 10 L/min with acceptable blood gases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: For a successful weaning outcome, the PaO2 and SaO2 should be ____, respectively, on an FIO2 < 40%.
q.e: The PaO2 and SaO2 should be >60 mm Hg and >90%, respectively, on FIO2 < 40% for a successful weaning outcome. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: For a successful weaning outcome, the PaO2/FIO2 should be ____.
q.e: A PaO2/FIO2 of ≥150 mm Hg suggests acceptable physiologic shunt and is listed as a weaning criterion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 522)

q.q: Which expression gives the physiologic shunt fraction QS/QT?
q.e: Subtract arterial oxygen content from end-capillary oxygen content for the numerator. Subtract mixed venous oxygen content from end-capillary oxygen content for the denominator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 523)

q.q: A patient’s calculated QS/QT is 24%. How does the chapter classify this value?
q.e: The chapter describes ≤10% as normal, 10% to 20% as mild, 20% to 30% as significant and >30% as critical or severe. It advises correcting significant or severe shunt above 20% before attempting weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 523)

q.q: The alveolar–arterial oxygen tension gradient is calculated by subtracting ____ from calculated PAO₂.
q.e: The gradient is PAO₂ minus PaO₂. A larger gradient reflects more severe hypoxemia or physiologic shunt. (Chang 4th ed., p. 523)

q.q: On room air, what is the expected upper limit for the P(A–a)O₂ gradient per decade of age?
q.e: On room air the expected gradient is less than 4 mm Hg for every 10 years of age. (Chang 4th ed., p. 523)

q.q: On 100% oxygen, a 50 mm Hg difference in P(A–a)O₂ corresponds to approximately what physiologic shunt?
q.e: Each 50 mm Hg corresponds to about 2% shunt on 100% oxygen. For weaning, the chapter gives a gradient below 350 mm Hg at that oxygen concentration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 523)

q.q: In mechanical ventilation, a P(A-a)O2 below what threshold while on 100% oxygen suggests a likelihood of weaning success?
q.e: A P(A-a)O2 of less than 350 mm Hg on 100% oxygen suggests a likelihood of weaning success; 350 mm Hg approximates a 14% shunt. (Chang 4th ed., p. 523)

q.q: A P(A-a)O2 of 350 mm Hg while on 100% oxygen approximates a shunt of about ____.
q.e: On 100% oxygen, every 50 mm Hg of P(A-a)O2 approximates 2% shunt, so 350 mm Hg approximates 14% shunt. (Chang 4th ed., p. 523)

q.q: Vital capacity includes tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume and ____.
q.e: Vital capacity is the maximum volume exhaled after maximal inspiration. The maneuver does not require forceful exhalation, and the chapter lists VC >10 mL/kg for successful weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 524)

q.q: Which setup matches the chapter’s maximum inspiratory pressure measurement?
o: Inhale against an occluded manometer for 20 sec
Exhale against an occluded manometer for 20 sec
Inhale through an open spirometer for 20 sec
Exhale through an open spirometer for 20 sec
q.e: MIP, also called negative inspiratory force, measures ventilatory muscle strength. The patient generates negative pressure in 20 seconds against an occluded device, and the chapter gives at least −30 cm H₂O as the target. (Chang 4th ed., p. 524)

q.q: Weaning will likely be successful if the patient can generate an MIP of at least ____.
q.e: The chapter states weaning will likely be successful if the patient can generate an MIP of at least −30 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 524)

q.q: In the 11 studies cited in the chapter, the MIP averaged ____ for weaned patients versus −30 cm H2O for nonweaned patients.
q.e: The results of 11 studies showed that MIP averaged −37 cm H2O for weaned patients versus only −30 cm H2O for nonweaned patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 524)

q.q: To calculate static lung compliance, divide corrected tidal volume by ____.
q.e: Static compliance is ΔV ÷ ΔP, with ΔP equal to plateau pressure minus PEEP. In this discussion, lower compliance increases the work of breathing and 30 mL/cm H₂O or greater is the stated minimum consistent with successful weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 525)

q.q: Which expression estimates airway resistance when inspiratory flow is constant?
o: Peak minus plateau pressure, divided by flow
Plateau minus PEEP, divided by flow
Peak minus PEEP, divided by flow
Peak plus plateau pressure, divided by flow
q.e: Airway resistance is estimated using the difference between peak inspiratory and plateau pressures divided by constant inspiratory flow in L/sec. The normal range is 0.6–2.4 cm H₂O/L/sec, and resistance may be higher during ventilation because of conditions such as bronchospasm or resistance from the tubing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 525)

q.q: Pressure support ventilation augments spontaneous tidal volume by applying a preset pressure plateau during ____.
q.e: PSV applies preset positive pressure during spontaneous inspiration. The initial level can be titrated to a spontaneous VT of 10 to 15 mL/kg or a spontaneous rate of ≤25/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 525)

q.q: For a successful weaning outcome, the static compliance should be ____.
q.e: For a successful weaning outcome, the compliance should be >30 mL/cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 525)

q.q: Which expression gives the deadspace-to-tidal-volume ratio?
q.e: The numerator is arterial minus mixed expired carbon dioxide tension, and the denominator is arterial carbon dioxide tension. The margin lists VD/VT <60% as a favorable weaning criterion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 526)

q.q: To obtain an average spontaneous tidal volume for RSBI, divide measured minute expired volume by ____.
q.e: Chang calls for at least 3 minutes to stabilize spontaneous breathing with mandatory frequency off and without PSV if tolerated. Measure expired volume and frequency for 1 minute, then divide minute volume by frequency to obtain average VT in liters. (Chang 4th ed., p. 526)

q.q: A therapist records an RSBI of 80 breaths/min/L at a spontaneous rate of 24/min. Which average tidal volume is consistent with that entry?
q.e: Because RSBI is frequency divided by average VT in liters, 24/min divided by 80 breaths/min/L gives 0.30 L. An RSBI below 100 predicts weaning success, while one above 100 correlates with failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 526)

q.q: For a successful weaning outcome, the VD/VT ratio should be ____.
q.e: For a successful weaning outcome, the VD/VT ratio should be 60% or less. (Chang 4th ed., p. 526)

q.q: The major diagnostic test used to assess readiness for extubation and weaning is the ____.
q.e: The spontaneous breathing trial evaluates readiness for extubation and weaning. Low-level pressure support of ≤8 cm H₂O, CPAP or automatic tube compensation may augment spontaneous breaths. (Chang 4th ed., p. 527)

q.q: Which patient response matches the chapter’s criteria for passing an SBT?
o: Normal breathing, adequate gas exchange, stable hemodynamics
Normal breathing, adequate gas exchange, unstable hemodynamics
Normal breathing, inadequate gas exchange, stable hemodynamics
Rapid shallow breathing, adequate gas exchange, stable hemodynamics
q.e: Passing requires adequate gas exchange, stable hemodynamics and a normal respiratory pattern without rapid shallow breathing. Patients who fail often do so in the first 20 to 30 minutes and may show agitation, anxiety, diminished mental status, sweating, cyanosis or increased work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 527)

q.q: In SIMV, the timing of mandatory breaths is synchronized with the patient’s ____.
q.e: SIMV allows spontaneous breaths between ventilator breaths and times mandatory breaths to the patient’s inspiratory efforts. The chapter advises against SIMV as a stand-alone weaning modality. (Chang 4th ed., p. 527)

q.q: During an SBT, spontaneous breathing may be augmented with low-level (____) pressure support, CPAP, or automatic tube compensation.
q.e: An SBT may use low-level (≤8 cm H2O) pressure support, CPAP, or ATC to augment spontaneous breathing, and may last up to 30 minutes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 527)

q.q: Which set lists the criteria for passing an SBT?
o: Normal respiratory pattern, adequate gas exchange, and hemodynamic stability
Normal chest radiograph, adequate gas exchange, and normal temperature
Normal respiratory pattern, normal hemoglobin, and stable mental status
Adequate cough, normal hemoglobin, and absence of secretions
q.e: The criteria for passing an SBT include a normal respiratory pattern (no rapid shallow breathing), adequate gas exchange, and hemodynamic stability. (Chang 4th ed., p. 527)

q.q: What maximum pressure-support levels may be used to augment spontaneous breathing during an SBT for an adult and a child, respectively?
q.e: An SBT may use a T-tube, CPAP or ATC for up to 30 minutes of spontaneous breathing. Low-level pressure support may be added up to 8 cm H₂O for adults and 10 cm H₂O for pediatric patients, and satisfactory blood gases and vital signs after a tolerated trial support considering extubation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 528)

q.q: When weaning by reducing SIMV support, what step size and final mandatory rate are used?
q.e: SIMV frequency is reduced by 1 to 3 breaths/min to a rate of 2 to 4/min. Monitor SpO₂, obtain blood gases as needed and consider extubation when the reduced rate is tolerated with satisfactory gases and vital signs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 528)

q.q: During weaning with PSV, how is the pressure-support level reduced once the patient tolerates it?
o: Reduce by 3–6 cm H₂O toward 5 cm H₂O
Reduce by 3–6 cm H₂O toward 10 cm H₂O
Reduce by 1–2 cm H₂O toward 10 cm H₂O
Reduce by 6–9 cm H₂O toward 5 cm H₂O
q.e: Start at 5 to 15 cm H₂O and titrate, up to 40 cm H₂O, for a VT of 10 to 15 mL/kg or a rate of ≤25/min. When tolerated, reduce support in 3 to 6 cm H₂O intervals toward 5 cm H₂O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 528)

q.q: Between weaning efforts, the chapter advises providing ____ at night so the patient can rest.
q.e: The chapter advises full ventilatory support at night to allow rest regardless of the weaning approach. (Chang 4th ed., p. 528)

q.q: Weaning with PSV is done by starting the pressure support level at ____ and adjusting it gradually until a desired spontaneous VT is obtained.
q.e: PSV weaning starts the pressure support at 5 to 15 cm H2O and adjusts it gradually (up to 40 cm H2O) until the desired spontaneous VT (10 to 15 mL/kg) is obtained. (Chang 4th ed., p. 528)

q.q: Automatic tube compensation is designed to offset the airflow resistance imposed by the ____.
q.e: ATC compensates for resistance from an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube and can reduce the work of breathing during weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 529)

q.q: The pace of reducing SIMV support is determined by the patient’s ____.
q.e: The chapter describes checking arterial blood gases or SpO₂ after at least 30 minutes at a setting and further reducing the rate if pH stays near normal, above 7.30 or 7.35. Patient condition and tolerance govern the pace. (Chang 4th ed., p. 529)

q.q: At FIO₂ ≥0.50, which pair gives the oxygenation cutoffs listed for SBT failure?
q.e: Chang gives PaO₂ ≤60 mm Hg or SaO₂ <90% as oxygenation criteria for SBT failure while FIO₂ is at least 50%. (Chang 4th ed., p. 529)

q.q: Which set gives the PaCO₂ and pH thresholds that indicate failure of a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT)?
o: PaCO₂ >50 or rise >8 mm Hg, pH <7.32 or fall ≥0.07
PaCO₂ >45 or rise >8 mm Hg, pH <7.35 or fall ≥0.05
PaCO₂ >50 or rise >10 mm Hg, pH <7.30 or fall ≥0.10
PaCO₂ >55 or rise >12 mm Hg, pH <7.28 or fall ≥0.12
q.e: SBT failure is indicated by PaCO₂ >50 mm Hg or a rise >8 mm Hg, and pH <7.32 or a drop ≥0.07. Changes are measured from the SBT baseline. (Chang 4th ed., p. 529)

q.q: Which spontaneous rate threshold is an indicator of SBT failure?
q.e: SBT failure is indicated by a rate above 35/min or a rise of at least 50% from baseline. Another indicator is f/VT >100 breaths/min/L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 529)

q.q: Which set gives the cardiovascular criteria for failure of a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT)?
o: HR >140/min or rise ≥20%, systolic BP >180 or <90 mm Hg or rise ≥20%
HR >160/min or rise ≥30%, systolic BP >200 or <85 mm Hg or rise ≥30%
HR >150/min or rise ≥25%, systolic BP >190 or <95 mm Hg or rise ≥25%
HR >130/min or rise ≥15%, systolic BP >170 or <80 mm Hg or rise ≥15%
q.e: SBT failure HR thresholds are >140/min or a rise of ≥20%. The systolic BP thresholds are >180 mm Hg or a rise of ≥20%, or <90 mm Hg; cardiac arrhythmias are also a failure sign. (Chang 4th ed., p. 529)

q.q: Volume support automatically adjusts the level of ____ to achieve a preset tidal volume.
q.e: Volume support adjusts pressure support to achieve the target tidal volume. Volume-assured pressure support combines inspiratory PSV with conventional volume-assisted cycles to maintain a preset tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 530)

q.q: Mandatory minute ventilation guarantees the target minute ventilation by automatically adjusting ____.
q.e: MMV adjusts frequency to achieve the target minute ventilation. Decreasing the MMV level increases the patient’s share of spontaneous breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 530)

q.q: When the frequency of pressure release in APRV is reduced to zero, the patient is effectively on ____.
q.e: In APRV, the pressure gradient determines tidal volume, and exhalation occurs during pressure release. Weaning can proceed by reducing release frequency until zero releases produce CPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 530)

q.q: Which set captures the three elements the chapter generally expects in a weaning protocol?
o: Readiness conditions, weaning procedure, outcome assessment
Ventilator setup, cuff management, discharge assessment
Gas exchange targets, sedation orders, nutrition schedule
Equipment selection, airway placement, follow-up testing
q.e: Weaning protocols generally cover the conditions for attempting weaning, the process and how to evaluate outcomes. The chapter recommends applying the criteria as guidelines with individual patient differences in mind. (Chang 4th ed., p. 530)

q.q: In APRV, the higher airway pressure is, for example, 10 cm H2O, and the lower release pressure is usually ____.
q.e: APRV has two pressure levels: a higher airway pressure (e.g., 10 cm H2O) and a lower release pressure (usually 0 cm H2O). (Chang 4th ed., p. 530)

q.q: Which set gives the oxygenation and acid–base readiness thresholds in step 1 of a weaning protocol for mechanical ventilation?
o: P/F >150 mm Hg, PEEP <8 cm H₂O, pH ≥7.25
P/F >100 mm Hg, PEEP <8 cm H₂O, pH ≥7.30
P/F >150 mm Hg, PEEP <10 cm H₂O, pH ≥7.30
P/F >200 mm Hg, PEEP <5 cm H₂O, pH ≥7.35
q.e: Step 1 requires some reversal of the underlying cause, inspiratory effort, hemodynamic stability, adequate oxygenation and acid–base status, and light sedation or better. The listed gas-exchange thresholds are P/F >150 mm Hg, PEEP <8 cm H₂O and pH ≥7.25. (Chang 4th ed., p. 531)

q.q: In a weaning protocol, which setup is used in step 2 to measure the rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI)?
o: Mandatory rate off, PS ≤8, PEEP ≤5, measure after ≥3 min
Mandatory rate off, PS ≤5, PEEP ≤8, measure after ≥2 min
Mandatory rate off, PS ≤10, PEEP ≤6, measure after ≥4 min
Mandatory rate on, PS ≤8, PEEP ≤5, measure after ≥1 min
q.e: Step 2 measures RSBI with mandatory frequency off, PS ≤8 cm H₂O and PEEP ≤5 cm H₂O after at least 3 minutes of spontaneous breathing. An RSBI <100 breaths/min/L allows progression to the SBT. (Chang 4th ed., p. 531)

q.q: During a weaning protocol's spontaneous breathing trial step, a patient breathes at 36/min for five consecutive minutes. What does the protocol indicate?
q.e: Step 3 uses an SBT of up to 30 minutes, with termination for a spontaneous frequency >35/min for 5 minutes. The protocol also lists SpO₂ <90%, HR >140/min or 120% of baseline, systolic pressure >180 or <90 mm Hg, anxiety and accessory muscle use. (Chang 4th ed., p. 531)

q.q: Tachypnea and accessory muscle use are early signs of weaning failure, along with ____ abdominal movement.
q.e: The chapter lists tachypnea, accessory muscle use and paradoxical abdominal movements as early signs. Dyspnea, chest pain, chest–abdomen asynchrony, diaphoresis and delirium may also indicate difficulty sustaining the work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 532)

q.q: A patient becomes anxious and hyperventilates during weaning. What does the chapter advise against doing solely on the basis of a PaCO₂ that shows hyperventilation?
q.e: Hypoxia, pain, anxiety or inappropriate ventilator settings may cause hyperventilation. If the patient cannot tolerate weaning, return to full support for rest and reassess before trying again. (Chang 4th ed., p. 532)

q.q: Which set of gas-exchange values indicates weaning failure?
q.e: Gas-exchange indicators of weaning failure are PaCO₂ >50 mm Hg, pH <7.30, PaO₂ <60 mm Hg, SpO₂ <90% and P/F <150 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 532)

q.q: Which set gives the vital-sign warning thresholds that indicate weaning failure?
o: BP changes of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic, HR rise of 20/min or HR >110/min
BP changes of 15 systolic or 5 diastolic, HR rise of 15/min or HR >120/min
BP changes of 10 systolic or 20 diastolic, HR rise of 20/min or HR >140/min
BP changes of 25 systolic or 5 diastolic, HR rise of 15/min or HR >130/min
q.e: Weaning failure is indicated by a change of 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic and an HR increase of 20/min or a rate >110/min. An abnormal ECG with arrhythmias is also an indicator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 532)

q.q: Which respiratory pattern crosses all three VT, f and f/VT warning cutoffs for weaning failure?
q.e: Warning signs are decreasing VT below 250 mL, increasing f above 30/min and increasing f/VT above 100 breaths/min/L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 532)

q.q: Which set of MIP, static compliance and VD/VT values indicates weaning failure?
o: MIP <−20 cm H₂O, compliance <30 mL/cm H₂O, VD/VT >60%
MIP <−35 cm H₂O, compliance <40 mL/cm H₂O, VD/VT >50%
MIP <−30 cm H₂O, compliance <25 mL/cm H₂O, VD/VT >55%
MIP <−25 cm H₂O, compliance <35 mL/cm H₂O, VD/VT >65%
q.e: Respiratory indicators of weaning failure include a decreasing MIP (<−20 cm H₂O), decreasing static compliance (<30 mL/cm H₂O) and increasing VD/VT (>60%). (Chang 4th ed., p. 532)

q.q: The three general causes of weaning failure are increased airflow resistance, decreased compliance and ____.
q.e: These three mechanisms can leave the patient unable to sustain the work of spontaneous breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 533)

q.q: When appropriate for the patient’s size, what minimum endotracheal tube size does the chapter recommend to reduce artificial-airway resistance?
q.e: The chapter advises size 8 or larger when appropriate, giving cross-sectional areas of 50 mm² for an 8-mm tube and about 66 mm² for the adult glottis. It reports an increase in work of breathing of 54% to 240%, depending on tube size and ventilator flow. (Chang 4th ed., p. 533)

q.q: The chapter expresses respiratory work as transpulmonary pressure multiplied by ____.
q.e: The equation for respiratory work is PTP × VT. (Chang 4th ed., p. 533)

q.q: Which work-of-breathing threshold is associated with weaning failure in ventilator-dependent patients?
q.e: The chapter associates failure with 1.7 kg·m/min or higher. It gives 1.6 kg·m/min or less as the work threshold normally needed before ventilator-dependent patients can assume adequate spontaneous breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 534)

q.q: Prolonged full ventilatory support can cause respiratory muscle dysfunction through disuse and lead to diaphragmatic ____.
q.e: Muscle disuse during prolonged full support may lead to diaphragmatic atrophy, and the chapter links ventilation-induced oxidative stress to proteolysis and contractile dysfunction. Short T-tube trials may improve respiratory muscle strength, and PSV may improve diaphragmatic endurance. (Chang 4th ed., p. 534)

q.q: Which pairing correctly classifies causes of decreased compliance?
q.e: The static group includes atelectasis, ARDS, tension pneumothorax, obesity and retained secretions in the lungs. The dynamic group includes bronchospasm, ET tube kinking, airway obstruction and retained secretions in the airways. (Chang 4th ed., p. 534)

q.q: A care team decides against starting mechanical ventilatory support. What term describes this decision in the chapter?
q.e: Withholding means the patient is never placed on mechanical ventilatory support. Terminal weaning refers to withdrawal of mechanical ventilation that results in the patient’s death. (Chang 4th ed., p. 534)

q.q: To support an informed decision about terminal weaning, consent discussions should take place ____.
q.e: The chapter recommends open, honest discussions over time so emotion, pain and other factors do not interfere. Informed consent includes understanding the potential consequences of removing life support, including death. (Chang 4th ed., p. 535)

q.q: Which set captures the four concerns the chapter says to evaluate when considering terminal weaning?
o: Informed request, medical futility, suffering, fear or distress
Decision timing, medical futility, oxygen delivery, nutrition
Informed request, oxygen delivery, suffering, ventilator settings
Decision timing, equipment choice, suffering, fear or distress
q.e: The four concerns are informed request, medical futility, relief of pain and suffering, and fear or distress. The chapter cites a proposal that an intervention may be considered futile if it was useless in the last 100 similar cases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 535)

q.q: Before withdrawal, immediate caregivers who are uncomfortable with the process should be offered the chance to ____.
q.e: Caregivers who are uncomfortable may leave the case. The patient’s pastor or hospital chaplain should be notified. (Chang 4th ed., p. 535)

q.q: Which equipment should remain available when preparing for terminal withdrawal?
o: Basic vital-sign monitoring, oxygen and IV access
Basic vital-sign monitoring, alarms and feeding tubes
Invasive monitoring, oxygen and IV access
Invasive monitoring, alarms and feeding tubes
q.e: The chapter calls for removal of invasive monitoring, alarms and unnecessary lines and tubes. Basic vital-sign monitoring, oxygen and IV access for analgesics and sedatives remain. (Chang 4th ed., p. 536)

q.q: During ventilator withdrawal, the family should be offered the opportunity to ____.
q.e: The family may stay with the patient while the physician and chaplain are encouraged to attend. Analgesics and sedatives are provided for comfort and relief of anxiety. (Chang 4th ed., p. 536)

q.q: After the weaning process starts, treatment adjustments are guided by continued monitoring of the patient’s ____.
q.e: No absolute criteria guarantee successful weaning, and the chapter associates meeting more criteria with a greater likelihood of success. Continued monitoring provides trends for adjusting ventilator settings and treatment. (Chang 4th ed., p. 536)

q.q: At 5 minutes an infant has an Apgar score of 6. What scoring schedule follows while the score stays below 7?
q.e: Scores range from 0 to 10 and are obtained at 1 and 5 minutes while resuscitation continues. A score of at least 7 at 5 minutes ends scoring. (Chang 4th ed., p. 546)

q.q: Which set of Apgar findings earns one point each for respiratory effort, muscle tone, and reflex response?
o: Gasping, some flexion, and a grimace
Apnea, flaccid limbs, and no response
Gasping, well-flexed limbs, and a cough
Crying, some flexion, and a grimace
q.e: The middle column pairs a slow heart rate with irregular respirations, some flexion, a grimace, and blue extremities with a pink body. (Chang 4th ed., p. 546)

q.q: In the chapter’s delivery-room criteria, meconium at delivery is an indication for intubation when the newborn is ____.
q.e: Findings include heart rate below 100/min, inadequate respirations, or poor tone. Other indications include inadequate or prolonged bag-mask ventilation, persistent bradycardia during compressions, endotracheal medication, and extreme prematurity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 546)

q.q: For a term newborn, a preemie, and a micropreemie, respectively, the Miller blade sizes are ____.
q.e: Blade size decreases across the three groups. A second person assists with equipment, monitoring, and timing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 547)

q.q: For newborns weighing 900, 1,500, 2,500, and 3,500 g, which sequence gives the recommended ETT internal diameters in millimeters?
q.e: The corresponding gestational-age bands are below 28, 28–34, 34–38, and above 38 weeks. (Chang 4th ed., p. 547)

q.q: An intubation attempt in a preterm infant has lasted 20 seconds without tube placement. What does the chapter advise next?
o: Withhold ventilation until the next attempt
Insert the tube without viewing the cords
q.e: Each attempt is limited to 20 seconds, with oxygenated bag-mask ventilation between attempts. (Chang 4th ed., p. 547)

q.q: Which SpO2 range does the chapter give for infants born before 32 weeks to minimize retinopathy of prematurity?
q.e: The chapter uses gestational age to specify this saturation target. Oxygen can be weaned using SpO2 and clinical signs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 547)

q.q: As the laryngoscope blade enters the mouth of an infant in the sniffing position, it sweeps the tongue ____.
o: toward the tip of the chin
q.e: Free-flow oxygen is provided during the procedure. The blade tip advances just beyond the tongue base, and the entire blade is lifted slightly. (Chang 4th ed., p. 547)

q.q: A 1.5-kg infant needs an unmarked ETT. What estimated depth at the lips follows from the chapter’s rule?
q.e: Add 6 to weight in kilograms to estimate depth in centimeters. With a marked tube, the marking lies at or just beyond the cords, and a chest radiograph confirms depth. (Chang 4th ed., p. 548)

q.q: Surfactant deficiency increases alveolar surface tension and thereby increases ____.
q.e: Surfactant lowers surface tension. Its deficiency is the primary cause of neonatal RDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 548)

q.q: The component of phosphatidylcholine credited with lowering alveolar surface tension is ____.
q.e: About 90% of surfactant is phospholipid, and about 60% of phosphatidylcholine is DPPC. Cholesterol is the predominant neutral lipid, and proteins A through D make up 5%–10% of surfactant. (Chang 4th ed., p. 548)

q.q: When intubation is performed specifically for meconium removal, the chapter advises omitting the ____.
q.e: For other intubations, bilateral breath sounds and a color change on a CO2 detector help verify placement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 548)

q.q: Once ETT placement is verified, prophylactic surfactant is delivered by ____.
q.e: The micropreemies described are usually under 30 weeks and weigh 500–1,000 g. The chapter describes dosing within 15 minutes of birth after radiographic verification. (Chang 4th ed., p. 549)

q.q: Which infant meets all three criteria (gestational age, PaO₂/PAO₂ ratio and birth weight) for prophylactic surfactant in the most premature group of candidates?
q.e: The most premature group is gestation ≤26 weeks with PaO2/PAO2 <0.22 and weight <1,250 g; only 25 weeks, 0.21 and 1,200 g meets all three. A ratio of 0.22 or a weight of 1,250 g misses the cutoff, and 27 weeks exceeds the gestational age limit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 550)

q.q: A 32-week infant has grunting, retractions, and escalating oxygen needs. Which radiographic finding supports rescue surfactant therapy?
q.e: The rescue criteria include signs of RDS, a positive film, and increasing oxygen or ventilatory needs. Gestation is generally under 34 weeks, and the listed arterial/alveolar ratio is below 0.22. (Chang 4th ed., p. 550)

q.q: Of the natural surfactants listed, the preparation obtained from porcine lung tissue is ____.
q.e: Survanta, Infasurf, and Alveofact are bovine preparations. Surfaxin is synthetic. (Chang 4th ed., p. 550)

q.q: The synthetic surfactant discontinued in 2008 was ____.
q.e: Surfaxin was approved in 2012 and supplied in 8.5-mL vials. Each milliliter contained 30 mg phospholipids, 4.05 mg palmitic acid, and 0.862 mg sinapultide. (Chang 4th ed., p. 550)

q.q: What is the recommended intratracheal dosing schedule for lucinactant (Surfaxin)?
q.e: Lucinactant is given at 5.8 mL/kg, up to four total doses in the first 48 hours of life, with any two doses at least 6 hours apart. (Chang 4th ed., p. 551)

q.q: For Survanta and Infasurf, respectively, which pair gives the doses used at 6-hour intervals?
q.e: Both schedules allow up to four doses. The table specifies the first 48 hours for Survanta. (Chang 4th ed., p. 551)

q.q: After the initial 2.5 mL/kg dose of Curosurf, the repeat schedule is ____.
q.e: Up to two additional doses are listed. Each dose is divided into halves given 30 seconds apart. (Chang 4th ed., p. 551)

q.q: Surfactant replacement for neonatal RDS is associated with a decrease in ____.
q.e: Reported benefits include reduced RDS severity, pulmonary interstitial emphysema, epithelial necrosis, and mortality. Some infants have a transient response or no response. (Chang 4th ed., p. 551)

q.q: For an infant with sustainable spontaneous breathing and mild to moderate shunting, nasal CPAP reduces V/Q mismatch by increasing ____.
q.e: CPAP supplies continuous pressure without mechanical breaths and reduces shunting. The chapter lists RDS, apnea of prematurity, obstructive sleep apnea, bronchiolitis, aspiration pneumonia, MAS, CHF, TTN, and postoperative support. (Chang 4th ed., p. 552)

q.q: Bubble CPAP generates pressure by means of ____.
q.e: The underwater seal produces chest vibration. A flow-generating CPAP device uses flow and has no exhalation valve. (Chang 4th ed., p. 552)

q.q: Which initial pressure and flow ranges are given for most infants on nasal CPAP?
q.e: For RDS the suggested starting pressure is 6 cm H2O. All CPAP devices require humidification. (Chang 4th ed., p. 552)

q.q: An infant with RDS on nasal CPAP has persistent respiratory acidosis with pH 7.18. What escalation does the chapter suggest considering?
q.e: Persistent pH below 7.20 or unsatisfactory PaO2 on more than 50% oxygen with nasal CPAP supports considering intubation and surfactant. (Chang 4th ed., p. 553)

q.q: Following a rapid improvement in compliance after surfactant, the pressure-controlled ventilator’s PIP should be ____.
q.e: At a preset PIP, delivered volume varies with compliance and resistance. Improved compliance can produce excessive tidal volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 553)

q.q: With volume-controlled ventilation, a fall in compliance while tidal volume remains constant can result in ____.
o: loss of the preset volume target
q.e: Peak pressure alarms help protect the infant. The chapter gives 5 mL/kg as a typical initial volume within a range of 3–7 mL/kg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 553)

q.q: Circuit expansion during inspiration, expressed in mL/cm H2O, is called the ____.
q.e: Gas retained in the circuit is unavailable to the infant. Low-compliance circuits and low-compressible-volume wick humidifiers minimize the loss. (Chang 4th ed., p. 554)

q.q: Which gas conditions are ideal at the trachea during neonatal mechanical ventilation?
q.e: A nonheated circuit may require heating the gas 3 or 4 degrees above target to compensate for heat loss. (Chang 4th ed., p. 554)

q.q: A heated inspiratory wire reduces the accumulation of condensate by ____.
q.e: Cooling against the tubing wall causes rain-out. Accumulated water increases resistance, risks contamination, and can drain into the lungs. (Chang 4th ed., p. 554)

q.q: The wire heater switches off as gas enters a warm incubator, and the inspiratory tubing collects water. Where should the distal temperature probe be placed?
o: Inside the incubator at the ETT
q.e: The servo-controller regulates the heated wire. Keeping the probe just outside the inlet prevents incubator heat from causing premature shutdown. (Chang 4th ed., p. 555)

q.q: The three general indications for neonatal ventilatory support are apnea, hypercapnia, and ____.
q.e: Ventilation supports gas exchange when spontaneous breathing cannot maintain adequate blood gases. It also prevents or corrects atelectasis and maintains FRC. (Chang 4th ed., p. 555)

q.q: Which finding on supplemental oxygen meets the chapter’s arterial oxygen criterion for starting mechanical ventilation?
q.e: The cutoff is an acute PaO2 below 50 mm Hg. Other indications include acutely rising PaCO2 with falling pH and apnea due to prematurity, intraventricular hemorrhage, or drug depression. (Chang 4th ed., p. 556)

q.q: At a constant inspiratory flow of 6 L/min and an inspiratory time of 0.3 second, what VT does the chapter’s flow-time calculation give?
q.e: Multiply inspiratory time by flow expressed in volume per second. At 6 L/min the flow is 100 mL/sec. (Chang 4th ed., p. 556)

q.q: When an air leak is present, the suggested ventilator strategy pairs low pressure with ____.
q.e: Low compliance generally requires higher initial pressure, whereas an air leak calls for low pressure and high frequency. (Chang 4th ed., p. 556)

q.q: For initial neonatal mechanical ventilation, which PIP/PEEP combination is recommended for normal compliance, in cm H2O?
q.e: For normal compliance, initial neonatal settings use a PIP of 15–20 cm H2O and PEEP of 3–5 cm H2O; for low compliance, initial settings use a higher PIP of 20–30 cm H2O and PEEP up to 8 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 557)

q.q: When initiating neonatal ventilation, which estimated VT ranges are used for normal and low lung compliance, respectively?
q.e: These values apply when the ventilator can provide a preset tidal volume. Both compliance groups use flows of 6–8 L/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 557)

q.q: When initiating neonatal ventilation in an infant with normal lung compliance, which initial I:E range is used?
q.e: Normal compliance calls for 25–40 breaths/min with an inspiratory time of 0.3–0.5 second. With low compliance the rate may reach 150/min, especially with air leak, and inspiratory time is adjusted to maintain 1:1. (Chang 4th ed., p. 557)

q.q: In either compliance group, FIO2 is adjusted to keep the infant pink with SpO2 of ____.
q.e: The table gives both groups the same saturation target and allows appropriate PEEP when needed. (Chang 4th ed., p. 557)

q.q: In the weight-based settings, which initial rate applies to low- and very-low-birth-weight infants compared with term infants?
q.e: All three groups start at 5 mL/kg within a 3–7 mL/kg range, with inspiratory time 0.3–0.5 sec and PEEP 4–8 cm H2O. (Chang 4th ed., p. 557)

q.q: Which umbilical arterial blood gas profile falls within all three usual targets in the chapter?
q.e: Usual targets are PaO2 >50 mm Hg, PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg, and pH 7.3–7.45. Higher PaCO2 may be accepted in chronic lung disease. (Chang 4th ed., p. 558)

q.q: Which heel-stick result generally requires a different measurement technique to assess the same physiologic variable?
q.e: Capillary PCO2, pH, and bicarbonate roughly correlate with arterial values. Pulse oximetry or transcutaneous PO2 monitoring can assess oxygenation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 558)

q.q: High frequency ventilation can maintain gas exchange even when the tidal volume is ____.
o: equal to the entire lung capacity
q.e: Small volumes can be delivered at relatively low pressures, which reduces barotrauma risk. The cited comparison found fewer new pulmonary leaks with HFOV and no significant mortality difference. (Chang 4th ed., p. 558)

q.q: Which frequency sequence correctly identifies HFPPV, HFJV, and HFOV, respectively?
q.e: One hertz equals 60 cycles/min, giving ranges of 60–150, 240–660, and 480–1,800 cycles/min respectively. (Chang 4th ed., p. 559)

q.q: HFPPV delivers conventional breaths whose tidal volume exceeds dead space, moving gas principally by ____.
q.e: HFPPV is indicated for hypoxemia or hypercapnia despite adequate conventional ventilation. Increasing rate can support minute ventilation while limiting peak pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 559)

q.q: Increasing HFPPV frequency while holding the other settings constant raises ____.
q.e: Mean airway pressure averages pressure over a complete cycle and depends on frequency, I time, PIP, and PEEP. Higher mPaw increases risks of barotrauma, cardiac compromise, and intracranial bleeding. (Chang 4th ed., p. 560)

q.q: Which delivery arrangement directs the HFJV pressure pulse into the ETT?
o: A jet adaptor or specially designed ETT
A piston pump across an expiratory filter
q.e: The gas pulse exits inside the tube. Indications include severe lung disease complicated by air leaks, pulmonary hypoplasia, restrictive lung disease, and persistent pulmonary hypertension. (Chang 4th ed., p. 560)

q.q: For rectangular pressure breaths with PIP 22, PEEP 4, frequency 40/min, and I time 0.5 second, what is the calculated mPaw in cm H2O?
q.e: Multiply the inspiratory fraction of the cycle by the difference between PIP and PEEP, then add PEEP. Here the inspiratory fraction is 40 × 0.5 / 60, or one third. (Chang 4th ed., p. 560)

q.q: During HFJV, why does the conventional ventilator maintain continuous flow at the ETT?
o: To supply gas for jet entrainment
To produce the high-pressure jet pulses
To remove gas actively on expiration
To measure pressure at the carina
q.e: Sighs help prevent microatelectasis and stimulate surfactant production. Continuous gas flow at the ETT is available for entrainment. (Chang 4th ed., p. 561)

q.q: Repeated high-pressure jet pulses striking the large airway walls may cause ____.
q.e: Internal jet delivery through a special catheter or triple-lumen ETT limits tracheal injury. Other hazards include gas trapping, hyperinflation, secretions obstructing the airway, and hypotension. (Chang 4th ed., p. 561)

q.q: On HFJV, chest vibration diminishes and PaCO2 rises while PaO2 stays stable. Which problem does this pattern suggest?
q.e: During HFJV, diminished chest vibration and rising PaCO₂ with stable PaO₂ indicate ETT obstruction or malposition. A concurrent fall in PaO₂ would suggest decreased lung compliance or pneumothorax. (Chang 4th ed., p. 561)
