q.q: In an oscillator, the negative stroke assists ____ while the positive stroke assists inspiration.
q.e: Positive and negative strokes assist both phases. The oscillator is inline with the ETT, and the gas source enters the tube perpendicularly. (Chang 4th ed., p. 562)

q.q: During HFV, movement of gas between inflated alveolar units as they equilibrate is called ____.
q.e: Pendelluft may improve gas exchange through enhanced diffusion. The chapter describes the mechanisms of HFV gas exchange as incompletely understood. (Chang 4th ed., p. 562)

q.q: For an infant under 1,000 g on conventional ventilation, which combination crosses all three thresholds for escalating to HFOV?
q.e: The thresholds are FIO2 >50%, frequency >30/min, and PIP >20 cm H2O. For infants over 1,500 g the table describes PIP in the high twenties. (Chang 4th ed., p. 563)

q.q: For a nitric oxide candidate with pulmonary hypertension, which minimum oxygen index makes the infant a candidate for HFOV?
q.e: The listed criterion is an oxygen index ≥15. A rapidly rising oxygen requirement without pneumothorax has a separate entry with an oxygen index >10. (Chang 4th ed., p. 563)

q.q: HFOV combined with surfactant in the first hours of life may reduce the incidence and severity of ____.
q.e: Early HFOV at optimal lung volume may also improve oxygenation in acute RDS and reduce surfactant requirements. Air leaks and lack of early improvement indicate poor prognosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 563)

q.q: When transferring an infant with diffuse alveolar disease to HFOV, the general starting guideline places mPaw ____ the conventional value.
q.e: The general starting table suggests mPaw 3–4 cm H2O above conventional mPaw for diffuse alveolar disease and at or below conventional mPaw for nonhomogeneous disease or air leak. (Chang 4th ed., p. 564)

q.q: Which initial HFOV bias flows correspond to a 1,600-g infant and a 2,400-g infant, respectively?
q.e: The general settings table divides bias flow at 2,000 g. Power is adjusted in 2–4 cm H2O increments until the chest wiggle is adequate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 564)

q.q: Which HFOV starting frequencies are recommended at 800, 1,200, 1,800, and 2,400 g, in order?
q.e: The smallest infants receive the highest initial frequencies. Decreasing frequency increases delivered volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 564)

q.q: A neonate receiving HFOV develops pallor, bradycardia, hypotension, and greater respiratory effort. What do these bedside findings indicate?
o: Readiness for a lower bias flow
q.e: Cardiopulmonary assessment is difficult during jet ventilation and oscillation. Cyanosis is another sign of deterioration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 564)

q.q: During HFOV, alveolar hyperinflation combined with high PEEP can compromise ____ and increase barotrauma risk.
q.e: Pressure measured at the carina may differ from alveolar pressure. The chapter also identifies limited equipment and training in level I and II nurseries. (Chang 4th ed., p. 564)

q.q: Which initial HFOV profile applies to a premature infant with diffuse alveolar disease?
o: Adequate wiggle, mPaw 1–2 cm H2O above conventional, 10–15 Hz
Adequate wiggle, mPaw 2–4 cm H2O above conventional, 8–10 Hz
Minimal wiggle, mPaw 1–2 cm H2O below conventional, 10–15 Hz
Minimal wiggle, mPaw 2–4 cm H2O below conventional, 8–10 Hz
q.e: For a term or near-term infant the same table specifies adequate wiggle, mPaw 2–4 cm H2O above conventional, and 8–10 Hz. Chest wiggle is assessed down to the eighth ribs or umbilicus. (Chang 4th ed., p. 565)

q.q: A neonate with meconium aspiration and air trapping is switched to HFOV. Which starting profile is recommended if tolerated?
o: 2–4 cm H2O below conventional and 10–15 Hz
2–4 cm H2O above conventional and 8–12 Hz
q.e: Both meconium aspiration patterns use good to adequate wiggle and 6–10 Hz. Diffuse disease permits mPaw 2–4 cm H2O above conventional, while focal pneumonia uses adequate wiggle, equal or 1 cm H2O lower mPaw, and 8–10 Hz. (Chang 4th ed., p. 565)

q.q: Which initial HFOV profile is suggested for pulmonary interstitial emphysema in a premature infant?
o: Minimal wiggle, 1 cm H2O below conventional mPaw, 10–15 Hz
Minimal wiggle, 2 cm H2O above conventional mPaw, 6–10 Hz
Adequate wiggle, 2 cm H2O below conventional mPaw, 10–15 Hz
Adequate wiggle, 1 cm H2O above conventional mPaw, 8–10 Hz
q.e: For PIE in a premature infant, use minimal chest wiggle, mPaw 1 cm H2O below conventional mPaw if tolerated, and 10–15 Hz. For gross air leak, premature infants use adequate wiggle and equal or 1 cm H2O higher mPaw at 10–15 Hz; term or near-term infants use equal or 2 cm H2O higher mPaw at 8–10 Hz if tolerated. (Chang 4th ed., p. 565)

q.q: For uniform pulmonary hypoplasia, the suggested initial HFOV frequency is ____.
q.e: Start with minimal wiggle and conventional mPaw, raising pressure if needed for saturation. Nonuniform disease starts at 10 Hz with minimal wiggle and mPaw equal to or up to 2 cm H2O above conventional, guided by the good lung. (Chang 4th ed., p. 565)

q.q: On HFOV, increasing amplitude or decreasing frequency increases tidal volume and ____.
q.e: Power determines oscillation amplitude, tidal volume, and ventilation. A power change affects mPaw, which needs readjustment, and frequency may need adjustment after amplitude or mPaw changes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 566)

q.q: During routine HFOV weaning, how often does the chapter suggest changing mPaw?
q.e: Most pressure changes are made in 1–2 cm H2O increments. Changes may be more frequent when expansion beyond nine posterior ribs persists. (Chang 4th ed., p. 566)

q.q: An HFOV inspiratory time of 33% produces an I:E ratio of ____.
q.e: Inspiratory time percentage is seldom changed. Initial FIO2 may be 100%, followed by titration to SpO2 of 90%–95% after stabilization. (Chang 4th ed., p. 566)

q.q: A breath that combines features of pressure-controlled and volume-controlled ventilation is called a ____ breath.
q.e: Fixed flow in VCV may fail to meet demand, whereas PCV tidal volume can vary as mechanics change. The chapter lists PRVC, VAPS, APRV, Machine Volume, and Volume Guarantee as examples of dual control. (Chang 4th ed., p. 566)

q.q: In AVEA Machine Volume, the inspiratory pressure needed to deliver the target VT is determined ____.
o: at the first breath of each minute
q.e: A proximal flow sensor is required. After adjusting pressure in PCV to reach the target volume, monitor uncorrected Vdel and set Machine Volume at or slightly below Vdel. (Chang 4th ed., p. 567)

q.q: Volume Guarantee adjusts the PIP for the next breath using the ____.
q.e: The clinician sets VT and maximum PIP. The ventilator uses the lowest pressure needed to deliver the target volume, with the goal of reducing volutrauma and barotrauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 567)

q.q: During Volume Guarantee, in which mode do the infant’s lung mechanics limit inspiratory time?
q.e: In PSV inspiration ends when the lungs are full. In SIMV and SIPPV the clinician sets inspiratory time, and the chapter identifies SIPPV with assist/control. (Chang 4th ed., p. 567)

q.q: The liquids described as carrying more oxygen and removing carbon dioxide more easily than a gas are ____.
q.e: Potential applications of liquid ventilation include RDS, aspiration syndromes, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, and pneumonia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 568)

q.q: Which prediction places an infant in the mortality-risk group the chapter reserves for ECMO evaluation?
o: An 82% mortality risk with conventional care
A 72% mortality risk with conventional care
A 78% mortality risk with conventional care
A 68% mortality risk with conventional care
q.e: The chapter reserves extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for high predicted mortality. Severe PPHN, meconium aspiration, sepsis, and congenital diaphragmatic hernia are candidate conditions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 568)

q.q: Which infant meets the chapter’s gestational age, weight, and intracranial bleeding requirements for ECMO consideration?
q.e: Gestation below 34 weeks, weight below 2,000 g, or existing intracranial hemorrhage excludes an infant. Systemic heparinization can worsen bleeding, and coagulopathy must be corrected first. (Chang 4th ed., p. 568)

q.q: Before ECMO was used in infants, membrane oxygenation of blood outside the body was developed for ____.
q.e: The surgical application dates to the 1950s, long-term use followed in the 1960s, and the first infant use was described in 1971. (Chang 4th ed., p. 568)

q.q: For neonatal ECMO selection, Chang gives a minimum predicted mortality risk of ____ with conventional methods.
q.e: The clinical criteria for ECMO select only infants who are at an 80% or greater risk of mortality with conventional methods. (Chang 4th ed., p. 568)

q.q: A neonate with reversible lung disease becomes ineligible for ECMO under the chapter’s duration criterion after more than ____ of mechanical ventilation.
q.e: Prolonged ventilation makes chronic lung disease more likely, and ECMO cannot reverse it. Candidates should also be free of significant cardiac disease. (Chang 4th ed., p. 569)

q.q: On 100% oxygen, barometric pressure is 760 mm Hg, PaCO2 is 50 mm Hg, and PaO2 is 48 mm Hg. What A-a gradient does the chapter’s ECMO formula give?
q.e: Subtract 47, PaCO2, and PaO2 from barometric pressure. A gradient of 605–620 mm Hg for 4–12 hours on 100% oxygen is an ECMO criterion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 569)

q.q: Using the chapter’s fractional FIO2 convention, what oxygen index corresponds to mPaw 20 cm H2O, FIO2 0.90, and PaO2 45 mm Hg?
q.e: Divide mPaw times FIO2 by PaO2. The ECMO table gives an index of 0.35–0.6 for 30 minutes to 6 hours. (Chang 4th ed., p. 569)

q.q: Which sustained blood gas finding meets the chapter’s pH-based ECMO criterion?
o: pH 7.26 for 1 hour with normal pressure
q.e: The pH criterion is below 7.25 for 2 hours with hypotension. The separate PaO2 criterion is 35–50 mm Hg for 2–12 hours. (Chang 4th ed., p. 569)

q.q: In venoarterial ECMO, blood drained from the right atrium through the internal jugular vein returns to the ____.
o: aortic arch via the right common carotid artery
right ventricle via the internal jugular vein
right atrium via a catheter in the femoral vein
pulmonary artery via the right common carotid artery
q.e: Pump-supported return to the aortic arch supports cardiac function as well as oxygenation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 570)

q.q: In the two-catheter venovenous route described, oxygenated blood returns through the femoral vein to the ____.
q.e: Blood is withdrawn from the right atrium via the right internal jugular vein. This route oxygenates blood and leaves cardiac output dependent on the heart. (Chang 4th ed., p. 570)

q.q: In a basic ECMO circuit, the component that moves blood from the reservoir to the membrane oxygenator is the ____.
q.e: The circuit diagram identifies a reservoir bladder, roller pump, membrane oxygenator, and heat exchanger. (Chang 4th ed., p. 571)

q.q: Which complication and frequency are paired correctly in the chapter’s ECMO reports?
q.e: The reported frequencies are 14% for ICH in one study, about 7% for hypertension, roughly 6% for positive blood cultures, and approximately 10% for mechanical complications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 571)

q.q: On ECMO, consumption of blood components by the membrane oxygenator can cause anemia, leukopenia, and ____.
q.e: Pulmonary complications include edema and hemorrhage. Mechanical complications include pump failure, tubing rupture, membrane failure, and cannula problems. (Chang 4th ed., p. 571)

q.q: In the hospital-stay comparison cited in the chapter, what were the average stays for ECMO and conventional care, respectively?
q.e: ECMO requires continuous monitoring by specially trained personnel. A shorter hospital stay can offset its high cost. (Chang 4th ed., p. 572)

sections.title: Ch 18 · Mechanical Ventilation in Nontraditional Settings

q.q: For air transport of critically ill patients, pressure compensation reduces fluctuations in ____.
q.e: Pressure-compensated ventilators limit changes in delivered volume under hypobaric conditions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 581)

q.q: During the U.S. poliomyelitis epidemics, the iron lung supported breathing by applying ____.
q.e: The iron lung was a negative-pressure ventilator. (Chang 4th ed., p. 582)

q.q: A home program costs less than hospital care. Which additional goal should the team discuss with the patient before transfer?
o: Improving quality of life in familiar surroundings
Maintaining the hospital schedule of blood tests
Limiting participation by family and friends
q.e: Home care aims to extend life, improve its quality and support rehabilitation in familiar surroundings. (Chang 4th ed., p. 582)

q.q: Before committing a patient to invasive home ventilation, the team assesses stability, ongoing ventilatory need and the suitability of ____.
o: serial blood gases or daily radiographs
q.e: The needs assessment includes alternatives to an artificial airway and mechanical ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 583)

q.q: A family can operate the ventilator but cannot manage the artificial airway. Which requirement for home care still needs attention?
o: Caregiver ability to manage the airway
Daily access to pulmonary function tests
Patient ability to manage the ventilator alone
q.e: Caregivers must be willing and able to care for the patient, airway, ventilator and related supplies as part of the team. (Chang 4th ed., p. 583)

q.q: Home ventilation should be deferred when an unstable condition requires ____.
o: a detailed discharge plan or family instruction
a portable ventilator or wheelchair access
trained relatives or community support groups
q.e: An unstable condition requiring specialized care is a contraindication. Frequent progressive arrhythmias are an example. (Chang 4th ed., p. 583)

q.q: Which patient characteristic supports evaluating a person for long-term invasive home ventilation?
o: Persistent inability to wean after a high cervical injury
An unstable condition requiring complicated monitoring
A brief need for ventilation during a scheduled procedure
q.e: Persistent ventilatory failure and inability to wean are reasons to assess the need for home support. The patient must be stable enough for care outside an acute setting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 583)

q.q: Which finding argues against starting home ventilation even when equipment is available?
o: The patient declines ventilation at home.
The patient has restrictive lung disease.
The patient has chronic airflow obstruction.
q.e: Patient unwillingness and inadequate financial or human resources are contraindications. Severe desaturation unresponsive to low or moderate FIO₂ or PEEP also argues against transfer. (Chang 4th ed., p. 584)

q.q: After pneumonia or major surgery, a patient with compensated respiratory acidosis may develop superimposed ____.
q.e: An acute illness or surgical complication can precipitate acute ventilatory failure in COPD. (Chang 4th ed., p. 584)

q.q: Which features of COPD help explain prolonged ventilator weaning?
o: Air trapping and loss of elastic recoil
q.e: Airflow obstruction, loss of recoil and air trapping impair ventilation and gas exchange in COPD. (Chang 4th ed., p. 584)

q.q: Before hospital-to-home transfer in COPD, which saturation does the chapter use as the cutoff for investigating significant desaturation?
q.e: The cause of SaO₂ or SpO₂ below 90% must be identified and corrected before transfer. (Chang 4th ed., p. 585)

q.q: With restrictive lung disease, rapid shallow breathing increases ____.
q.e: Limited expansion reduces tidal volume. Rapid shallow breathing increases deadspace ventilation, while low compliance increases the work of breathing. (Chang 4th ed., p. 585)

q.q: Between infections, what lung function would be expected when polyneuropathy is the primary cause of ventilatory failure?
q.e: The ventilatory muscles are impaired, but the lungs generally remain healthy unless infection occurs. Pneumonia and atelectasis can complicate infection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 585)

q.q: A COPD patient in acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure has pH 7.27, PaCO₂ 74 mm Hg and PaO₂ 43 mm Hg. Which HCO₃⁻ value accompanies these results?
q.e: By comparison, stable COPD has HCO₃⁻ of about 30 mEq/L (pH 7.36) and acute failure in a previously normal patient about 26 mEq/L (pH 7.30). The acute-on-chronic example has the highest bicarbonate and PaCO₂; pH 7.27 with PaCO₂ 74 mm Hg corresponds to HCO₃⁻ ≈ 33 mEq/L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 585)

q.q: In central hypoventilation syndrome, variable periods of apnea or hypoventilation result from failure of ____.
q.e: Impaired autonomic control may require support during sleep or continuously. Persistent poor expansion predisposes to infection and atelectasis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 586)

q.q: A patient feels isolated from professional care and is too distressed to discuss discharge. When should the team revisit the decision?
o: When the patient can understand the implications
As soon as the family accepts financial responsibility
As soon as the family completes airway training
When the home ventilator is ready for delivery
q.e: The patient needs time to make an informed decision. Hypoxia, confusion and emotional distress interfere with that discussion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 586)

q.q: Successful adaptation to home ventilation depends on family commitment and ____.
q.e: The family assumes much of the care. Successful home ventilation requires commitment and communication. (Chang 4th ed., p. 586)

q.q: In contrast to many patients who recover from ventilatory muscle dysfunction, prolonged support may be necessary after injury at ____.
q.e: The chapter identifies high spinal injury as an exception to recovery without prolonged ventilation. Aggressive airway care and bronchopulmonary hygiene help prevent complications. (Chang 4th ed., p. 586)

q.q: Which is described as a disadvantage of leaving the hospital for home mechanical ventilation?
o: The feeling of isolation from professional care
q.e: Home care lets the patient stay close to family in a familiar environment; one disadvantage is the feeling of isolation from professional care, with medical care assumed mainly by family members. (Chang 4th ed., p. 586)

q.q: Which categories of resources should the discharge team assess for home ventilation?
o: Physical resources, technical support and emotional support
Ventilator settings, airway pressures and blood gases
Insurance coverage, rental rates and staffing costs
Respite hours, work schedules and vacation coverage
q.e: The home needs space and outlets, technical support with around-the-clock coverage, and emotional support for patient and family. (Chang 4th ed., p. 587)

q.q: The first consideration in selecting a home ventilator is whether it meets ____.
q.e: Patient needs take priority. Ease of use and maintenance are secondary, while equipment and professional care affect total cost. (Chang 4th ed., p. 587)

q.q: When considering a backup home ventilator, the chapter distinguishes total ventilator dependence from ____.
q.e: Part-time users may not need a backup system. Total ventilator dependence may justify one. (Chang 4th ed., p. 588)

q.q: Compared with the chest cuirass, the airtight wrap negative pressure ventilator used after the polio epidemic covers a larger area and provides ____.
q.e: The cuirass is a shell over the chest. The wrap seals at the arms, hips and neck and generally requires help to put on. (Chang 4th ed., p. 588)

q.q: Inflation of a pneumobelt compresses the abdomen and moves the diaphragm ____.
q.e: The belt alternates between positive and ambient pressure. A rocking bed uses movement to displace the abdominal contents. (Chang 4th ed., p. 588)

q.q: In diaphragmatic pacing, which structure receives stimulation from the electrode connected to the implanted receiver?
q.e: The external transmitter communicates with a subcutaneous receiver. Stimulation of the phrenic nerves contracts the diaphragm to augment spontaneous ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 588)

q.q: For a patient receiving mechanical ventilation at home, a backup ventilator may be necessary when the patient ____.
o: is totally dependent on mechanical ventilation
breathes independently while awake and uses ventilation during sleep
has a tracheostomy but breathes spontaneously
q.e: Total ventilator dependence may warrant a backup ventilator. Patients who breathe independently while awake and use ventilation during sleep may not need one. (Chang 4th ed., p. 588)

q.q: Which alarm set does the chapter specifically identify for a dependable, low-maintenance home ventilator?
o: High pressure, low pressure and ventilator failure
High humidity, high temperature and battery charge
High pressure, low humidity and high temperature
Low pressure, low temperature and cuff leakage
q.e: Home ventilators need high-pressure, low-pressure and failure alarms that caregivers can understand. Built-in rechargeable batteries help during brief outages. (Chang 4th ed., p. 589)

q.q: An earthquake or act of terrorism meets the chapter’s definition of a mass casualty incident when the severely injured or dead exceed ____.
o: the capacity for a timely regional response
the number of patients at one emergency department
the number of vehicles at the scene
the capacity of a single transport crew
q.e: The definition depends on regional response capacity. Both natural and human-caused events may qualify. (Chang 4th ed., p. 589)

q.q: Victims of primary blast injury to the lungs may need fluid management and supportive care along with ____.
q.e: Primary or compressive blast lung injury can require mechanical ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 590)

q.q: Nerve-agent exposure can cause apnea and flaccid paralysis because inhibition of acetylcholinesterase leads to ____.
q.e: Acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. A sudden surge can cause unconsciousness, seizures, flaccid paralysis and apnea. (Chang 4th ed., p. 590)

q.q: Which complication created a need for mechanical ventilation in many confirmed cases during the 2009 H1N1 outbreaks?
q.e: Influenza can spread across large regions in a pandemic. Many confirmed H1N1 patients developed acute lung injury or ARDS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 590)

q.q: An infectious disease spreading through human populations across a continent meets the chapter’s definition of a ____.
q.e: A pandemic extends across a large region, a continent or the world. (Chang 4th ed., p. 590)

q.q: Modern triage uses predetermined criteria and gives high priority to severely ill patients who ____.
q.e: Modern triage prioritizes seriously ill patients likely to survive. Earlier military systems favored the less wounded who could return to battle. (Chang 4th ed., p. 591)

q.q: In a modification of START, responders assess perfusion by checking the radial pulse in place of ____.
q.e: START uses respiration, perfusion and mental status. JumpSTART is the pediatric version. (Chang 4th ed., p. 591)

q.q: In both pandemic scenarios, the projected share of the 90 million ill people who would need outpatient care was ____.
q.e: Both scenarios projected illness in 30% of the population and outpatient care for 45 million people. (Chang 4th ed., p. 591)

q.q: In U.S. projections for moderate and severe pandemic influenza scenarios, which pair gives hospital admissions rather than the subset needing ICU care?
q.e: Projected hospitalizations rose from 865,000 to 9,900,000 across scenarios. ICU demand rose from 128,750 to 1,485,000. (Chang 4th ed., p. 591)

q.q: In the pandemic projections, which moderate-to-severe change describes demand for mechanical ventilation?
q.e: Mechanical ventilation was projected for 64,875 and 742,500 people. The corresponding death projections were 209,000 and 1,903,000. (Chang 4th ed., p. 591)

q.q: In START mass-casualty triage, the category with priority over both delayed and minor is ____.
q.e: In START triage, Immediate has a higher treatment priority than Delayed and Minor. (Chang 4th ed., p. 592)

q.q: Which intervention belongs to the prehospital SALT assessment alongside hemorrhage control, opening the airway and giving an auto-injector antidote?
q.e: SALT combines sorting and assessment with immediate lifesaving interventions before treatment or transport. (Chang 4th ed., p. 592)

q.q: An ICU team wants an initial and ongoing assessment for hospitalized patients with sepsis or hypoperfusion. Which system fits this setting?
q.e: The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment uses six criteria to assess critically ill hospitalized patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 592)

q.q: During SALT global sorting, which group is assessed between those with an obvious life threat and those who can walk?
o: People who wave or move purposefully
People who can walk on command
People showing an obvious life threat
q.e: Still patients or those with an obvious life threat are assessed first, patients making purposeful movements second and walkers third. (Chang 4th ed., p. 593)

q.q: Using the chapter’s historical allocation scheme, how is a patient with a SOFA score of 9 prioritized?
q.e: In the chapter’s scheme, scores of 8–10 receive highest critical-care priority and scores of 7 or less receive intermediate priority. Scores of 11 or more are associated with 95% mortality and priority for palliation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 593)

q.q: In SALT mass-casualty triage, when the airway is opened as a lifesaving intervention for a child, the responder is directed to consider ____.
q.e: SALT lifesaving interventions include controlling major hemorrhage, opening the airway (considering two rescue breaths if the patient is a child), and chest decompression. (Chang 4th ed., p. 593)

q.q: The CDC program described as centrally storing medicines, medical supplies and approximately 10,000 ventilators for emergencies is the ____.
o: Homeland Security Exercise and Evaluation Program
Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment system
q.e: The stockpile can deliver many ventilators quickly after an isolated disaster, although clinicians may lack brand-specific experience. (Chang 4th ed., p. 594)

q.q: SOFA scores each organ at the most severe category its value meets. What respiratory score corresponds to a PaO₂/FIO₂ ratio of 180 mm Hg?
q.e: A PaO₂/FIO₂ of 180 mm Hg meets both the ≤300 and ≤200 mm Hg categories; the most severe category it meets, ≤200 mm Hg, scores 3 points. (Chang 4th ed., p. 594)

q.q: A platelet count of 18 × 10³/μL gives a coagulation SOFA score of ____.
q.e: The table assigns 4 points for a platelet count of 18 × 10³/μL. (Chang 4th ed., p. 594)

q.q: In the SOFA score, what liver score corresponds to a bilirubin of 4.0 mg/dL?
q.e: A bilirubin of 2.0–5.9 mg/dL (33–100 µmol/L) earns 2 liver SOFA points, so 4.0 mg/dL scores 2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 594)

q.q: On the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA), what cardiovascular score corresponds to dobutamine infusion at any dose alone?
q.e: The SOFA cardiovascular component assigns 2 points for dopamine ≤5 or dobutamine infusion at any dose. (Chang 4th ed., p. 594)

q.q: A Glasgow Coma Score of 8 gives a neurologic SOFA score of ____.
q.e: The table assigns 3 points for a Glasgow Coma Score of 8. (Chang 4th ed., p. 594)

q.q: SOFA scores the kidney by the worse of creatinine or urine output. What renal score corresponds to a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL with urine output of 180 mL/day?
q.e: Creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL alone would score 2, but urine output <200 mL/day scores 4, and the worse value is used, so the renal score is 4. (Chang 4th ed., p. 594)

q.q: The LP-10 and Uni-Vent Eagle 754 in the federal stockpile were being replaced by the LTV 1200 and the ____.
q.e: The chapter identifies the LTV 1200 and Newport HT50 as replacements. It dates discontinuation of the LP-10 to November 2006. (Chang 4th ed., p. 595)

q.q: Under the 2007 New York shortage criteria, which cardiac history meets an objective exclusion criterion?
o: A remote episode of self-limited tachycardia
A single episode of uncomplicated syncope
q.e: Unwitnessed, recurrent, refractory and trauma-related arrests are listed. The criteria address clinical conditions when ventilator demand exceeds supply. (Chang 4th ed., p. 595)

q.q: In the 2007 New York pandemic ventilator-allocation exclusion criteria, what burned body surface area accompanies severe inhalation injury in the severe-burn entry?
q.e: The table specifies more than 40% body surface area and lists severe inhalation injury. It also lists metastatic malignancy with poor prognosis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 595)

q.q: In the 2007 New York pandemic ventilator-allocation exclusion criteria, which set gives the cardiac, pulmonary and hepatic end-stage criteria, respectively?
q.e: The table lists class III or IV heart disease, severe chronic lung disease with FEV₁ below 25%, and MELD above 20. (Chang 4th ed., p. 595)

q.q: Alongside a severe irreversible neurologic event with high expected mortality, the 2007 New York ventilator-allocation exclusion criteria list renal failure requiring ____.
q.e: Dialysis dependence is the listed renal criterion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 595)

q.q: The program that helps state and local governments develop, conduct and evaluate emergency preparedness exercises is ____.
q.e: Homeland Security developed HSEEP to support preparedness exercises. Planning also includes services such as evacuation, infection control and waste disposal. (Chang 4th ed., p. 596)

q.q: The term for a hyperbaric enclosure designed to treat several patients at once is ____.
q.e: A multiplace hyperbaric chamber treats more than one patient at a time. HBO supplies oxygen under increased ambient pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 596)

q.q: At an FIO₂ of 0.21, approximately how much of the normal 20 vol% blood oxygen content is carried in plasma?
q.e: Plasma normally carries about 0.3 vol%. At 100% oxygen the chapter gives about 2 vol% dissolved at one atmosphere and 6 vol% at three atmospheres, enough to meet the stated tissue minimum. (Chang 4th ed., p. 596)

q.q: In the chapter’s 100% oxygen example, which expression gives the alveolar oxygen pressure used in the dissolved-oxygen calculation?
q.e: The result is 673 mm Hg. Multiplication by 0.003 gives about 2 vol% dissolved oxygen at 1 ATA. (Chang 4th ed., p. 597)

q.q: At 33 ft below sea level, the water column and surface atmosphere produce a total pressure of ____.
q.e: The water column adds another atmosphere to the surface pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 597)

q.q: For decompression sickness after rapid ascent from depth or to altitudes above 18,000 ft, rapid recompression is followed by ____.
q.e: Rapid decompression allows dissolved gases to form bubbles. Treatment uses rapid recompression followed by gradual decompression. (Chang 4th ed., p. 597)

q.q: In mild to moderate CO poisoning, the chapter continues 100% oxygen by mask until the COHb level is ____.
q.e: The stated endpoint is COHb below 5%. Severe poisoning may require HBO to raise dissolved oxygen and treat tissue hypoxia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 597)

q.q: HBO can supplement antibiotics in clostridial myonecrosis because oxygen enrichment ____.
q.e: An oxygen-enriched environment can suppress anaerobic pathogens in gas gangrene. (Chang 4th ed., p. 597)

q.q: A patient will undergo compression and decompression with an endotracheal tube in place. What cuff filling does the chapter describe?
q.e: A fluid-filled cuff helps prevent cuff overdistension and rupture during decompression. (Chang 4th ed., p. 597)

q.q: Under hyperbaric conditions, closer monitoring of neuromuscular blockade is warranted because the agents have ____.
q.e: A shorter half-life may call for lower doses given more frequently. (Chang 4th ed., p. 597)

q.q: To obtain more stable tidal volumes during chamber compression and decompression, the preferred mode is ____.
q.e: Pressure control provides a constant pressure. During volume control, gas compression reduces delivered volume and may require an increased setting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 598)

q.q: Among ventilators suitable for multiplace hyperbaric chambers, the Omni-Vent Series D was tested in VCV only to 6 ATA. Which other ventilator has the same testing profile?
q.e: Both the Impact Uni-Vent Eagle 754 and Omni-Vent Series D were tested in VCV only to 6 ATA. The Bird Avian (VCV only) was tested only to 2.5 ATA, while the Lifecare PLV-100 and Servo 900 C were tested in both VCV and PCV. (Chang 4th ed., p. 598)

q.q: Among ventilators tested in VCV and PCV for use in multiplace hyperbaric chambers, which model was also tested in CPAP and PSV modes at 2.8 ATA?
q.e: EVITA 4 was tested in CPAP and PSV. The PLV-100 and Servo 900 C were tested to 6 ATA, with SIMV and assist also listed for the PLV-100. (Chang 4th ed., p. 598)

q.q: When adjusting the volume setting during hyperbaric treatment, a Wright respirometer provides a bedside estimate of delivered volume by measuring ____.
q.e: Expired tidal volume approximates delivered volume and can guide adjustments during changes in pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 598)

q.q: Before an electrically powered monitor is used in an oxygen-enriched hyperbaric chamber, it must be ____.
o: connected to an internal discharge unit
q.e: Electrical equipment may generate a voltaic arc. Devices must be tested before patient use. (Chang 4th ed., p. 599)

q.q: How should the pressure transducer be prepared for intravascular pressure monitoring in a chamber?
o: Fill it with fluid, calibrate it and expose it to chamber pressure.
Fill it with air, calibrate it and expose it to chamber pressure.
Fill it with air, zero it and keep it outside the chamber.
Fill it with fluid, calibrate it and keep it at sea-level pressure.
q.e: Systemic and pulmonary pressures can be measured when the calibrated, fluid-filled transducer is also under hyperbaric conditions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 599)

q.q: A single-patient hyperbaric enclosure with limited space for defibrillation precautions is called a ____.
q.e: A monoplace chamber treats a single patient. Electrical discharge or arcing during defibrillation poses a fire hazard. (Chang 4th ed., p. 599)

q.q: During volume ventilation in a hyperbaric chamber at 12 breaths/min, which sequence of set volumes maintained 500 mL delivered as pressure rose from 1.0 to 1.3, 1.6 and 1.9 ATA?
q.e: The set volume rose by 50 mL at each of these steps while delivered volume stayed at 500 mL. (Chang 4th ed., p. 599)

q.q: In the hyperbaric volume study at 12 breaths/min, which settings maintained a delivered volume of 500 mL at 2.2, 2.5 and 2.8 ATA, respectively?
q.e: Progressively higher settings were needed at these three pressures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 599)

q.q: During HBO, pulse oximetry in a patient without cardiovascular deficits is chiefly useful for monitoring ____.
q.e: Oxygen saturation is generally already full under these conditions. ECG signals can be transferred outside the chamber for monitoring. (Chang 4th ed., p. 600)

q.q: Which blood pressure and temperature monitoring methods are favored inside a hyperbaric chamber?
q.e: The manual method avoids a potential electrical fire hazard. Thermistors should be safe, while mercury poses a toxicity risk under pressure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 600)

q.q: To avoid falsely high mainstream end-tidal CO₂ readings caused by increased gas density in a hyperbaric chamber, monitoring favors ____.
o: sidestream sampling from the inspiratory limb
q.e: Sidestream measurement outside the chamber using decompressed expiratory tubing is preferred. Transcutaneous PO₂ and PCO₂ are also suitable for monitoring oxygenation and ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 600)

q.q: Which device can monitor both airway pressure and exhaled tidal volume during mechanical ventilation in a hyperbaric chamber?
q.e: An electric spirometer such as the Ohmeda 5420 may be used to monitor both airway pressure and exhaled tidal volume. The Wright mechanical respirometer measures exhaled tidal volume alone. (Chang 4th ed., p. 600)

q.q: During defibrillation in an air-compressed multiplace chamber, the chamber FIO₂ must stay below ____.
q.e: The chamber is compressed with air and its oxygen fraction kept below 21.5% to reduce fire risk. (Chang 4th ed., p. 601)

q.q: Which electrical arrangement is specified for defibrillation inside a multiplace hyperbaric chamber?
o: External discharge unit with a large-diameter, low-resistance cable
Internal discharge unit with a small-diameter, high-resistance cable
Internal discharge unit with a large-diameter, low-resistance cable
External discharge unit with a small-diameter, high-resistance cable
q.e: The defibrillator and switches stay outside. Gel provides conduction at the large adhesive plates, and flammables must be kept away. (Chang 4th ed., p. 601)

q.q: During multiplace defibrillation, one team member attaches the paddle inside and another operates the discharge unit outside. The third operates the ____.
q.e: The table assigns one member of the three-person team to fire suppression. (Chang 4th ed., p. 601)

q.q: The chapter describes most implanted pacemakers as safe at chamber pressures below ____.
q.e: Continuous ECG monitoring and an available defibrillator are recommended. An untested temporary external pacemaker is kept outside with wires through the wall. (Chang 4th ed., p. 601)

q.q: After initial stabilization, a ventilated casualty may need aeromedical evacuation to receive comprehensive care and rehabilitation at ____.
q.e: The stated strategy is to stabilize the wounded and evacuate them to a centralized location. (Chang 4th ed., p. 601)

q.q: At 8,000 ft, the chapter pairs a calculated alveolar oxygen pressure of 59 mm Hg with a barometric pressure of ____.
q.e: An acute fall in barometric and alveolar oxygen pressures contributes to illness in unacclimatized people. (Chang 4th ed., p. 602)

q.q: After rapid ascent, a hiker reports insomnia and nausea. Which additional symptom completes the chapter’s description of acute mountain sickness?
q.e: Headache accompanies at least one gastrointestinal disturbance, insomnia, dizziness or fatigue. (Chang 4th ed., p. 602)

q.q: Cerebral vasodilation, overperfusion and inadequate buffering by cerebrospinal fluid contribute to ____.
q.e: Descent and supplemental oxygen are initial treatments. Further descent or a portable hyperbaric chamber may be needed if cerebral edema persists. (Chang 4th ed., p. 602)

q.q: Which medications may relieve symptoms of acute mountain sickness when descent or oxygen is unavailable?
q.e: The chapter lists acetazolamide and dexamethasone for these circumstances. (Chang 4th ed., p. 602)

q.q: A climber develops resting tachycardia, tachypnea and bloody sputum. Which mechanism fits high-altitude pulmonary edema?
o: Noncardiogenic edema with elevated pulmonary capillary pressure
Cardiogenic edema with reduced systemic vascular resistance
Cardiogenic edema with elevated left atrial pressure
Noncardiogenic edema with reduced pulmonary artery pressure
q.e: High-altitude pulmonary edema is associated with pulmonary hypertension and raised capillary pressure. Cold can increase pulmonary artery pressure through sympathetic stimulation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 602)

q.q: When descent, supplemental oxygen and a portable chamber are unavailable for high-altitude pulmonary edema, the chapter describes use of ____.
q.e: Nifedipine can lower pulmonary artery pressure. High-altitude pulmonary edema accounts for most high-altitude illness fatalities. (Chang 4th ed., p. 602)

q.q: Although aircraft generally cruise at 25,000–40,000 ft, what range of cabin pressure altitudes does the chapter describe?
q.e: The cabin is generally pressurized to an altitude of 8,000 ft or less. (Chang 4th ed., p. 602)

q.q: In the chapter’s account of pilot oxygen requirements, what pair of cabin altitudes applies for exposure over 30 minutes and for continuous use, respectively?
q.e: The chapter gives 12,500 ft for over 30 minutes and continuous use above 14,500 ft. Its normal maximum operating cabin altitude is 8,000 ft. (Chang 4th ed., p. 603)

q.q: Which tolerated SpO₂ ranges correspond to cabin pressure altitudes of sea level, 10,000 ft and 13,000 ft, in that order?
q.e: Tolerated SpO₂ is 95–100% at sea level, about 88–93% at 10,000 ft (also cited as 88–92%), and 83–88% at 13,000 ft; tolerated saturation falls below sea-level values as altitude increases. (Chang 4th ed., p. 603)

q.q: What SpO₂ ranges are tolerated at cabin pressure altitudes of 16,000 ft and 20,000 ft, respectively?
q.e: Tolerated SpO₂ is 75–80% at 16,000 ft and 70–75% at 20,000 ft. A separate supplemental oxygen guideline compares the reading with the person’s usual home-altitude value. (Chang 4th ed., p. 603)

q.q: For the chapter’s 10%-below-baseline guideline for in-flight oxygen, the comparison value is the person’s usual SpO₂ at ____.
q.e: The guideline uses normal saturation at the person’s home altitude as the reference. (Chang 4th ed., p. 603)

q.q: With falling ambient pressure in a hypobaric environment, both measured tidal volume and peak flow may ____.
q.e: Ascent can increase delivered tidal volume through gas expansion and cause hyperinflation. Hypobaric pressure is below one atmosphere. (Chang 4th ed., p. 603)

q.q: A ventilator that adjusts pressure or volume output automatically as atmospheric pressure changes has ____.
q.e: Pressure compensation helps stabilize tidal volume, peak inspiratory flow, proximal airway pressure and minute ventilation at altitude. (Chang 4th ed., p. 604)

q.q: After a significant change in cabin altitude, a noncompensating ventilator is being recalibrated. How is ventilation often maintained during the procedure?
q.e: Manual ventilation may be needed during recalibration. Another approach is to monitor output and adjust tidal volume and frequency during ascent and descent. (Chang 4th ed., p. 604)

q.q: At 2,500, 5,000, 8,500 and 10,000 ft, which sequence gives measured tidal volume with the Evita 4 set to 500 mL throughout?
q.e: Measured values increased as pressure fell from 695 to 633, 554 and 524 mm Hg. Displayed values were 371, 355, 307 and 353 mL. (Chang 4th ed., p. 604)

q.q: Which sequence gives peak flow at 2,500, 5,000, 8,500 and 10,000 ft in the simulator study?
q.e: Peak flow increased at each successive altitude in the study. (Chang 4th ed., p. 604)

q.q: Which feature takes priority when choosing a portable ventilator for air travel?
o: Modes and settings that meet the patient’s needs
A housing that fits the smallest carry-on bag
The lowest available weight and smallest footprint
The longest available internal battery duration
q.e: Battery life, weight, dimensions and alarms matter after confirming that the device can provide the needed ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 605)

q.q: An airline requests information about a passenger’s portable ventilator. What should accompany the physician’s approval to travel?
o: Device specifications and manufacturer contact information
A battery purchase receipt and a wheelchair serial number
The physician’s fee schedule and oxygen delivery receipts
Rental charges and the home agency’s billing address
q.e: Airline engineering and medical staff may review the specifications. The passenger should distinguish a ventilator from portable oxygen and arrange care at the destination. (Chang 4th ed., p. 605)

q.q: Because the airline decides whether a passenger may use aircraft electrical power, a ventilator user should bring ____.
q.e: The ventilator and extra batteries should fit under the seat. If the ventilator does not fit, the chapter describes holding it or purchasing another seat. (Chang 4th ed., p. 605)

q.q: A traveler uses BiPAP only during sleep and will not need it during the flight. How does the chapter advise transporting the machine?
o: Pack it as a carry-on item.
q.e: The ventilator is delicate and should travel as carry-on baggage. Travelers needing suctioning or IV support may require a personal companion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 605)

q.q: The LTV 800, listed for pediatric patients weighing more than 5 kg, has a tidal volume range of ____.
q.e: The LTV 800 lists rates of 10–100/min, PEEP of 0–20 cm H₂O, one hour of internal battery life and a weight of 12.9 lb. (Chang 4th ed., p. 606)

q.q: The 13-lb UniVent Eagle 754 has a three-hour internal battery and a respiratory rate range of ____.
q.e: The Eagle 754 lists VT of 0–3,000 mL, PEEP of 1–20 cm H₂O and A/C, SIMV and CPAP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 606)

q.q: The 20.8-lb V-Leonardo offers tidal volumes of 100–1,600 mL and an internal battery duration of ____.
q.e: The listed rate range is 5–99/min and PEEP range is 0–15 cm H₂O. The external power specification is 12 VDC. (Chang 4th ed., p. 606)

q.q: The 35-lb LP-10 has a one-hour internal battery and an external deep-cycle battery rated for ____.
q.e: The internal battery lasts one hour. The LP-10 lists VT of 100–2,000 mL, rate ranges of 1–20 or 22–38/min and no PEEP setting. (Chang 4th ed., p. 606)

q.q: Cabin pressure altitude falls 2,000 ft during descent. Using the study estimate, what change in set VT would offset compression with a noncompensating ventilator?
q.e: The study estimates a 3% increase per 1,000 ft of descent and a 3% decrease per 1,000 ft of ascent. (Chang 4th ed., p. 607)

q.q: For intermittent ventilator users at altitude, oxygen during spontaneous breathing is recommended to reduce ____.
q.e: Altitude hypoxia particularly affects people with heart or lung disease. Prophylactic oxygen can reduce breathing effort and help prevent ventilatory failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 607)

q.q: Which concentrator listed at less than 10 lb has a maximum battery duration of 12 hours?
q.e: The chapter lists 12 hours for the 8.5-lb EverGo, 10 hours for the FreeStyle, eight for the Inogen One G2 and seven for the XPO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 607)

q.q: A passenger plans six hours of one-way travel using a portable oxygen concentrator. What minimum battery duration follows the chapter’s rule of thumb?
q.e: The rule is at least 150% of one-way travel time. The chapter says airlines need not supply oxygen or DC power and the POC and batteries must fit under the seat or on the lap. (Chang 4th ed., p. 607)

q.q: Outside the hospital, providers often work alone or in small teams and must adapt ventilator settings to ____.
q.e: Nontraditional settings may lack the range of monitors, equipment and professional support available in a hospital. (Chang 4th ed., p. 608)

q.q: The asthma case reports blood gases at an elevation of 4,400 ft. What barometric pressure applies to these measurements?
q.e: Cases 2 through 14 report blood gases at a barometric pressure of 640 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 615)

q.q: The patient with emphysema can breathe comfortably only when sitting upright. This symptom is called ____.
q.e: Orthopnea is difficulty breathing comfortably unless upright. (Chang 4th ed., p. 616)

q.q: The patient with COPD gains weight suddenly and develops dependent edema. Which complication do these findings suggest?
q.e: Sudden weight gain with dependent edema suggests cor pulmonale in this case. (Chang 4th ed., p. 616)

q.q: The patient with COPD develops a more pronounced abdominal paradox as his respiratory rate reaches 36/min and PaCO2 rises. Which process explains this change?
q.e: The rising rate, increasing PaCO2 and abdominal paradox indicate fatigue and impending acute ventilatory failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 617)

q.q: In the emphysema case, which finding supports the use of corticosteroids according to the chapter?
q.e: The chapter links corticosteroid benefit in COPD to evidence of reversible airway disease. (Chang 4th ed., p. 617)

q.q: In the COPD case, which drug is described as potentially improving diaphragmatic function?
q.e: The chapter notes a possible benefit of aminophylline for diaphragmatic function in COPD. (Chang 4th ed., p. 617)

q.q: An alert, cooperative patient with COPD needs ventilatory assistance. Which additional finding supports a trial of mask ventilation?
q.e: The case identifies intact airway defenses as a condition for noninvasive support in an alert, cooperative patient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 618)

q.q: For the patient receiving theophylline for COPD, the chapter gives a target serum concentration of ____.
q.e: The case uses a serum range of 5 to 15 mcg/mL to minimize toxicity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 619)

q.q: At discharge the patient with COPD asks what his comprehensive rehabilitation program will teach. Which topic belongs in that program?
q.e: Rehabilitation covers the disease, self-care, diet, activity and smoking cessation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 620)

q.q: In acute asthma, aminophylline is commonly used to reverse severe bronchospasm that has not responded to which drug?
q.e: Aminophylline is commonly used to reverse severe bronchospasm in acute asthma that has not responded to epinephrine. (Chang 4th ed., p. 620)

q.q: During a severe asthma attack, the patient continues to breathe rapidly, but her initially low PaCO2 rises toward normal. What does this trend suggest?
q.e: As hyperventilation becomes unsustainable, a rise in PaCO2 toward normal signals fatigue and possible ventilatory failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 621)

q.q: The pregnant patient with refractory asthma is switched to PC-IRV. Which I:E ratio did the team select to improve oxygenation?
q.e: The team selected a 2:1 inverse ratio to improve oxygenation and limit barotrauma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 622)

q.q: A chest radiograph of a patient with status asthmaticus shows widened spaces between the ribs. Which accompanying finding supports hyperinflation?
q.e: Widened intercostal spaces and a depressed diaphragm are radiographic signs of hyperinflation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 623)

q.q: Which inhaled drug was added in the asthma case to prevent further mast cell degranulation?
q.e: Cromolyn was used prophylactically to prevent mast cell degranulation and future attacks. (Chang 4th ed., p. 624)

q.q: A patient is wheezing in the middle of an acute asthma episode. Why is Intal (cromolyn) not given at this time?
o: It is a prophylactic drug for airway hyperreactivity
It requires a continuous IV infusion
It causes rebound bronchospasm in hypoxemic patients
It interacts with aminophylline to cause seizures
q.e: Intal is not given in acute asthma episodes; it is used as a prophylactic measure to control airway hyperreactivity. (Chang 4th ed., p. 624)

q.q: Before abdominal surgery the patient has a low hematocrit, weakness and reduced exercise tolerance. The case links these symptoms to ____.
q.e: The low hematocrit contributes to tissue hypoxia, which can explain the fatigue and exertional symptoms. (Chang 4th ed., p. 625)

q.q: The abdominal surgery patient’s white cell count is elevated. In addition to infection, which event does the chapter identify as a possible cause of transient leukocytosis?
q.e: The case notes that leukocytosis is generally transient and can occur after hemorrhage. (Chang 4th ed., p. 625)

q.q: The postoperative patient previously left the hospital with chronic CO2 retention. What PaCO2 did the team use as her baseline for ventilator adjustments?
q.e: Her previous discharge PaCO2 of 50 mm Hg served as the target for subsequent measurements. (Chang 4th ed., p. 626)

q.q: When comparing the postoperative patient’s capnogram with her arterial gas, the chapter places normal PETCO2 about ____ PaCO2.
q.e: The case gives a normal PETCO2 approximately 2 mm Hg below PaCO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 626)

q.q: The postoperative patient’s CVP stays at 10–12 mm Hg. Which reference range did the team use to interpret this finding?
q.e: The reported CVP exceeds the case’s normal range of 1–7 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 626)

q.q: For a patient with normal blood pressure, the postoperative case lists an endotracheal cuff pressure range of ____.
q.e: The chapter gives 27–40 cm H2O and specifies lower pressures for patients with hypotension. (Chang 4th ed., p. 626)

q.q: After abdominal surgery, spontaneous frequency is 16/min and mean VT is 476 mL. What rapid shallow breathing index do these values yield?
q.e: Dividing 16 breaths/min by 0.476 L gives approximately 34/min/L, below the case’s threshold of 100/min/L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 627)

q.q: After head trauma the patient has no spontaneous eye opening, limb movement or speech. Her Glasgow coma score of 3 corresponds to ____.
q.e: The case interprets a Glasgow coma score of 3 as severe coma. (Chang 4th ed., p. 628)

q.q: In a patient with head trauma, pupils that are reactive to light mean that ____ are adequate.
o: cardiac output and systemic blood pressure
spinal cord function and brainstem reflexes
q.e: Pupils that are reactive to light mean that cerebral circulation and oxygenation are adequate. (Chang 4th ed., p. 628)

q.q: The head-injury patient’s intracranial pressure ranges from 6 to 8 mm Hg. What upper boundary did the team want it to stay below?
q.e: The case gives a desired intracranial pressure below 10 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 629)

q.q: On an otherwise normal chest radiograph, small round markings in the lung fields represent ____.
q.e: The vessels run parallel to the X-ray beam and produce round markings. (Chang 4th ed., p. 629)

q.q: According to the head-injury case, which finding would justify an exception to the stated restriction on PEEP?
q.e: The case reserves PEEP for severe hypoxemia in this head-injured patient. (Chang 4th ed., p. 630)

q.q: In the head-injury case, the PaCO2 target during mild hyperventilation was ____.
q.e: The team used mild hyperventilation to maintain PaCO2 between 34 and 35 mm Hg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 630)

q.q: After head injury, ____ may be drained to minimize the rise of intracranial pressure from subsequent swelling of the brain.
q.e: Cerebrospinal fluid may be drained to minimize the rise of intracranial pressure from subsequent brain swelling. (Chang 4th ed., p. 630)

q.q: A man found confused in a smoke-filled room has soot around his mouth. Besides carbon monoxide, which inhaled poison does the case identify as a concern?
q.e: The listed complications include cyanide and carbon monoxide poisoning, bronchospasm and infection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 631)

q.q: The smoke-inhalation patient has a reassuring SpO2 despite suspected carbon monoxide poisoning. Why can the reading be falsely high?
o: The oximeter counts carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin.
The oximeter calculates saturation from respiratory frequency.
The oximeter measures plasma oxygen instead of saturation.
The oximeter substitutes venous saturation for arterial saturation.
q.e: Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin. The case uses arterial oxygen content to assess oxygenation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 632)

q.q: A smoke-inhalation burn patient's admission chest radiograph shows normal lungs. What complication could subsequently change the lung findings?
q.e: The lungs typically are not affected on the chest film unless edema forms secondary to smoke inhalation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 632)

q.q: A smoke-inhalation victim is breathing adequately on his own. What is the initial supportive measure?
q.e: With adequate spontaneous ventilation, the initial supportive measure for smoke inhalation is 100% O2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 632)

q.q: For the smoke-inhalation patient, which sequence gives the HbCO half-lives on room air, on 100% oxygen at 1 atm and on 100% oxygen at 3 atm, respectively?
q.e: The listed half-life decreases as inspired oxygen concentration and then atmospheric pressure increase. (Chang 4th ed., p. 633)

q.q: The fire victim is still breathing spontaneously. Which anticipated complication prompted elective intubation?
q.e: Intubation secured the airway before swelling could obstruct it. (Chang 4th ed., p. 633)

q.q: For the patient exposed to carbon monoxide, breathing 100% oxygen at 3 atm can raise dissolved oxygen to about ____.
q.e: The chapter describes 6 vol% dissolved oxygen as sufficient to sustain cerebral metabolism. (Chang 4th ed., p. 634)

q.q: After tricyclic overdose, the patient is intubated and an end-tidal CO2 of 20 mm Hg is detected. What does this finding suggest in the case?
q.e: The detected end-tidal CO2 supports placement of the tube in the trachea. (Chang 4th ed., p. 635)

q.q: After aspiration in the overdose case, peak and plateau pressures both rise. Which change does the chapter associate with this pattern as ARDS develops?
q.e: Decreasing compliance raises peak and plateau pressures. Intrapulmonary shunting increases the oxygen requirement. (Chang 4th ed., p. 636)

q.q: Watery brown material is suctioned from the overdose patient’s endotracheal tube. The initial PEEP of 5 cm H2O was intended to prevent ____.
q.e: The case links the initial PEEP to prevention of atelectasis after suspected aspiration. (Chang 4th ed., p. 636)

q.q: The overdose patient changes from CMV to PCV. Relative to the previous peak inspiratory pressure, where does the case suggest starting the pressure setting?
q.e: The case suggests starting PCV pressure 10 cm H2O below the peak inspiratory pressure on CMV. (Chang 4th ed., p. 637)

q.q: After the overdose patient changes to pressure control, the team tracks minute volume closely. Besides pressure and inspiratory time, minute volume in this mode depends primarily on ____.
q.e: The case names pressure, inspiratory time and lung compliance as the primary determinants of minute volume during PCV. (Chang 4th ed., p. 637)

q.q: In the overdose case, PaCO2 is allowed to reach 80 mm Hg as tidal volume falls to about 450 mL. This strategy is called ____.
q.e: Permissive hypercapnia reduces the pressure and volume required for ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 638)

q.q: The patient with a right hemopneumothorax has a systolic pressure of 70 mm Hg, a pulse of 120/min and bloody chest drainage. What do the two vital signs suggest?
q.e: Hypotension and tachycardia are common signs of inadequate circulating volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 639)

q.q: A chest radiograph of a patient with tension hemopneumothorax shows a white (opaque) area over the right hemithorax. Which material accounts for the opacity?
q.e: Blood in the pleural space appears white on the radiograph, whereas pleural air would appear dark. (Chang 4th ed., p. 640)

q.q: As the hemopneumothorax patient loses blood, hemoglobin falls from 15.8 to 10.7 g%. Which oxygen measurement falls from 20.9 to 15 vol%?
q.e: The decrease in hemoglobin diminishes the arterial oxygen content despite a high PaO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 641)

q.q: After massive transfusion, limited 2,3-DPG in stored blood shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left. What happens at the tissues?
q.e: The left shift reduces oxygen unloading and can contribute to tissue hypoxia. (Chang 4th ed., p. 642)

q.q: After major blood loss in the hemopneumothorax case, which pair of measurements did the team use to assess circulating volume?
q.e: Cardiac output and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure helped assess the adequacy of circulating blood volume. (Chang 4th ed., p. 642)

q.q: The patient recovering from hemopneumothorax has an MIP of −52 cm H2O. Which accompanying f/VT value supports a weaning attempt?
q.e: The case associates this MIP and an f/VT below 100/min/L with successful weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 643)

q.q: Following blunt chest trauma, an internal injury to lung tissue beneath unbroken skin is called a ____.
q.e: The case defines pulmonary contusion as an internal parenchymal injury with intact skin. (Chang 4th ed., p. 644)

q.q: After chest trauma, a chest radiograph shows a right-sided rib fracture, greater density of the left lung field, loss of the left diaphragm shadow, and the mediastinum and trachea drawn toward the left. Which finding accounts for the pull to the left?
q.e: Left-sided atelectasis (volume loss) pulls the mediastinum and trachea toward the affected left side; tension pneumothorax or hemothorax would push them away. (Chang 4th ed., p. 645)

q.q: The chest-trauma patient receives inverse-ratio pressure control. Which pressure pattern does the chapter associate with this mode?
o: Mean airway, central venous and pulmonary artery pressures rise.
Central venous pressure falls while the other two pressures rise.
Pulmonary artery pressure rises while the other two pressures fall.
Mean airway pressure rises while both vascular pressures fall.
q.e: PC-IRV increases all three pressures and may cause hemodynamic instability. (Chang 4th ed., p. 646)

q.q: In pressure control-inverse ratio ventilation (PC-IRV), what is the inverse I:E ratio intended to do?
o: Increase inspiratory time and lung expansion to improve oxygenation
Lower central venous pressure to improve venous return
Shorten inspiratory time to reduce mean airway pressure
Lengthen expiratory time to reduce air trapping
q.e: Use of an inverse I:E ratio is intended to increase inspiratory time and lung expansion, and to improve oxygenation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 646)

q.q: While adjusting ventilation after chest trauma, the team follows ventilation and oxygenation. What additional factor should guide changes in settings?
q.e: The case includes hemodynamic status among the factors guiding ventilator adjustments. (Chang 4th ed., p. 647)

q.q: The chest-trauma patient is improving but still requires high FIO2 and PEEP. The chapter suggests reducing FIO2 to about ____ before weaning PEEP.
q.e: The suggested sequence lowers FIO2 to about 40% before reducing PEEP. (Chang 4th ed., p. 648)

q.q: During a chest-trauma weaning trial, the patient takes rapid, shallow breaths. Which region may receive most of this ventilation?
q.e: Rapid, shallow breaths may ventilate only the conducting airways and provide little effective alveolar ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 649)

q.q: The patient progressing toward ARDS can no longer sustain hyperventilation. Which arterial gas trend suggests impending ventilatory failure?
o: PaCO2 rises as pH and PaO2 fall.
PaCO2 falls as pH and PaO2 rise.
PaCO2 rises as pH and PaO2 rise.
PaCO2 falls as pH and PaO2 fall.
q.e: The case describes a rising PaCO2 accompanied by decreasing pH and PaO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 650)

q.q: An iron supplement is used to increase the ____ of hemoglobin.
q.e: An iron supplement is used to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin. (Chang 4th ed., p. 650)

q.q: The patient with evolving ARDS has a PaO2 of 58 mm Hg on 100% oxygen and a PaCO2 of 33 mm Hg. Which change specifically addressed her hypoxemia?
q.e: The team increased PEEP for hypoxemia despite 100% oxygen and reduced the ventilator rate for the low PaCO2. (Chang 4th ed., p. 651)

q.q: What is the primary concern with prolonged CPAP use in critically ill patients?
q.e: CPAP requires adequate spontaneous breathing; development of respiratory muscle fatigue is the primary concern for prolonged CPAP use in critically ill patients. (Chang 4th ed., p. 651)

q.q: The ARDS patient has pulmonary edema and a normal wedge pressure. Which explanation does the chapter favor?
q.e: Pulmonary edema with a normal PCWP suggests parenchymal injury such as ARDS. The chapter gives a PCWP above 18 mm Hg as typical of cardiogenic edema. (Chang 4th ed., p. 652)

q.q: For a woman with ARDS, the chapter’s tidal-volume equation uses 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight. Which expression gives that weight in kilograms when height is measured in inches?
q.e: The female equation starts at 45.5 kg for 60 inches and adds 2.3 kg per additional inch. The male equation starts at 50 kg. (Chang 4th ed., p. 652)

q.q: The ARDS patient receives dornase alfa for thick yellow secretions. Which other agent in her regimen served the same purpose?
q.e: Mucomyst and Pulmozyme were used to mobilize retained secretions. (Chang 4th ed., p. 653)

q.q: After repeated unsuccessful weaning attempts in the ARDS case, VT is reduced to 380 mL. The stated purpose of low VT is to minimize ____.
q.e: The chapter links low tidal volume to lower airway pressures. (Chang 4th ed., p. 654)

q.q: In the trial summarized after the ARDS case, approximately how did deaths change with small tidal volumes compared with large tidal volumes?
q.e: The case discussion reports approximately 25% fewer deaths with small tidal volumes. (Chang 4th ed., p. 655)

q.q: In the myasthenia case, the initial gas shows acute ventilatory failure and elevated bicarbonate. Which process explains the bicarbonate elevation?
o: Resolution of chronic carbon dioxide retention
New bicarbonate loss from the gut
q.e: The case attributes the elevated bicarbonate to compensation for preexisting ventilatory failure. (Chang 4th ed., p. 656)

q.q: A patient with myasthenia gravis aspirated barium into the left lung. A chest radiograph also shows a flat right hemidiaphragm with a poorly defined right costophrenic angle. What could explain the right-sided finding?
q.e: The barium is on the left; the flat right hemidiaphragm with a poorly defined costophrenic angle may be caused by pleural effusion. (Chang 4th ed., p. 657)

q.q: A Glasgow coma score of ____ or lower indicates severe brain injury or neurological deficit.
q.e: A Glasgow coma score of ≤8 indicates severe brain injury or neurological deficit; a score of 15 rules out neurological deficit. (Chang 4th ed., p. 657)

q.q: During a CPAP/pressure-support trial in the myasthenia case, the patient develops marked accessory muscle use after four hours. How did the team respond?
o: Maintained CPAP for another four hours
q.e: Extreme accessory muscle use prompted the team to take him off CPAP/PS. (Chang 4th ed., p. 658)

q.q: The myasthenia patient’s biopsy is positive for cytomegalovirus. Which medication was started to target the infection?
q.e: Ganciclovir is an antiviral used to treat or prevent cytomegalovirus infection. (Chang 4th ed., p. 659)

q.q: In the myasthenia case, the recorded MIP values on days 2, 3, 4 and 5 are −24, −12, −26 and −29 cm H2O, respectively. On which day was his inspiratory muscle strength weakest?
q.e: The least negative MIP reflects the weakest inspiratory effort. Day 3 had the least negative MIP (−12 cm H2O), even though his vital capacity that day was 4.02 L. (Chang 4th ed., p. 659)

q.q: On day 6 the myasthenia patient can complete only part of his spontaneous parameters (MIP −28 cm H2O; VC 1.1 L, down from 3.4 L on day 5). What happened during his CPAP/PS trial that day?
o: Extreme dyspnea and accessory muscle use after 90 minutes
Stable breathing at 15–17/min with VT in the low 400s
Successful extubation followed by nasal cannula at 3 L/min
Comfortable, unlabored breathing through two 2-hour trials
q.e: With his vital capacity down to 1.1 L, he tolerated only 90 minutes of CPAP/PS before becoming extremely short of breath, with increased work of breathing and marked accessory muscle use. (Chang 4th ed., p. 659)

q.q: Along with myasthenia gravis and aspiration pneumonia, ____ contributed to the patient’s earlier failed weaning attempts.
q.e: The chapter identifies poor nutritional intake as the third contributor to unsuccessful early weaning. (Chang 4th ed., p. 660)

q.q: The myasthenia patient receives neostigmine to improve muscle tone. This drug acts as an inhibitor of ____.
q.e: Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to improve muscle tone in myasthenia gravis. (Chang 4th ed., p. 660)

q.q: In the adolescent with Guillain-Barré, FEV1 and FVC both decline. Which FEV1/FVC pattern does the chapter associate with restriction?
q.e: A reduction in both FEV1 and FVC typically preserves the FEV1/FVC percentage in restriction. (Chang 4th ed., p. 661)

q.q: When following the adolescent’s vital capacity, the chapter identifies an absolute threshold for ventilation when VC falls below ____.
q.e: The case gives a VC below 1,000 mL or twice predicted tidal volume as an indication for mechanical ventilation. (Chang 4th ed., p. 661)

q.q: After intubation for Guillain-Barré, which setting did the team adjust to match inspiratory demand while preserving alveolar ventilation?
q.e: The team adjusted peak flow to meet the patient’s inspiratory demand. (Chang 4th ed., p. 662)

q.q: In the Guillain-Barré case, how much rehabilitation does the chapter associate with each week of muscle immobility?
q.e: The chapter estimates four weeks of rehabilitation for each week of immobility. (Chang 4th ed., p. 663)

q.q: The four breathing patterns below were recorded on days 2 through 5 of ventilation for Guillain-Barré. Which pattern produced the highest rapid shallow breathing index (f/VT)?
q.e: Day 3 combined the highest frequency with the smallest tidal volume. Its f/VT of 833 exceeded the other three values of 264, 312 and 287. (Chang 4th ed., p. 664)

q.q: On days 26, 28 and 32 in the Guillain-Barré case, spontaneous frequency is 6, 10 and 23/min while spontaneous VT measures 410, 440 and 70 mL, respectively. What happens to f/VT across those measurements?
o: It rises from 23 to 328, then falls to 15.
It falls from 328 to 15, then rises to 23.
q.e: Chang shows a much higher f/VT on day 32, when VT fell to 70 mL and frequency reached 23/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 664)

q.q: In the Guillain-Barré case, spontaneous breathing measures 30/min with VT 135 mL on day 36, 29/min with VT 110 mL on day 42, and 32/min with VT 85 mL on day 46. Which f/VT sequence do these measurements yield?
q.e: The recorded f/VT rose at each measurement as tidal volume decreased. (Chang 4th ed., p. 664)

q.q: In the Guillain-Barré case, spontaneous breathing values are: day 52 (f 27/min, VT 200 mL), day 54 (f 23/min, VT 210 mL), day 56 (f 32/min, VT 115 mL) and day 58 (f 21/min, VT 240 mL). On which day is the rapid shallow breathing index (f/VT) highest?
q.e: On day 56, 32/min divided by 0.115 L gives an f/VT of about 278 breaths/min/L, the highest of the four days (about 135, 110 and 88 on days 52, 54 and 58). (Chang 4th ed., p. 664)

q.q: Across ventilator days 60, 62, 64, 66 and 68 in the Guillain-Barré case, recorded MIP values progress from −23 to −24, −26, −30 and −37 cm H2O. What does this trend indicate?
o: Peak inspiratory strength on day 60 followed by decline
q.e: Increasingly negative MIP readings (from −23 to −37 cm H2O) reflect steadily improving inspiratory muscle strength. (Chang 4th ed., p. 664)

q.q: The adolescent with Guillain-Barré is expected to require long-term ventilation. Which airway procedure does the case associate with that expectation?
q.e: The case identifies anticipated long-term mechanical ventilation as the reason for tracheotomy. (Chang 4th ed., p. 665)

q.q: Late in the Guillain-Barré case, pressure support is adjusted against spontaneous breathing. Which pair of targets does the chapter give as alternatives?
q.e: The specified targets are a spontaneous VT of 10–15 mL/kg or a spontaneous frequency below 25/min. (Chang 4th ed., p. 666)

q.q: On ventilator day 40 the adolescent begins brief T-piece trials to exercise his respiratory muscles. What initial schedule does the case describe?
q.e: The initial trials could be as brief as 10–15 minutes every 2–4 hours. By day 54 he tolerated 30–60 minutes twice daily. (Chang 4th ed., p. 666)
